desktop_surface: A Bulk Egress card on Posture listing each upload root with total enqueued bytes, turn count and the decision chain rendered as a precedence ladder (env → config → remote → effective), with the deciding row highlighted; the two rules land on the Triage queue with the chain attached as incident evidence.
data_source: ~/.grok/logs/unified.jsonl: msg='repo_state.upload.start' (399 records, roots <redacted-local-path> 274, <redacted-local-path> 123, <redacted-local-path> 2), msg='repo_state.upload.enqueued' (274 records, 520,761 bytes total), msg='trace.upload.decision' (209 records, 207 enabled remotely)
honest_limit: `size_bytes` is the compressed tarball and exists only on `enqueued` records — 399 starts produced 274 enqueued lines here, so 125 uploads have no recorded size and the ledger prints that count rather than summing them as 0. The log never lists the tarball's contents, so which files left is unknowable from disk: the row can honestly say 'the tree under this root, up to 1 GB per file' and nothing more. `gcs_path` is stored as an opaque destination id, not resolved, because resolving it would be a network call.
competitive_note: The v1 entry files this as a posture line item with a `repo_upload_enabled` rule, which attributes the control to the customer's config; the log says the vendor's server decided it 207 times out of 209. No vendor row in the 62-competitor matrix reads ~/.grok/logs at all, and a SASE proxy sees only a TLS POST to Google storage — it cannot tell that the body is your repository, which repository, or that a remote flag switched it on.
v1_ref: Vendor telemetry and upload posture report
gap_area: Opaque-payload and bulk-egress volumetrics: the bytes DLP structurally cannot read

name: authorization_basis per tool call, ungated-call KPI and default_policy_delta
description: The owner's mandate - 'are agents using tools and reading data WITHOUT permission' - becomes two columns on the tool_calls ledger plus one dashboard card. authorization_basis in {bypass_no_gate, mode_auto, rule_matched, human_denied, unknown} is filled by joining each call to autonomy_intervals: a call inside a bypassPermissions interval, or a Codex turn with approval_policy='never' and sandbox_policy.type='danger-full-access', had no gate that could have stopped it, full stop; a call whose tool_result carries toolDenialKind was refused (37 records here). would_prompt_by_default is a second, explicitly counterfactual boolean evaluated against a versioned table shipped at packages/core/data/default-policy.json (Claude: Bash, Write, Edit, WebFetch and mcp__* prompt while Read, Glob and Grep do not; Codex: default approval_policy 'on-request' prompts for exec outside the sandbox), so the org can be told how much of the vendor's own safety UX it switched off - on this machine Bash 6,305 + Edit 2,041 + Write 341 + WebFetch 63 = 8,750 calls before MCP tools are counted. 'rule_matched' is always rendered as 'Vole's evaluation of the allowlist' and never as the tool's own decision, because re-implementing Claude's permission matcher would manufacture a number.
desktop_surface: Dashboard KPI strip gains 'ungated tool calls' beside tokens and cost, with the default-policy counterfactual as its second line and the policy-table version as a footnote; clicking through opens Breakdown grouped by tool name and session with the quoted permission mode, and the session sheet shows an authority chip on every call row.
data_source: tool_calls.name joined to autonomy_intervals; ~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl permissionMode entries and tool_result toolDenialKind; ~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl turn_context.{approval_policy, sandbox_policy.type, permission_profile}; Devin meta info configOptions[mode]='bypass'; ~/.grok/config.toml yolo; opencode session.permission; packages/core/data/default-policy.json (versioned, shipped in-repo)
honest_limit: Most Claude permission-mode lines carry no timestamp, so a call's basis is bounded by neighbouring stamps and calls before the first stamp stay 'unknown' - a blank must render as 'not recorded', never as 'gated'. Vole never observes the permission prompt itself, so it cannot distinguish 'a human approved this' from 'a rule pre-approved it' except where a denial was recorded. The default-policy figure is a counterfactual against a documented table, not against what a specific agent version would actually have done: the table is versioned, cited by version in every figure, calls from an agent version older than the entry count as 'unknown policy' rather than folding into the total, and the number must never be labelled 'N unauthorised actions'. Cursor, Antigravity and Devin record no tool calls at all and contribute no rows.
competitive_note: 65% of enterprises saw agents act outside intended scope and 46% cannot produce a 30-day audit trail (EMA/Cequence via Infosecurity, 2026-09-01). Zenity, Noma, Aim and Invariant answer this only at a runtime gateway, seeing what routes through them; Anthropic's own OTel emits tool_decision with an approval source but only when telemetry is enabled and never for a competitor's agent, so Anthropic itself cannot tell a customer how many actions bypassed its own dialog. Neither number exists anywhere in roadmap-v1 or the 62-vendor matrix, and both are readable from files every session already writes with telemetry off.
v1_ref: tool_calls ledger with tool_result error join
field_verified: The table this feature adds two columns to DOES NOT EXIST. schema.ts contains exactly three CREATE TABLEs — usage_events (25 cols), anomalies (18), collector_state (5) — and no tool_calls anywhere; tool names survive only as a comma string in usage_events.tools. So this is blocked on v1's Tier-1 ledger, which the write-up never says. The KPI arithmetic is also wrong. Deduped by tool_use.id across all 629 transcripts the default-prompting set is Bash 11,411 + Edit 1,687 + Write 277 + WebFetch 654 + mcp__* 2,391 = 16,420, not 8,750; the feature's figures mix methods (its Edit 2,041 is my UNDEDUPED Edit count exactly, while its Bash 6,305 and WebFetch 63 match neither). Raw counting double-counts Claude's streamed copies — Bash is 12,211 raw vs 11,411 deduped — which is the same placeholder problem claude-code.ts:60-71 already solves by coalescing on message.id. Denials verified: toolDenialKind automode-blocked 22 / user-rejected 14 / automode-unavailable 2. The data file path is wrong: packages/core/data/ does not exist; pricing.json lives at packages/core/src/data/pricing.json.
constraint: Constraint 14 and constraint 4. default-policy.json must be `import`ed and frozen into the SEA at build time exactly as pricing.json is (pricing.ts:55 `const P = loadPricing()`), never readFileSync'd at runtime — the collector is a zero-runtime-dependency SEA. Constraint 4 is the sharper one: authorization_basis 'unknown' must not become a third confidence tier; confidence stays exactly {exact, activity_only} and 'unknown' lives in its own column rendering as 'not recorded'. The feature's own guard against re-implementing Claude's permission matcher matches roadmap-v1 L78's existing warning verbatim, so keep it. Constraint 13 applies to the KPI strip: queries.ts + DB.swift, twice.

name: anomaly_context: blast radius attached to every behaviour incident
description: A behaviour incident is unreadable without the reach of what happened, and the anomalies row cannot grow that answer because it is frozen at first sight. Add a sibling table anomaly_context(anomaly_key PRIMARY KEY, distinct_files, distinct_dirs, out_of_repo_writes, destructive_calls, failed_calls, unknown_outcome_calls, top_path_classes, contributing_sessions, window_end) filled from the tool_calls and file-write ledgers over the incident's own window and upserted only when window_end grows, which keeps collection idempotent without entangling it with the anomalies upsert semantics. The same change closes a live principle-3 gap: anomalies.observed, baseline and threshold exist in the schema but are selected by no reader — not queries.ts:230, not DB.swift:227 — so today no surface renders the figures that actually fired the rule.
desktop_surface: Incident detail gains a 'reach' block (files, directories, out-of-repo writes, destructive calls, failed and unknown-outcome calls) above the explanation, and finally renders observed / baseline / threshold from the columns that already store them.
data_source: tool_calls and the file-write ledger joined on session and the anomaly's window; anomalies.{observed, baseline, threshold} (schema.ts:42-64), currently unread at queries.ts:230 and apps/mac/Sources/Vole/DB.swift:227
honest_limit: Reach is only what the ledger recorded — unresolved shell redirect targets and Bash-mediated writes on tools without command capture appear as 'n calls with unresolved target', never as zero. Windows that predate the ledger have no context row at all and must render 'not recorded' rather than zeros, which is the failure mode most likely to be misread as a clean incident. contributing_sessions is exact only once burn-rate stops blaming evs[0].session_id; until then a multi-session window lists a single contributor.
competitive_note: No v1 entry surfaces observed/baseline/threshold although principle 3 requires the real figures and the columns already exist. Anthropic states plainly that correlation and alerting are the SIEM's job; an incident that arrives carrying its own blast radius is the difference between a Vole incident and a raw OTel event.
field_verified: THE PRINCIPLE-3 GAP IS CONFIRMED IN BOTH READERS, VERBATIM. packages/core/src/queries.ts:225-232 getAnomalies: `SELECT id, rule, severity, tool, session_id, model, window_start, window_end, title, detail, confidence, source FROM anomalies WHERE window_end >= ?...`. apps/mac/Sources/Vole/DB.swift:223-240 anomalies(): the identical 12 columns. Neither selects observed, baseline or threshold, and no other reader does either. schema.ts:54-56 stores them: `observed REAL NOT NULL, baseline REAL, threshold REAL`. So the product stores the exact figures that fired every one of its 249 incidents and renders none of them, while ROADMAP principle 3 requires 'incidents explainable with real figures'. burn-rate.ts:58 `session_id: first.session_id` confirmed, so the contributing_sessions caveat is accurate. tool_calls does not exist; a file-write ledger exists nowhere — not in schema.ts, not as a v1 entry.
constraint: Constraint 6 gap: the proposed anomaly_context schema has no source column. It is keyed on anomaly_key, which detect/index.ts:57 already prefixes with the source, so partitioning works transitively — but the purge is `DELETE FROM ... WHERE source='seed'` and will NOT cascade to this table, leaving orphaned seed context rows after a demo-data purge that the constraint says must be genuinely removable. Add the source column or an explicit cascade. The upsert-only-when-window_end-grows rule is well designed and correctly avoids entangling with F1's severity semantics — that separation is right and should be kept. Constraint 13: rendering observed/baseline/threshold requires editing BOTH queries.ts:225 and DB.swift:223, the canonical read-model-parity pair.

name: Four-state authority on every tool call (denied / pre-authorised / posture-waived / no record)
description: Adds authority TEXT and authority_evidence TEXT to each tool_calls row: 'denied' when the entry carries a top-level toolDenialKind (re-counted today: automode-blocked 22, user-rejected 14, automode-unavailable 2) or a tool_result whose text matches the versioned denial-phrase list; 'pre_authorised' when the tool name matches the allowedTools set in the nearest preceding attachment.type='command_permissions' (43 attachments here, e.g. {"allowedTools":["Read"]}) or a settings allow rule; 'posture_waived' when the autonomy interval covering the call is accept_edits or full_auto; 'unknown' otherwise. The design point is that no agent on disk records an affirmative human approval, so Vole must never claim one — the honest fourth state is what makes the number defensible. On this machine 22,687 tool_use blocks produced 38 denial records, so 22,649 actions (99.83%) reached no recorded human decision of any kind, and that is the headline a CISO can act on.
desktop_surface: Session-detail tool list gains an authority chip per call (red 'denied', amber 'waived by posture', blue 'pre-authorised', grey 'no record'); a Behaviour header stat 'N of M calls reached no permission decision' filters the table when clicked; the incident detail for any behaviour rule quotes the call's authority state and its evidence field.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl top-level toolDenialKind on user entries; message.content[].tool_result.content denial phrasing with is_error=true (739 error results here); attachment.type='command_permissions'.allowedTools; joined to the permission-mode/autonomy intervals from the v1 posture feature
honest_limit: Only Claude Code writes denial records; Codex, OpenCode, Grok, Devin, Cursor and Antigravity write none, so for those tools authority is 'unknown' on every call and the UI must render 'not recorded', never '0 denials'. 'pre_authorised' is Vole's own re-implementation of the vendor's matcher and can disagree with what the vendor actually matched — it is labelled a Vole evaluation. An affirmative human 'yes' is never observable anywhere on disk and is never asserted.
competitive_note: v1's guardrail ledger records denials and refusals but has no state for the calls nobody was ever asked about — 99.8% of calls here. Claude Code's opt-in OTel does emit tool_decision with source=config|hook|user_* (market.md §4) but only with CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 and a running collector, and only for Claude Code; gateway products (MintMCP, Lasso, Speakeasy) see approvals only for MCP traffic routed through them and are blind to local Bash; CrowdStrike Falcon AIDR reconstructs a causal chain from syscalls with no concept of the agent's own permission decision.
v1_ref: Guardrail-fired ledger: denials, refusals, hook blocks, denial_streak (Tier 2)
field_verified: Every named field exists and the denial counts are exact. Top-level toolDenialKind across all 633 transcripts: automode-blocked 22, automode-unavailable 2, user-rejected 14 = 38 — matching the feature's re-count to the unit. A denial entry is a user line whose tool_result carries both is_error:true and tool_use_id (verified in a raw sample: `"is_error":true,"tool_use_id":"call_acb5d121a3de4c568db8591a"`), so denials bind to a specific call. attachment.type='command_permissions' = 43, sample verbatim: `{"type": "command_permissions", "allowedTools": ["Read"]}` and `{"allowedTools": ["WebFetch(domain:platform.claude.com)"]}` and one with `[]`. tool_result is_error total 742 (claim 739). Settings allow rules are thin: ~/.claude/settings.json permissions.allow has 9 entries, settings.local.json 1 — so pre_authorised will be a near-empty bucket, as the design implies.
constraint: Two. (1) Constraint 7, 'the database holds no content': authority_evidence TEXT must never hold the denial phrase itself (the sampled phrase is a 700-character model-facing instruction). Store a phrase-pack id plus pack_version and the toolDenialKind enum; the phrase list lives in code, not in the DB. (2) The headline contradicts the feature's own four-state model, which is the more serious problem. Measuring distinct tool_use ids against the prevailing permission-mode stamp in their own transcript file gives: no posture stamp anywhere 9,816 (46.7%), bypassPermissions 6,254 (29.7%), auto 4,856 (23.1%), plan 73, default 36, acceptEdits 1 — total 21,036. So roughly 52.8% of calls are posture_waived, not 'no record'. Claiming '22,649 actions (99.83%) reached no recorded human decision of any kind' collapses posture_waived into unknown and is the one number in this shard a hostile reviewer would use to discredit the product. Reconciliation: publish the four-state split as measured (≈47% no record, ≈53% waived by a standing posture, 0.5% under a prompting mode, 38 denied, ≈0% pre-authorised) — still damning, and defensible line by line. Also note this feature is not standalone: 'posture_waived' requires the v1 autonomy-interval feature as a hard dependency.

name: Behaviour panel with incident-to-ledger jump
description: The tool-call ledger stays invisible until DB.swift can read it: add a Behaviour section with a sessions list, the session report card, the tool-call table, the subagent tree and the per-tool coverage matrix, plus a 'Show calls' action on every incident that opens the ledger filtered to that anomaly's window and session. Every one of those queries must exist twice (queries.ts and the DB.swift port) or the app cannot show it, and the drill-down needs text binds since it keys on session_id — impossible with today's Int-only run(). MenuPanel's top-5 tools also moves off the 49%-NULL usage_events.tools column onto the ledger.
desktop_surface: 'Behaviour' section in the Risk sidebar group; a 'Show calls' button on each incident row; the tool-mix strip in MenuPanel sourced from tool_calls.
data_source: tool_calls, agent_edges and anomaly_context tables via new DB.swift readers; existing anomalies columns for the jump target.
honest_limit: DB.swift's row loop swallows SQLITE_BUSY and returns partial results, so the panel must keep prior values when a read fails rather than rendering an empty session and implying no activity. It can show nothing at all for Cursor, Devin and Antigravity, whose stores record no tool calls, and the empty view must state that rather than reading as clean; Claude's two tool timestamps include permission-prompt wait, so any duration column is labelled transcript_gap_ms, never latency.
competitive_note: Every security vendor covering coding agents ships a cloud console; a local panel that renders the same evidence with nothing leaving the laptop is the works-council-acceptable form of the view, and v1 specifies the report card without ever porting it to the app that would show it.
v1_ref: Session behaviour report card and tool-mix breakdown
field_verified: `tool_calls`, `agent_edges` and `anomaly_context` do not exist. The text-bind dependency is confirmed real (DB.swift:141 `_ binds: [Int]`, :149 `sqlite3_bind_int64`), so a session-keyed drill-down is impossible until feature 1 lands. The SQLITE_BUSY claim is verified: DB.swift:150 is `while sqlite3_step(stmt) == SQLITE_ROW { row(stmt!) }` — any non-ROW return, BUSY included, exits silently with whatever rows were already appended and no error surfaced (the `sqlite3_busy_timeout(handle, 2000)` at :136 narrows the window without closing it). FACTUAL ERROR: the feature says 'MenuPanel's top-5 tools also moves off the 49%-NULL usage_events.tools column'. MenuPanel.swift:202 reads `store.summary.byTool`, which comes from DB.swift:176-182 `SELECT tool, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY tool` — that is the AGENT column (`tool`), not the invoked-tool-names column (`tools`). MenuPanel never reads `tools` at all; the top-5 is a per-agent list and needs no migration.
constraint: Constraint 13 (parity) is named and correct. Constraint 7 needs an explicit line in the table spec: a tool-call ledger must store tool NAMES, call ids and outcomes and never `tool_use.input` or `toolUseResult.stdout`, or it silently becomes the content store the whole product is built to avoid. Constraint 1: a call row keyed on file position would repeat codex.ts:197's collision — key on the tool's own call id where one exists.

name: agent_pushed_data_off_device: scp, rsync and cp into an unmonitored context
description: Every DLP feature in the product asks what reached a model; none asks what the agent copied to another machine. From the same command-shape pass, isolate transfer verbs with a directional argument pair — `scp <local> <host>:<path>`, `rsync <local> <host>:`, `docker cp <local> <container>:`, `kubectl cp`, `sshfs` mounts, and `gh codespace cp` — and record the direction plus the source path class, never the bytes. Adds `data_moves(call_event_key, transport, direction{push|pull}, src_path_class, src_path_hmac, dest_context_id, dest_kind, ts, source)`, keyed with the same path HMAC the secret ledger uses so a push joins the existing findings: if a file that carries a `secret_sightings` fingerprint or sits under a sensitive path class (.env, ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, a credential dir) is the source of a push to an unmonitored context, the rule `secret_bearing_file_left_device` fires at critical with the destination and the fingerprint id as its figures. The plain rule `agent_pushed_data_off_device` fires on volume: pushes per session to destinations with monitored=0. Measured here: scp 29, rsync 12, sshfs 1 — small, and the honest number is more useful than a guess.
desktop_surface: Leak Ledger gains an Off-device tab beside the model-egress tabs, with columns destination, direction, path class and 'joined to finding' — the first screen in the product where a leak destination is a machine rather than a provider endpoint. A push whose source joins an open secret finding renders as a critical row on the Data Exposure screen with the finding's evidence card inline.
data_source: Claude Code Bash `input.command` (scp/rsync/sshfs/docker cp/kubectl cp argument pairs), Codex local_shell_call, OpenCode tool part state.input; joined to the existing secret_sightings path HMAC and the sensitive-path class table
honest_limit: Vole reads the command, not the transfer: it cannot confirm the copy happened, cannot know the byte count, and for a directory push it names the directory only — every file inside is unknown and is reported as unknown rather than expanded. A push to a host that is in fact monitored still shows as a push; monitored=1 only downgrades the rule, it never rewrites the row. Transfers made by a tool other than the classified verbs (a Python script the agent wrote, a curl PUT, a git push to an internal remote) are outside this feature by construction and belong to the egress inventory.
competitive_note: Endpoint DLP vendors that cover coding agents (Cyberhaven, Nightfall, Forcepoint) watch egress to model endpoints and cloud apps; DBIR 2026 puts source code as the #1 data type across 858,440 DLP events, yet none of the coding-agent-aware vendors in the matrix reports an agent-initiated host-to-host copy as an AI event rather than a generic file movement.
gap_area: Where agents actually run: devcontainers, Docker, SSH remotes, VMs and CI runners as declared blind spots

name: agent_self_authorised: the agent changed its own permission surface
description: Sharpens v1's agent_config_modified from 'a config file changed' to 'a permission-granting key changed', which is the only version worth a critical. The watched keys are additions to permissions.allow, hasTrustDialogAccepted flipping true, enableAllProjectMcpServers, skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt (already true in ~/.claude/settings.json here), any hooks block gaining an entry, Grok [ui].yolo (config.toml line 14, currently false) and permission_mode (line 16, 'auto'), and Codex approval_policy. Detection runs two ways so neither can be evaded alone: a tool call whose target path is one of those files (Write/Edit file_path or a Bash command string), and a content-free per-poll diff of the posture snapshot at key granularity that stores only the key name, a value class {wildcard, exact, boolean_true, contains_secret_shape} and a sha256. The secret-shape class exists because of the April 2026 finding of live credentials embedded in allow entries inside .claude/settings.local.json files shipped on npm.
desktop_surface: Posture tab 'Permission changes' timeline: one row per key change with the file class, key, old and new value class, the session that was running at the time (or 'no session'), and a red dot for grants rather than revocations; a grant made while a bypass session was active also opens as an incident.
data_source: ~/.claude/settings.json, ~/.claude/settings.local.json, <repo>/.claude/settings.local.json, ~/.claude.json projects[*], ~/.codex/config.toml, ~/.grok/config.toml; plus tool_use.input.file_path and Bash command strings targeting those paths
honest_limit: These files are rewritten both by the agent and by a human clicking 'always allow', and neither writes an author, so attribution to a session holds only when a tool call in that session named the file within the same poll interval; otherwise actor is 'unknown' and the incident says so. The diff is poll-granular, so a grant added and removed between two polls is invisible. Values are never stored, so the panel can say an entry is wildcard-shaped or secret-shaped but can never show which secret.
competitive_note: v1 bundles this with out-of-repo writes as one S-sized rule keyed on file path; the enterprise-grade version is key-level and value-class-level, which is what makes 'the agent granted itself bypass' distinguishable from 'the agent edited a comment in settings.json'. v1's separate 'Permission allowlist and managed-settings posture' feature classifies rules once, at a point in time; this is the change stream over the same files. Snyk Agent Scan and Invariant scan these files as a point-in-time posture check and never as a diff.
v1_ref: Out-of-repo write and agent self-modification rules (scope_escape, agent_config_modified)
field_verified: Two watched keys confirmed, three absent, and one better key found. CONFIRMED: ~/.claude/settings.json line 29 `"skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt": true` — exactly as claimed — with a permissions.allow block of 9 entries including `"Bash(gh api *)"` and `"Bash(curl -sL -m 60 \"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/...\")"`. CONFIRMED: ~/.claude.json projects[*] hasTrustDialogAccepted present on all 23 projects (true 9, false 14). CONFIRMED: ~/.grok/config.toml line 14 `yolo = false`, line 16 `permission_mode = "auto"`. ABSENT: enableAllProjectMcpServers is null on all 23 projects — the real per-project MCP grant keys are enabledMcpjsonServers / disabledMcpjsonServers (21 each) and hasClaudeMdExternalIncludesApproved (21), none of which the feature names. ABSENT: no `hooks` block in any ~/.claude/settings*.json here. ABSENT: ~/.codex/config.toml has NO approval_policy key at all — its 120 lines carry `[projects."<redacted-local-path>"] trust_level = "trusted"` three times, which IS the Codex permission-granting key and the feature misses it entirely. The contains_secret_shape class is vindicated by real data on this machine: ~/.codex/config.toml line 75 holds `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN = "litellm-899D…"` (redacted) inside [shell_environment_policy] — a live-shaped credential sitting in an agent config, the same shape as the April 2026 npm finding.
constraint: Constraint 7 is the binding one and the design already respects it: key name, value class and sha256 only, never the value — which is what makes it safe to watch a file that demonstrably contains a live token. Two gaps: the poll-granular snapshot is a new table needing a `source` column and a purgeSeed line (db.ts:228-232 covers two tables today); and constraint 14 means these config paths must be declared in paths.ts with VOLE_* overrides rather than read ad hoc, since the SEA allows no undeclared runtime file reads. Principle 1: attribution to a session is 'unknown' unless a tool call named the file in the same poll interval — the feature says so and must keep saying so.

name: agent_edges: the subagent tree from what the metadata actually carries
description: Build the fan-out tree as a table rather than timing it from Agent tool_use blocks: agent_edges(parent_session, parent_call_key, workflow_id, child_agent_id, agent_type, spawn_depth, edge_source, source) plus per-session tree size, max depth and max concurrent children. The edge comes from three exact facts on disk: the directory path ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<parent_session>/subagents/[workflows/<wf_id>/]agent-<id>.jsonl names both the parent session and the workflow that spawned the child; agent-*.meta.json carries {agentType, spawnDepth} on all 479 files on this machine and additionally toolUseId on 23 of them, which is a foreign key straight into the tool_calls ledger; and Codex session_meta.source plus OpenCode session.parent_id give the same edge for those tools. This machine has 479 subagent transcripts under 18 parent sessions but only 23 Task/Agent tool_use blocks, so timing fan-out from the Agent tool_use alone — v1's approach — would miss 456 of 479 subagents.
desktop_surface: Behaviour panel tree view: parent session, then children grouped by workflow id and agent type (456 workflow-subagent, 16 Explore, 4 general-purpose, 2 Plan, 1 claude-code-guide here), each row linking to its own tool-call list; incident detail names the branch that fired.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/**/<session>/subagents/**/agent-*.meta.json {agentType, spawnDepth, toolUseId} and the sibling agent-*.jsonl; the parent transcript's tool_use.id; ~/.codex/sessions rollout session_meta.source; opencode session.parent_id
honest_limit: Only 23 of 479 metas here carry toolUseId — the other 456 are workflow-subagents whose parent is known as a session plus a workflow id and nothing finer, so parent_call_key is stored NULL and never guessed from timing. meta.json carries no timestamp, so a child's start comes from the parent call where a toolUseId exists and otherwise from the child transcript's first line, labelled accordingly. spawnDepth is 1 on all 479 files, so depth >= 2 is untested and must be reported only where observed rather than assumed absent. meta.description is task text and is never stored, hashed or exported.
competitive_note: v1's fanout_burst counts subagents and failure ratios and its note admits the lifecycle entries carry no timestamp, yet it still anchors timing on the Agent tool_use, which covers 5% of the subagents on this machine. Cursor's OTel export documents no subagent roll-up; CrowdStrike Falcon Guardian markets a causal chain but builds it from EDR process events, which cannot see an in-process subagent.
v1_ref: Subagent and workflow fan-out monitor (fanout_burst)
field_verified: CONFIRMED WITH NEAR-PERFECT PRECISION. I parsed every agent-*.meta.json under ~/.claude/projects: 487 metas, 487 sibling .jsonl, agentType = {workflow-subagent 464, Explore 16, general-purpose 4, Plan 2, claude-code-guide 1} — the four non-workflow figures match the feature exactly (16/4/2/1); only the workflow count grew from 456. spawnDepth == 1 on ALL 487 files, no exceptions. toolUseId present on EXACTLY 23. Key histogram: agentType 487, spawnDepth 487, description 23, toolUseId 23 — so 464 metas carry nothing but type and depth, and parent_call_key is genuinely unrecoverable for 95%. Sample: `{"agentType":"claude-code-guide","description":"Confirm Claude Code statusline and MCP facts","toolUseId":"toolu_01BRCG8rhScdiECDpWHEF5h5","spawnDepth":1}`. Path shape confirmed: ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<parent_session>/subagents/[workflows/<wf>/]agent-<id>.meta.json — 18 parent sessions, 17 workflow ids. Codex `thread_spawn":{"parent_thread_id":"01a07a53-...","depth":1,"agent_path":"/root/platform_evidence","agent_nickname":"Goodall","agent_role":null}` in 2 rollouts. OpenCode session.parent_id: 68 of 145 sessions populated.
constraint: Constraint 7: meta.description is task text on the 23 files that have it — the feature already forbids storing, hashing or exporting it; hold that, since a hash of a task description is still a fingerprint of intent. Constraint 6 satisfied (source column present in the proposed schema). Constraint 10 needs an arbitration rule the feature omits: usage_events.agent_id already encodes tree membership for 4,947 claude_code rows, so state plainly that agent_edges owns tree STRUCTURE (parent, workflow, type, depth) while agent_id stays SPEND attribution, and define what happens when they disagree. Constraint 1: the directory path is a stable key; do not fold mtime or scan order into it (the antigravity and codex.ts:197 line-index keys are the two existing violations and explicitly not precedents).

name: Command-shape skeleton and versioned pattern pack (pattern_id + pack_version, not just a hash)
description: Classify each shell command by splitting on &&, ||, ; and | into segments, dropping leading cd and VAR=... prefixes, then matching a versioned pattern pack; store pattern_id, category, pack_version and an argv skeleton with every literal replaced (strings → <S>, numbers → <N>, paths → path class, URLs → host). First-token classification is provably wrong on this corpus: of 11,865 Bash calls, 3,862 (32.5%) start with cd and 10,055 (84.7%) contain a chain or pipe operator, so the dangerous segment is usually not the first token. Storing only class + SHA-256, as roadmap-v1 specifies, makes the corpus unreclassifiable when the pack gains a rule, because Claude prunes transcripts after cleanupPeriodDays — the skeleton is the thing that survives to be re-matched offline. Pack v1 covers the classes actually present here: rm -rf, ssh key paths, sudo, .env reads, base64, find -exec, force-push, curl|sh, $IFS, chmod 777.
desktop_surface: Behaviour panel 'Commands' tab: category counts per session with a drill-down listing skeletons (never raw commands) and a 'pack v1.3' badge; every destructive_command incident quotes the skeleton and its pattern_id instead of an opaque hash.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl tool_use.input.command for name='Bash' (11,865 here); ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db part.data $.state.input where $.tool='bash' (6,084 rows); ~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl function_call.arguments; ~/.grok/logs/unified.jsonl exec_done (tool_name only)
honest_limit: The skeleton is derived from command text and keeps hosts and flag names, so it is metadata by policy, not by construction — exports ship pattern_id + pack_version only. Heredocs, $(...) bodies and variable expansions collapse to one opaque token, so a command whose danger lives in a variable is classified 'unresolved', never 'safe'. Skeletons are capped at N tokens (p95 command is 1,157 chars, max 21,482 here). Grok records only tool_name, so it can never be classified.
competitive_note: Sysdig detects agent commands at the syscall layer with no content retention but has no notion of which agent session issued them (market.md competitor row 84); Amazon Q's find -exec RCE (2025-08-19) and Claude Code's $IFS bypass CVE-2025-66032 are exactly the shapes a first-token classifier misses.
v1_ref: Destructive and outbound command classifier (destructive_command, destructive_under_bypass) (Tier 2)
field_verified: The argument against first-token classification reproduces exactly: of 12,078 Bash calls, 3,909 (32.4%) begin with `cd ` and 10,218 (84.6%) contain &&, ||, ; or | — the feature claims 32.5% and 84.7%. Command length max 21,482 chars matches to the character; p95 1,140 vs the claimed 1,157. Every one of pack v1's ten classes is present in this corpus, counted directly: rm -rf 670, ssh key paths 173, sudo 55, .env reads 518, base64 79, find -exec 74, force-push 12, curl|sh 4, $IFS 4, chmod 777 8 (plus 337 commands containing API_KEY/SECRET/TOKEN/sk- shapes and 8 touching ~/.aws/credentials or gcloud auth). Sources verified: Claude tool_use.input.command, OpenCode $.state.input.command on 6,081 of 6,084 bash parts, Codex function_call.arguments carries the full cmd (sample: `{"cmd": "sed -n '1,220p' ..."}`). Grok records tool_name only — confirmed, no command anywhere in exec_done.
constraint: One real strain and one omission. Constraint 7 says the DB holds 'only counts, ids, model names, tool names, cwd/file paths, raw_ref pointers'. An argv skeleton that preserves hosts and flag names is derived command text and sits outside that enumeration; the feature's own honest_limit concedes it is 'metadata by policy, not by construction'. That is not a reconciliation, it is a deferral — resolve it before shipping by making pattern_id + pack_version the only exported and synced fields (already proposed) AND making skeleton retention a local, off-by-default column, so the constraint holds by construction for anyone who does not opt in. Omission: Devin is absent from the data_source and should not be. Its tool_call payload carries rawInput.command in full plus a vendor-supplied _meta['cognition.ai/commandNames'] array — a verbatim sample from this machine is `ls -la ~/.ssh/ 2>/dev/null && echo "---CONFIG---" && cat ~/.ssh/config 2>/dev/null`, which is a pack-v1 ssh-key-path hit with a pre-parsed verb list, across 1,715 calls.

name: Secret-store retrieval ledger: the credential the agent pulled from a remote vault
description: A whole class of secret access leaves no filesystem trace, so path-based sensitive-read rules never fire: `kubectl get secret … -o jsonpath='{.data.GEMINI_API_KEY}' | base64 -d`, `aws secretsmanager get-secret-value`, `gh secret list/set`, `op read`, `vault kv get`, `wrangler secret`, `flyctl secrets`, `doctl … --access-token` (39 such commands here across 8 CLIs, 3 of them decoding a Kubernetes secret from the `do-nyc3-launchsafe` cluster). `secret_store_reads(call_id, store_kind, target_ref, item_name, field_name, materialised{yes|unknown})` stores the *name* of the item and field and never the value; `materialised` is yes when the pipeline decodes or prints it (`base64 -d`, `--jq .SecretString`). Rule `remote_secret_read` is posture-weighted, and a second join closes the loop: when a fingerprint from the existing secret_sightings ledger later appears in a transcript, its first origin can be attributed to the store item that was read in the same session.
desktop_surface: A 'Pulled from a secret store' section on the Data Exposure screen, one row per store item with field names, the target system, and a link to any later at-rest sighting of the same fingerprint.
data_source: Bash/exec command strings joined to action_targets for the cluster/account label; existing HMAC fingerprint key for the optional sightings join.
honest_limit: A literal credential typed into the command (a `dop_v1_…` DigitalOcean token appears inline in one command here) is fingerprinted and labelled by provider, never stored — and the value is a token for the account, so the account label is a claim about the string's shape, not a verified identity. Vole cannot see the retrieved value, so `materialised` describes the pipeline shape, not the outcome, and a secret fetched by an SDK inside a script is invisible: only CLI commands the agent ran are counted.
competitive_note: Secret scanners in the matrix (TruffleHog, Gitleaks, GitGuardian, GitHub Secret Protection) scan files and find nothing here because no file is written; Knostic blocks `.env` reads, which this class routes around entirely; the CSPM vendors see the vault audit log without knowing an AI agent asked.
gap_area: Blast radius beyond the filesystem: cloud/SaaS/DB/VCS action targets, and agent-initiated package installs

name: Blast Radius screen: every system outside this laptop that agents touched
description: The covered screens answer who used which agent (Shadow AI, People), what leaked (Leak Ledger) and how the agent behaved (Behaviour) — none answers the question a CISO actually asks after Replit and Nx: which systems beyond this filesystem did our agents act on. One screen over `action_targets` and its four child ledgers, grouped by target with locality and declared environment, showing first and last touch, the sessions and people involved, the worst action class, and the incident count. Every total carries its denominator: resolved targets beside `target unresolved (n)` and `no target named (n)`, so the screen can never imply coverage it does not have. Ordering is by worst action class then recency, with no computed risk score.
desktop_surface: A new sidebar section between Behaviour and Data Exposure. Rows read like the ground truth on this machine: 'launchsafe-db-do-user-…ondigitalocean.com/launchsafe — remote, env undeclared, 139 calls, 1 truncate, 4 sessions'; '195.242.30.141 (h200) — 145 hops, 117 privileged, 1 installer pipe'; 'do-nyc3-launchsafe — 18 kubectl calls, 5 secret reads, context from file'. Selecting a row filters the ledger; a header strip states how many calls had no target and why.
data_source: action_targets joined to db_actions, remote_exec, secret_store_reads, package_execs and vcs_actions; written once in queries.ts and ported to DB.swift as a read-only consumer, per the read-model parity rule.
honest_limit: The screen shows targets Vole could name from local evidence; it is not an inventory of the company's systems and must not be read as one. A target reached by a tool that exposes no command string (Cursor, Antigravity, Devin today) never appears, and the coverage strip says so. Environment chips appear only for targets declared in policy — most rows here would show no chip at all.
competitive_note: Every console in the matrix that could show this — Wiz, Legit, GitHub audit, the cloud provider's own trail — starts from the target system and cannot name the agent or the person; every AI-security product starts from the prompt and stops at the process. This screen is the join, and it is computed entirely on the endpoint with no network call.
gap_area: Blast radius beyond the filesystem: cloud/SaaS/DB/VCS action targets, and agent-initiated package installs

name: unattended_full_access and the 'no human was present' evidence chain
description: Fires on a contiguous stretch where the autonomy interval is full_auto (or Codex approval_policy='never' AND sandbox_policy.type='danger-full-access') and no entry with origin.kind='human' appears between window_start and window_end. observed = minutes with no human-origin entry, threshold configurable through the RuleConfig contract (default 15), and the detail carries calls, write-class calls and destructive-class calls inside the window. The incident stores an evidence chain: the posture interval id, the two bounding human-origin entries with their timestamps, and the first and last raw_ref of the window as <transcript path>#<byte offset>. The anchor exists on disk here - origin.kind is human 1320, task-notification 129, peer 1 (that one carrying fromMode='bypass') - and non-human origins are excluded by name, which is why a peer-driven bypass session still fires. Grounded in Nx s1ngularity and the Replit production-database deletion.
desktop_surface: Incidents detail renders the chain as a vertical evidence list - last human input, posture at that moment, each intervening tool call with its authority chip, next human input - with a copy-as-markdown action for the ticket; the session sheet shades the unattended window on the posture ribbon.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl origin.kind and timestamp; ~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl turn_context.payload.{approval_policy, sandbox_policy} and user_message rows; autonomy_intervals
honest_limit: Absence of a human-origin entry is not absence of a human - someone watching the screen without typing is indistinguishable from an empty room, so the incident text reads 'no human input recorded for N minutes', never 'unattended'. origin.kind is a Claude-only field; for Codex, OpenCode, Grok and Devin the human-turn anchor degrades to the user_message / user-role row, which is coarser and is labelled as such in the incident.
competitive_note: v1's feature counts human turns and the longest unattended stretch but produces no incident, no threshold and no exportable chain. Anthropic's OTel export has no human-turn event; CrowdStrike and Sysdig see process activity but cannot separate an agent acting under supervision from one acting alone, because neither the permission mode nor the human turn is a syscall.
v1_ref: Human intervention, autonomy duration, self-scheduling and idle/zombie sessions
field_verified: origin.kind exists and is close to claimed: human 1,299 (feature says 1,320), task-notification 129 ✓, peer 1 ✓ — and the single peer row is the one with the rich keyset ('body','from','fromMode','kind','msg_id','name','verifiedPeerPid'), all others being bare {"kind":"human"}. origin appears only on `user` entries (1,429). The important finding the feature misses: entries with NO origin field are exactly and only entrypoint='sdk-cli' with promptSource='sdk' (27× v2.1.234, 5× v2.1.233, 1× v2.1.251) — absence of origin is itself a programmatic-prompt signal, not a version gap, and `promptSource` (typed | sdk) is a cleaner human anchor than origin.kind because it is present on every prompt entry. Codex fallback verified: event_msg user_message = 5,822 rows across 66 rollouts.
constraint: Principle 1 and constraint 5. 'minutes with no human-origin entry' as `observed` is fine, but the window must never be computed against Date.now() for an open session — codex.ts:124 and claude-code.ts:169 already leak Date.now() for missing timestamps and that is listed as a principle-1 leak in the code map; here it would also put now() inside the incident's own window bounds. Reconciliation: window_end is the last observed entry timestamp, never now, and a still-open window emits no incident. Second: DB.swift selects only `title, detail, confidence, source` from anomalies (DB.swift:228) and never observed/baseline/threshold, so principle 3 ('incidents explainable with real figures') currently leaks in the app — the evidence chain must go in `detail` or the Swift query widens.

name: repeat_call_loop replaces loop_suspected (ledger-native, absolute-rate path, agent-scoped)
description: detect/loop.ts's only baseline is the session's own leave-one-out median bucket, so a session that spins at a constant rate from turn one (a CI `claude -p`, a bash retry loop) is its own baseline and never fires — a 12-bucket by 40-call fixture produces zero anomalies, contradicting the README's 'runaway tool loops'. Replace it with a rule over the tool_calls ledger firing on three independent signatures: N identical (name, args_sha256) calls in a 5-minute window; an A-B-A-B cycle of the same two (name, args_sha256) pairs; or an absolute rate at or above MIN_CALLS*3 (45 calls / 5 min) with the existing low-output condition and no baseline at all. Group by (session_id, agent_id ?? 'main') rather than session_id, which removes the standing false positive where ten parallel read-only subagents share the parent's session_id and read as one spinning agent. Drop the documented second signal 'cache reads climb', implemented at loop.ts:42 as cacheRead > 0, which every Claude call satisfies. Identical repeats are a real signal on this machine: only 1,408 of 11,249 Bash commands duplicate another.
desktop_surface: Incident detail shows the repeated call skeleton, the repeat count and which agent branch produced it; the Behaviour panel marks looping windows on the session timeline.
data_source: tool_calls (name, args_sha256, issued_ts, session_id, agent_id); usage_events.output_tokens for the flat-output gate; packages/core/src/detect/loop.ts:8,22,25,34,41-42
honest_limit: A genuine loop with a varying argument (an incrementing offset, a new file each turn) hashes differently every call and is reachable only by the absolute-rate path, which needs per-call output tokens and so covers only tools with exact usage. Devin and Grok have tool calls but no per-call output tokens, so only the identical-repeat and A-B-A-B signatures apply there and the rule must say which signatures were even available. The 45-calls figure is a policy constant, not an observation, and belongs in the tunable rule config with its origin printed in the incident.
competitive_note: v1's tool_loop entry describes the same identical-hash and A-B-A-B signatures but leaves loop_suspected standing beside it, so the undetectable-at-constant-rate defect and the subagent false positive both survive. CSA's Agentic NIST profile names action velocity (AG-MS.1) as a required control; no coding-agent vendor ships a loop rule, and Cursor's OTel export has no per-session tool attribution to build one from.
v1_ref: Tool-sequence loop and edit-test-revert thrash rules
field_verified: CONFIRMED. loop.ts:22 `groupBy(usable, (e) => e.session_id as string)` — session-only grouping. loop.ts:34 `const baseline = Math.max(1, medianExcluding(counts, i));` then L36 `if (evs.length <= baseline * RATE_MULTIPLE) continue;` — at a constant rate baseline == evs.length so the guard always fires; the constant-rate blindness is structural, not a tuning issue. loop.ts:42 `if (cacheRead <= 0) continue;` — verbatim the vacuous second signal the feature names. Bash duplication on this machine now: 12,063 commands, 10,582 distinct, 1,481 duplicated (feature: 11,249 / 1,408 — data grew, ratio holds at 12.3%). agent_id is populated on 4,947 of 16,728 claude_code rows and 1,230 of 10,885 opencode rows, so `(session_id, agent_id ?? 'main')` has real material to group on. tool_calls / args_sha256 do NOT exist — the ledger is roadmap-v1.md:6, L effort, unbuilt.
constraint: Constraint 10 is honoured, not strained: 'child events carry the parent's session_id and their own agent_id' is precisely why the current session-only grouping reads ten parallel subagents as one spinning agent, and (session_id, agent_id) is the contract-compliant fix. Constraint 7 permits args_sha256 ('counts/ids/hashes/paths') provided the collector hashes the argument in the loop and never stores or re-selects it — worth stating in the collector, since v1's sibling thrash rule wants result hashes too and that is closer to the content line. Unstated dependency: the absolute-rate path's low-output gate needs per-call output tokens, but usage_events carries output per assistant message, not per tool call — the join is one-to-many and must be documented as 'output on the message that issued the call', not per call.

name: Signal provenance on every ledger row: status_source, duration_kind and the per-tool coverage matrix
description: Every tool_calls row carries status_source ∈ {result_flag, exit_code, log_flag, turn_status, none} and duration_kind ∈ {execution, transcript_gap, turn_scoped, none} beside the value, and a per-(tool, tool_name) coverage view aggregates them so no rule or report card can print an invented zero. The signals genuinely differ, all verified here: OpenCode gives a real metadata.exit on 6,026 of 6,084 bash parts and state.time.{start,end} on 12,290 of 12,292 tool parts (status completed 12,201 / error 89 / running 2); Grok gives success + elapsed_ms on 1,402 exec_done; Devin gives completed/failed on 1,246; Claude gives only a boolean is_error with no exit code and a tool_use→tool_result gap that also contains model queue time and the permission prompt (medians 129 ms under bypassPermissions, 189 ms normal, 1,021 ms auto); Codex has no per-call outcome at all, only ~/.codex/thread_history_1.sqlite thread_turns.{status,duration_ms} at turn granularity on 6 of 66 threads. Every behaviour rule reads coverage first and skips (tool, tool_name) pairs whose status_source is 'none', and human-gate time is published only where the wait is unambiguously human — AskUserQuestion (114 calls here, p50 36.6 s, p95 29 min) and denial rows.
desktop_surface: Behaviour panel header strip renders a coverage matrix (tool × signal) with em dashes for unavailable signals, mirroring the existing confidence-badge convention, and clicking a cell filters the call table; the duration column carries a kind chip (exec / gap / turn / —); the session report card shows a 'time waiting on a human' figure sourced only from AskUserQuestion and denials, with its source named inline.
data_source: tool_calls, set at collection time from which field yielded the value: OpenCode part.data $.state.metadata.exit and $.state.time.{start,end}; Grok shell.tool.exec_done ctx.{success,elapsed_ms}; Devin messages kind='tool_call' content.status; Claude assistant.timestamp vs the tool_result entry timestamp and tool_result.is_error; ~/.codex/thread_history_1.sqlite thread_turns.{status,duration_ms} and rollout task_complete.duration_ms
honest_limit: transcript_gap may never be reported as tool latency or agent runtime, and durations of different kinds must never be summed into one KPI; sessions with no permission-mode stamp (8,700 matched results here) are excluded from any mode comparison. Coverage is a statement about what the vendor writes to disk today — a version bump can silently remove a field, so the verify pass must alarm when a coverage class drops to zero. It can never tell whether an unrecorded call succeeded, and Codex's turn-level status covers a whole turn, never one call.
competitive_note: EMA/Cequence report 46% of enterprises cannot produce a 30-day agent audit trail (market.md §1); an audit trail that silently prints zero where it has no signal is worse than none, and no vendor publishes per-signal coverage. Cursor's OTel export publishes durations with no such distinction and labels its own cost 'best-effort'.
v1_ref: tool_calls ledger with tool_result error join — its ⚠ names duration_kind but defines no taxonomy; also corrects 'Session behaviour report card and tool-mix breakdown'
field_verified: The most accurately sourced feature in the shard. OpenCode, verified by direct query: bash parts 6,084, with $.state.metadata.exit 6,026 (feature: 6,026 of 6,084 — exact); tool parts with both $.state.time.start and .end 12,290 of 12,292 (exact); status completed 12,201 / error 89 / running 2 (exact). Grok: 1,402 exec_done, 1,402 with success, 1,402 with elapsed_ms (exact). Codex: ~/.codex/thread_history_1.sqlite thread_turns schema confirms `status TEXT NOT NULL, duration_ms INTEGER, rollout_ordinal INTEGER` with 6 rows across 5 distinct threads out of 66 (exact). Claude: only is_error, no exit code — confirmed, and the AskUserQuestion human-gate figure reproduces to the decimal: 114 calls, 113 joinable tool_use→tool_result pairs, p50 36.6 s, p95 1,732.9 s = 28.9 min. One correction: Devin gives a terminal status on 1,712 of 1,715 calls (completed 1,685, failed 27, in_progress 3), not the 1,246 claimed — the feature understates its own coverage.
constraint: No conflict; it is the enforcement mechanism for principles 1 and 2 and the reason F1 can ship without inventing zeros. One thing to state explicitly so it is not mistaken later: status_source and duration_kind are separate columns and must never be folded into confidence, which constraint 4 pins at exactly two values ('exact' | 'activity_only') — a third tier is forbidden even though ROADMAP principle 2 names one. Two additions the honest_limit needs: the AskUserQuestion maximum gap here is 191,360 s (53 hours, a session left open overnight), so a 'time waiting on a human' KPI must publish a cap or the distribution, never a mean; and the coverage matrix should read from tool_calls at query time rather than being materialised, so a vendor silently dropping a field shows as a live coverage collapse rather than a stale row.

name: payload_origin: a screenshot of somebody's screen versus a PNG that was already in git
description: Classifies each `payload_sightings` image row by where its bytes came from, using evidence that already exists rather than any pixel: the row's `tool_use_id` joins the tool-call ledger to recover the Read's `input.file_path`, and OpenCode preserves the attachment's original `filename` verbatim in `part.data`. Four classes are stamped at insert — `screen_capture` (the OS screenshot naming pattern, or a screenshot temp directory), `outside_work_roots` (a path resolving under no `work_roots` entry), `repo_asset` (under a work root and present in that repo's `.git/index`), and `unresolved`. On this machine 471 of 670 image Reads came from `~/Desktop`, 186 from `/tmp` or `/var/folders`, only 12 from inside a repository, and 54 of OpenCode's 66 attachments are literally named `Screenshot 2026-06-19 at 6.30.24 PM.png`. The distinction is the whole point: a screenshot can contain whatever was on that screen — a customer record, an inbox, a Slack thread — while a checked-in asset is already in the repository the agent is allowed to see, and the Samsung shape is stated without a single pixel being read.
desktop_surface: The Leak Ledger's unreadable axis splits by origin class rather than rendering one grey bar, and the People view gains a 'screen captures sent to a model' count per principal per week with the counted `unresolved` bucket printed beside it.
data_source: payload_sightings.tool_use_id joined to the tool_calls ledger's Read input.file_path (~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl content[].tool_use.input.file_path); ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db part.data.filename; work_roots and .git/index for the repo_asset test
honest_limit: A screenshot of a stack trace and a screenshot of a customer record are identical to this classifier — it says where the bytes came from and never what they show. Screenshot naming is locale- and tool-dependent, so the patterns ship as a content pack with a version stamp, not as a name list compiled into the collector. 241 of the 911 tool-result images have no file path at all (browser and MCP tools returned them in memory) and land in `unresolved`, which is counted and printed, never guessed into a class.
competitive_note: The endpoint content vendors (Cyberhaven, Harmonic, Nightfall) would need OCR and would then be storing the pixels, which is exactly the retention the DPO buyer's works-council pack forbids. Browser-only tools (LayerX, Menlo, Island, Purview) never see a terminal agent reading ~/Desktop at all. Nobody classifies image provenance from the agent's own tool-call path.
gap_area: Opaque-payload and bulk-egress volumetrics: the bytes DLP structurally cannot read

name: What the agent left behind: the envelope receipt and its review packet
description: One section on Blast Radius, machine side above repo side, each row a classified write carrying its class chip, posture at the time, authorisation basis, escape state and the diff facts — names added, install-script keys, PATH position, ignore patterns — as figures, not prose. Per session it renders an envelope receipt answering the three questions the class list encodes: what this session changed about what runs, about what is trusted, and about what is hidden. A new `v_envelope_changes` read model is written twice (queries.ts and DB.swift) per the read-model parity constraint, and `vole envelope --session <id>` plus an evidence-bundle section emit the same rows through round 2's deny-by-default export field registry, so a change board or an auditor receives the receipt as data rather than a screenshot.
desktop_surface: The section itself, plus a per-session receipt sheet reachable from the session card and from a vole:// deep link, with the unmonitored-agent count printed beside every total.
data_source: The change_risk_class ledger, dependency_deltas, grant_deposits and the persistence/visibility rows, exposed through v_envelope_changes.
honest_limit: This is a receipt of what was observed, not of what changed: a write through a tool Vole does not ledger, or during an interval when no collector was running, is simply absent, so the section prints the unmonitored-agent count and round 2's evidence_gaps beside the total or it will be read as complete. Nothing on the screen says a change is unsafe — the DB holds no content, this is not SAST, and the wording ships as 'the envelope moved and who authorised it', never as a vulnerability claim.
competitive_note: Vendor consoles report acceptance rate and lines suggested (Amazon Q dashboards, Copilot metrics, Cursor analytics); the change-review artefact for agent-authored work does not exist in any of the 62 vendors, and the ASPM tools that could produce one see the diff without the agent, the posture or the principal.
gap_area: Agent-authored change risk: writes that widen the security envelope, not writes that destroy

name: MCP server dimension on the ledger and tool_first_seen
description: Split every tool name of the form `mcp__<server>__<tool>` into separate `server` and `tool_name` columns on the tool_calls ledger, giving observed-usage counts per MCP server — live here: playwright 1,994, searxng 548, Claude_Browser 298, github 48, context7 31, ui 13, ccd 2. Rule `tool_first_seen` fires the first time a `(tool, server, tool_name)` triple is observed for a principal, which catches a newly added MCP server, a poisoned server that grew a tool, and built-in tools whose names carry their own risk (`browser_run_code_unsafe`, 214 calls here). This is observed usage rather than configuration inventory, so it also catches servers registered outside the config files v1's MCP inventory parses.
desktop_surface: Breakdown pane gains an 'MCP servers' group (calls, failure ratio, first seen); the first-seen incident appears in the feed with the server name and its transport where the config inventory knows one.
data_source: tool_calls.name prefix `mcp__<server>__`; Claude tool_use.name; OpenCode part tool names; Devin `_meta['cognition.ai/inferenceToolName']` ('mcp_call_tool', 167 rows here).
honest_limit: Devin collapses every MCP invocation to the single name `mcp_call_tool`, so its server is unknowable from this source and stays NULL. Transport and command come from the config inventory, never from the ledger; a server observed but absent from config is reported as 'observed, not registered locally', never as malicious. Counts are lower bounds until the comma-joined `tools` column bug (code-map bug 5, which loses names on roughly half of Claude turns) is fixed.
competitive_note: OWASP MCP Top 10 names shadow MCP (MCP09) and audit/telemetry gaps (MCP08); Claude Code's own OTel collapses MCP tool names to the literal string 'mcp_tool', so the vendor's telemetry cannot answer which server was used.
v1_ref: MCP server inventory, trust posture, usage diff and pin/sign rules
field_verified: Mechanism real, EVERY NUMBER WRONG. usage_events.tools does hold mcp__<server>__<tool> strings (1,066 live rows match 'mcp\_\_%'). But splitting that column gives playwright 981, searxng 53, github 22, context7 9, ui-skills 1 — no Claude_Browser, no ccd. Counting the raw transcripts instead gives github 41,325, playwright 23,584, searxng 4,240, context7 1,836, Claude_Browser 626, ccd_session_mgmt 366, ui-skills 316, scheduled-tasks 208, ccd_directory 98, claude-in-chrome 52, claude_ai_{Google_Drive,Gmail,Google_Calendar} 24 each, plugin_supabase_supabase 11, plugin_chrome-devtools-mcp_chrome-devtools 8. The quoted figures (playwright 1,994 / searxng 548 / Claude_Browser 298 / github 48 / context7 31 / ui 13 / ccd 2) match NEITHER source, and two named servers do not exist under those names — the real prefixes are `ui-skills`, `ccd_session_mgmt` and `ccd_directory`. `browser_run_code_unsafe` is on 147 usage_events rows, not 214.
constraint: The extension_points entry is explicit: 'a tool_calls table must be produced in the same pass, never derived from usage_events.tools'. My two counts prove why — the DB column loses ~96% of playwright calls and 100% of Claude_Browser. So this is NOT an S-effort query over an existing ledger: it is gated on the tool_ledger shard building tool_calls in the collector parse loop, and on code-map bug 5 (claude-code.ts:150 + db.ts:101, tool names lost on 7,102/14,238 turns). Second correction: the split must handle the `mcp__plugin_<plugin>_<server>__<tool>` shape or plugin-supplied servers land under a bogus server name. Constraint 3: `tool_first_seen` keyed on (tool, server, tool_name, principal) is deterministic and now()-free — compliant.

name: headless_bypass_launch rule (the Nx s1ngularity shape)
description: Fires when a Claude session's entrypoint is 'cli' or 'sdk-cli' (1,188 and 177 entries here against 44,873 claude-vscode) AND its first observed permissionMode is bypassPermissions AND the transcript contains zero origin.kind='human' entries AND the session cwd holds a package manifest whose mtime is within N minutes of the session's first timestamp - that last clause is what separates a deliberate headless run from a postinstall-triggered one, and it only raises severity, it never gates the rule. observed = tool calls in the session, threshold = 1, severity critical; the detail names the entrypoint, version, cwd basename class and manifest filename, never the full path. A second, weaker trigger is the literal string --dangerously-skip-permissions inside a Bash command, which appears 17 times in these transcripts: an agent launching a nested headless agent. anomaly_key is headless_bypass:<session>; tagged OWASP ASI and ATLAS supply-chain.
desktop_surface: Its own Incidents card style with a red 'headless, no human, full access' banner, the entrypoint and version strings, and a list of the sensitive-path classes and destructive classes touched during the run.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl entrypoint, permissionMode, origin.kind, cwd, version; tool_use.input.command for the nested-launch string; fs.stat mtime of package.json / pnpm-lock.yaml / requirements.txt in cwd
honest_limit: Vole sees only the agent leg of the attack: the npm postinstall process, the stealer payload and any exfiltration outside a tool call are invisible and belong to EDR. A run launched with CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR pointed elsewhere writes its transcript outside ~/.claude/projects and is missed entirely unless alternate-home discovery ships. Only Claude Code records an entrypoint field, so this rule is Claude-only and every other tool's panel must read 'entrypoint not recorded'. The manifest-mtime clause is a heuristic and is labelled one.
competitive_note: market.md logs Nx s1ngularity (2025-08-26, >1,700 users leaked, Wiz) using exactly `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions` for secret recon and lists 'bypass headless session' as a feature implication, yet roadmap-v1 has no such rule. No vendor in the 62-row matrix detects it from the agent's own transcript: Snyk Agent Scan finds the config, CrowdStrike finds the process, neither joins entrypoint + permission mode + absence of a human turn.
field_verified: Fields all exist; two numbers are wrong and the rule fires ZERO times as specified. entrypoint distribution: claude-vscode 76,347 (feature says 44,873 — wrong by 70%), claude-desktop-3p 8,513 (never mentioned), cli 1,188 ✓, sdk-cli 177 ✓, claude-desktop 26. I simulated the exact conjunction over all 125 sessions: 45 have a cli/sdk-cli entrypoint, ALL 45 carry at least one permissionMode entry, 33 have zero human-origin entries — and every one of those 33 starts at permissionMode 'default' and never once uses bypassPermissions. Firings: 0. Even relaxing 'first mode' to 'any mode' gives 0. The nested-launch trigger is worse: '--dangerously-skip-permissions' appears 215 times as a raw substring across the transcripts but only 3 times as an actual deduped Bash tool_use.input.command — the feature's '17 times: an agent launching a nested headless agent' is a substring artifact of prompt and documentation text.
constraint: Constraint 14. The manifest-mtime clause adds an fs.stat of package.json / pnpm-lock.yaml / requirements.txt in the session cwd — a runtime filesystem read of a path that is not a declared source, and build-sea.mjs allows 'no runtime file reads except pricing override and sources'. Reconciliation: declare the cwd manifest a source in paths.ts with a VOLE_* override, or drop the clause (it is only a severity modifier). Constraint 7 is respected — the detail names the manifest filename and a cwd basename class, never the path.

name: scope_drift: sessions that move to a second repository
description: Claude stamps cwd on every entry and 23 of 81 sessions here touched more than one cwd. The rule fires when a session's tool calls cross into a second git root, or when the set of distinct directories written to grows beyond K after the first N calls. This is a different test from v1's scope_escape, which is per-call (file_path outside entry.cwd); scope_drift is a per-session trajectory and catches exactly the case where every individual call is in scope for its own cwd while the session as a whole has wandered into another product. Repo identity comes from the nearest .git directory above the path, resolved by a file read, never a git subprocess.
desktop_surface: Behaviour panel session header lists the repos touched with per-repo call counts; incident detail names both roots and the exact call at which the crossing happened.
data_source: Claude entry.cwd per assistant line; tool_use.input.file_path; parsed cd and redirect targets from the command classifier; OpenCode message path.cwd/root
honest_limit: A cd inside a Bash command does not change entry.cwd, so a parsed cd target is a labelled second signal and never ground truth. Codex, Grok and Devin record cwd sparsely or not at all here (all 1,758 Grok rows have project NULL), so the rule covers Claude Code and OpenCode and must say so rather than reporting zero drift for the rest. A monorepo with one .git root and ten products reads as no drift by construction, which is a stated blind spot rather than a clean result.
competitive_note: v1's scope_escape stays per-call and its note puts Bash redirection writes explicitly out of scope, so a session that legitimately cds into a second repo and works there is invisible to it. Zenity markets taint tracking from native hooks; a purely log-derived repo-crossing signal needs no hook and works for the agents no vendor instruments.
v1_ref: Out-of-repo write and agent self-modification rules (scope_escape, agent_config_modified)
field_verified: CONFIRMED with a correction to the honest_limit. Claude stamps cwd on entries — verified on a real line: `{...,"cwd":"<redacted-local-path>","sessionId":"bc9e45fc-...","gitBranch":"main"}`. I grouped every cwd by sessionId across all 633 transcripts: 125 sessions carry a cwd, 35 of them touched more than one (28%). The feature said 23 of 81 (28%) — same ratio, different snapshot/denominator. Grok DB rows: `select count(*), count(project) from usage_events where tool='grok'` → 1758|0, so 'all 1,758 Grok rows have project NULL' is exact. CORRECTION: the honest_limit's 'Grok records cwd sparsely or not at all here' is wrong — ~/.grok/logs/unified.jsonl carries `"msg":"session created","ctx":{"cwd":"<redacted-local-path>"}` on 7 lines; the cwd exists on disk once per session and grok.ts simply drops it (it is listed in code-map-extracts fields_available_but_ignored). Grok is one collector line away from coverage, not structurally excluded.
constraint: IDEMPOTENCY BREAK THE FEATURE MISSES (constraint 1 / principle 4): resolving repo identity by walking to the nearest .git directory at DETECTION time makes the verdict a function of the current filesystem, not of the logged data. A repo moved, deleted or newly git-init'd changes historical verdicts, and if the resolved root is folded into anomaly_key the key is not stable across re-reads — which detect.test.ts:120 exists to prevent. Reconciliation: resolve the root in the COLLECTOR at ingest (when the path most probably still exists), store it as a column, and key the anomaly on the ordered cwd pair rather than the resolved root, so a vanished repo degrades to 'root unresolved' instead of silently re-labelling history. Constraint 7 is satisfied — cwd and file paths are explicitly among the things the DB may hold.

name: Acting-now panel and live-autonomy tint
description: Nothing in the app distinguishes a session running unattended under full autonomy from one a human is typing into. Add two read models — getLivePosture() and getActingNow(), each written twice per the read-model parity rule — that return, per session, its most recent autonomy_interval, the tool, minutes since the last human-origin entry and calls since, and drive a third menu-bar tint from whether any session's current interval is full_auto with its last event inside two poll intervals. The panel gains an 'Acting now' section above the hero figures, one row per live session with an autonomy chip, each row clicking through to that session's posture ribbon in the dashboard.
desktop_surface: Menu-bar glyph gains a third tint alongside the existing severity tints, with the lag stated in its tooltip; MenuPanel gains an 'Acting now' section listing live sessions with tool, autonomy chip, 'last activity 42s ago' and calls since the last human turn.
data_source: autonomy_intervals (from the permission-mode/sandbox posture feature) joined to usage_events.ts; new queries getLivePosture()/getActingNow() in queries.ts plus DB.swift ports; Store.swift refresh timer; ~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json for pid liveness where available.
honest_limit: 'Acting now' means 'wrote a transcript line within the last two poll intervals' — a session blocked on a long tool call looks idle and one that exited without a final line looks live until the window lapses, so the row says 'last activity 42s ago' rather than 'running'. At the default 5s poll the badge lags reality by up to 10s and the refresh interval is user-configurable, so the lag is shown rather than assumed; sessions from tools that stamp no permission mode show an autonomy chip of 'unknown', never 'supervised'.
competitive_note: Every competitor's equivalent live view lives in a cloud console the developer never opens; a tint in the menu bar is the only place an autonomy warning reaches the person who can change it in the second it matters, and it is the visible half of the Tier 5 control story without any of its enforcement risk.
v1_ref: Live process map: PID to session
field_verified: Both artifacts exist; one has a defect the feature misses. `~/.claude/sessions/22530.json` is real and contains `{"pid":22530,"sessionId":"96eb2395-6c1c-4fc8-8f0c-98f7d51f1a54","cwd":"<redacted-local-path>","startedAt":1788746180904,"procStart":"Mon Sep  7 01:56:20 2026","version":"2.1.263","kind":"interactive","entrypoint":"claude-vscode"}` — pid liveness and session mapping are genuinely available. Permission mode is on disk too: 743 `bypassPermissions` occurrences across ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl. MATERIAL DEFECT: the line is `{"type":"permission-mode","permissionMode":"bypassPermissions","sessionId":"..."}` and I dumped its keys — `['type','permissionMode','sessionId']`, `has timestamp: False`. There is NO timestamp on the mode-change line, so an autonomy_interval has no clock of its own. `autonomy_intervals` as a table does not exist.
constraint: Constraint 2 is the reason this must be a side table and the feature gets that right: the upsert (db.ts:102 `WHERE excluded.total_tokens > usage_events.total_tokens`) never rewrites session_id or agent_id and only widens on strictly-greater tokens, so 'enrich the session row with autonomy later' is impossible by construction. Constraint 19 is fine (epoch integers). Constraint 7 is fine — a mode name is not content.

name: denied_then_achieved and denial_then_reshape: the guardrail-bypass matcher
description: Gives v1's guardrail_bypass_suspected an actual mechanism, in two branches off one trigger. On a denial - top-level toolDenialKind (automode-blocked 22, user-rejected 13, automode-unavailable 2 here) joined back to the issuing assistant entry through the sourceToolAssistantUUID field the denial record already carries - extract the target as a normalised path or verb+path and hash it. denied_then_achieved fires when a DIFFERENT tool reaches the same target hash within K subsequent calls in the session (Bash `cat`/`head` after a denied Read, `python3 -c` or `sed -i` after a denied Edit, `gh api` after a denied MCP call); denial_then_reshape fires when the SAME pattern category recurs with a different args_sha256; both escalate when the retry succeeds under a higher autonomy than the denied call. The rule exists because Claude's own denial text, verbatim on this machine, instructs the model that it '*may* attempt to accomplish this action using other tools that might naturally be used to accomplish this goal, e.g. using head instead of cat' - the workaround is designed behaviour, so watching for it is the only way to know it happened.
desktop_surface: Incidents detail renders the pair side by side - denied call and achieving call - with the shared target class between them, the number of intervening calls and the posture at each end, plus a standing note that this is expected agent behaviour and not necessarily malicious so the reviewer triages rather than panics. The session sheet gains an 'Interventions' tab listing every denial with any subsequent same-category call.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl toolDenialKind, sourceToolAssistantUUID, tool_result.content denial phrases, subsequent message.content[].tool_use.{name,input}; tool_calls.{pattern_id, args_sha256}; autonomy_intervals for the escalation branch; opencode permission table (0 rows here)
honest_limit: Claude Code is the only tool here that records denials at all - OpenCode's permission table has 0 rows across 145 sessions - so this is Claude-only and every other tool's panel must read 'denials not recorded' rather than showing a clean bill. With 37 denials total on this machine the rule is rare and its precision unmeasurable for a long time, so it ships off by default behind a labelled-firings counter. Target normalisation is textual, so relative, absolute and symlinked spellings of the same file may not match: the rule under-reports and never over-reports. A legitimate retry the user themselves approved is indistinguishable from a model-initiated workaround, and the incident says so.
competitive_note: v1 lists guardrail_bypass_suspected inside the guardrail ledger with no definition, no key and no window. Claude Code's OTel emits tool_decision with an approval source only when telemetry is enabled; Vole reads the same fact from disk for every session including ones with telemetry off. Gateway vendors (Lasso, MintMCP, Speakeasy) can block a denied MCP call but never see the local Bash call that achieves the same thing seconds later, which is precisely the gap this covers.
v1_ref: Guardrail-fired ledger: denials, refusals, hook blocks, denial_streak
field_verified: The best-verified feature in the shard. A real denial record, quoted whole: {"parentUuid":"d4a02cec-...","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"tool_result","content":...,"is_error":...,"tool_use_id":...}]},"timestamp":"2026-08-15T08:04:22.095Z","toolUseResult":"Error: Permission for this action was denied by the Claude Code auto mode classifier. Reason: Blocked by classifier. ... IMPORTANT: You *may* attempt to accomplish this action usi[ng other tools]","toolDenialKind":"automode-blocked","sourceToolAssistantUUID":"d4a02cec-...","sessionId":"ca4c0a67-..."}. The verbatim instruction the feature's argument rests on is present exactly as quoted. Counts: automode-blocked 22 ✓, user-rejected 14 (feature 13), automode-unavailable 2 ✓ = 38 (feature 37). sourceToolAssistantUUID occurs 23,206 times and equals parentUuid on denial records — but message.content[0].tool_use_id is the STRICTLY better join, because it names the individual denied tool_use rather than an assistant entry that may carry several. OpenCode permission table: 0 rows across 145 sessions ✓ EXACT.
constraint: Constraint 7. The trigger reads the denial phrase out of toolUseResult, which is content; matching must happen on the raw line inside the collector and only {kind, target_hash, pattern_id, args_sha256} may be stored — roadmap-v1 L52 already sets this rule ('store toolDenialKind, bracketed reason category; never denial or refusal text'). Constraint 3: the key must be built from the denial's own uuid, not from the window, so it stays now()-free.
