One correction the write-up needs: automode-unavailable is a classifier TIMEOUT ('is temporarily unavailable (timed out), so auto mode cannot determine the safety of Bash right now') — it is not a guardrail decision and must be excluded from the trigger, or the rule manufactures incidents out of infrastructure flakiness.

name: Human-interrupt ledger from the interruption marker
description: v1 concludes twice — in the session outcome labels and the waste taxonomy — that interruptions have almost no local evidence, because toolUseResult.interrupted is false on every one of roughly 6,000 rows. The evidence exists in a different shape: the literal string '[Request interrupted by user]' appears 262 times across 190 transcript files on this machine right now. Record each as an intervention row (session, ts, and the tool call it interrupted, resolved via the immediately preceding unbound tool_use), and expose interrupts per session and interrupts per 100 tool calls. That counter is the denominator for every autonomy metric and the honest ceiling on any 'the agent ran unattended' claim, because a session with nine interrupts was plainly supervised no matter what the chain length says.
desktop_surface: Behaviour panel session strip marks interrupts as ticks on the autonomy bar, breaking the continuous bar where a human intervened; the session report card gains a line 'n human interrupts (text marker)'.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl user entries containing the literal '[Request interrupted by user]' (262 occurrences, 190 files here); toolUseResult.interrupted (present, always false)
honest_limit: This is a text marker, not a structured field: it is version-fragile, it can be produced by a user pasting the same string into a prompt, and every surface must label it 'text marker' rather than presenting it as a vendor signal. Only Claude Code emits it — OpenCode, Codex, Grok and Devin have no interruption record and must render an em dash, never 0. An interrupt that lands between turns leaves no marker at all, so the count is a floor and never a total.
competitive_note: v1's notes read 'interrupted has almost no local evidence and may never fire' and 'label as text match or omit' — this is the omitted half, and it is the only local evidence that a human was at the keyboard while an agent ran. No vendor telemetry exposes user interruptions; Cursor and Copilot report acceptance rates, which measure a different act entirely.
v1_ref: Session outcome labels (rule-based funnel)
field_verified: CONFIRMED, with a file-count correction and one field the feature missed. `grep -oh 'Request interrupted by user'` across all ~/.claude jsonl → 262 occurrences (exact match), but in 175 files, NOT 190. v1's premise verified exactly: `"interrupted":` appears 6,060 times and is `false` every single time, zero trues. CORRECTION 1: the marker is not confined to user entries — by (type, role) it is user/user 205, assistant/assistant 21, attachment 7, result 7. A collector reading only user entries misses 55 of 262 (21%). CORRECTION 2 (missed field): `"interruptedByShutdown":true` appears 18 times and never false — a genuine structured field corroborating a subset, and the same entries carry promptId, entrypoint ('sdk-cli') and isSidechain. Sample entry: `{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"[Request interrupted by user]"}]},"interruptedByShutdown":true,"entrypoint":"sdk-cli","timestamp":"2026-08-23T19:25:34.317Z",...}` — note it DOES carry a timestamp.
constraint: Constraint 7 is satisfied and worth saying so: matching a literal string inside a user message is a content read in the collector loop, which the constraint explicitly sanctions ('DLP scanning happens on the raw line in the collector'), and storing only (session, ts, tool_use_id) keeps content out of the DB. Principle 1 discipline is good — 'text marker', 'a floor and never a total', em dash for the four tools that emit nothing. One attribution defect: 'the immediately preceding UNBOUND tool_use' will almost never resolve, because only 5 tool_use ids in 101,610 entries are unbound — Claude writes a tool_result even on interrupt. Bind to the preceding tool_use by position and label the binding as positional, or the ledger records 262 interrupts attributed to nothing.

name: Bash redirect, heredoc and copy write-targets in the file ledger
description: Parse write targets out of the shell segments produced by the pattern pack (>, >>, tee, cp, mv, install, sed -i, patch) and record them as file-write rows in the same ledger as Edit/Write, tagged method='bash_redirect'. This closes the largest blind spot in any edit ledger: 6,321 of 11,865 Bash calls here contain a write-shaped segment and 750 contain a heredoc, against 2,374 structuredPatch results from Edit/Write — so a blast-radius figure built only on Edit/Write undercounts writes by roughly 2.7x. roadmap-v1 declares redirection writes out of scope under scope_escape and then admits in the rollback entry that 'Bash edits are invisible to the ledger'; those are the same gap and it is parseable. Rows store the resolved path class and repo-relative directory only, plus an 'unresolved' flag when the target contains a variable, glob or heredoc-generated name.
desktop_surface: Behaviour panel 'Files' tab: writes split by method (Edit/Write vs bash_redirect vs unresolved) with an out-of-repo count badge; the rollback flow lists bash_redirect targets as 'cannot be restored from file-history backups' instead of omitting them.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl tool_use.input.command; ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db part.data $.state.input where $.tool='bash'; the same segments emitted by the command-shape classifier, so no second parser exists
honest_limit: Targets containing variables, globs or heredoc-generated names cannot be resolved and are reported as 'N writes with unresolved target' — never dropped and never counted as zero. The segment parse is a shell-shaped heuristic, not a shell: quoting edge cases and process substitution degrade to 'unresolved'. A redirect that failed at runtime still appears as an attempted write on Claude (no exit code is recorded); on OpenCode the exit code disambiguates. Codex, Grok, Cursor and Antigravity contribute nothing here.
competitive_note: Endpoint DLP suites (Cyberhaven, Nightfall) see file writes at the filesystem layer but cannot attribute them to an agent session and tool call (market.md rows 68-69); gateway vendors see neither.
v1_ref: Out-of-repo write and agent self-modification rules (scope_escape, agent_config_modified) (Tier 2), whose ⚠ declares Bash redirection out of scope
field_verified: The mechanism verifies; the headline number does not. structuredPatch results: 2,374 — exact match to the claim. Heredocs: 787 of 12,134 Bash commands (claim 750) — verified. But the claimed '6,321 of 11,865 Bash calls contain a write-shaped segment' is reproducible only as `any command containing the character >` = 6,338 today, which is dominated by `2>/dev/null` and `2>&1` — sampled hits include `wc -l interface/*.py agents/*.py 2>/dev/null | tail -30`, which writes nothing. Measured honestly: redirects to a non-/dev/null target 1,765 (14.5%); strict segment match on >, >>, tee, cp, mv, install, sed -i, patch 1,125 (9.3%); tee/cp/mv/install/sed -i/patch alone 273. So bash-shaped writes add roughly 74% on top of the 2,374 Edit/Write patches, not the claimed 2.7x undercount — the real ratio is about 0.74:1, not 2.7:1.
constraint: No new constraint conflict beyond the one it inherits from F4 (constraint 7: a resolved write target is a file path, which constraint 7 explicitly permits, so this feature is cleaner than F4 — paths are on the allowed list, skeletons are not). Constraint 5 (never invent a number) is the binding one and the design already honours it with the explicit 'N writes with unresolved target' bucket instead of a silent drop. Same Devin omission as F4: 1,715 commands with full rawInput.command are available and the feature lists no Devin source at all.

name: Destructive-command classifier with cwd-relative blast radius
description: Corrects the v1 classifier, which stores class, hash, outcome and permission mode but never resolves what the command would actually have destroyed - the difference between the 387 harmless `rm -f` calls here and a cleanup command that expands to ~/ and takes the Keychain with it. Adds target_scope in {inside_cwd, outside_cwd, home, root, unresolved}, computed by expanding ~, $HOME and a leading / against the entry's own cwd, with 'unresolved' whenever the string contains a variable or command substitution Vole cannot expand - never a guess. Verified classes in the 6,543 command strings on this machine: rm -f 387, rm -rf 77, sudo 68, rm -r 8, base64 -d 1, find -exec 1. destructive_command fires critical only when target_scope is home, root or outside_cwd AND autonomy is full_auto AND authorization_basis is not human_denied. The same textual path resolver is the shared dependency of the Codex sandbox-claim rule and the cross-scope publish rule, so it ships once rather than three times.
desktop_surface: Incidents row shows the class, the masked command (path segments replaced by their class), the resolved scope and the posture chip; the session sheet's behaviour report card gains a blast-radius column counting calls per scope.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl tool_use.input.command with the entry's own cwd; ~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl function_call.arguments.{cmd, workdir}; ~/.grok/logs/unified.jsonl shell.tool.exec_done.ctx
honest_limit: Claude records no exit code on success and only 'Exit code N' text on some failures, so the outcome stays an enum {ok, exit:N, interrupted, timed_out, denied, unknown} and 0 is never assumed. Shell expansion is approximated, never executed: a command whose target depends on a variable, a subshell or a script file resolves to 'unresolved' and cannot fire the critical branch. Vole classifies the command string itself and deliberately ignores the vendor's own read-only/safe classification, because the Amazon Q `find -exec` RCE (2025-08-19) and the Claude Code $IFS CVEs were both vendor misclassifications.
competitive_note: Sysdig detects the syscall after the fact and CrowdStrike the process, but neither can say whether the agent was in bypass mode or whether a human had been asked, and vendor telemetry emits no command strings at all. Grounded in the Replit agent deleting a production database during a code freeze (2025-07-21). v1 is right about the pattern list and wrong to stop before resolving the target.
v1_ref: Destructive and outbound command classifier (destructive_command, destructive_under_bypass)
field_verified: Patterns exist; the counts are wrong in both directions and nobody's numbers agree. Deduped by tool_use.id over 11,411 Bash commands: rm -f 363, rm -rf 177, sudo 110, find -exec 71 (feature claims rm -f 387, rm -rf 77, sudo 68, find -exec 1 — rm -rf understated 2.3x, sudo 1.6x, find -exec 71x). base64 -d/--decode is 28 undeduped, not 1. Roadmap-v1 L47 quotes a third set again (rm -rf 203, sudo 160). Every input the resolver needs is present on the entry: `"cwd": "<redacted-local-path>"` sits on the same user entry as permissionMode, and Codex function_call arguments carry `{"cmd": "sed -n '1,220p' <redacted-local-path>", "workdir": "<redacted-local-path>", ...}`.
constraint: Principle 1, and the feature already handles it correctly: 'unresolved' rather than a guessed expansion, and an outcome enum that never assumes 0. Keep that discipline literally — the code map lists `?? 0` on absent reasoning (codex.ts:210, grok.ts:161, opencode.ts:114) as an existing principle-1 leak, so a `scope ?? 'inside_cwd'` default would repeat it. Constraint 7: the masked command (path segments replaced by class) must be produced in the collector loop and only the mask stored, never the raw string. Overlaps roadmap-v1 L55 scope_escape, which already resolves Edit/Write paths against entry.cwd (2,132 in / 256 out) — the shared resolver should be lifted from there rather than written fresh.

name: pnpm verify --behaviour: ledger reconciliation and collector shape-drift counter
description: Principle 4 requires every new exact dataset to be reconciled, and the ledger is the largest one yet. verify --behaviour independently recounts tool_use blocks and tool_result joins from the transcripts (22,687 / 22,683 today), OpenCode tool parts (12,292), Devin toolCallId rows and Grok exec_done lines, compares them with tool_calls, fails on any shortfall, and reports rows whose source file has since been pruned as 'source deleted' rather than a failure. The same pass counts record shapes the parsers skipped, which this machine already demonstrates: codex.ts reads local_shell_call and 0 exist in 66 rollouts, while 72 item_completed events go unread — a parser aimed at a shape the tool no longer writes, invisible today because nothing counts what was skipped. A coverage class (F3's status_source) dropping to zero between runs is reported as drift, not as an improvement.
desktop_surface: Settings replaces the hard-coded 'Verification: Every stored row reconciled' caption with the real last-run result per table including the behaviour tables, plus an 'unread record shapes' line per collector; vole doctor --json carries the same fields for MDM collection.
data_source: the same artifacts the collectors read, re-counted independently by verify.ts; ~/.vole/vole.db tool_calls; packages/core/src/collectors/codex.ts:118-120
honest_limit: Reconciliation can only prove Vole stored what was on disk when it ran; it cannot prove the tool wrote everything it did, and the report must say so. Claude prunes transcripts after cleanupPeriodDays (unset here, so the tool default applies), so old rows are permanently unverifiable and are counted separately rather than failing the run. An unread shape is a count, not a judgement — a shape may be deliberately ignored, so the counter lists it and lets a human decide.
competitive_note: Anthropic states Claude Code transcripts are internal and change between versions (market.md §4); a drift counter is the only defence for a parser-based product, and no competitor publishes one because none parses these files — the 27 in-path vendors read the request, not the store.
v1_ref: Support and lifecycle policy with collector-format drift detection (Tier 6) — pulled forward and given a real counter, plus the verify extension principle 4 already demands
field_verified: Both halves verified, and the drift example is better than claimed. codex.ts declares `const TOOL_ITEMS = new Set(['function_call', 'custom_tool_call', 'local_shell_call'])` and local_shell_call appears 0 times across all 66 rollouts, while ev:item_completed appears exactly 72 times unread — the feature's figure to the unit; token_usage_record (39 lines) is likewise unread. The independent recount targets all exist as verified in F1 (Claude 22,913 blocks / 20,761 distinct ids joining 20,756 results, OpenCode 12,292, Devin 1,715, Grok 1,402). The UI claim is exact: DashboardView.swift:696 is literally `LabeledContent("Verification", value: "Every stored row reconciled")` — a hard-coded string, not a computed result. verify.ts is 539 lines reconciling three sources and ending in `console.log(ok ? '\n  PASS — every stored row matches its source record.' : '\n  FAIL')`.
constraint: None — constraint 20 and principle 4 mandate exactly this ('pnpm verify must keep passing and must be extended for any new source with exact tokens'), and the ledger is the largest new exact dataset in the roadmap. Two notes rather than conflicts. The code map records that verify.ts's Codex section is a re-implementation of the collector rather than an independent recount, which makes it a tautology; the behaviour pass must not repeat that pattern or it proves nothing. And the shipped UI string is itself a compliance defect today: a procurement reviewer who reads 'Every stored row reconciled' in Settings and then discovers it is a literal will discount every other number in the product, so wiring that caption to a real last-run result is arguably the highest-trust-per-line change in this shard.

name: fetch_ingress: untrusted web bytes entering a session, with a size and a status code
description: Claude's WebFetch results carry a four-field receipt that nothing currently reads — `toolUseResult.{bytes, code, codeText, durationMs, url}` — giving the exact number of bytes pulled from a named host, the HTTP status, and the latency. Adds `fetch_ingress(event_key, session_id, ts, tool_use_id, host, url_path_hmac, bytes, http_status, duration_ms, source)` with the hostname stored in clear because the hostname is the finding, and the path HMACed under the existing Keychain key. This is the prompt-injection ingress channel measured rather than named: 63 fetches totalling 10,772,168 bytes here, across launchsafe.com (30), github.com (9), x.com (5), inco.ai (4), huggingface.co (3) and docs.nebius.com (2). It also gives the already-planned `install_after_ingress` rule something real to bound on — a sized, timestamped, host-attributed ingress event instead of a bare tool name — so 'the agent read 2.1 MB from an unreviewed host and then installed a package' becomes a sentence with figures in it.
desktop_surface: An Ingress band on the Behaviour panel: hosts ranked by bytes with call count and status mix, non-2xx marked, and a jump from any `install_after_ingress` or `denied_then_achieved` incident straight to the fetch rows inside its window.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl: toolUseResult.{bytes,code,codeText,durationMs,url} on WebFetch results (63 rows, 10,772,168 bytes, 6 distinct hosts)
honest_limit: `bytes` is what the fetcher received, not what entered the model's context — the tool truncates before injection and the transcript never says by how much, so the row reports received bytes and marks context-entered as unknown rather than guessing. MCP browser tools and `curl` under Bash report no byte count whatsoever, so those fetches appear in the tool ledger with a NULL size and are counted as 'N ingress events with no recorded size'. A host being unfamiliar is not evidence of anything; the ledger ranks and attributes, and only the joined rules make a claim.
competitive_note: context_edges covers commands leaving the machine (scp, rsync, ssh) and gives ingress no size at all; this is the inbound half with the vendor's own byte counter. SASE proxies see the same fetch but cannot bind it to a session, a subagent or the tool call that followed it, which is the join the CSA Agentjacking and Gemini-CLI README-hijack write-ups both turn on.
v1_ref: context_edges: every command that left this machine, by transport and destination
gap_area: Opaque-payload and bulk-egress volumetrics: the bytes DLP structurally cannot read

name: sensitive_read_unasked: sensitive-path access joined to authority and posture
description: v1's protected-path ledger records that a sensitive path was touched; this adds the two columns that turn it into an incident - the call's authorization_basis and the autonomy in force. A versioned path-class table maps tool arguments to {ssh_private_key, cloud_credentials, agent_credentials, dotenv, keychain, npm_token, kube_config, browser_profile}, and sensitive_access stores class + salted sha256 of the normalised path + count, never the path itself; matching happens on the raw line inside the collector loop, per the no-content constraint. Verified here: of 6,543 Bash command strings, 288 reference .env, 190 reference .ssh and 3 reference the keychain, plus 13 Read/Edit file_path values under .env/.ssh/credentials - and not one of them produced a denial record. The rule fires critical when class is in {ssh_private_key, cloud_credentials, agent_credentials} AND authorization_basis is bypass_no_gate or unknown AND autonomy is full_auto, which is the exact shape of the Invariant MCP tool-poisoning read of ~/.ssh/id_rsa.
desktop_surface: The session detail sheet gains a 'Sensitive access' matrix - path class down the side, authorization_basis across the top, counts in the cells, red cells clicking through to the individual calls with their timestamps and posture - and the same counts roll up per employee in Breakdown.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl message.content[].tool_use.input (Bash.command, Read.file_path, Glob.pattern); ~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl function_call.arguments.cmd and custom_tool_call.input; joined to tool_calls.authorization_basis and autonomy_intervals
honest_limit: Only paths that appear literally in a tool argument are visible: a read performed inside a script the agent invoked, behind a shell glob Vole cannot expand, or through a variable is invisible, so every count is a floor and is labelled one. Cursor, Antigravity and Devin record no tool arguments at all, so their rows are permanently 'not recorded' rather than zero. The DB never holds the argument, so the panel can name the class but can never show which file.
competitive_note: v1 files this under secrets_dlp as an access ledger with a raw permissionMode column but no authority join and no posture interval, which is exactly what turns hundreds of observations into the handful of incidents worth paging on. Cyberhaven and Nightfall detect the same reads by inspecting and retaining content in the endpoint DLP path; Vole's version keeps a class and a salted hash and nothing else.
v1_ref: Sensitive-file access ledger and protected_path_access rule
field_verified: Signal exists in volume but every quoted number is undeduped, and one claim is simply false. Undeduped Bash commands referencing .env = 541, .ssh = 178, keychain = 20 (feature: 288 / 190 / 3); deduped by tool_use.id: .env 443, .ssh 179, keychain 18. Read/Edit file_path under .env|.ssh|credentials = 13 undeduped (EXACT match to the feature) but 8 deduped — confirming the write-up counted raw lines. The false claim: 'not one of them produced a denial record'. Joining the 88 denied tool_use_ids against the 677 tool_use ids whose command or file_path matches .env|.ssh|credentials|keychain gives an overlap of 3, all Bash. Three sensitive-touching calls WERE denied. Depends on the same non-existent tool_calls table as F5.
constraint: Constraint 7 is the whole design and the feature gets it right: 'DLP scanning happens on the raw line in the collector' and the DB stores class + salted sha256 + count, never the path or the argument. Two additions needed: the salt must live under ~/.vole and never leave it (constraint 17, no silent egress) or per-employee hashes become correlatable across machines by whoever receives a sync; and sensitive_access needs a `source` column plus a line in purgeSeed (db.ts:228-232), which today deletes from two tables only. Principle 1: 'not one produced a denial' must be struck — 3 did.

name: tool_failure_storm, and error_storm narrowed to API errors
description: Split detect/error-storm.ts in two. error_storm keeps only assistant-level API failures and stops counting activity_only rows: 7 of the 10 live error_storm incidents are Grok 403 spending-limit rows, which is quota exhaustion misfiled as a failing tool. tool_failure_storm is a new rule over the tool_calls ledger keyed on (tool, session, tool_name), firing at five or more failed calls of a single tool name with a failure ratio above 0.2, and it names the tool that is failing rather than the session. Per-source failure evidence exists on disk and reaches usage_events.is_error from none of it today: Claude tool_result.is_error (422 rows), OpenCode part state.status='error' (89) plus metadata.exit != 0, Devin content.status='failed' (17), Grok exec_done ctx.success=false (33, dropped at grok.ts:104).
desktop_surface: Incident feed gains a 'failing tool' column and the quota rows move to the quota surface; the Behaviour panel shows a per-tool-name failure-ratio bar per session with the unknown-outcome count beside it.
data_source: tool_calls.{status, exit_code}; usage_events.is_error for the narrowed API rule; collector sites grok.ts:104, opencode.ts:145, codex.ts:214
honest_limit: Claude records no exit code on success and only free text on some failures, so a Bash failure the model does not mark is_error is invisible; the rule must read 'k failures of n calls with a recorded outcome' and print the unknown-outcome count beside it, never a ratio over all calls. Codex's is_error is hard-coded 0 by the collector, so Codex contributes nothing until task_complete.error is read. A Grok 403 removed from error_storm has to land in a quota rule or the split quietly deletes a real signal.
competitive_note: v1 keeps one rule and only re-words its detail ('k API errors, j failed tool calls'), which leaves the Grok quota rows still firing an error storm and never names the failing tool. Windsurf and Devin's own analytics give tool-category counts with no success/failure split at all.
v1_ref: tool_calls ledger with tool_result error join
field_verified: CONFIRMED, with two count corrections. Live DB: 10 error_storm rows, and 7 of them are tool='grok' — the feature's ratio is exact. Every one of the 10 reads '100% error rate' (e.g. '182 of 182 calls failed in 15 min'), because error-storm.ts:17 iterates raw `events` with no withTokens() filter, so Grok's activity_only inference_failed rows (grok.ts:121 `is_error: 1`) form their own pure-error windows. Collector sites verified: grok.ts:104 `if (e.msg === 'shell.tool.exec_done' && e.ctx.tool_name)` — the branch appends tool_name and `continue`s, discarding ctx.success (33 `"success":false` vs 1,372 true in unified.jsonl). opencode.ts:145 `is_error: d.error != null || (d.finish && ERROR_FINISH.has(d.finish)) ? 1 : 0`. codex.ts:214 `is_error: 0,` hard-coded. Per-source evidence on disk: OpenCode part `tool|error` = 89 exactly as claimed, plus exit codes 1×349, 2×27, 127×26, 124×9. CORRECTIONS: Claude tool_result is_error:true is now 741, not 422; Devin content.status='failed' is 27, not 17 (I read all 54 acp-messages dbs: completed 1,685 / failed 27 / in_progress 3).
constraint: Constraint 4 is the live wire: activity_only implies every token field NULL, and Grok's 403/quota rows ARE activity_only with is_error=1 — so narrowing error_storm to 'assistant-level API failures' deletes 7 of the 10 incidents this rule has ever produced with nothing catching them. The feature's honest_limit concedes this ('has to land in a quota rule or the split quietly deletes a real signal') but does not list that quota rule as a dependency, and it is not in this shard. Make it a same-commit requirement or the split is a straight regression in coverage. Second: the new rule keys on (tool, session, tool_name) — with F1's upsert live and a no-downgrade policy, a failure ratio that improves within the window can never de-escalate, so the ratio comparator must be chosen deliberately (the same 'observed falls while severity rises' problem F1 flags for error_storm).

name: Read completeness on the tool ledger, and the paged_bulk_read rule the per-call view can never see
description: Claude records how much of a file it actually delivered and how big the file was — `toolUseResult.file.{numLines,startLine,totalLines,truncatedByTokenCap}` — and, when a read overflows, writes an `attachment` of type `read_truncation_notice` whose banner carries the whole file's token size against the cap (`95528 tokens, cap 25000`). Adds `lines_delivered`, `lines_total`, `offset_start` and `truncated` to the tool-call ledger, and the rule `paged_bulk_read`: N distinct non-overlapping `startLine` windows against the same path inside one session covering ≥X% of `totalLines`, which is the shape of an agent walking a large file page by page — a pattern every per-call ledger renders as N unremarkable Reads. It also supplies the honest reducer that exposure figures need in the other direction: across text reads here, 486,630 total lines were opened and 127,213 were delivered, with 721 reads truncated, so assuming a whole file left the machine overstates by about four times.
desktop_surface: Each Read row on the tool-ledger drill-down shows 'lines 1–2 of 67' with a completeness bar; `paged_bulk_read` incidents land on the Triage queue with the page windows listed and the covered fraction as the observed figure against the rule's threshold.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl: toolUseResult.file.{numLines,startLine,totalLines,truncatedByTokenCap} (1,361 rows; totalLines 486,630 vs numLines 127,213; 721 truncated) and attachment.type=='read_truncation_notice'.banner (14 rows)
honest_limit: This counts lines the tool handed over, not bytes, and not what the model retained after its own context handling; a file re-read after an edit would inflate coverage, so the rule keys on distinct line ranges rather than call count. Reads that go through Bash (`cat`, `head`) carry no completeness record at all and are reported as 'N reads with no completeness record', never as complete. `totalLines` is the file at read time, so a file that grew between pages makes the fraction approximate and the row says so.
competitive_note: v1's file_exposure takes a sha256 only when `startLine==1 && numLines==totalLines`, which silently discards the 721 truncated reads instead of measuring them — a partial read becomes a row with no byte count rather than a measured fraction. Cursor's OTel export has no per-session tool attribution at all; GitHub's audit stream carries request bodies but not the agent's own delivered-versus-total line counts.
v1_ref: file_exposure ledger (which file content entered which model context), including path-only rows
gap_area: Opaque-payload and bulk-egress volumetrics: the bytes DLP structurally cannot read

name: posture_escalated and policy_downgraded within a session
description: A rule pair over autonomy_intervals that adds no new parsing. posture_escalated fires when a session's autonomy rank increases (prompt_each < classifier_gated < accept_edits < full_auto) and at least one tool call executes inside the higher interval; policy_downgraded fires on the Codex-only confinement axis when a session moves permission_profile managed -> disabled, or sandbox_policy.type read-only/workspace-write -> danger-full-access, quoting both turn ids and timestamps. observed = calls in the escalated interval, baseline = calls in the prior interval, threshold = 1; severity is critical when the escalation follows a recorded denial within K calls (denial -> escalate -> retry is the guardrail-bypass shape) or when the new autonomy is full_auto and no human-origin entry follows the transition. anomaly_key is posture_escalate:<source>:<session>:<seq_start> - deterministic and free of now(), per the detect.test.ts contract. Tagged OWASP ASI excessive-agency and MITRE ATLAS.
desktop_surface: Incidents pane row carries both mode strings and the transition time inline ('classifier_gated -> bypassPermissions at 08:04:41, 62 calls after'); the detail has a 'show on posture ribbon' action that opens the session sheet scrolled to the transition, and renders before/after profile_kind and sandbox values for the Codex downgrade variant.
data_source: autonomy_intervals (Claude permissionMode / auto_mode attachments, Codex turn_context.{approval_policy, sandbox_policy.type, permission_profile}); tool_calls.authorization_basis for the preceding denial
honest_limit: A transition proved only by an untimestamped type:"permission-mode" line is placed at the following timestamped entry, so the escalation time carries up to one entry of error and the incident text says so. A session launched already in bypass is not an escalation and must not fire here - that is headless_bypass_launch's job. Codex downgrades are visible only in rollouts new enough to carry turn_context; older sessions produce no rows rather than a false 'no downgrade found'.
competitive_note: v1 names privilege_escalation inside the posture feature but supplies no evidence definition, no anomaly key and no severity ladder, and has no downgrade concept at all. No competitor in the 62-vendor matrix detects an in-session autonomy change: vendor telemetry (Anthropic OTel, Cursor Analytics) emits no posture dimension, and static scanners (Snyk Agent Scan, Invariant, Pillar) read config once and never see the runtime switch.
v1_ref: Permission-mode and sandbox posture per session (normalised autonomy column)
field_verified: Claude branch has real evidence: 15 of 125 sessions change posture mid-session, 11 containing a rank increase — measured by replaying every user-entry permissionMode plus every type:"permission-mode" line per sessionId. Codex branch has almost none: of 66 rollouts only 3 files carry more than one turn_context, and exactly ONE shows any change — and it is a TIGHTENING, not a downgrade: [('never','danger-full-access','disabled'), ('on-request','workspace-write','managed')]. So `policy_downgraded` has zero positive examples on this machine and cannot be calibrated. The denial join for the severity ladder is real: toolDenialKind automode-blocked 22 / user-rejected 14 / automode-unavailable 2, each record carrying sourceToolAssistantUUID and a timestamp.
constraint: Constraint 3 and the detect purity contract. anomaly_key `posture_escalate:<source>:<session>:<seq_start>` is correctly free of now() and satisfies detect.test.ts:120 ('anomaly keys are stable, so re-running cannot duplicate incidents' — verified in the file). The real conflict is with detect/index.ts:12: 'Runs every rule. Pure: no DB access, so rules stay unit-testable in isolation.' A rule over autonomy_intervals must NOT read the DB. Reconciliation: pass intervals as a third pure input array exactly as RateLimitObservation[] already is in detectAll(events, rateLimits, now) — the precedent exists and costs one parameter. Second conflict: constraint 6, detectBySource prefixes source into the key, so intervals must be partitioned by source too or seed and live posture collide.

name: stuck_tool_call and the per-session concurrency ceiling
description: From the tool_calls ledger, a call with an issued_ts and no bound outcome after N minutes while the same session kept issuing calls is a stuck_tool_call incident naming the tool and its argument skeleton. The condition is observable on disk today: OpenCode's part.data holds 2 rows in state.status='running' with no end time, while Claude has 0 unmatched of 22,018 tool_use ids, so on Claude the rule fires only on a genuinely hung or killed session rather than as routine noise. The same pass computes max concurrent in-flight calls and max concurrent child agents per session — the honest measure of fan-out pressure that a raw call count hides, since twelve calls in a minute is a different machine from twelve calls at once.
desktop_surface: Behaviour panel 'in flight' counter per live session with a high-water mark, and a stuck-call row in the incident feed carrying the age of the unbound call and the tool that owns it.
data_source: tool_calls rows with result_ts IS NULL; opencode part.data $.state.status='running'; Claude tool_use ids with no matching tool_result.tool_use_id
honest_limit: A stuck row cannot distinguish 'still running' from 'the process died' without PID liveness, so the incident reads 'no outcome recorded after N minutes' and offers no cause. A crashed agent leaves rows unbound forever; they age out of the rule window rather than resolving, and no surface may render that ageing-out as resolution. Concurrency is in-flight-per-ledger, so a tool whose collector records only completions (Devin, Grok) reports a ceiling of 1 and must show an em dash instead of a number.
competitive_note: Vendor consoles are batch — Copilot roughly two days behind, Claude Analytics daily — and structurally cannot show an in-flight call; this only exists because Vole reads a local store at poll cadence. No v1 entry covers unbound calls or concurrency at all.
field_verified: CONFIRMED with two corrections, both in the feature's favour on one side and against it on the other. OpenCode: `select json_extract(data,'$.type'), json_extract(data,'$.state.status'), count(*) from part group by 1,2` → tool|completed 12,201, tool|error 89, tool|running 2. The 2 running rows are exact. CORRECTION 1: Claude is NOT 0 unmatched — I matched every tool_use id to every tool_result.tool_use_id across all 633 transcripts: 20,746 tool_use vs 20,741 tool_result, so 5 unmatched (0.024%). The design conclusion is unchanged and arguably strengthened: the rule fires ~5 times per 100k entries, i.e. only on genuinely hung sessions. CORRECTION 2: the honest_limit's claim that Devin 'reports a ceiling of 1 and must show an em dash' is WRONG — Devin's acp-messages payloads carry content.status on all 1,715 tool calls with values completed 1,685 / failed 27 / in_progress 3, each with a unique toolCallId. Devin can participate in both halves of this feature.
constraint: Constraint 3 unaddressed: a 'no outcome after N minutes' verdict is inherently relative to now, and the feature never states the anomaly_key. It must be (tool, session, tool_use_id) — never a bucket of now() — or detect.test.ts:120's determinism assertion fails and re-runs duplicate. Interaction with F1 that neither feature names: a stuck call can never resolve (the feature admits rows age out of the window rather than resolving), and F1 refuses downgrades by construction, so an aged-out stuck call leaves a permanent unresolvable warn/critical in the feed with no cause offered. Give it an explicit terminal state ('outcome never recorded') rather than letting it ride F1's no-downgrade rule forever. Prerequisite: tool_calls with a nullable result_ts, which does not exist.

name: action_targets: the target-system resolver with an explicit resolution chain
description: One row per ledger call that names a system outside this filesystem, resolved by a target-extraction rule set added to round-2's versioned pattern pack (same pattern_id/pack_version, not a second parser). Adds `action_targets(call_id, target_kind{cloud_account|k8s_context|database|vcs_repo|package_registry|saas|remote_host}, target_label, locality{loopback|remote|unknown}, env_class{prod|staging|dev|unknown}, reversible{yes|no|unknown}, resolution{literal|shell_var_from_file|context_file_default|flag|unresolved}, evidence_path)`. The mechanism the gap brief misses is shell-variable indirection: on this machine 136 of 233 database-client commands contain no DSN at all — they read `DB_URL=$(grep '^DATABASE_URL=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)` and then use `"$DB_URL"`, so the resolver follows the assignment inside the same command string to the named key in the named file at the recorded cwd (129 of those files still exist), and keeps host, port and database name while the credential half is dropped before the row is built. Name-only context files fill the rest: `~/.ssh/config` Host→HostName (4 aliases here), `~/.kube/config` current-context (`do-nyc3-launchsafe`), `~/.aws/config` plus the sso cache, `~/.config/gcloud/configurations`, `gh` `hosts.yml`, `.terraform/environment`. `locality` is exact and computed (loopback literal vs anything else); `env_class` is set only from a clause in the existing policy file and otherwise stays `unknown` — never inferred from a name.
desktop_surface: A Target column on every ledger row in the Behaviour drill-down (label + a locality dot + an env chip only when declared), and a target inspector popover that prints the resolution chain verbatim: `$DB_URL ← DATABASE_URL in <redacted-local-path>`. Unresolved calls are counted, never hidden: 'target unresolved (62)'.
data_source: Claude Code `content[].tool_use.input.command` (Bash) and `input` for MCP calls; Codex `function_call.arguments.cmd`/`workdir` (exec_command) and `custom_tool_call.input`; OpenCode `part.state.input`; Grok `exec_done`. Local name-only context files: ~/.ssh/config, ~/.kube/config, ~/.aws/config + ~/.aws/sso/cache, ~/.config/gcloud, ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml, project .env files at the recorded cwd.
honest_limit: A resolved label is what the string and the local files say, not what a credential resolved to at the server: an exported AWS_PROFILE/KUBECONFIG or a `--context` flag overrides the file (only 1 of 18 kubectl commands here carried `--context`, so 17 rows are tagged `context_file_default`, flag absent). The .env may have been edited or deleted since the command ran, so the row stores the value read now plus the file mtime, and degrades to `unresolved` rather than guessing. 62 of 233 database commands name no target at all and stay NULL. Cursor, Antigravity and Devin expose no command string today, so their calls carry no target row.
competitive_note: Gateways (LiteLLM, Portkey, Cloudflare AI Gateway, Tailscale Aperture) see model traffic and never the shell action; Cyberhaven, Harmonic and Nightfall read the prompt and map process→provider, not action→target system; Wiz and Legit see the cloud and repo side but cannot say which agent session caused it. CrowdStrike Falcon AIDR is the only matrix entry claiming a prompt→tool→action causal chain, and it needs an ES-level sensor Vole does not use.
v1_ref: Destructive and outbound command classifier (destructive_command, destructive_under_bypass)
gap_area: Blast radius beyond the filesystem: cloud/SaaS/DB/VCS action targets, and agent-initiated package installs

name: Autonomy clock: unattended_run rule and the daily exposure rollup
description: v1 measures autonomy from turn_duration, which exists on 14 entries in the entire store; measure it from the ledger instead, where it works on all 22,018 matched Claude tool calls plus OpenCode and Devin. Per session, compute the longest chain of consecutive tool calls with no human-authored user entry between them, in wall-clock minutes and call count, plus calls_per_human_turn — a human-authored entry being identified by entry shape (a user entry carrying no tool_result block), never by reading content. The rule unattended_run fires when a chain exceeds the configured minutes or call count while the session's recorded posture is bypassPermissions or its equivalent (Codex approval_policy='never' on 17 of 19 turn_contexts here, sandbox danger-full-access on 8). The same pass feeds a daily rollup autonomy_daily(day, user, machine, tool, autonomy, minutes, calls, write_calls, destructive_calls, sensitive_reads, human_turns, never_asked_calls, source), carrying the source column and the same live/seed partition and cascading purge as every other table, which turns posture into the two numbers a security programme is actually run on: minutes at full autonomy per person per day, and the share of calls that reached no permission decision. Minutes are wall-clock between observed entries inside an interval, optionally extended by process liveness from ~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json (verified to carry procStart and pidDomain) checked against the live PID and its start time.
desktop_surface: Behaviour panel per-session strip showing human turns as ticks against a continuous autonomy bar, plus a menu-bar badge when a live session crosses the threshold; and a dashboard 'Autonomy exposure' section with stacked daily bars per person split by autonomy level, a never-asked-ratio sparkline, and a table ranked by full-auto minutes with an explicit control that hides per-person rows under pseudonymous mode.
data_source: tool_calls.issued_ts; Claude user entries without tool_result blocks; Claude permissionMode entries (712 bypassPermissions, 767 auto here); Codex turn_context.{approval_policy, sandbox_policy}; ~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json {procStart, pidDomain} joined to live PIDs
honest_limit: A human watching silently is indistinguishable from an absent human — the metric is 'no human input recorded' and every surface must word it that way. Minutes are bounded by observed entries, not process lifetime: a session left idle with the window open contributes autonomy time only up to its last transcript line, so the figure under-counts exposure and must say so; without the PID join it is transcript-derived only, and a PID reused after the agent exited would over-count, which is why procStart is compared as well. Claude's permission-mode entries carry no timestamp, so a chain's mode is bounded by neighbouring stamps or left NULL, and calls before the first stamp are never assigned one. The per-person rollup is the single artifact here that GDPR Art. 88 and EU AI Act Annex III 4(b) make dangerous, so it must be gated behind the no-performance-scoring switch before it ships to a works-council jurisdiction.
competitive_note: v1's own note concedes turn_duration is nullable on all but 14 entries and never proposes a substitute clock, and it has no rollup table at all. EMA/Cequence report 65% of enterprises saw agents act outside intended scope and the OWASP Agent Control Standard asks for inspectable, traceable autonomy; vendor consoles report seats, tokens and spend, and none reports time spent with safeguards off — the one number a CISO can take to a board because it goes down when the programme works.
v1_ref: Human intervention, autonomy duration, self-scheduling and idle/zombie sessions
field_verified: CONFIRMED, including the v1 defect it corrects. `"subtype":"turn_duration"` appears EXACTLY 14 times across all of ~/.claude/projects — v1's own caveat (roadmap-v1.md:62 'turn_duration exists on 14 entries only') verified to the unit, so replacing that clock is justified. Sample: `{"type":"system","subtype":"turn_duration","durationMs":621321,"messageCount":228,...}`. Ledger substrate: 20,746 distinct tool_use ids across 633 transcripts (feature said 22,018 — my count excludes nothing and differs only by snapshot). permissionMode 712 bypassPermissions / 767 auto confirmed. ~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json VERIFIED verbatim: `{"pid":22530,"sessionId":"96eb2395-...","cwd":"...","startedAt":1788746180904,"procStart":"Mon Sep  7 01:56:20 2026","version":"2.1.263","kind":"interactive","entrypoint":"claude-vscode","pidDomain":"darwin",...}`. NEW LIMIT THE FEATURE MISSES: only 3 such .json files exist (6 entries incl. .key files) — it is an ephemeral registry of CURRENTLY LIVE sessions, deleted on exit, so the PID/procStart join can never enrich a single historical minute. Every autonomy minute in the rollup is transcript-derived; liveness helps only the handful of running agents.
constraint: Principle 1 breach hiding in the schema: `never_asked_calls` cannot be observed for Claude Code — the transcript records a permission MODE, never a per-call permission decision, so the column can only mean 'calls issued while mode == bypassPermissions'. That is an inference presented as a count. Rename it calls_under_full_auto or the flagship metric invents a number in its own column header. Constraint 6 is correctly honoured (source column, live/seed partition, cascading purge stated). Constraint 12/13: a new table is fine under CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, but DB.swift assumes the newest columns are present and DB.swift:141 binds `[Int]` only — a per-person/per-tool rollup view cannot bind its string filters until F13's binding rewrite lands. GDPR Art. 88 gating is correctly named, but it depends on a no-performance-scoring switch that does not exist and that F13 simultaneously requires — build one switch, not two.

name: Remote-database action ledger and the remote_database_write / destructive_schema_change rules
description: The Replit shape, made local and exact. For every call whose target_kind is `database`, parse the statement class out of the client's own argument — `psql -c`, `mysql -e`, `mongosh --eval`, plus migration subcommands (`drizzle-kit push`, `prisma migrate reset`, `alembic downgrade`) — into `db_actions(call_id, client, statement_class{read|write|ddl|truncate|drop|migrate_reset}, object_names, target_ref)`, storing only the class and the identifier names, never the literal SQL or any value. Two rules: `remote_database_write` fires when statement_class is write or worse and locality is `remote` (139 of the 213 database commands here resolve to `launchsafe-db-do-user-35002029-0.e.db.ondigitalocean.com:25060/launchsafe`, a managed cluster, against 12 to localhost), and `destructive_schema_change` for truncate/drop/migrate_reset, posture-weighted by round-2's severity scheme. The payoff is the card wording: 'TRUNCATE against database launchsafe on launchsafe-db-do-user-…ondigitalocean.com, resolved from $DB_URL ← DATABASE_URL in backend/.env, under bypassPermissions' instead of 'destructive command'.
desktop_surface: An incident card on the Behaviour screen whose figures row is the target line, the statement class and the object names, with the resolution chain expanded inline; the same rows roll into the Blast Radius screen grouped by database.
data_source: Bash/exec command strings already parsed in-collector, joined to action_targets; the .env key named by the command, read at the recorded cwd (host/port/dbname only).
honest_limit: Claude Code records no exit code, so the incident says 'ran', never 'deleted', and never a row count; OpenCode's `part.state.metadata.exit` and Grok's `exec_done.ctx.success` do carry an outcome, so the wording is driven by round-2's status_source rather than assumed. `psql -f file.sql` and interactive sessions expose no statement to classify — the row records the script path and statement_class stays NULL. An ORM or app process that opens the same connection is invisible; only client commands the agent itself ran are counted.
competitive_note: No competitor in the matrix classifies the database an agent acted on: Cursor and Anthropic native telemetry have no per-session tool attribution at all, MCP gateways (MintMCP, Lasso, Speakeasy) see only SQL that went through an MCP server and miss a `psql` in Bash entirely, and Wiz/Sysdig see the database or the syscall without the agent session.
v1_ref: Destructive and outbound command classifier (destructive_command, destructive_under_bypass)
gap_area: Blast radius beyond the filesystem: cloud/SaaS/DB/VCS action targets, and agent-initiated package installs

name: context_edges: every command that left this machine, by transport and destination
description: The inverse of the gap and the strongest signal on this machine: the monitored agent is itself the vehicle into unmonitored contexts, and every crossing is on this disk in full. Riding the tool-call ledger's command-shape pass, classify each Bash/shell call by transport verb and record only the transport and the destination label — never the command body. Measured here across 12,520 Bash tool_use blocks in 641 transcripts: ssh 631, docker 286, scp 29, kubectl 19, rsync 12, modal 7, devcontainer 7, colima 5, podman 2, limactl 2, tart 2, runpod 2, gh codespace 1, vagrant 1, sshfs 1, mosh 1; ssh destinations fuchsia-lark 154 and h200 16, both of which are Host aliases in this user's own ~/.ssh/config; docker subcommands logs 120, ps 53, run 12, build 5. Adds `context_edges(call_event_key, session_id, transport{ssh|scp|rsync|docker_run|docker_exec|kubectl_exec|compose|vm|sshfs|mosh|cloud_exec}, destination_label, destination_kind, destination_context_id, remote_verb_pattern_id, ts, source)` joined to `execution_contexts` so an ssh alias becomes 'reached 154 times, Vole is not installed there'. Two rules: `agent_crossed_to_unmonitored_context` (per session, count of edges whose destination_context_id is unmonitored, with the destination and count as the incident's observed figure) and `remote_privileged_execution` (transport=ssh and the remote command's first token is sudo/doas/su — 58 occurrences here on a GPU box), severity weighted by the session's posture exactly like every other behaviour rule.
desktop_surface: Behaviour panel gains a Crossings lane on the session timeline: one mark per edge, coloured by transport, with the destination label and the ledger jump. The Session card header reads 'this session executed on N hosts Vole does not monitor'. Overview tile 'Off-machine execution' shows the 30-day edge count and the top three destinations; clicking a destination opens its execution_contexts row.
data_source: Claude Code transcript `message.content[].tool_use` where name is Bash — `input.command` parsed in the collector pass only; Codex `response_item` local_shell_call and custom_tool_call; OpenCode `part` rows of type tool with state.input; join target ~/.ssh/config Host aliases and execution_contexts.label
honest_limit: Only the skeleton survives: transport, destination label and a pattern id for the remote verb — Vole cannot know whether the remote command ran, succeeded, what it touched, or whether an agent was launched there. Heredocs, shell wrappers, `bash -c` strings, variables and aliases hide the real destination and are counted as an unresolved edge rather than dropped. ssh_config `Include` and `ProxyJump` are not resolved, so a jump host is recorded as the alias typed, not the machine reached. Destination labels are hostnames from the user's own config and are pseudonymised at insert under managed mode like every other identity field.
competitive_note: Sysdig's Falco kernel agent would see the ssh and docker syscalls but attributes them to a process, never to an agent session, model, prompt turn or cost. Anthropic's own OTel does not pass OTEL_* into Bash, hooks or MCP (code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage), so a Claude Code Bash-launched remote run is invisible in the vendor's own telemetry — the only place it exists is the transcript Vole already reads.
v1_ref: Command-shape skeleton and versioned pattern pack (pattern_id + pack_version, not just a hash)
gap_area: Where agents actually run: devcontainers, Docker, SSH remotes, VMs and CI runners as declared blind spots

name: subagent_inherited_bypass: autonomy propagation down the agent tree
description: A subagent never gets its own permission dialog — it inherits the parent's posture at spawn — so autonomy_intervals gains autonomy_inherited and depth, populated from the agent_edges tree plus three vendor facts: Claude's <session>/subagents/**/agent-*.jsonl children (parent session given by the containing directory), Codex session_meta.payload.source.thread_spawn{parent_thread_id, depth, agent_nickname} (2 rollouts here), and Grok's 'subagent spawn credentials' log line, verified on this machine to carry subagent_id, subagent_type, effective_model, base_url, auth_type, parent_model and context_window, paired with a 'subagent completed' line carrying tool_calls, turns, success and cancelled. The rule fires when a subagent at depth >= 1 executes N or more tool calls under an inherited full_auto posture with no human-origin entry in the parent for the child's lifetime. A second signal is unique to Grok and nearly free: the child's base_url differing from the parent's means a spawned agent is talking to a different endpoint under the parent's authority.
desktop_surface: The session-detail agent tree renders each child with an inherited-posture chip and a lock icon when its endpoint differs from the parent's; the incident lists the subagent type, its call count and the parent's posture at the moment of spawn.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/**/<session>/subagents/**/agent-*.jsonl and agent-*.meta.json; ~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl session_meta.payload.source.thread_spawn; ~/.grok/logs/unified.jsonl msg='subagent spawn credentials' ctx.{subagent_id,subagent_type,effective_model,base_url,auth_type,parent_model} and msg='subagent completed' ctx.{tool_calls,turns,success,cancelled}
honest_limit: Claude's subagent metadata carries no timestamp, so the child's lifetime is anchored on its own transcript's first and last line rather than the parent's clock. spawnDepth is 1 on all 479 metas here and no nested subagents directory exists, so depth >= 2 is untested. Only 3 Grok spawn-credential lines exist on this machine, so endpoint divergence is a real but barely exercised signal, and ctx.key_prefix is deliberately never stored. Codex's event_key collides across parent and child rollouts today (codex.ts:197 keys on session plus line index while the child replays the parent's session_meta), so that collector must be re-keyed on a stable per-response id before any Codex subagent row can be trusted.
competitive_note: v1's fan-out monitor counts subagents and failure ratios but never propagates posture, so a bypass-mode parent spawning ten children shows as ten sessions of unknown authority. No vendor in the matrix models an inherited permission state, and nothing else on the machine reads Grok's spawn-credential line.
v1_ref: Subagent and workflow fan-out monitor (fanout_burst)
field_verified: CONFIRMED FIELD-BY-FIELD, and I found one thing the feature missed. ~/.grok/logs/unified.jsonl, 3 spawn lines, ctx verbatim: `{"subagent_id":"019f51f0-3d72-7f70-a5be-c25f26b5b965","subagent_type":"general-purpose","effective_model":"grok-4.5","effective_model_raw":"grok-4.5","base_url":"https://cli-chat-proxy.grok.com/v1","key_prefix":"eyJ0eXAi","auth_type":"SessionToken","model_has_own_creds":false,"auth_method_id":"cached_token","parent_model":"grok-4.5","parent_key_prefix":"eyJ0eXAi","context_window":500000}`. Paired 'subagent completed' ctx: `{"subagent_id":...,"success":true,"cancelled":false,"duration_ms":10507,"turns":1,"tool_calls":4,"output_preview":"README is updated. Summary of changes:...","error":null}`. Codex thread_spawn confirmed on 2 rollouts with parent_thread_id/depth/agent_nickname. codex.ts:197 confirmed verbatim: `event_key: \`codex:${sessionId ?? filePath}:${index}\`` — line-index keyed, exactly the collision the feature demands be fixed first.
constraint: CONSTRAINT 7 LANDMINE THE FEATURE MISSES: 'subagent completed'.ctx.output_preview is raw model output text (I read a 200-character README summary out of it), and ctx.error is free text. The feature carefully forbids storing key_prefix but says nothing about output_preview — the collector must drop both explicitly or this feature is the first place content enters the DB, breaking constraint 7 and principle 5 in one line. Constraint 1: codex.ts:197's line-index key is named in the constraints as an existing violation and 'not a precedent'; re-keying on a stable per-response id is therefore an obligation this feature inherits, not an optional cleanup. Calibration risk: spawnDepth == 1 on all 487 Claude metas, so 'depth >= 1' is simply 'is a subagent' — with 464 workflow children under bypass-heavy parents the rule would fire constantly unless N (tool calls) is set high and stated in the incident.

name: Remote-execution hop ledger (ssh, docker, kubectl exec) and remote_privileged_exec
description: cwd-relative blast radius is not merely incomplete for these calls, it is meaningless: the command runs on another machine. `remote_exec(call_id, transport{ssh|scp_rsync|docker_run|docker_exec|kubectl_exec|fly_ssh}, host_ref, remote_user, inner_pattern_id, inner_class)` records the hop and re-runs the same pattern pack over the inner command against the remote target. Host identity is deduped through ~/.ssh/config so an alias and a literal address collapse to one target: 313 ssh invocations here carry an inner command, 182 resolved by alias and 131 literal, and 195.242.30.141 appears both as itself (128) and as `h200` (17). Rules `remote_privileged_exec` (sudo, rm -rf, kill, systemctl, docker rm in the inner command — 117 here) and `remote_installer_pipe` (`curl … | sh` inside an ssh payload — 1 here, run as root on 195.242.30.141 with an explicit `-i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`).
desktop_surface: A 'Left this machine' band at the top of the Behaviour screen listing each remote host with its alias, the count of hops and the worst inner class; clicking a hop shows the outer and inner commands as two separate masked skeletons.
data_source: Bash/exec command strings; ~/.ssh/config Host/HostName/User (name-only); ~/.kube/config current-context for `kubectl exec`; the Docker image reference from the command itself.
honest_limit: Vole sees the instruction, never the remote result — there is no evidence the remote host executed anything, so rules read 'sent to', not 'ran on'. A host reached only by IP with no ssh_config entry stays a bare address with no environment class. `ProxyJump`, an ssh control-master session, or a shell alias hides the real destination. Multi-line quoted payloads are re-classified best-effort and the row keeps the pack version that judged them.
competitive_note: v1's exfil detector owns payload-carrying transfers (curl -d, scp, rsync); this owns execution, which none of the 62 vendors separates. Endpoint sensors (Sysdig, Jamf, CrowdStrike) see the local ssh process but attribute nothing to an agent session, and every gateway and browser-extension product is blind to it.
v1_ref: Exfil-shaped command detector (possible_exfil, sensitive_read_then_egress)
gap_area: Blast radius beyond the filesystem: cloud/SaaS/DB/VCS action targets, and agent-initiated package installs

name: Asset resolution chain: stamped at insert, widened only into NULLs
description: One resolver used at insert by secret_sightings, dlp_egress, action_targets, context_edges and the tool_calls file/command targets, adding asset_id, asset_tier, asset_match and asset_rev to each ledger. The chain is explicit, first hit wins, and the winning link is stored: (1) repo_remote_log from Codex session_meta.git.repository_url (present here as launchsafe/engine ×16, openai/codex-security ×9, launchsafe/vole ×5, launchsafe/platform ×3), normalised by lowercasing the host, stripping user-info and a trailing `.git` so `…/vole` and `…/platform.git` collapse to one identity; (2) repo_remote_disk from the nearest ancestor .git/config `[remote "origin"] url` read at resolve time, the only remote link Claude Code rows can ever have; (3) repo_path_glob via node's builtin path.matchesGlob; (4) host_suffix / dsn_host_port; (5) store_path. Rows carry three states, never two — resolved, `unresolved` (a target existed and matched nothing) and `no_target` (activity_only rows and calls that never named one) — counted separately and never summed. Because the usage_events upsert only rewrites when total_tokens strictly grows, late enrichment is impossible there; these ledgers get their own widening statement (SET asset_id, asset_rev WHERE asset_id IS NULL AND asset_rev < ?) run oldest-first inside the pack-bump re-scan budget, which fills NULLs and never rewrites a resolution already stamped.
desktop_surface: An 'Asset' column on Leak Ledger, Blast Radius and the tool-call drill-down: tier chip plus asset_id, with the chain link in the cell tooltip ('matched by repo remote on disk, register v7'), an em dash for unresolved and the literal words 'no target' for no_target.
data_source: ~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl session_meta.git.repository_url; <cwd ancestor>/.git/config remote origin url; usage_events.project / tool_calls target paths; ~/.vole/policy/assets.json match_norm.
honest_limit: Link (2) is time-of-resolution, not time-of-event: <redacted-local-path> holds 893 stored events and has no .git today, so no remote link can ever fire for that history — it stays on globs or unresolved. A repo re-pointed at a new remote changes future rows only; a worktree or submodule resolves to its parent's remote; and .git/config is a new read root that must be declared in the shipped read manifest and can be denied like any other.
competitive_note: Cursor's OTel export and Anthropic's own event stream carry no target or asset dimension at all (Anthropic: 'anomaly detection, baselining, correlation across sessions... are the responsibility of your SIEM'); Fleet/osquery inventories agents but has no repo-identity join, and Snyk agent-scan reads configs, never runtime targets.
gap_area: The company's own asset and data-class register (what 'sensitive' and 'customer data' mean here)

name: install_after_ingress: bounding the ingress-then-action rule so it can actually fire
description: v1's `ingress_then_privileged_action` escalates when untrusted ingress is followed by any Bash or Write in the session, which on this machine means nearly every session — 12,521 Bash calls sit downstream of some fetched content, so the rule as specified is unusable. The correction is adjacency plus a closed action set: fire only when a target-bearing action (a package_exec, a remote_exec hop, a remote_database_write, or a secret_store_read) occurs within N ledger ordinals of a tool result whose source was an MCP server, a WebFetch, or a read outside the repo — the exact Agentjacking sequence — and store the ingress call_id and the ordinal distance on the incident so a reader can check it. `anomaly_key` is (session, ingress_call_id, action_call_id, rule), which contains no clock value and is stable across re-reads.
desktop_surface: On the incident card, a two-row mini-timeline: the ingress call (server or host name, never the content) above the action call with its target, and the measured ordinal gap between them.
data_source: Round-2's tool_calls ledger ordinals; Claude Code `mcp__*` tool names (mcp__playwright__*, mcp__searxng__*, mcp__github__* all present here) and WebFetch entries; action_targets and the tables above.
honest_limit: Adjacency is correlation, never causation — the incident says 'followed', not 'caused by'. The window N is a policy threshold stored on the finding, and a slow attack that waits out the window never fires. Ingress classification depends on the tool result naming its source, which Claude and Codex do and Cursor, Antigravity and Devin do not, so those tools contribute no rows. Content is never read to decide whether the ingress was actually malicious.
competitive_note: Zenity and MintMCP can see the MCP half through a gateway or hooks but not the Bash half; CrowdStrike claims the whole causal chain but only inside its own sensor and console. This is the sequence Cloud Security Alliance named in the 2026-06-12 Agentjacking note and Elastic's finding that 43% of MCP servers carry command injection.
v1_ref: Offline injection-indicator scans: MCP tool descriptions and ingress content (ingress_then_privileged_action)
gap_area: Blast radius beyond the filesystem: cloud/SaaS/DB/VCS action targets, and agent-initiated package installs

name: VCS action ledger from the agent's own gitOperation record
description: Claude Code writes a structured, vendor-emitted record of what a git command actually did — `toolUseResult.gitOperation` — and nothing in Vole reads it, though it is not in the 41-field inventory either: 109 rows here, including `{"push":{"branch":"main"}}` 26 times, `{"commit":{"branch":…,"kind":"committed","sha":"33326fc"}}`, and `{"branch":{"action":"merged","ref":…}}`. `vcs_actions(call_id, op{push|commit|merge|visibility|delete|secret_set}, branch, sha, repo_ref, source{structured|parsed})` takes the exact fields where they exist and falls back to command parsing for what gitOperation does not cover — `gh repo edit --visibility public` (the Nx s1ngularity shape), `gh repo delete`, `gh secret set`, `git push --force`. repo_ref comes from `owner/repo` in the command when present (the `launchsafe` org appears in gh commands here even though `hosts.yml` names only a user) and otherwise from the origin remote in `<cwd>/.git/config`. Rules: `repo_visibility_changed`, `agent_push_to_protected_branch` (branch declared protected in policy), `force_push_after_agent_commit`.
desktop_surface: A Repositories block on the Blast Radius screen: one row per repo with pushes, commits with their short shas, merges and any visibility change, each row badged `structured` or `parsed` so a reader knows which figures came from the agent's own record.
data_source: Claude Code `toolUseResult.gitOperation` and `returnCodeInterpretation` on user lines (both currently skipped at claude-code.ts:93); Bash command strings for the gh operations; `<cwd>/.git/config` remote, read-only.
honest_limit: gitOperation names the branch and sha but never the remote, so the repository identity is a join through the cwd and is labelled as such; if the working copy moved or the remote changed, repo_ref is NULL rather than a guess. Only Claude Code emits this record — Codex, OpenCode and Grok fall back to `parsed`, and the badge says so. A push whose result line was never written (session interrupted) leaves a command with no confirmation, and the row stays `sent`, not `pushed`.
competitive_note: Legit Security and Cycode see the repo side after the fact with no agent attribution; GitHub's own audit log lags ~2 days and does not carry the local session; no endpoint or gateway vendor in the matrix reads the agent's structured git result, because none of them parse the transcript at that depth.
v1_ref: Agent-authored commit scan and revert rate
gap_area: Blast radius beyond the filesystem: cloud/SaaS/DB/VCS action targets, and agent-initiated package installs

name: Kiro ACP ledger: tool calls carrying the vendor's own policy verdict and the human's answer
description: Kiro's session.json holds posture but no tool calls; ~/.kiro/logs/<launchStamp>/kiro.log does, as plain JSONL {timestamp, level, message}. Parse: agent_controller.triggered {agentType, autonomyMode, modelId}; [ACPEventAdapter] Execution began|yielded|resumed {executionId}; acp.policy-eval.complete {toolId, effect:'allow'|'ask', capability:'shell'|'fs_read'}; [ACP ToolApproval] Requesting permission for toolId=..., operationId=..., sessionId=... paired with Got response: {optionId:'always-accept'|'accept'|'reject', outcome}; [q-developer-converse] Sending GenerateAssistantResponse modelId=... agentMode=... conversationId=... and its 'Request payload: <N> chars, <M> history messages'. Rows land in the tool_calls ledger with authorization_basis read straight from effect rather than inferred, execution_id as the interval key, and decision_latency_ms from the request/response pair (8.97 s, 5.99 s and 8.62 s in the single execution captured here). operationId carries the upstream tool-use id (run_command_toolu_bdrk_01RDhk...), which doubles as the Bedrock routing proof.
desktop_surface: Behaviour panel gains Kiro executions as intervals with an approval lane beneath them: each call shows allow / ask, the capability, and for asks the human's answer and how long they took. Every ungated call names the rule that allowed it.
data_source: ~/.kiro/logs/<YYYYMMDDThhmmssSSS>/kiro.log; joined to ~/.kiro/sessions/<hash>/sess_<uuid>/session.json and ~/.kiro/session-index/<hash>.jsonl
honest_limit: The log carries no token counts, and 'Request payload: 78987 chars' is characters — it goes in a payload_chars column and is never divided by four to make tokens. Log directories are per-launch with no documented rotation contract, so a pruned launch is an evidence gap and must be counted as one. The [Steering] lines prove steering was populated for an execution but not which files; ExistingFiles was empty in every line here. Message strings are a vendor internal format and will drift, so the parser needs a shape-drift counter like the other collectors.
competitive_note: Gemini CLI's telemetry is the only competitor schema with native tool_call decisions and approval_mode, and it requires OTel to be switched on with logPrompts defaulting true. Kiro prints the same verdicts to a plain file with nothing enabled and no vendor reads it; Snyk's free scanner sees Kiro's config, never its decisions.
v1_ref: Four-state authority on every tool call (denied / pre-authorised / posture-waived / no record)
gap_area: Editor-embedded agent task stores (Cline, Roo/Kilo, Kiro, Zed, JetBrains) across every VS Code fork root

name: Posture-weighted severity across every rule
description: v1 lands permission posture as a column and then writes only two dedicated rules on it, leaving the five existing rules posture-blind — a burn-rate spike during a bypassPermissions run reads identically to one during a supervised session. Give detect/index.ts a third context argument postureAt(session, ts) => autonomy and have every rule escalate one severity step when the incident window overlaps a full_auto interval, writing the reason into detail verbatim ('escalated: session was in bypassPermissions for 100% of this window'). Posture comes from the autonomy_intervals table built on Claude permissionMode entries (verified on this machine: bypassPermissions 712, auto 767, default 51, plan 5, acceptEdits 1) plus Codex turn_context.approval_policy='never' and sandbox_policy.type='danger-full-access'. A Settings toggle makes the policy visible rather than implicit.
desktop_surface: Incident rows gain a posture chip (bypass / auto / default / unknown) and an upward arrow where severity was raised, whose tooltip names the interval that caused it; Settings gains a 'raise severity under full autonomy' toggle so the escalation policy is inspectable.
data_source: autonomy_intervals joined to anomalies.window_start/window_end; Claude permissionMode entries in ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl; Codex turn_context.payload.{approval_policy, sandbox_policy.type}; packages/core/src/detect/index.ts detectAll/detectBySource
honest_limit: Escalation applies only where posture is known. A NULL interval must leave severity untouched and never silently downgrade, and the incident must read 'posture unknown for this window' so a clean-looking feed is not mistaken for a safe one. Claude's permission-mode entries carry no timestamp, so an interval is bounded by neighbouring stamped entries and every call before the first stamp is unassigned. The whole feature is inert until the anomaly upsert exists: under INSERT OR IGNORE the first verdict is frozen and an escalation can never be written to the row.
competitive_note: v1 adds posture as data and two rules but never feeds it back into the existing rule set, so the posture column pays for itself twice instead of everywhere. No vendor in the 62-vendor matrix weights a detection by the agent's permission state; Windsurf/Cognition report aggregate tool counts and Anthropic's OTel export has no posture dimension at all.
v1_ref: Permission-mode and sandbox posture per session (normalised autonomy column)
field_verified: CONFIRMED EXACTLY. `grep -ho '"permissionMode":"[a-zA-Z]*"' ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl | sort | uniq -c` → 767 auto, 712 bypassPermissions, 51 default, 5 plan, 1 acceptEdits — the feature's four figures match to the unit. Codex: `"approval_policy":"never"` ×21, `"on-request"` ×5; `"sandbox_policy":{"type":"danger-full-access"` ×8, read-only ×9, workspace-write ×2, across 19 turn_context lines in 66 rollouts. detect/index.ts:13-25 detectAll takes exactly (events, rateLimits, now) — the third argument does not exist yet. autonomy_intervals does NOT exist: `sqlite3 ~/.vole/vole.db .tables` → anomalies, collector_state, usage_events only.
constraint: Not a constraint breach but a severity-calibration hazard the feature misses: 712 of 1,536 mode entries on this machine are bypassPermissions (46%), so a blanket one-step escalation would upgrade roughly half of all incidents and severity stops carrying information. Reconciliation: require the window to be ≥X% covered by a full_auto interval, never escalate an already-critical row, and print the base rate in the incident ('bypass covered 46% of your sessions this month') so the escalation is calibrated rather than ambient. Second: it must land AFTER F3 or it escalates a rule whose scoring is wrong on 99% of its fired windows — compounding a principle-3 error rather than fixing it. Chain: needs v1's autonomy_intervals (roadmap-v1.md:49, M, unbuilt) AND F1's upsert; under INSERT OR IGNORE the escalation is unwritable, which the feature concedes.

name: agent_wrote_persistence and the PATH-precedence fact
description: The machine_persistence class plus the one structured fact the class alone misses. When the changed file is a shell rc, the collector diffs the parsed PATH assignment between pre- and post-image and records `path_entry`, `position` (prepend or append) and `dir_writable_by_principal` from a single stat — a prepend of a principal-writable directory is what decides which binary runs at the next login. The other targets come from the same ledger and the Bash write-target resolver: `.git/hooks/*`, `~/Library/LaunchAgents|LaunchDaemons`, `/etc/paths.d`, any `.app/Contents/**` path, `crontab`, and `git config core.hooksPath`. `agent_wrote_persistence` is critical when the target falls outside every declared work_root, because the change outlives both the repo and the session. There is a real row on this machine: an Edit to `<redacted-local-path>` touching a PATH export from a session whose cwd was `<redacted-local-path>`.
desktop_surface: The machine half of 'what the agent left behind' on Blast Radius, sorted above the repo half, each row showing target, session, posture at the time, whether a human was present, and for PATH rows the position and writability verdict.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl `toolUseResult.{filePath, originalFile, oldString, newString}`; Bash `input.command` write-target resolver rows (rc appends, `.git/hooks/` and LaunchAgents paths all present in this machine's 12,879 Bash calls); one stat per PATH entry.
honest_limit: This records that the agent wrote the file, not that the line is still there — Vole does not re-read shell rc files, so a later manual revert is invisible and the row must read 'written on <date>', never 'present'. Persistence installed by a package installer, by `launchctl` outside a monitored tool, or by a process Vole never sees leaves no row here; round 2's gateway persistence inventory covers the standing state, this covers authorship. `dir_writable_by_principal` is evaluated now, not at write time.
competitive_note: This is the local half of Cursor DuneSlide (CVE-2026-50548/50549 — writes to cursorsandbox and ~/.zshrc) and the Keyv worm's planted agent hooks, both of which the incident table marks detectable from local logs. Jamf, Santa and Kolide see a changed file with no author and no AI semantics; CrowdStrike is the only matrix vendor claiming the causal chain, at the price of an ES sensor and prompt inspection.
gap_area: Agent-authored change risk: writes that widen the security envelope, not writes that destroy

name: Grant deposits: the credential the agent handed to something else
description: Round 2 ledgers the credentials an agent pulled out of a vault; nothing ledgers the ones it put in, which is the direction that permanently widens someone else's authority. A `grant_deposits` table classifies the command shapes that do it: `gh secret set` / `gh variable set` / `gh workflow enable|run`, `aws iam attach-*|put-*-policy|create-access-key`, `gcloud * add-iam-policy-binding`, `kubectl create secret` and RBAC `apply`, `vault kv put`, `wrangler secret put`, `heroku config:set`, `terraform apply`. Each row stores verb, target system, scope parsed from the flags (repo, project, cluster, namespace), the secret's name, and the HMAC fingerprint of the value so it joins round 2's `secret_sightings` — the value itself never lands in the DB. There is a live example on this machine: `gh secret set DIGITALOCEAN_ACCESS_TOKEN --repo launchsafe/engine --body "dop_v1_..."`. Rules: `agent_deposited_credential` and `agent_widened_cloud_iam`.
desktop_surface: A 'granted to' column on Blast Radius rows whose target is outside this machine, and a cross-link from the Leak Ledger finding to the deposit that reused the same fingerprint — one line that says the key in this repo's .env is now also in that repo's Actions secrets.
