data_source: Bash/exec `input.command` strings already in the tool-call ledger (Claude `content[].tool_use.input.command`, Codex `exec_command.arguments.cmd`, OpenCode `part` tool `bash` `state.input.command`); fingerprint join to secret_sightings.
honest_limit: Parsed from the command string, so it records an attempt to deposit, not confirmation: Claude gives an outcome enum from stdout/stderr and interruption but no exit code on success, so `outcome` stays `unknown` rather than `ok`. A credential passed by file, env var or stdin has no name to record and `secret_name` is NULL. CLI flag grammars drift by version, so unrecognised shapes go to an explicitly counted `unclassified` bucket rather than being dropped.
competitive_note: Secret scanners (TruffleHog, GitGuardian, GitHub Secret Protection) hunt secrets at rest in code and by design ignore a secret correctly placed in a CI secret store — exactly the transfer of authority a reviewer needs to see. No vendor in the 62-row matrix ledgers deposits; MCP gateways see only what routes through them, and `gh` does not.
gap_area: Agent-authored change risk: writes that widen the security envelope, not writes that destroy

name: sandbox_claim_violated and network_claim_violated (Codex declared vs observed)
description: Codex is the only agent here that writes a machine-readable confinement claim per turn - turn_context.payload.sandbox_policy.type, permission_profile.file_system.entries[].access, permission_profile.network and workspace_roots (present in 14 rollout files here) - and the collector discards every one of them today (codex.ts:113-116). The rule falsifies the claim against the observed call: sandbox_claim_violated fires when function_call.arguments.workdir (present on 254 lines here, optional per call, falling back to workspace_roots[0]) or a path resolved out of exec_command.cmd falls outside workspace_roots while sandbox_policy.type is 'read-only' or 'workspace-write'; network_claim_violated fires when permission_profile.network='restricted' and the command carries a network verb aimed at a non-loopback host. Verified distribution on this machine: sandbox read-only 9 / workspace-write 2 / danger-full-access 8, permission_profile managed 14 / disabled 12, approval_policy never 21 / on-request 5.
desktop_surface: The Posture tab gains a per-session 'declared vs observed' strip: declared sandbox and network policy on the left, counts of conforming and non-conforming calls on the right, and each non-conforming call listed with its resolved scope and the turn id that declared the claim.
data_source: ~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl turn_context.payload.{sandbox_policy.type, permission_profile.file_system.entries, permission_profile.network, workspace_roots}; function_call.arguments.{cmd, workdir}; custom_tool_call.input; function_call_output.output for the outcome enum
honest_limit: Codex's own sandbox may well have blocked the call: Vole sees the attempt and, from function_call_output, whether it errored, but never the sandbox's reason, so the incident reads 'attempted outside the declared root' plus the outcome enum and never 'the sandbox failed'. turn_context appears in only a couple of dozen rows across all rollouts here because it is a newer field, so older sessions have no claim to compare against and are skipped rather than assumed permissive. workdir is optional per call; when it is absent the comparison falls back to the session's workspace_roots and the row is marked lower confidence. Path extraction from a shell string is textual and marks unresolvable targets rather than guessing.
competitive_note: roadmap-v1 mentions Codex approval/sandbox fields only as inputs to a posture column, never as a claim to be falsified. OpenAI's own Codex telemetry reports usage, not sandbox conformance, and no endpoint vendor in the 62-row matrix parses turn_context. It is the local analogue of the Cursor DuneSlide sandbox escape (CVE-2026-50548/9, 2026-07-02), where writes landed outside the declared working directory.
field_verified: The DECLARED side is verified beyond what the feature claims; the OBSERVED side barely exists. Declared, quoted verbatim: {"type":"managed","file_system":{"type":"restricted","entries":[{"path":{"type":"special","value":{"kind":"root"}},"access":"read"},{"path":{"type":"path","path":"<redacted-local-path>"},"access":"write"},{"path":{"type":"special","value":{"kind":"tmpdir"}},"access":"write"}]},"network":"restricted"} — permission_profile.file_system.entries[].access and permission_profile.network exist exactly as specified, and the entries list is RICHER than workspace_roots (which is a bare ["<redacted-local-path>"]), so the rule should key on entries, not roots. Observed side collapses: `arguments.workdir` appears on exactly ONE real call in all 66 rollouts (the 684 'workdir' substring hits are tool-schema description text), total Codex tool calls are 38 (32 custom_tool_call 'exec' + 6 function_call), and the exec input is not JSON at all but JavaScript source: "input": "text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:\"cat <redacted-local-path>\"}))". There are no exec_command_begin/exec_command_end event_msg types on this machine (event_msg is agent_message 72,680 / task_started 5,830 / task_complete 5,827 / user_message 5,822 / token_count 118 / item_completed 72). turn_context is 19 rows in 16 of 66 files, not 'present in 14 rollout files' with 26 policy values.
constraint: Principle 1 above all. With one usable workdir and cmd strings embedded in JS, any 'non-conforming calls' count would be an extraction artifact dressed as a measurement. Reconciliation: the rule emits a count only for calls whose path resolved cleanly, and reports 'N of M calls unresolvable' beside it — never folding unresolved into conforming. Constraint 7: permission_profile entries contain absolute paths including user directories, so the stored form is a class or salted hash, not the path list. codex.ts:113-116 does discard these fields today, so the extension point is real.

name: cross_scope_read_then_publish rule
description: The GitHub MCP toxic-agent flow in rule form: within one session, a read-class call whose target resolves to scope A is followed within a bounded window by a publish-class call to a different scope B. Scopes come from MCP tool arguments (owner, repo, url, path, host) and from filesystem paths resolved relative to cwd, reusing the destructive rule's path resolver; publish-class tool names come from a versioned list covering mcp__*__create_pull_request, create_or_update_file, push_files, add_issue_comment and mcp__*__send*, plus Bash `git push`, `gh pr create` and `gh issue comment`. The incident stores the two tool names, the two salted scope hashes, the elapsed seconds and the posture - never the arguments. Severity is critical when the read scope is private-shaped (a path outside cwd, or a repo the session never wrote to) and the publish scope is public-shaped.
desktop_surface: Incidents detail draws a two-node arrow - read scope, elapsed time, publish scope - above the list of calls in between, with that window's segment of the posture ribbon rendered underneath.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl tool_use.name and tool_use.input for mcp__* tools (the local MCP census includes github push_files, create_pull_request and add_issue_comment); ~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl custom_tool_call.input and function_call.arguments.cmd; Bash command strings
honest_limit: Scope resolution is only as good as the server's argument names: an MCP server that calls its repository argument something else resolves to scope 'unknown' and the rule does not fire, so this under-reports by design rather than guessing. Whether a repository is actually private is not knowable locally without a network call, so 'private-shaped' is a labelled heuristic derived from prior session behaviour. Exfiltration through any channel that is not a tool call is invisible.
competitive_note: v1's detector is aimed at shell shapes (curl -d/-F/-T, base64|curl, scp, nc); this is the MCP-to-MCP variant behind the 2025-05-26 GitHub MCP toxic flow (private repo -> public PR, Invariant Labs), which was enabled by 'Always Allow' and is therefore inseparable from the authority state. Zenity does taint tracking for this class but as a SaaS that ingests MCP content; Vole matches on argument-derived scope hashes only and stores neither.
v1_ref: Exfil-shaped command detector (possible_exfil, sensitive_read_then_egress)
field_verified: The Bash arm is well-sourced; the MCP arm's stated premise is false. Deduped publish-class Bash commands: git push 128, gh api 108, gh pr create 19, gh issue comment 1, plus scp 25 and nc 7. But the claim 'the local MCP census includes github push_files, create_pull_request and add_issue_comment' does not survive: the full census of 46 distinct MCP tools actually invoked contains only READ-class github calls — search_code 13, get_file_contents 10, issue_read 5, list_commits 4, pull_request_read 3, get_release_by_tag 3, list_releases 3, search_issues 2, search_repositories 1 — and ZERO invocations of push_files, create_or_update_file, create_pull_request or add_issue_comment. Those tools are offered by the server; they have never been called here. The heaviest MCP traffic is playwright (browser_run_code_unsafe 268, browser_evaluate 320) and searxng (web_url_read 466), which are themselves egress-shaped and go unmentioned.
constraint: Principle 1 and constraint 17. 'private-shaped' derived from prior session behaviour is an inference presented as a scope property; it must render as a labelled heuristic with its basis quoted, and it must never trigger a network call to check repo visibility (constraint 17 forbids silent egress, and UpdateChecker.swift:27 is already flagged as the existing violation — do not add a second). Constraint 7: scope hashes only, never owner/repo/url values.

name: Shadow MCP: servers called but present in no local config
description: Set-difference between the servers the agent actually called and the servers any local config declares. Left side: distinct `mcp__<server>__` prefixes from the tool_calls ledger — playwright 1,994, searxng 548, Claude_Browser 298, github 48, context7 31, ui 13, ccd 2. Right side: `posture_mcp_servers` identities from `~/.claude.json` (four here: searxng, playwright, context7, github), `.mcp.json`, Codex config.toml, opencode.jsonc, Cursor. Servers on the left with no identity on the right — Claude_Browser, ui, ccd here — are cloud or dynamic connectors that a config-file inventory structurally cannot see, and `claudeAiMcpEverConnected` independently names three more with no local endpoint at all. Rule `mcp_server_unregistered` writes one incident per server with its call count and first-seen date.
desktop_surface: Supply Chain → MCP splits into two lists, 'Configured' and 'Observed only (no local config)', the second badged amber with call counts; the menu-bar panel surfaces the first unregistered server seen in the last 24h.
data_source: tool_calls / usage_events.tools LIKE 'mcp\_\_%'; ~/.claude.json mcpServers and claudeAiMcpEverConnected; posture_mcp_servers.
honest_limit: A server reached through the vendor's own proxy leaves no command, no URL, no transport and no version locally — Vole can name it and count its calls and nothing more; the endpoint fields are NULL, never guessed. The inverse is equally bounded: 'configured but unused' means 'no call observed on this machine in range', not 'unused by this employee'. Counts inherit the tools-column truncation bug and are lower bounds.
competitive_note: v1 Tier 3 defines 'unused' (configured, never called) but not the inverse, which is the OWASP MCP Top 10 MCP09 shadow-MCP case. Gateway vendors (Lasso, MintMCP, Speakeasy, Bifrost) see only the servers routed through them and openly admit the rest is shadow AI.
v1_ref: MCP server inventory, trust posture, usage diff and pin/sign rules
field_verified: Both sides verified, and the gap is much larger than claimed. Right side: ~/.claude.json mcpServers = 4 global (searxng, playwright, context7, github) plus exactly one project-scoped server across all 23 project entries (`ui-skills`); `find ~/Developer -maxdepth 3 -name .mcp.json` returns nothing. Left side (raw transcripts): observed-but-unregistered = Claude_Browser 626, ccd_session_mgmt 366, scheduled-tasks 208, ccd_directory 98, claude-in-chrome 52, claude_ai_Google_Drive/Gmail/Google_Calendar 24 each, claude_ai_Cortellis_Regulatory_Intelligence 13, plugin_supabase_supabase 11, claude_ai_Cortellis_CMC 9, plugin_chrome-devtools-mcp_chrome-devtools 8, claude_ai_Synthesize_Bio 8, claude_ai_Synapse_org 8. The thesis holds emphatically; the named trio ('Claude_Browser, ui, ccd') is wrong on two of three names.
constraint: The adversarial finding is a false-positive cliff, not a constraint breach. Most of that unregistered set is NOT shadow: ccd_session_mgmt/ccd_directory/scheduled-tasks/claude-in-chrome/Claude_Browser read as Claude Code's own bundled servers, and the plugin_* entries are supplied by ~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json plus settings.json `enabledPlugins` (ponytail@ponytail here — verified present). A naive set-difference fires `mcp_server_unregistered` on thirteen servers, most of them the vendor's own features — a demo that cries wolf. Reconciliation: subtract a shipped first-party built-in list AND the plugin inventory (roadmap-v1 L101) before firing, and label the residue 'observed, not registered locally', never malicious. Dependencies: posture_mcp_servers does not exist (v1 L93 defines it) and tool_calls does not exist — this is gated on two other items, so not S.

name: Offered-tool-surface ledger (what the model was actually handed)
description: Config says which servers are registered; the transcript says which tools reached the model. A posture_tool_surface table stores one row per (session, ts, kind, name, action) from three Claude attachment types re-counted today: deferred_tools_delta (761) carrying addedNames/addedLines/removedNames/readdedNames plus pendingMcpServers[], agent_listing_delta (129) carrying addedTypes/addedLines, and skill_listing (608) carrying the full skill roster. That answers 'which tools existed in this session's context at the moment of the incident', which no config inventory can. The rule tool_appeared_unconfigured fires when a name enters the surface whose server prefix appears in no local config and no observed registration.
desktop_surface: Session detail gains a 'tool surface' strip: a timeline of tools added and removed during the session, with names not traceable to a config file marked unconfigured; Supply Chain → MCP shows configured-but-never-offered servers as 'pending', and an incident's detail names the tools that were on offer when it fired.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl attachment.type in {deferred_tools_delta, agent_listing_delta, skill_listing}
honest_limit: Names only — the ledger records that a tool was offered, never its schema or description, so it cannot support tool-poisoning analysis. pendingMcpServers means 'registered, not yet connected at this point in the session', which is not the same as failed; a server that never connects looks identical to one that connects after the last delta. Only Claude Code emits these deltas; for every other tool the strip is 'not recorded'.
competitive_note: Gemini CLI's OTel schema carries mcp_server_name and tool_type, but Claude Code's OTel collapses MCP names to 'custom'/'mcp_tool' (market.md §4), so the transcript is the only place the real names survive locally; Zenity and Snyk inventory MCP config, not what the model was handed mid-session.
v1_ref: System-prompt and injected-context census (Tier 3), which hashes these attachments for drift but builds no per-session tool-availability ledger
field_verified: All three attachment types exist with the exact field names claimed. deferred_tools_delta: 785 (claim 761, one day of growth), verbatim sample carries `addedNames`, `addedLines`, `removedNames`, `readdedNames` and `"pendingMcpServers": ["context7", "github", "playwright", "searxng"]`. agent_listing_delta: 129 exactly, keys present on all 129 rows are type/addedTypes/addedLines/removedTypes/isInitial/showConcurrencyNote — so the claimed addedTypes and addedLines are real, plus two the feature did not know about. skill_listing: 620 (claim 608). Also present and adjacent: mcp_instructions_delta 466.
constraint: One hard conflict with constraint 7, hiding inside a field name. deferred_tools_delta.addedLines is just names, but agent_listing_delta.addedLines is full prose — verbatim from this machine: `"- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming"`. The description says the table stores addedLines while the honest_limit says 'names only'; those cannot both be true. Reconciliation: store addedTypes/addedNames plus a SHA-256 of the lines blob (which is all the drift rule needs anyway), never the lines themselves. Second, smaller point: v1's system-prompt census (Tier 3) already hashes these same attachments plus mcp_instructions_delta for drift, so this must be built as a join onto that table rather than a second reader of the same lines — two parsers over one artifact is how the two features silently disagree.

name: MCP registration sweep keyed on endpoint identity, not server name
description: One posture_mcp_servers(source, config_path, client, server_name, mcp_identity, transport, command, argv, url, cwd, enabled, env_key_names, first_seen, last_seen) table covering every MCP client on the machine, keyed on mcp_identity = sha256 over the normalised endpoint (transport, resolved command, argv array, cwd, url and the sorted KEY NAMES of env/headers) and never on the display name the user chose. Clients swept: ~/.claude.json global mcpServers and projects[*].mcpServers, repo .mcp.json, ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json (a client Vole has no collector for at all), ~/.codex/config.toml [mcp_servers.*], ~/.cursor/mcp.json, ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json (present but empty here), Kiro ~/.kiro, Zed settings, Cline/Roo globalStorage, VS Code mcp.json, opencode.jsonc. Two drift rules: mcp_endpoint_changed when the same (config_path, server_name) resolves to a new mcp_identity - the MCPoison shape, where the approved name survives and the command underneath is swapped - and mcp_name_reused when one identity appears under two names. Verified live: Codex registers node_repl at /Applications/ChatGPT.app/Contents/Resources/cua_node/bin/node_repl with 14 env keys including NODE_REPL_TRUSTED_CODE_PATHS, plus computer-use with the relative command './Codex Computer Use.app/Contents/SharedSupport/.../SkyComputerUseClient' and cwd '.'.
desktop_surface: Supply Chain > MCP: one row per identity with a transport glyph, the command or URL, enabled state, the list of client config files that registered it, and first/last seen; a red identity-changed badge opens a drill-down showing the old and new identity hashes side by side with their two timestamps.
data_source: ~/.claude.json mcpServers and projects[*].mcpServers; repo .mcp.json; ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json; ~/.codex/config.toml [mcp_servers.*]; ~/.cursor/mcp.json; ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json; opencode.jsonc; VS Code / Zed / Kiro / Cline globalStorage config files.
honest_limit: An `npx -y <pkg>` identity is stable while the package contents change on every run - the hash proves the registration did not change, never that the code did not. Relative commands resolve differently per cwd, so their identity is recorded as-written and flagged unresolvable. Env and header VALUES are never read, so a server authenticating with a bearer token shows the key name and nothing else, and a remote HTTP server's actual behaviour is entirely unobservable from its endpoint. Servers registered only through a vendor cloud connector have no local endpoint and never appear here. Config discovery on its own is commodity - Snyk's free agent-scan covers the same clients - so this table only earns its place joined to observed calls.
competitive_note: v1 stores command and binary hash but never states the identity key and scopes its rules to the server name - the exact field MCPoison (CVE-2025-54136) leaves untouched - and its client list (Claude, Codex, opencode, Cursor) omits Claude Desktop, Gemini, Kiro, Zed, Cline/Roo and VS Code, precisely the clients an employee installs without asking. Cyberhaven, Nightfall, Zenity, Lasso, MintMCP and Speakeasy all publish MCP inventories keyed on server name; the gateway vendors only ever see servers routed through them.
v1_ref: MCP server inventory, trust posture, usage diff and pin/sign rules
field_verified: Verified, with a coverage correction. `~/.claude.json` global mcpServers holds exactly 4: searxng (`npx -y mcp-searxng`, env SEARXNG_URL), playwright (`npx -y @playwright/mcp@latest`), context7 (`npx -y @upstash/context7-mcp`), github (`type: http`, `url: https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/`, headers `Authorization: Bearer gho_...` — a live token in the file). `~/.codex/config.toml` `[mcp_servers.node_repl]` command `/Applications/ChatGPT.app/Contents/Resources/cua_node/bin/node_repl` with 15 env keys (not 14) including `NODE_REPL_TRUSTED_CODE_PATHS = "<redacted-local-path>:/Applications/ChatGPT.app/..."`, and `[mcp_servers.computer-use]` `command = "./Codex Computer Use.app/.../SkyComputerUseClient"`, `cwd = "."`, `enabled = false` — exactly the relative-command case. COVERAGE CORRECTION: of the 11 named clients, 8 yield nothing here — `~/.cursor/mcp.json` does not exist; `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json` is 0 bytes; no `.mcp.json` exists anywhere under ~/Developer or ~/Desktop; no Zed/Cline/Roo globalStorage matches; and `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json` exists but its top-level keys are only `['coworkUserFilesPath','preferences']` — `mcpServers` is absent (null). Only 1 project of 23 in ~/.claude.json has a non-empty mcpServers (`<redacted-local-path>` -> ['ui-skills']); enabledMcpjsonServers is empty on all 21 that carry the key.
constraint: C7 (the DB holds no content; credentials must never be stored or held beyond the collector loop) — the github registration's Authorization value is a live `gho_` token sitting in the parse path. Reconciliation: the normaliser must project to key names before the object leaves the parse function, and the value must never reach a note, an error string, or a thrown exception message (C11 aborts the whole batch on a bad bind, and a stack trace carrying the header is the leak). C6: posture_mcp_servers must carry a source column and be covered by purgeSeed. C1/C3: mcp_identity is the idempotency key and must be a pure function of the endpoint — no now(), no file mtime.

name: Vendor lever cards: each tool's own permission config, observed value beside the hardened one
description: Instead of reinventing process control for tools with no hook seam, read each tool's native lever and show the literal config line to change, with a copy button; Vole writes nothing (SECURITY.md: writes only under ~/.vole). Real values on this machine: opencode.jsonc has permission {edit:'allow', bash:'allow', webfetch:'allow', external_directory:'allow'} — all four wide open; ~/.grok/config.toml has yolo=false and permission_mode='auto'; ~/.codex/config.toml has notify=[...] but no approval_policy and no sandbox_mode key at all, so those rows must render 'not set — tool default applies' rather than a guessed default; ~/.claude/settings.json carries permissions.allow (long Bash allowlist), skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt and remoteControlAtStartup. Add a tool_levers table (tool, lever_key, config_path, observed_value, recommended_value, file_sha256, first_seen, last_seen) keyed idempotently on (tool, lever_key, config_path) so a lever loosening between polls is drift, not a new row.
desktop_surface: A 'Harden this tool' card on the incident drill-down showing only the levers relevant to the rule that fired, and a Settings > Levers matrix: one row per tool per lever with observed value, recommended value, copy button, and a drift badge when the value changed since first seen. Tools with no readable permission config render 'no lever exposed', never a blank that reads as safe.
data_source: ~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc permission block; ~/.grok/config.toml yolo, permission_mode; ~/.codex/config.toml approval_policy, sandbox_mode, notify; ~/.claude/settings.json permissions, skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt, remoteControlAtStartup; per-project .claude/settings.local.json and repo-level opencode.jsonc
honest_limit: A config file proves what is written, not what runs: a project-level config, a CLI flag, an env var or an MDM-managed profile can override it and Vole sees none of those at the process level, so a card can say 'hardened' about a session that is not. Keys absent from the file are rendered 'not set', never filled in with the vendor's default. Vole never edits these files, so every card is advice until a human pastes the line — and there is no confirmation the paste happened beyond the next poll's re-read. Cursor, Devin and Antigravity expose no readable permission config here at all.
competitive_note: v1's adapter maps PIDs by argv, lsof cwd and recency and then SIGSTOPs the inferred match — one wrong signal against a developer's session ends the pilot, and market.md's positioning is explicitly 'coexist with CrowdStrike/Zscaler, do not compete on sensors'. Snyk Agent Scan / Invariant already does config discovery across Claude, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode and Antigravity, so this is table stakes rather than a differentiator, but it is the honest form of control for tools where Vole has no seam.
v1_ref: Cross-tool control adapters (Codex, OpenCode, Grok)
field_verified: Every named value is real, quoted from this machine. ~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc: "permission": {"edit": "allow", "bash": "allow", "webfetch": "allow", "external_directory": "allow"} — all four wide open, exactly as claimed. ~/.grok/config.toml: `yolo = false` and `permission_mode = "auto"`, both under the [ui] table (not top-level — matters for any parser). ~/.codex/config.toml: `notify = [...]` present; grep confirms NO approval_policy and NO sandbox_mode key, so 'not set — tool default applies' is the correct render. ~/.claude/settings.json: `"skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt": true`, `"remoteControlAtStartup": false`, and a 9-entry permissions.allow Bash allowlist — all three confirmed. TWO UPGRADES the feature misses, both verified. (1) Codex records the EFFECTIVE policy per turn in the rollout the collector already parses: in ~/.codex/sessions/2026/09/06/rollout-2026-09-06T22-24-34-01a07a53.jsonl I counted 3 turns of "approval_policy":"never" and 4 of "on-request", plus "sandbox_policy":{"type":"danger-full-access"} and "workspace-write" — one session flipping between full-access and workspace-write mid-run. code-map.md:119 lists exactly these as ignored-but-present. That is observed enforcement state, not advice, and it closes the feature's own honest limit for Codex. (2) Claude Code does the same: grepping this session's own transcript ~/.claude/projects/-Users-shiva-Developer-vole/c1641660-*.jsonl gives "permissionMode":"auto" x1 and "permissionMode":"bypassPermissions" x14, and code-map.md:112 confirms a whole `permission-mode` line type (bypassPermissions) is ignored today. Live proof of the file-vs-runtime gap: settings.json says nothing about bypass, while `ps` shows the running process as `claude ... --permission-mode auto --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions`. NEGATIVE result, so the card must not overclaim: OpenCode's runtime signal is empty here — its `permission` table exists (cols id, project_id, action, resource, time_created, time_updated) with COUNT(*)=0, and session.permission is NULL on all 5 most recent sessions, so for OpenCode the config file genuinely is the only lever.
constraint: #7 (no content, no credentials) is the sharp one and the feature walks straight into it: ~/.codex/config.toml contains `[shell_environment_policy.set] ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN = "litellm-899D6018-..."` in plaintext, and opencode.jsonc has apiKey "{file:~/.config/opencode/secrets/qwen38-h200-key}". A generic observed_value column over 'each tool's config' will store a live token on someone's machine. Reconcile by making observed_value an allowlist of named lever keys with enum-ish values only (allow|ask|deny|never|on-request|true|false|not-set); anything off the list is counted, never copied, and file_sha256 covers change detection. #14 (SEA: zero runtime deps, node: builtins only, no runtime file reads beyond pricing override and sources) — Node has no TOML parser and JSON.parse dies on a real .jsonc; adding a parser dep breaks a package.json that today has devDependencies only (esbuild, postject, @types/node). Reconcile the lazy way: regex the fixed lever-key list out of the TOML, strip // and /* */ before JSON.parse for the jsonc, and for Codex skip config.toml entirely in favour of the turn_context fields the collector already parses. Config files also become new source paths, which the paths.ts + VOLE_* env-override pattern must cover. #1/#6/#13 as usual: key tool_levers on (tool, lever_key, config_path) with no mtime in the key, carry a source column, port the query twice.

name: content_packs registry: verified offline load with an unremovable builtin floor
description: Adds `content_packs(kind TEXT PRIMARY KEY, version, built_at, source, ring, sha256, signed_by, entry_count, installed_at, load_state)`, written by the collector once per poll from `/Library/Application Support/Vole/packs/<kind>.json` plus a detached `<kind>.json.sig`, verified with `crypto.verify(null, bytes, spki, sig)` against an Ed25519 SPKI pinned in the SEA — confirmed working on this machine under the bundled node v26.7 with `node:crypto` alone and a 60-char base64 SPKI key, so no native module and no dynamic require. Loading reuses `pricing.ts` `loadPricing()`'s exact merge shape (builtin object spread first, pack on top, malformed input silently ignored), which makes the builtin pack an unremovable floor: a tampered, unsigned, missing or group-writable pack degrades to shipped content rather than to nothing, recorded in `load_state` ∈ builtin|pack|rejected_signature|rejected_perms|malformed. A file that is not root-owned and 0644-or-stricter is rejected on `fs.statSync` before parse. This deliberately widens the SEA constraint "no runtime file reads except the pricing override and sources" to a third read of one fixed directory; that widening belongs in DECISIONS.md, not smuggled in.
desktop_surface: Settings → Content: one row per pack kind with version, built date, age in days, ring, signer fingerprint and a load_state chip; a rejected pack shows the literal reason and states that shipped content is still running. About shows the pinned key fingerprint so a support call can confirm which binary is trusting what.
data_source: New: /Library/Application Support/Vole/packs/<kind>.json and <kind>.json.sig (root-owned, MDM-delivered). Existing precedent: packages/core/src/data/pricing.json frozen into the SEA by scripts/build-sea.mjs, and the ~/.vole/pricing.json override at paths.ts:21. Ownership/mode via node:fs statSync; signature via node:crypto.
honest_limit: A signature proves the pack came from whoever holds the key, not that its content is correct or complete. Anyone who can write /Library can also replace the app, so this is tamper-evidence for non-root users and drift-evidence for MDM, never a defence against root. On an unmanaged Mac — this one reports `MDM enrollment: No` — there is no admin-owned channel at all and every kind resolves to builtin; the screen says that rather than showing an empty table.
competitive_note: Every gateway and EDR in the 62-vendor matrix updates detection content from its own cloud on a continuous cadence (CrowdStrike Falcon Guardian, 2026-09-01); none ships an offline channel because none needs one. Vole's constraint puts it with Fleet/osquery and Santa, where rules arrive by MDM — the differentiator is reporting its own content age instead of implying freshness.
v1_ref: Policy-as-code file with local enforcement, drift report and vole_policy check
gap_area: Detection-content lifecycle: how packs, CVE floors and allowlists reach the fleet offline, age, and re-score history

name: Suppression register: turn a detector off centrally, keep counting what it hid
description: v1's policy.json lists `suppressions` with no accounting, which makes "0 findings" indistinguishable from "0 reported" — unacceptable in a product whose whole claim is that a number is never invented. A suppression entry `{kind, entry_id, reason (required), set_by, expires_at?, mode}` ships in an admin_authored pack: `mode=mute_report` still evaluates the detector and increments `suppressed_counts(day, kind, entry_id, n)` while writing no finding and sending no notification, whereas `mode=mute_scan` skips the work entirely and writes NULL — never 0 — into that counter. Every aggregate that could read as clean renders the suppressed count beside it. Expiry is advisory by design: Vole stops honouring the entry at `expires_at`, and an MDM that keeps pushing the pack simply re-applies it, which is the admin's decision, visible in the register.
desktop_surface: Policy screen gains a Suppressions table (entry, reason, set_by, expires, hits hidden in range); every zero-finding figure on Data Exposure and the Behaviour board carries a "+N suppressed" affordance that opens it, and a mute_scan entry renders "— not evaluated" rather than a count.
data_source: suppressions block of the admin pack under /Library/Application Support/Vole/packs; counters incremented in the same collector pass that evaluates the detector, so no second scan is needed.
honest_limit: The counter counts matches, not true positives: a suppression hiding a real leak looks identical to one hiding noise, and the count is the only evidence either way. mute_scan cannot be counted at all by construction, which is why it renders as unknown rather than zero.
competitive_note: Gitleaks and Betterleaks let a rule be disabled in config with no accounting, and enterprise DLP consoles (Nightfall, Proofpoint) show nothing about what a disabled detector would have caught. Counting the suppressed matches is the works-council-defensible version and the only thing that makes a zero meaningful.
v1_ref: Policy-as-code file with local enforcement, drift report and vole_policy check
gap_area: Detection-content lifecycle: how packs, CVE floors and allowlists reach the fleet offline, age, and re-score history

name: Pricing as a pack kind, and the user override that must lose in managed mode
description: `~/.vole/pricing.json` (paths.ts:21, `$VOLE_PRICING`) is today unsigned, user-writable, unversioned and read once at import in `loadPricing()`, and `repriceUnpriced` (db.ts:199) rewrites historical `cost_usd` in place — so on a managed laptop a developer can change their own showback and nothing anywhere records that they did. Pricing becomes content_pack kind `pricing` with precedence managed_pack > user override > builtin; the resolved revision is stamped into `cost_basis` at insert as `pricing_rev`; in managed mode a user override loads only when the admin pack sets `allow_user_pricing`, otherwise it is recorded as `load_state=override_ignored` with its sha256 so the attempt is evidence rather than silence. Repricing writes a `reprice_runs(from_rev, to_rev, rows, ts)` row instead of mutating silently, and any total spanning two revisions is labelled mixed-rev rather than restated.
desktop_surface: Costs screen footer names the pricing revision behind every total and shows a "mixed pricing revision" chip when the range spans a bump; Settings → Content lists the pricing pack like any other kind, including an ignored user override with its checksum.
data_source: packages/core/src/data/pricing.json (builtin, inlined into the SEA at build); ~/.vole/pricing.json or $VOLE_PRICING (absent on this machine, so builtin is what runs today); /Library/Application Support/Vole/packs/pricing.json; usage_events.cost_usd and the cost_basis stamp.
honest_limit: Every figure remains a list-price equivalent, not a bill; a rate bump changes what past usage "would have cost", so Vole labels mixed ranges instead of pretending one number covers both. It can detect that a rate changed, never that a rate is wrong.
competitive_note: No competitor prices subscription-auth agents at all — market.md finding 1: none of the 27 agent-security vendors offers exact per-session token or cost. The risk that the party being charged can edit their own rate card is unique to a local-first design and has to be closed deliberately, not inherited.
v1_ref: What-if per project/session with third-party rate cards
gap_area: Detection-content lifecycle: how packs, CVE floors and allowlists reach the fleet offline, age, and re-score history

name: Repos band on Posture: four readability states and a printed denominator
description: A band on the existing Posture screen that renders the registry with the same honesty the coverage strip already demands: roots known, roots readable, roots skipped by policy, roots not present, and the byte receipt from repo_scan_state, with the denominator sentence written out — 'artifact findings cover 24 readable roots of 58 known; 34 roots are not present on disk and their last-known state is from <date>'. Every count is a real query, never a bare zero: a root with no artifacts renders 'none of the 18 declared paths present', a root that could not be opened renders 'unreadable', and a root with an over-budget file renders its em-dash sha with the skip reason. Requires the read-model written twice per the parity constraint — queries.ts view plus its DB.swift port — and a getRepos read model returning per-root artifact counts, worst artifact state and the scan receipt.
desktop_surface: Posture screen, Repos band: a sortable root list with kind, origin, classification, last agent activity and artifact-count chips; expanding a root shows the artifact ledger with tracked-state and sha; a persistent footer carries the receipt and the denominator sentence; each artifact row deep-links via vole:// to the incident that cites it.
data_source: work_roots, root_cwds, repo_artifacts, repo_scan_state (all local); no new source read
honest_limit: The band can only show roots that produced agent evidence, so its 'known' figure is itself a lower bound and is labelled as one rather than presented as a repo inventory. Artifact counts describe this laptop at the last scan cursor; a root scanned before a manifest bump shows its old manifest_version and is not silently re-badged as covered.
competitive_note: Fleet/osquery renders inventory tables with no readability denominator. The console vendors show a repo or project list without ever stating how many roots were unreadable, excluded, or gone, which is exactly the number an auditor asks for.
v1_ref: Posture screen with three-state controls and an evidence coverage ratio
gap_area: The repo registry: enumerating repo-local agent artifacts at all

name: Crown-jewel-scoped rule variants: same detection, escalated only on a tiered target
description: No new matching — a join and a distinct rule id, so a SOC can route tier-1 separately without retuning a single threshold: crown_jewel_read_unasked (sensitive_read_unasked where the path resolves to tier ≤ 2), crown_jewel_egress (dlp_egress whose class × tier crosses the register's declared line), tier1_remote_write (action_targets remote_database_write against a declared production DSN — this machine's transcripts name launchsafe-db-do-user-35002029-0.e.db.ondigitalocean.com 39 times and a second landing DB 30 times) and crown_jewel_left_device (context_edges whose destination is off-device carrying a tier-1 target). Each variant fires with its parent's observed/baseline/threshold figures plus the asset row, and every parent keeps firing: the variants are additional keys, not replacements, so muting tier-1 routing can never silence the base rule.
desktop_surface: A 'Crown jewels' filter pill on Leak Ledger and the Behaviour board; each incident card shows the parent rule and the variant together with the register entry's basis.
data_source: secret_sightings / dlp_egress / action_targets / context_edges rows carrying asset_id and asset_tier; register dsn, domain, path and repo entries from ~/.vole/policy/assets.json.
honest_limit: Shape near-misses are the real failure mode: the same transcripts contain db-xxxx.b.db.ondigitalocean.com 25 times plus HOSTNAME_OR_IP_ADDRESS and host:25060 placeholders, all of which look like a production DSN. Matching is therefore on the exact declared host:port, and a near-miss is written to the preflight worksheet as near_match — never fired as an incident.
competitive_note: Cyberhaven and Harmonic can only fire on content they inspect and retain; these fire on a target string plus a declared register with no prompt stored anywhere — the out-of-path, exact, prompt-free intersection market.md's white-space analysis says no vendor occupies.
v1_ref: sensitive_path_class_exposed rule (destination-aware)
gap_area: The company's own asset and data-class register (what 'sensitive' and 'customer data' mean here)

name: Grant widening by one click: the always-accept that wrote a wildcard shell rule
description: The sequence is on disk in full: Got response: {'optionId':'always-accept'} followed within 130 ms by [PolicySession] Persisted allow rule for shell matching 'echo *' at scope=workspace, then 'git *' at scope=user, then 'head *' at scope=session, with rebuild() complete: 17 then 18 then 19 rules parsed. The results are still there — ~/.kiro/settings/permissions.yaml holds capability: shell / effect: allow / match: [git *] and ~/.kiro/workspace-roots/<hash>/permissions.yaml holds 'echo *'. Adds grant_events(ts, tool, root_id, session_id, capability, match_pattern, scope, rule_count_before, rule_count_after, origin, source) with origin in {approval_click, file_edit}, and the rule blanket_grant_created keyed (tool, capability, match_pattern, scope, bucket) — never now() — firing when a persisted pattern has no argument constraint or when scope='user', which authorises every future workspace from a click made inside one. The same rule covers the inverted shape in VS Code: agent-host-config.json editAutoApprovePatterns is {'**/*': true} with 14 deny globs (**/.env, **/.mcp.json, **/.claude/settings.json, **/.github/hooks/**, **/*.lock), so a removed deny glob is a widening event too.
desktop_surface: Posture > Grants lists each pattern with its scope, the timestamp, whether a click or a file edit created it, and the rule-count delta; the two shapes sit side by side (Kiro's allow-list growth and VS Code's shrinking deny-list) so a reviewer sees the same event in both idioms.
data_source: ~/.kiro/logs/<stamp>/kiro.log ([ACP ToolApproval] Got response, [PolicySession] Persisted allow rule ... at scope=...); ~/.kiro/settings/permissions.yaml; ~/.kiro/workspace-roots/<hash>/permissions.yaml; <editor root>/User/globalStorage/agent-host-config.json editAutoApprovePatterns and permissions.{allow,deny}
honest_limit: The log gives the pattern and the scope, not who clicked beyond the OS user already stamped at insert. A rule typed directly into permissions.yaml produces no event, only a file mtime, so origin='file_edit' carries a coarser timestamp and cannot be pinned to a session. scope='session' rules disappear with the session and exist only in the log — once that launch directory is pruned they are unprovable. Whether a pattern is 'too broad' is policy, so the floor lives in the policy pack and the incident quotes it.
competitive_note: The covered ledger reads the grant files at rest; this is the creation event with its 130 ms causal link and the click latency. Nothing in the 62-vendor matrix ledgers the moment a wildcard grant is born: Snyk and Cisco scan configs at rest, Harmonic-class tools block inline and never explain what the user widened.
v1_ref: Grant and override ledger: which file granted this authority, and what weakens the guardrails
gap_area: Editor-embedded agent task stores (Cline, Roo/Kilo, Kiro, Zed, JetBrains) across every VS Code fork root

name: security_envelope_changed: posture- and authority-weighted, not count-weighted
description: One rule over the classified rows, scored by who authorised the change rather than how many changes there were. Each envelope-class write joins round 2's four-state `authorization_basis` (denied / pre-authorised / posture-waived / no record) and the `autonomy_intervals` timeline covering the write's timestamp: info when the write sits under an explicit grant in `default` mode, warn under `acceptEdits` or `auto`, critical when the covering interval is `bypassPermissions` and the unattended evidence chain holds. anomaly_key is `<source>:security_envelope_changed:<session_id>:<change_risk_class>:<bucket>` — posture, pack_version and asset tier stay out of it, and a later escalation travels through round 2's separate escalation channel rather than a second row. observed/baseline/threshold carry real figures: writes in this class this window, the principal's own 30-day median for the same class, and the posture multiplier applied.
desktop_surface: Incident card on the Triage queue whose drill-down lands directly on the 'what the agent left behind' section filtered to that session and class, with the posture interval drawn as a band under the write's timestamp.
data_source: The change_risk_class ledger joined to autonomy_intervals and authorization_basis; posture from Claude `permissionMode` lines (712 bypassPermissions, 767 auto, 51 default here) and Codex `turn_context.payload.{approval_policy, sandbox_policy.type}`.
honest_limit: Three of the 25 envelope writes here sit in sessions that also carry bypassPermissions, but Claude records the mode as its own line type rather than per tool call, so posture at the instant of the write is an interval lookup and is NULL when no interval covers it — never defaulted to 'default', and a NULL posture degrades the rule to warn. Codex is the mirror image: rich approval_policy and sandbox_policy, no per-write path, so its rows arrive posture-rich and target-poor and are counted separately.
competitive_note: v1's scope_escape fires on 'outside cwd', which misses every envelope change made inside the repo — the CI file, the manifest, the .npmrc — and its own note put Bash redirection writes out of scope, a hole round 2 already closed. CrowdStrike Falcon AIDR's prompt-to-tool-to-action causal chain is the nearest commercial equivalent and needs an ES-level sensor plus inline prompt inspection to build it.
v1_ref: Out-of-repo write and agent self-modification rules (scope_escape, agent_config_modified)
gap_area: Agent-authored change risk: writes that widen the security envelope, not writes that destroy

name: Cross-agent credential and base-URL injection
description: One agent can silently reconfigure another, and modelling each agent's config in isolation misses it entirely. ~/.codex/config.toml [shell_environment_policy.set] is injected into every shell Codex spawns, and on this machine it sets ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4141, ANTHROPIC_MODEL=claude-opus-4.6 and ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL=gpt-4 (verified, with inherit="core") -- so a `claude` launched from inside a Codex session talks to a different endpoint under a different token than the same command run from a normal terminal. Parse every env-injection surface (Codex shell_environment_policy, Claude settings.json env block and its ccr backups, MCP server env maps and header key names, plugin install scripts) and emit agent_env_redirects_other_agent when a variable whose name belongs to agent A is set by agent B's config, quoting the variable name, the parsed target host and the config file path -- never the value.
desktop_surface: Supply Chain -> Environment: a matrix of 'set by' agent versus 'affects' agent, each cell listing the variable names and the destination host; a cell containing a credential-shaped variable name renders critical with the config file path and a Reveal in Finder action.
data_source: ~/.codex/config.toml [shell_environment_policy].inherit and [shell_environment_policy.set] (verified live on this machine); ~/.claude/settings.json env block (empty here) plus its 5 ccr/reset backups; mcpServers[].env and headers key names in ~/.claude.json (github carries an Authorization header) and ~/.codex/config.toml
honest_limit: Only variable NAMES, the parsed host and the config path are stored; the token value stays in memory for the scan and never reaches vole.db. The finding proves the injection is configured, not that any child agent actually ran under it -- proving that needs the live process map, and the incident must say so. Variables exported from a shell rc file rather than an agent config are outside this surface entirely, and a config file is a snapshot of now, so it must never be stamped onto historical sessions.
competitive_note: v1's Tier 3 model-route integrity detects base-URL overrides per agent but treats each agent's config in isolation; the cross-agent direction -- B's config rewriting A's provider and token -- is modelled nowhere in the roadmap or the 62-vendor matrix. This is the local shape of CVE-2026-21852 (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL redirecting API traffic with the Authorization header, Check Point 2026-02-24).
v1_ref: Model-route integrity and allowlist (model_provider_rerouted, model_switch, model_not_allowed)
field_verified: VERIFIED LIVE, verbatim, and it is the most alarming fact on this machine. ~/.codex/config.toml ends with `[shell_environment_policy] inherit = "core"` followed by `[shell_environment_policy.set] ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN = "litellm-899D6018-53B8-4827-8F49-F2A824B72558", ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL = "http://localhost:4141", ANTHROPIC_MODEL = "claude-opus-4.6", ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL = "gpt-4"` — Codex's own config rewrites Claude Code's endpoint, token and model for every shell it spawns. ccr backups CONFIRMED: settings.json.bak-pre-ccr, two .ccr-backup-*, .ccr-original, .reset-backup — 5 files. ~/.claude.json mcpServers.github.headers.Authorization CONFIRMED (47 chars). Minor correction: the Claude settings.json `env` block is ABSENT, not 'empty here'.
constraint: Constraint 3 — the incident's anomaly_key must be (config path, file sha256, variable name); a config re-read every 5 s would otherwise re-fire on a stable file. Constraint 7 (no content) — variable NAMES, parsed host and config path only; note that ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN's value must not even be fingerprinted into the Data Exposure ledger without the UI saying that a config value was hashed. Constraint 18 (config is a snapshot of now) — it must never be stamped onto historical sessions, which again makes this depend on v1 #222's time-versioned provider_configs.

name: Plugin always-on context tax, priced per model per session
description: Claude Code caches the marketplace catalog at `~/.claude/plugins/plugin-catalog-cache.json` with, per plugin, `tokens:{<model>:{always_on, on_invoke}}`, `components`, `unique_installs` and `marketplace_sha`. Store it as a `posture_plugin_catalog` table keyed on (marketplace_sha, plugin) and compute, per enabled plugin, the exact always_on token cost it adds to every request on this machine multiplied by the session count from usage_events in range — a figure that comes from the vendor's own catalog and is therefore counted, not estimated. This is the only feature in the product that attributes context-window cost to an installed extension, and it is the reason a first-call context number can finally be decomposed rather than merely reported.
desktop_surface: A FinOps 'context tax' row under Breakdown listing always_on tokens per plugin per model and the running total across sessions in range, rendered as an em dash wherever the catalog lists no figure for the model actually in use.
data_source: ~/.claude/plugins/plugin-catalog-cache.json — verified here: fetchedAt 2026-08-29T07:17:37Z, catalog.generated_at 2026-08-28, marketplace_sha 0620a687…, catalog.models ['claude-opus-4-7','claude-sonnet-4-6'], plugins[].tokens.<model>.{always_on, on_invoke} (e.g. 1081 always_on / 25462 on_invoke on opus-4-7 for one plugin), plugins[].components.{commands,agents,skills,hooks,mcpServers,lspServers}.
honest_limit: The catalog is a cache with a fetchedAt and lists token figures only for the models it was generated against (two models here), so a session on any other model gets NULL and never a substituted figure. It covers marketplace plugins only — a locally installed or inline plugin has no catalog entry at all. always_on is the plugin's declared cost, not a measured delta in this machine's requests, and multiplying it by session count assumes the plugin was enabled for every one of them, which the cache cannot prove.
competitive_note: No roadmap-v1 entry reads plugin-catalog-cache.json, and v1's first-call context view explicitly refuses to split context among MCP servers because it has no per-component figure — this file supplies one. Vendor consoles report credits or seats (JetBrains, Windsurf, Copilot per market.md §4); none attributes context-window cost to an installed extension.
v1_ref: Context cost views: first-call context per session and growth following each tool
field_verified: The catalog verifies perfectly and the installed set makes it empty. ~/.claude/plugins/plugin-catalog-cache.json (476 KB, `-rw-------`): `{version, fetchedAt: '2026-08-29T07:17:37.379Z', catalog: {generated_at: '2026-08-28T11:07:01.934Z', marketplace_sha: '0620a687ddd518871772eefd78573baff2dcb8cb', models: ['claude-opus-4-7', 'claude-sonnet-4-6'], plugins: {…}}}` — **290 plugins**, all 290 carrying `tokens`, e.g. 42crunch-api-security-testing `tokens: {claude-opus-4-7: {always_on: 1081, on_invoke: 25462}, claude-sonnet-4-6: {always_on: 796, on_invoke: 19014}}`, `unique_installs: 2843` — the feature's example figures verbatim ✓. **But**: `~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json` lists exactly **one** installed plugin, `ponytail@ponytail` (a user-scope marketplace), which has **no catalog entry**; and the catalog prices only claude-opus-4-7 / claude-sonnet-4-6 while every session on this machine runs `claude-opus-5[1m]` or Fable. Both NULL conditions fire simultaneously: zero catalogued plugins installed, and zero sessions on a catalogued model.
constraint: Principle 1, and this is the sharp edge. `always_on × session count in range` is not a count — it is a product of a vendor's declared figure and an assumption (that the plugin was enabled for every one of those sessions) that the cache demonstrably cannot support. The description calls it 'a figure that comes from the vendor's own catalog and is therefore counted, not estimated'; only the multiplicand is counted. Reconciliation: render always_on per plugin per model as the counted fact, render session count as the counted fact, and show the product only on demand with both inputs and the enablement assumption printed — the same discipline feature 15 applies to its implied-value line. Otherwise this is the shard's most quotable invented number.

name: Rule provenance and control-framework mapping on every incident
description: Every rule ships a static provenance record in its definition — {incident_name, incident_date, url, detectability, framework_ids[]} — plus a rule_controls(rule, framework, control_id, control_title, mapping_version) table in packages/core/data/controls.json, joined to anomalies.rule at read time so one Vole incident lands in a SIEM already carrying the control id the auditor asks about. Seeded mappings: privilege_escalation_mid_session and unattended_full_access to OWASP ASI excessive agency (ASI02/03); sensitive_read_unasked and cross_scope_read_then_publish to OWASP MCP tool poisoning and MITRE ATLAS CS0045; mcp_endpoint_changed to MCPoison CVE-2025-54136 and the OWASP MCP rug-pull entry; hook_command_first_seen to the Keyv worm; hidden-Unicode instruction findings to the Rules File Backdoor; agent_env_redirects_other_agent to CVE-2026-21852; the destructive classifier to NIST AI 600-1 and NIST 800-53 SI-4/AU-6; the whole pack to ISO 42001 A.6.2.8 and SOC 2 CC6/CC7. The ids travel in the evidence bundle, in vole posture --json and in every export.
desktop_surface: Framework chips on each incident row and a framework filter in the incident feed; a collapsed 'Why this rule exists' footer on every incident card showing the source incident name, its date, a copyable URL and its detectability verbatim; a rules index on the Supply Chain screen listing every rule with its provenance and current firing count; and a 'Controls covered' summary naming which control ids have evidence in the retention window and which have none.
data_source: Static provenance metadata compiled into detect/*.ts alongside each rule's thresholds; packages/core/data/controls.json versioned in the repo; joined to anomalies.rule at render time; ids sourced from OWASP ASI, OWASP MCP Top 10, MITRE ATLAS (CS0045 Cursor MCP config exfiltration, CS0053 postmark-mcp), NIST AI 600-1, ISO 42001, SOC 2.
honest_limit: The mapping is Vole's editorial judgement about which control a rule provides evidence for — not a certification and not an assessor's opinion — so it is versioned, shown with its version and the framework version it was written against, and worded 'evidence toward', never 'compliant with'. A control with zero incidents means the rule found nothing, which is not the control being satisfied, and the summary states that rather than showing a green tick. Citing a dated incident does not mean the rule would have caught that instance: several sourced incidents are only partially detectable from local logs and the card prints that detectability verbatim.
competitive_note: v1's evidence pack maps the product to frameworks at document level and would otherwise have to invent the per-rule mapping at export time; mapping at rule level is what lets an auditor sample individual incidents. market.md §9 item 5 asks for OWASP/ATLAS tagging on the behaviour rule pack and it never became a v1 entry. Most competitors ship a compliance PDF; almost none put the control id on the alert, and it is the cheapest answer to the questionnaire question every vendor gets — 'what does this rule actually detect'.
v1_ref: Compliance evidence pack export
field_verified: anomalies.rule exists (schema.ts:45 `rule TEXT NOT NULL`) so the join key is real. Every cited incident is in market-extracts.incidents with a detectable_from_local_logs field, so 'prints its detectability verbatim' is sourceable: 'ATLAS CS0045: Cursor MCP config exfiltration' (2025-06-24, 'Yes: Bash tool call reading ~/.cursor / .mcp.json followed by curl'), 'ATLAS CS0053: poisoned postmark-mcp' (2025-09, 'Partially'), 'Cursor MCPoison CVE-2025-54136 / CurXecute CVE-2025-54135' (2025-08-05), 'Rules File Backdoor' (2025-03-18), 'Keyv npm worm plants Claude Code and VS Code hooks' (2026-08-04), CVE-2026-21852 (2026-02-24). OWASP ASI ASI02/03/05/10 confirmed at market.md L157. BUT of the ~10 rules mapped, ONE exists: the shipped rules are burn_rate_spike, loop_suspected, error_storm, rate_limit_pressure, context_pressure. privilege_escalation_mid_session, unattended_full_access, sensitive_read_unasked, cross_scope_read_then_publish, mcp_endpoint_changed, hook_command_first_seen and the destructive classifier do not exist. Path error: the shipped data dir is packages/core/src/data/, not packages/core/data/.
constraint: C14: controls.json must be `import`ed like pricing.json so it is frozen into the SEA blob at build time, not runtime-read -- trivially satisfiable but must be stated or the collector loses zero-runtime-dependency. C3 unaffected (mapping is join-time, not key-time).

name: repo_carried_grant: the permission allowlist that travels with the clone
description: The already-planned allowlist scans score a grant's content; this scores its distribution. Join repo_artifacts rows of kind claude_settings, claude_settings_local, cursor_hooks, mcp_json or vscode_settings where tracked_state='tracked' to the existing grant-and-override ledger and to work_roots.origin_slug, and fire repo_carried_grant keyed (root_id, artifact_sha256, rule_text_hash) — deterministic, no now() — because a committed grant installs itself on every clone, every teammate's checkout and every CI runner without any of them seeing an approval prompt. Severity rides the covered posture-weighted scale and escalates when the grant is blanket-shaped: this machine's tracked platform/.claude/settings.json carries Bash(env) and Bash(python3 -), its tracked settings.local.json carries a bare Bash(python3), and engine's untracked file carries Bash(gh api *) and Read(//tmp/**). This is the Lakera shape, where 428 npm packages shipped a .claude/settings.local.json and 33 of them held live credentials, seen before the package is ever published.
desktop_surface: A 'travels to every clone' column on the Repos band showing origin slug and tracked-file count, and an incident card on the Behaviour feed quoting the literal rule text, the artifact path, its sha256 and the origin — with the observed/baseline/threshold figures selected, not dropped.
data_source: repo_artifacts rows for .claude/settings.json, .claude/settings.local.json, .mcp.json, .cursor/hooks, .vscode/settings.json joined to tracked_state from .git/index and to work_roots.origin_slug from <root>/.git/config; measured literal rules quoted above
honest_limit: Vole reads this laptop's index, so it cannot know whether the commit was pushed or how many clones exist — the incident says 'staged in this repo', never 'installed on N machines'. origin_slug NULL (apiup here has a .git and no remote) means the blast radius is unknown, not one. The rule text is quoted, never evaluated against the vendor's real permission matcher, so 'what this actually authorised' stays a Vole reading.
competitive_note: Cursor's enterprise hooks.json and Anthropic's managed-settings.json are the vendors' own answer to repo-controlled permissions, but neither reports that a repo-local grant is committed and travelling. Legit and Cycode would see it only after a push, and only in repos they are wired to.
gap_area: The repo registry: enumerating repo-local agent artifacts at all

name: Data-class entries: what 'customer data' means here, as validators and salted hashes
description: The second half of the same pack: `class` entries that state what this company's customer data looks like — a regex plus one of dlp_detectors' shipped offline checksum validator ids (Luhn, mod-11, IBAN), a table/column name list, a filename shape such as customers*.csv, or a `literal` supplied as HMAC-SHA256 under a pack-declared salt so the register on every laptop is never a file of live values. Hits land in secret_sightings with class_entry_id and validator_checked, and the two never aggregate into one figure: a checksum-validated customer id and an unvalidated shape guess stay in separate columns everywhere they are rendered. Load-time refusal: a literal whose declared plaintext length and charset fall under the entropy floor is rejected with the reason shown, because the pack salt ships to every endpoint and a low-entropy hash (a customer name, a project code name) is offline-guessable by anyone holding the pack.
desktop_surface: Data Exposure gains a 'Company classes' section beside the builtin detectors — per-entry counts split validated vs shape-only, with the entry's basis; the Privacy Center field dictionary lists class_entry_id and states that no matched value is ever stored.
data_source: ~/.vole/policy/assets.json `class` entries; the existing dlp_scan_state cursors, keyword prefilter and byte budget; the Keychain-held fingerprint key for the sighting fingerprint (distinct from the pack salt used for literal matching).
honest_limit: Exact matches only. A paraphrase, a re-encoded or joined export, a screenshot, a summarised row set or a column renamed in transit is invisible, and the count is rendered with that sentence beside it rather than implying recall. A shape-only entry with no validator produces false positives at a rate nobody can compute in advance — which is what the preflight exists for.
competitive_note: TruffleHog, Gitleaks and detect-secrets accept customer regex but have no agent context and their findings usually contain the secret; Presidio-style PII needs the on-device NER Vole deliberately refuses to run, so the validator + salted-literal split is what keeps this a metadata-only product.
gap_area: The company's own asset and data-class register (what 'sensitive' and 'customer data' mean here)

name: Register coverage on every asset-scoped figure, and the unresolved worklist
description: A view v_asset_coverage(ledger, period, resolved, unresolved, no_target, coverage_pct) computed per ledger over a declared denominator, because an implicit one lies: this machine's transcripts touch 2,670 distinct hosts, nearly all public documentation, so coverage is computed over eligible targets (write, egress, secret-sighting and remote-action rows) and the denominator's definition is printed next to the number. An absent register renders 'No asset register loaded — every severity is posture-only', never '0 critical assets', so an empty register is visible rather than silently making everything low. A register that stops growing while unresolved volume rises surfaces through the existing content_stale state for kind `assets`, not as a new rule that fires daily.
desktop_surface: A coverage strip on Blast Radius, Leak Ledger and Data Exposure, matching the attribution-coverage strip on People and the cost_basis strip on Costs; plus an 'Unresolved targets' worklist ranked by row count, each with a copy-as-entry button that emits a candidate register line.
data_source: asset_id / asset_match / asset_rev columns on the five ledgers; the assets table's pack_version; content_packs registry state for kind `assets`.
honest_limit: Coverage measures how much of what Vole saw resolves — not how much of the company's estate is declared. A perfect 100% can still mean the admin declared only the three systems these agents happened to touch, and the strip says so.
competitive_note: No competitor publishes a coverage denominator at all: Cursor calls its cost 'best-effort', Copilot metrics lag ~2 days and depend on IDE telemetry, and none of the 62 vendors states what fraction of activity its console could not classify.

name: vole packs --preflight assets.json: score a candidate register before the fleet gets it
description: Reuses the existing pack preflight path to score a candidate register against this machine's retained evidence, emitting per entry: rows it would resolve, entries resolving zero rows (dead), entries claiming the same target (collision, naming which loses because chain order decides), near_match entries where an observed host differs from a declared one by a single label or matches a documentation placeholder, entropy-floor rejections for literals, and a severity delta — how many already-stored incidents would escalate under content_rev if this pack shipped. Grounded here: an entry for *.db.ondigitalocean.com:25060 would resolve 97 observed DSN mentions of which 25 are the docs placeholder db-xxxx.b.db.ondigitalocean.com, exactly the finding an admin needs before pushing a register to a fleet.
desktop_surface: Posture → Asset Register → 'Preflight a candidate' file picker, rendering the same worksheet the CLI prints, with a copyable diff and the severity-delta count.
data_source: a candidate ~/.vole/policy/assets.json; the five asset-bearing ledgers already in ~/.vole/vole.db; anomalies rows for the severity delta.
honest_limit: It scores against one machine's evidence, itself bounded by the evidence-expiry countdown, so an entry scoring zero here may be another team's crown jewel. The output is a worksheet, never a pass/fail gate, and the header states that before the first table.
competitive_note: Policy simulation exists in Purview and the DLP suites but runs server-side over content the vendor already holds; an offline preflight on the buyer's own laptop, against evidence that never leaves it, has no vendor analogue in the 62-row matrix.

name: change_risk_class: the envelope classifier on the file-write ledger
description: Adds nullable `change_risk_class`, `class_pattern_id` and `content_rev` columns to the existing file-write ledger, populated at insert from a versioned path pack loaded through round 2's content_packs registry. Every input is already in the ledger: Claude `toolUseResult.filePath` (2,374 write results over 358 distinct paths on this machine), OpenCode `part.data` rows of `type='patch'` (`files[]`, 971 here) and `tool.write|edit` `state.input.filePath`, plus the Bash redirect/heredoc/copy targets round 2 resolves for Codex and Grok, which have no structured write tool at all. Ten classes: ci_pipeline, dependency, registry_config, container, infra_iam, auth_crypto, visibility, test_gate, secret_material, machine_persistence — 25 rows on this machine match, among them `<redacted-local-path>` and `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. `pattern_id` lives on the row and `pack_version` in `content_rev`, never in any key, so a pack bump re-scores rows instead of duplicating them. This is the classification v1 never made: its edit ledger counted lines and cost per line, which answers a productivity question about a file whose only interesting property is what it decides.
desktop_surface: A class chip on every row of the file-write drill-down, and a new Envelope band on Blast Radius counting rows per class with the unclassified rows printed as their own count rather than folded into zero.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl `toolUseResult.filePath`; ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db `part.data` (`type='patch'.files[]`, `tool.write|edit .state.input.filePath`); round 2's Bash write-target resolver rows.
honest_limit: This is a path class, not a content risk: a file named auth.ts may hold nothing sensitive and a plain .ts may hold the whole authorisation policy. Cursor, Antigravity and Devin record no write target of any kind, so their sessions contribute zero rows and must render as an unmonitored denominator beside the total, never as 'no envelope changes'. The class list is admin-visible policy, versioned and arguable, and a file that matches two patterns takes the higher-tier class with both pattern_ids kept.
competitive_note: ASPM (Legit Security, Cycode) sees the same changed file but starts at the commit and cannot name the agent, session or posture that produced it; Sysdig watches syscalls with no notion of which file class was touched; and no vendor console — Cursor's OTel export, Copilot usage metrics, Anthropic's Compliance API — exposes a per-write file path at all.
v1_ref: Agent edit ledger with blast radius, time-to-first-edit and cost per lines written
gap_area: Agent-authored change risk: writes that widen the security envelope, not writes that destroy

name: envelope_change_escaped: did the widening leave the laptop
description: Joins the classified writes to the VCS action ledger inside the same session: Claude's own `toolUseResult.gitOperation.{commit.sha, commit.branch, push.branch}` (105 such results here, 43 carrying both a commit and a push), falling back to the parsed `git push` command shape for agents that record no gitOperation. Adds `escape_state` (local_only / committed / pushed) and `push_evidence` (gitOperation / command_shape / none) to the envelope row — a provenance column, not a confidence value, since confidence stays exactly two-valued. `envelope_change_escaped` fires when a class of ci_pipeline, dependency, infra_iam or registry_config reaches `pushed`, and escalates when `--no-verify` appears in the same session, which is the agent changing the pipeline and skipping the gate that would have reviewed the change in one motion.
desktop_surface: An escape chip (Local / Committed / Pushed) on every row of 'what the agent left behind', with the branch and short sha on the incident card so a reviewer can open the actual commit.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl `toolUseResult.gitOperation`; Bash `input.command` for `git push` / `git commit --no-verify` shapes; round 2's VCS action ledger.
honest_limit: gitOperation is Claude-only and appears only on the Bash results Claude chose to annotate, so `push_evidence='none'` is common and must render as 'not observed', never as 'not pushed'. A push from a terminal outside the agent, or a later push by a human, is invisible. `gitBranch` is the literal string HEAD on a large share of rows and must never be treated as a branch name.
competitive_note: v1's provenance ledger built the session-to-commit link for cost-per-PR; this reuses the same link for the containment question instead. GitHub's audit log records the push and Copilot's metrics record the seat, but neither can say which local agent authored the pipeline change under which posture, and the ~2-day lag on Copilot metrics rules out same-day triage.
v1_ref: Session to commit / PR provenance ledger
gap_area: Agent-authored change risk: writes that widen the security envelope, not writes that destroy

name: Hook execution ledger with first-seen command hashes
description: A posture_hook_runs(source, session_id, ts, hook_event, hook_name, command_sha256, argv0_basename, script_in_managed_dir, exit_code, duration_ms, prevented_continuation, level) table reconciling the two records Claude Code writes, with one correction that matters: attachment.type='hook_success' (741 here) carries {hookName, hookEvent, command, exitCode, durationMs, stdout, stderr, content, toolUseID} but its `command` field is the hook's DISPLAY LABEL, not the shell command - verified: {"hookName":"SessionStart:startup", "command":"Loading ponytail mode...", "exitCode":0, "durationMs":108}. The literal argv lives in type='system' subtype='stop_hook_summary'.hookInfos[].{command, durationMs} (459 here), e.g. '"<redacted-local-path>" ".../cth-hook.cjs"', alongside preventedContinuation, hookErrors and level. So command_sha256 and argv0_basename come from stop_hook_summary and the configured hooks blocks in settings*.json and plugin hooks/*.json, while hook_success contributes the outcome fields. hook_command_first_seen fires the first time a command_sha256 appears - the moment a worm-planted hook executes.
desktop_surface: Supply Chain > Hooks: rows grouped by hook event with run counts, median duration, exit-code distribution and a first-seen date; new-hash rows pinned to the top with a critical badge and the argv0 path; a prevented_continuation column links out to the sessions the hook stopped.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl attachment.type='hook_success' (741) and type='system' subtype='stop_hook_summary'.hookInfos[].command (459); attachment.type='hook_additional_context' (439); ~/.claude/settings.json and project .claude/settings*.json hooks blocks; ~/.claude/plugins/**/hooks/*.json; ~/.codex/config.toml notify (a SkyComputerUseClient argv here).
honest_limit: hook_success.stdout and .content carry the full injected prompt verbatim (verified: an entire multi-kilobyte instruction block), so only sha256 and length are ever stored. Only successful hooks leave a hook_success attachment - zero failure attachments exist here - so 'no hook observed' is never 'no hook configured', and a hook removed before the session leaves nothing at all. stop_hook_summary carries the literal command only for Stop-event hooks, so PreToolUse and PostToolUse argv must be matched from the settings blocks by hookName, and hook_additional_context has no command field, so PostToolUse context injection is counted but never attributed to a script. exitCode and durationMs are the tool's own figures, and a first-seen hash is a fact about this machine's recorded history, not a verdict: a legitimate new hook and a planted one look identical until a human classifies it.
competitive_note: v1 reconciles hook_success on {hookEvent, hookName, exitCode, durationMs} only, and would have hashed a display label had it reached for `command`; it also misses stop_hook_summary.hookInfos[].command, where the real argv lives, and the entire hook_additional_context channel. The Keyv npm worm (2026-08-04) plants exactly this kind of hook and fires it once a workspace is trusted; no gateway or vendor console observes a local hook run at all.
v1_ref: Hook inventory and execution ledger
field_verified: The central correction is verified exactly, and I found a second one. Across 406 `hook_success` attachments, ALL 406 carry all ten keys {type, hookName, toolUseID, hookEvent, content, stdout, stderr, exitCode, command, durationMs}, and `command` is indeed the display label: `{"hookName":"SessionStart:startup","hookEvent":"SessionStart","exitCode":"0","command":"Loading ponytail mode...","durationMs":"53"}`. NEW: exitCode and durationMs are STRINGS, not numbers. `stop_hook_summary` verified verbatim: `"hookInfos":[{"command":"\"<redacted-local-path>\" \"<redacted-local-path>\"","durationMs":69}]` alongside hookErrors, hookAdditionalContext, preventedContinuation, stopReason, hasOutput, `"level":"suggestion"`. Counts today: 406 / 67 / 355 (write-up said 741 / 459 / 439 — same transcript pruning). hookName distribution: SubagentStart:workflow-subagent 345, SessionStart:startup 28, UserPromptSubmit 27, SessionStart:compact 4 — NO PreToolUse or PostToolUse entries at all. And `~/.claude/settings.json` has no `hooks` block whatsoever: every hook that ran here was installed by the ponytail PLUGIN.
constraint: C5/Principle 1 — exitCode '0' and durationMs '53' arriving as strings means a naive INTEGER column silently coerces or, under C11 (node:sqlite strict binding throws on the wrong shape and aborts the whole batch), kills the insert. Parse with an explicit NULL fallback rather than a cast. C7: hook_success.content and .stdout carry the entire injected instruction block verbatim (verified — the full multi-kilobyte ponytail text) so sha256 and length only, never the body, and never into a collector note. C3: hook_command_first_seen keys on (command_sha256) alone, which is correct and stable.

name: Pack-bump re-scan of retained evidence, oldest-first and bounded, with the unscannable backlog counted
description: `dlp_scan_state` gains `pack_rev TEXT`; when the dlp_detectors version changes, the collector requeues only rows whose `raw_ref` file still exists, oldest-first, draining inside the byte budget the scan engine already enforces, so a bump degrades throughput rather than blocking a poll. `secret_sightings` gains `first_seen_pack` and `refired_by_pack` written as NULL-only widening updates, so the existing "rewrite only when total_tokens strictly grows" upsert rule is not violated, plus a `retro` flag so a finding surfaced today about three-week-old evidence is never rendered as new activity. A `content_rescan(pack_rev, requeued, scanned, unscannable, finished_at)` row records the bump, and the Data Exposure screen states its coverage as scanned/(scanned+unscannable) instead of declaring the store clean.
