desktop_surface: Data Exposure gains a "re-scanned for dlp_detectors <version>" banner carrying the coverage fraction and the count of findings tagged retro; the Leak Ledger filter bar gains a `retro` facet so an analyst can separate "new leak" from "new detector".
data_source: dlp_scan_state cursors; usage_events.raw_ref (file path plus byte offset stamped by every collector); existence checks against ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl, ~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl and the other five source roots resolved by paths.ts.
honest_limit: A new detector can only find what is still on disk. Claude Code deletes local transcripts after 30 days by default (anthropics/claude-code#23710), so for older sessions the honest answer is "not re-checked", never "no finding" — and the window between a leak and the pack that could have seen it is unrecoverable.
competitive_note: detect-secrets ships a hashed baseline precisely so a detector change can be replayed over old code (Yelp design doc, market.md L169). No AI-agent security vendor re-scans retained agent evidence on a detector bump because the inline vendors — Harmonic, Nightfall, Cyberhaven — scan in the request path once and keep nothing to re-scan.
v1_ref: Secret pattern scanner with entropy gate (secret_findings)
gap_area: Detection-content lifecycle: how packs, CVE floors and allowlists reach the fleet offline, age, and re-score history

name: assets.json: the admin-authored register, and the two entry kinds it refuses to load
description: Reads only ~/.vole/policy/assets.json, loaded through the content_packs registry as kind `assets` in the admin-authored trust class under the customer trust anchor — never vendor-signed, never inferred from evidence. Entries are {asset_id, tier, kind, match, owner, basis} where kind is repo (a normalised remote URL or a `github.com/<org>/*` prefix), path (glob), domain (host suffix), dsn (host+port), store (path prefix) or class (see the data-class feature); `basis` is a one-line admin sentence quoted verbatim in every incident that cites the asset. Materialises into `assets(pack_version, asset_id, tier, kind, match_norm, owner, basis, source)` so any stored resolution can be replayed against the register version that made it, plus `assets_rejected(pack_version, entry_ix, reason)` for load-time refusals. Two refusals ship: an entry whose `match` is itself a credential shape under dlp_detectors (this machine's transcripts carry the DigitalOcean managed-DB `doadmin` user 226 times and `AVNS_` password prefixes 72 times, so a register full of live DSNs is the obvious wrong turn), and a `literal` entry below the entropy floor. Tier is admin-declared policy, never computed, and every render says which pack version and entry declared it.
desktop_surface: Posture → Asset Register: a read-only entry table (tier chip, owner, basis, resolved-row count) matching the existing Policy screen's read-only-by-design rule, with a red 'Rejected entries' section naming the entry index and the refusal reason.
data_source: ~/.vole/policy/assets.json (admin-authored, signed under the customer trust anchor, loaded via the content_packs registry); validated against the shipped dlp_detectors credential shapes at load time.
honest_limit: The register is a declaration, not evidence: Vole can prove an agent touched github.com/launchsafe/platform, never that the org's tier-1 list is complete or correct. An absent file means 'no register loaded', never 'nothing here is critical'. In managed mode the admin pack wins and a user-local assets.json is ignored but counted; in personal mode there is no register at all and every rule falls back to posture weighting alone.
competitive_note: Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels are the closest analogue but need content inspection and M365 device onboarding; of the 27 vendors in market.md that cover coding agents (Cyberhaven, Nightfall, Harmonic, Zenity, CrowdStrike Guardian) every one classifies by content shape or lineage inline, and none exposes a customer-declared asset register that an out-of-path, prompt-free endpoint ledger joins to.
v1_ref: Policy-as-code file with local enforcement, drift report and vole_policy check
gap_area: The company's own asset and data-class register (what 'sensitive' and 'customer data' mean here)

name: Criticality as the second severity input — and why asset_tier must stay out of anomaly_key
description: Severity becomes f(posture, asset_tier): a rule firing against a tier-1 or tier-2 target escalates exactly one step above its posture-weighted level, and an unresolved target never de-escalates — it keeps the posture-only severity and the detail line reads 'target not in the register', never 'low value'. Adds anomalies.asset_id, asset_tier and asset_rev plus a severity_inputs template parameter so an incident reads 'critical: bypass posture + tier 1 (assets.json v7, entry prod-db: "customer database, DPA scope")'. The load-bearing constraint is that anomaly_key must contain neither asset_id nor asset_tier — otherwise every register edit duplicates every incident — so re-scoring after a register bump rides the escalation channel and content_rev, which is also the only path by which a register published after the fact can move an already-frozen INSERT OR IGNORE verdict.
desktop_surface: Severity chips gain a tier marker; the incident card shows a two-line severity derivation (posture input, asset input) with the register entry's basis quoted and a link straight to that entry in Posture → Asset Register.
data_source: anomalies rows joined to the ledger row's asset_id/asset_tier/asset_rev; ~/.vole/policy/assets.json tier and basis; existing posture weighting from autonomy_intervals.
honest_limit: Escalation is one declared step, never a computed risk score — the product stays out of Annex III 4(b) scoring territory by construction. An incident that fired before the register existed shows its original severity beside 're-scored at content_rev N', so the audit trail admits the verdict changed rather than pretending it was always critical.
competitive_note: Zenity does taint tracking but SaaS-side with no laptop CLI collector; every endpoint DLP vendor in the matrix weights severity by content class alone, which is precisely why an ~/.ssh read outranks the customer PII export in their consoles.
gap_area: The company's own asset and data-class register (what 'sensitive' and 'customer data' mean here)

name: Blast Radius sorted by asset tier, with a counted untiered bucket
description: The Blast Radius screen sorts and groups by asset tier, and the 'Untiered' group is always counted and expandable — never collapsed to zero, never hidden, and never sorted to the bottom, so an undeclared crown jewel is not buried by its own absence. Each row shows tier, asset_id, owner, the basis verbatim, the chain link that resolved it and the register version that made the match. A 'Propose as asset' action writes a candidate entry to ~/.vole/policy/assets.proposed.json and never touches the signed pack: in managed mode the register is admin-only, so the desktop's only write is a proposal an admin can accept or discard.
desktop_surface: Blast Radius with tier headers ('Tier 1 — 3 targets, 214 actions', 'Untiered — 61 targets, 1,908 actions'), the resolution link on every row, and the proposal button; the menu bar carries a count of tier-1 incidents only, never a score.
data_source: action_targets, context_edges and remote-execution rows joined to assets via asset_id; ~/.vole/policy/assets.proposed.json for the write.
honest_limit: Untiered is not safe — it is unknown, and the group header says exactly that. The proposal file is a suggestion with no authority: nothing in it affects severity until an admin signs it into the pack, and the screen must not imply otherwise.
competitive_note: CrowdStrike Falcon Guardian ships a shadow-agent inventory with a causal chain but ranks by its own risk score; this is the anti-score version of the same screen, where the bucket the score would have hidden is the one kept in view.
gap_area: The company's own asset and data-class register (what 'sensitive' and 'customer data' mean here)

name: write_then_hide: the change the agent made unreviewable
description: The visibility class, joined rather than alerted on alone. An addition to `.gitignore`, `.dockerignore`, `.npmignore` or `.git/info/exclude`, a `git update-index --assume-unchanged|--skip-worktree`, or a `git config` write is stored with the added pattern taken from the key-set delta. `write_then_hide` fires only in two shapes: a path the same session wrote is matched by a pattern the same session added, or the added pattern covers a path already present in round 2's `tracked_state` snapshot from `.git/index`. That is the line between routine housekeeping and removing a file from every reviewer's and every repo scanner's view. Seven `.gitignore` writes exist on this machine and none of them would fire, which is the point.
desktop_surface: Hidden paths rendered struck-through in 'what the agent left behind' with the ignoring pattern shown beside them, and an info-tier count of visibility writes that did not fire so the quiet ones are still visible.
data_source: The change_risk_class visibility rows, their pre/post images for the pattern delta, the same session's write ledger, and `tracked_state` from `.git/index`.
honest_limit: Adding build output to `.gitignore` is overwhelmingly the honest case, which is why the bare class stays info and only the join fires. The rule cannot see a file hidden by a pattern that was already there, nor one hidden by a human. Glob semantics are approximated locally, so negations and nested ignore files produce false negatives, counted in the pack's own coverage figure rather than assumed away.
competitive_note: Repo scanners and ASPM read what the repository shows them, so a path an agent added to .gitignore is invisible to them by construction — the local write ledger is the only place the hiding action itself is recorded. No matrix vendor claims this signal.
gap_area: Agent-authored change risk: writes that widen the security envelope, not writes that destroy

name: Window hunt: what entered this machine's agent surface between two timestamps
description: Half the advisories name an interval rather than an artifact — s1ngularity was "whoever installed in this window", the Keyv worm was a publication range — so the hunt takes [A,B] and returns every first appearance across the ledgers that already carry a first_seen: package executions, MCP registrations by endpoint identity, hook command hashes, tool_first_seen, ai_extensions, egress hosts on context_edges, plugin installs and work_roots. Adds the view `v_arrived_between(kind, identity, first_seen, last_seen, still_present, source_ledger, first_seen_floored)` and `vole hunt --between <a> <b>`, with still_present resolved against the current inventory sweep so "arrived and removed" separates from "arrived and still here". No new collection — it is a union over columns the round-2 ledgers already populate.
desktop_surface: A date-range picker on the Triage screen's hunt entry point producing a single grouped list, each row jumping to the ledger card that owns it; rows whose first_seen sits at the horizon are struck with a floor marker instead of a date.
data_source: first_seen columns on the existing package execution, MCP registration, hook, tool_first_seen, ai_extensions, context_edges, plugin and work_roots ledgers; answerable_from for the floor
honest_limit: first_seen is first observed, not first present: anything whose first observation coincides with the answerable_from floor is reported as floored and can never be claimed to have arrived inside the window. An artifact that arrived and was removed before the collector's first pass leaves nothing here — only the residue hunt can reach it.
competitive_note: Gateway and proxy vendors (LiteLLM, MintMCP, Portkey, Cloudflare AI Gateway) only ever see routed traffic and never see an install; EDR sees the process but, per the matrix, Jamf/Huntress/Santa are "process-level only; no AI semantics", so nobody can list what entered the agent surface in a window.
gap_area: Indicator retro-hunt: 'an advisory just named X — were we exposed, when, and what happened next'

name: Managed-policy coverage and precedence chain per agent
description: Answer the first question a platform lead asks: is any of this actually under management? Probe every managed layer that exists per tool and record presence, owner_uid, mode and sha256 into posture_policy_layers(source, layer, path, present, owner_uid, mode, sha256, checked_at), then render the precedence chain per tool with the layer that actually wins: /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json, the com.anthropic.claudecode defaults domain, /Library/Managed Preferences/<user>/*.plist, /Library/Application Support/GeminiCli/settings.json, /Library/Application Support/ampcode/managed-settings.json, /Library/Application Support/Cursor/hooks.json, ~/.codex/requirements.toml. Verified live on this device: it IS MDM-enrolled (/Library/Managed Preferences/shiva/ holds a root-owned complete.plist and com.apple.applicationaccess.plist from 2026-08-31) while /Library/Application Support contains no ClaudeCode, GeminiCli, ampcode or Cursor directory at all — 'managed device, zero managed agents' is the headline this feature exists to print.
desktop_surface: Supply Chain → Policy: one row per (tool, layer) with present/absent/unknown, file owner and mode, and the precedence order drawn as a chain with the winning layer highlighted; a headline chip reads 'device managed · 0 of 8 agents under policy'.
data_source: /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json; `defaults read com.anthropic.claudecode`; /Library/Managed Preferences/<user>/*.plist; /Library/Application Support/{GeminiCli,ampcode,Cursor}; ~/.codex/requirements.toml; ~/.grok/config.toml
honest_limit: Absence is only provable for paths Vole can read: under a Full-Disk-Access-denied state some /Library paths return EPERM and the row must read 'unknown', never 'absent' (the reduced-functionality pattern in market.md §7). Presence does not prove enforcement — Google states its own system settings are 'not a foolproof security boundary' — and owner/mode is the only tamper evidence available: a root-owned file edited by root is indistinguishable from a legitimate MDM push. The raw proposal's Grok evidence is wrong and is corrected here: ~/.grok/managed_config.lock is a zero-byte lock file, which proves the CLI has a managed-config code path, not that a policy file exists; Grok's actual settings live in ~/.grok/config.toml (user-owned here) and the row must say 'no managed layer known'.
competitive_note: v1 Tier 3 checks 'managed-settings.json presence and hash' for Claude Code alone; the MDM defaults domain, /Library/Managed Preferences, Gemini system settings, amp managed-settings, Cursor enterprise hooks.json and Codex requirements.toml are unlisted, as is the precedence chain that decides which layer wins. Fleet and Jamf report MDM enrolment; neither maps enrolment to per-agent policy coverage, which is the gap this row exposes on a device that is already enrolled.
v1_ref: Permission allowlist and managed-settings posture
field_verified: Headline CONFIRMED on this device. /Library/Managed Preferences/shiva/ contains `-rw-r--r-- 1 root wheel 168 Aug 31 18:47 com.apple.applicationaccess.plist` and `-rw-r--r-- 1 root wheel 835 Aug 31 18:47 complete.plist` — root-owned, dated 2026-08-31 exactly as claimed. /Library/Application Support/ contains no ClaudeCode, GeminiCli, ampcode or Cursor. `defaults read com.anthropic.claudecode` returns 'Domain com.anthropic.claudecode does not exist'. The Grok correction is right: `-rw-r--r-- 1 shiva staff 0 Jun 17 21:44 managed_config.lock` is zero bytes and `-rw-r--r-- 1 shiva staff 363 Jul 19 11:36 config.toml` is user-owned. So 'managed device, zero managed agents' is literally true here. NOT VERIFIED and undisclosed: ~/.codex/requirements.toml does not exist (52 entries in ~/.codex, no requirements.toml) — it is listed as a data source with no caveat, unlike the Grok path which was correctly caveated.
constraint: Constraint 14 (SEA: zero-runtime-dependency, node: builtins only, no native modules) — /Library/Managed Preferences plists are binary and node has no plist parser in stdlib, so this needs a `plutil -convert json` or `defaults read` subprocess from a hardened-runtime notarised binary; allowed via node:child_process but unstated and it is the first subprocess the collector would spawn. Constraint 6 (source column on posture_policy_layers). Constraint 13 — 'Supply Chain → Policy' does not exist; DashboardView.swift has four panes only (line 331-334), so this is a new pane plus a DB.swift port. Constraint 7 is respected: storing sha256 and owner/mode is hashes and paths, not content.

name: content_rev on incidents: re-score without duplicating, retire without lying
description: `anomalies` gains `content_rev` (the pack revision that first produced the row) and `rescored_rev`; `anomaly_key` deliberately excludes both, because including the pack version duplicates every open incident on every bump, while the row must carry it or an incident that appears with no new activity is unexplainable. Re-scoring rides the escalation channel that has to exist anyway to fix db.ts:137, where `INSERT OR IGNORE` freezes severity and observed at first sight: a newer pack scoring the same window higher widens severity/observed/rescored_rev, a newer pack scoring it lower changes nothing and records `rescore_declined`. A detector retired in a pack deletes no history — matching rows get `rule_retired_in` set, so no reader is ever shown a rule the current content no longer contains.
desktop_surface: Incident detail gains a provenance line "fired by dlp_detectors 2026.08.11, re-scored by 2026.09.03" beside the observed/baseline/threshold figures; the incident feed tags rows whose content_rev postdates their own window as `retro`; a retired rule appears struck through in the rule filter with its incidents intact.
data_source: anomalies table (schema.ts); content_packs.version read at detection time; the rule-to-pack mapping in the rule registry.
honest_limit: Only windows whose events are still in usage_events can be re-scored; older incidents keep the verdict the pack of the day produced and are labelled with it, so a threshold change is never retroactive across the whole history. Vole reports which pack changed the verdict, never why — it cannot tell a correction from a policy decision.
competitive_note: Anthropic states that anomaly detection, baselining and correlation are the SIEM's responsibility (code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage), so no vendor owns incident lifecycle across a detector change; SIEM rule edits re-fire and duplicate alerts, which is exactly the failure mode excluding pack_version from anomaly_key avoids.
gap_area: Detection-content lifecycle: how packs, CVE floors and allowlists reach the fleet offline, age, and re-score history

name: recipient resolution: the model name is not the recipient
description: The brief proposes keying the register on 'endpoint host and model-id shape', and on this machine that keying is actively wrong: 456 rows carry model `anthropic/claude-ccr-h7177656e2f7177656e332e382d3237622d667038`, whose hex alias decodes to a qwen model served from `http://195.242.30.141:30000/v1` — a cleartext raw-IP endpoint in an unnamed country that the model string calls 'anthropic'. Equally, 2,275 rows read `github-copilot/claude-opus-4.6`: an Anthropic model whose recipient is GitHub/Microsoft, with Anthropic as a downstream sub-processor. This resolves the recipient from model_routes/CCR config first and the model label last, and stamps a closed state on every egress row: `vendor_resolved | broker_truncated | self_hosted_unnamed | unattributable`. Adds column `recipient_state` and rule `unattributable_recipient`, which replaces the brief's single `untermed_vendor_received_data` bucket because a raw IP, a broker, a self-hosted GPU box and a vendor Vole simply has not packed are four different answers for a DPO.
desktop_surface: A recipient chip on every Leak Ledger row coloured by state, and a 'Recipients' lane on the Blast Radius screen grouping the four states with counts; broker rows expand to show 'chain truncated at hop 1 — downstream provider chosen per request by the broker' rather than a vendor name.
data_source: ~/.vole/vole.db usage_events.model, ~/.claude-code-router/config.sqlite app_config.value_json (base URLs: http://195.242.30.141:30000/v1, https://openrouter.ai/api/v1), model_routes alias map, ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db message.data.providerID
honest_limit: Where no route record exists, the state is `unattributable` and stays there — Vole will not name a vendor from a model string. A broker's downstream provider is chosen per request server-side and is unknowable from disk, so `broker_truncated` is a permanent ceiling, not a backlog item. An `ollama/…` row has no recipient at all and must render 'stayed on this device', never a vendor with blank terms.
competitive_note: Only Snyk's agent-scan reads local agent configs at all, and it scans for MCP/config risk, not for who received the traffic; the SASE vendors see the TLS destination but not the alias map that made a qwen box answer to the name 'anthropic'.
v1_ref: model_routes: resolving the local gateway's alias map, and the two rules it exposes
gap_area: AI-vendor processing register: where the data landed, under whose law, and on what default terms

name: Hunt-time fingerprinting: the pack carries the burned value, the store never does
description: An advisory that names a leaked credential publishes the value; Vole stores only HMAC-SHA256 fingerprints under a per-install Keychain key, so the two can never be compared unless the fingerprint is computed here, at hunt time. The pack (admin trust class only) carries the already-public value in memory; the hunt runs the existing pre-match normalisation at the recorded provenance rev, computes one fingerprint per retained key epoch, compares against `secret_sightings.fingerprint`, and discards the value — which never reaches the database, the log, the incident detail or the export, enforced by piping the hunt's own output through `verify --content` before anything is written. Epochs the store has rotated past return `not_comparable`, never `not_seen`; the same construction answers file_sha indicators against the at-rest sink hashes.
desktop_surface: On the Data Exposure screen, an "advisory match" band on a finding: which epoch matched, first and last sighting, the sinks it reached, and the rotation state from the existing credential-liveness sweep — with a visible "value not stored" receipt naming the verify --content run that proved it.
data_source: secret_sightings (fingerprint, epoch, detector id, sink, raw_ref byte offset); Keychain-held fingerprint key with epoch rotation; the normalisation layer's provenance rev; indicator pack values held in memory only
honest_limit: Matching can only find what was already a sighting: a credential shape no shipped detector recognised was never fingerprinted, so a negative here means "no fingerprint of this exists", not "this key was never in a transcript". Epochs rotated away are permanently unmatchable by design, and a normalisation-rev mismatch degrades to not_comparable rather than guessing.
competitive_note: Secret scanners in the matrix either hold the secret (TruffleHog, GitGuardian findings) or hash-only with no agent context (detect-secrets baseline); none can take a published advisory key and answer against an agent transcript corpus without ingesting the corpus. Vole answers without ever having stored either side in the clear.
gap_area: Indicator retro-hunt: 'an advisory just named X — were we exposed, when, and what happened next'

name: Successor window: the "and what happened next" half of the question
description: A hit answers "were we exposed" and "when"; the security team's next sentence is always "and what did it do". For each hit the hunt runs a bounded join forward from the matched evidence row — same session_id and the agent tree via agent_edges, default 30 minutes, declared on the view and never inferred — across context_edges and egress hosts, first-seen secret_sightings, action_targets remote writes, package executions, VCS actions, and the four-state authority of every tool call in between; ingress-kind indicators also get the backward leg. Adds `v_hunt_successors(hit_id, offset_ms, kind, identity, authority, raw_ref)` rendered with byte-offset provenance. Deliberately fires no rule of its own: adjacency is a filter over evidence, and the incident stays the indicator hit.
desktop_surface: An ordered strip beneath each hit on the hunt result — minute offsets on one axis, one chip per consequence, tinted by authority state — with the window length printed on the strip itself and a fixed "adjacency, not causation" caption; each chip opens the just-in-time evidence viewer at the byte offset.
data_source: tool_calls with authorization_basis; context_edges and the egress ledger; secret_sightings first_seen; action_targets and the remote-execution hop ledger; package execution and VCS action ledgers; agent_edges for the subagent tree
honest_limit: Nothing here is causal, and the caption must say so: the window is a time filter, so widening it strictly widens the noise and every count is printed with its window length. Consequences in another session, on another device, or after the agent exited are invisible, and a session whose tool ledger has coverage gaps yields a shorter strip that must not be read as a quieter aftermath.
competitive_note: CrowdStrike Falcon AIDR advertises a causal prompt→tool→action chain and is the closest thing in the matrix, but it inspects content inline and its retention is not stated; Vole reconstructs the same shape from evidence the agents wrote themselves, and refuses the causal claim its own data cannot support.
gap_area: Indicator retro-hunt: 'an advisory just named X — were we exposed, when, and what happened next'

name: Xcode bundled Claude Code posture: skip-permissions by default
description: The consequence of the multi-root gap, and the reason it matters more than a coverage percentage: Xcode's embedded Claude Code runs from its own config dir and, per the `IDEChatAgenticChatSkipPermissions` default, is launched with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`. Read `~/Library/Preferences/com.apple.dt.Xcode.plist` for that key (binary plist, so `defaults read` / `plutil -convert xml1 -o -` spawn), and when it is true write an `autonomy_intervals` row with `autonomy='full_auto'`, `granted_by='xcode_default:IDEChatAgenticChatSkipPermissions'` covering every session in that home — an autonomy grant that no human ever clicked. The highest-autonomy agent sessions on a Mac are exactly the ones Vole is structurally blind to today, and this is the pairing that makes that a finding rather than a footnote.
desktop_surface: The Agent-homes list in Settings shows a red badge on any home whose posture is full_auto by default rather than by user action; the session list shows those sessions with a 'permissions skipped (Xcode default)' chip, and the incident feed carries one info row the first day it is seen.
data_source: ~/Library/Preferences/com.apple.dt.Xcode.plist key IDEChatAgenticChatSkipPermissions; ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/CodingAssistant/ClaudeAgentConfig/projects/**/*.jsonl permissionMode stamps.
honest_limit: Verified on this machine: both the CodingAssistant directory and the preference key are absent, and `defaults read` returns 'does not exist' — so the correct stored value is NULL, never `false`, since Xcode's own default may differ from an unset key and may change between builds. The preference is a snapshot at scan time and cannot be stamped onto historical sessions. Reading a binary plist needs a subprocess, which the zero-dependency SEA bundle permits (node:child_process) but which fails silently under a restricted sandbox — that failure must render as 'not readable', not as 'not enabled'.
competitive_note: market.md's Xcode profile (community gist re-verified 2026-06-16) documents the skip-permissions default; roadmap-v1's shadow-agent item covers Claude Desktop scratch sessions but not this. Anthropic's Analytics and Compliance APIs cannot see the Xcode-bundled agent either (Xcode-managed, telemetry env disabled), so it is a bypass-permissions session that neither the vendor console, nor a gateway, nor Vole-as-shipped observes — the worst possible demo failure in front of a CISO.
v1_ref: Permission-mode and sandbox posture per session (normalised autonomy column)
field_verified: NEITHER named artifact exists on this machine — the feature says so, and it is right. `defaults read com.apple.dt.Xcode IDEChatAgenticChatSkipPermissions` -> 'The domain/default pair of (com.apple.dt.Xcode, IDEChatAgenticChatSkipPermissions) does not exist'. ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/CodingAssistant -> 'No such file or directory'. The preference file itself IS present: ~/Library/Preferences/com.apple.dt.Xcode.plist, 5,250 bytes — and `file` confirms /Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Info.plist is an 'Apple binary property list', consistent with the binary-plist subprocess requirement. So the entire feature rests on a community gist plus a shipped fixture; it cannot be demoed, regression-tested, or even sanity-checked on this endpoint.
constraint: Constraint 5 (never invent a number / absent is NULL not false) is correctly applied — the feature already insists the stored value is NULL when the key is unset, because Xcode's own default may differ from an unset key. Constraint 14: the plutil/defaults spawn is SEA-legal (node:child_process) but the feature is right that a sandbox failure must render 'not readable', not 'not enabled'. The undeclared dependency is the real issue: `autonomy_intervals` does not exist as a table — it belongs to roadmap-v1 L49 ('Permission-mode and sandbox posture per session, normalised autonomy column') — and the config root it reads only exists once feature 10 ships. So this is gated on two other items, not S standalone.

name: Native-telemetry and prompt-logging posture per agent
description: Before Vole exports anything, a security team needs to know whether the agents are already shipping telemetry somewhere unmanaged - and whether that telemetry includes prompts. Read the settings layers as a snapshot: ~/.claude/settings.json, settings.local.json and the managed-settings path for CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT / PROTOCOL / HEADERS (key names and host only, never header values) and OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS / OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT; ~/.codex/config.toml [otel] exporter; ~/.grok/config.toml plus the Grok trace.upload.decision log line's telemetry_mode / uploads_enabled / data_collection_disabled; and the ~/.claude/telemetry/ directory, which exists but is empty on this machine. Rows land in posture_snapshots(kind='telemetry', key, value, observed_at) with two rules: prompt_logging_enabled (critical) when a prompt- or tool-content-logging flag is on, and telemetry_endpoint_unmanaged (warn) when the OTLP host is outside the policy allowlist.
desktop_surface: Posture > a per-tool telemetry card reading 'native telemetry: on/off, endpoint <host>, prompt logging: ON' with the file and key that decided it, and a link into Supply Chain > History when a backup shows the flag was different before.
data_source: ~/.claude/settings.json and settings.local.json (verified present); /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json; ~/.claude/telemetry/ (exists, empty here); ~/.claude/debug/*.txt '[3P telemetry]' lines; ~/.codex/config.toml [otel]; ~/.grok/config.toml and ~/.grok/logs/unified.jsonl trace.upload.decision.
honest_limit: Config files are a snapshot of now and must never be stamped onto historical rows - a flag flipped yesterday says nothing about last week, and only backup replay recovers earlier states. Environment variables set in a shell profile, a launchd plist or a CI job override the files entirely and are invisible to a file read, so 'telemetry off' means 'no file turns it on'. Header values are deliberately never read, so Vole can name the host but never which tenant the telemetry lands in. Claude's debug lines exist only for sessions where debug logging was on (5 files here), so that row reads 'last observed at <ts>' or NULL, never 'disabled'.
competitive_note: v1 reports what already leaves via the vendor's channel but does not single out the prompt-logging flags, which are the ones that turn an observability exporter into a content pipeline: Gemini CLI defaults logPrompts to true and Cowork's OTel includes full prompts by default. Detecting a prompt-logging exporter already running on the laptop is a finding no gateway, SASE proxy or vendor console can produce, because they only see the traffic they themselves carry.
v1_ref: Vendor telemetry and upload posture report
field_verified: Verified, and the machine hands this feature a much stronger argument than it makes for itself. Claude side: `~/.claude/settings.json` contains no telemetry key at all (so native telemetry is off by absence, not by a flag); `~/.claude/telemetry/` exists and is empty; the debug channel is exact — `2026-08-21T21:52:37.967Z [DEBUG] [3P telemetry] isTelemetryEnabled=false (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=undefined)` and `[WARN] [3P telemetry] Event dropped (no event logger initialized): mcp_server_connection` across 4 debug .txt files. Codex has NO `[otel]` section in config.toml — that source is unverified here. Grok is the finding: `~/.grok/logs/unified.jsonl` carries 209 `trace.upload.decision` lines, 207 of them `"uploads_enabled":true`, and the full context reads `{"trace_upload":true,"trace_upload_source":"remote","telemetry_mode":"true","telemetry_source":"remote","in_env_trace_upload":null,"in_env_telemetry_enabled":null,"in_cfg_telemetry_trace_upload":null,"in_cfg_features_telemetry":null,"has_remote_settings":true,"uploads_enabled":true,"upload_reason":"proxy","data_collection_disabled":false}`.
constraint: Principle 1, and the feature's own honest limit is the thing that needs correcting. It says 'telemetry off means no file turns it on' — on Grok that reading is exactly inverted: every local input is null (`in_env_telemetry_enabled: null`, `in_cfg_features_telemetry: null`) and the vendor enabled uploads REMOTELY (`telemetry_source: "remote"`, `has_remote_settings: true`). A pure config read would report 'telemetry not configured' while 207 turns uploaded. Reconciliation: the card must be evidence-ranked — an observed log decision outranks a config file, a config file outranks absence, and absence renders 'unknown', never 'off'. C7/C5: read OTLP header KEY names and the host only, never values, so the card names the endpoint but never the tenant.

name: os_grants: which AI app can read the screen and the keystrokes
description: For a non-engineer, the most literal version of 'an agent read data from my system without permission' is an AI desktop app holding Screen Recording and Accessibility — it sees every window and every keystroke with no tool call, no MCP server and no agent transcript to parse. Open /Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db and ~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db read-only and select from table `access`: service, client, client_type, auth_value, auth_reason, last_modified, filtered to kTCCServiceScreenCapture, kTCCServiceAccessibility, kTCCServiceListenEvent, kTCCServicePostEvent, kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAllFiles and kTCCServiceMicrophone. `client` is a bundle id, which joins straight to the installed-AI-app census (verified installed here: com.openai.codex at /Applications/ChatGPT.app, com.anthropic.claudefordesktop, com.anthropic.operon, com.electron.wispr-flow). Adds os_grants(bundle_id, service, auth_value, auth_reason, granted_at, db_scope) joined to ai_surfaces; auth_reason is the field that separates a user click from an MDM PPPC push, which is the sanctioned-versus-unsanctioned split the buyer actually needs. Rule ai_app_screen_or_input_grant fires on an AI surface holding ScreenCapture, Accessibility or ListenEvent, and escalates when it holds two of the three, because that combination reads every window and every keystroke on the device.
desktop_surface: Posture screen, OS band, plus a Blast Radius entry per AI app: the systems this application can reach with no agent, tool call or network of its own, sorted by asset tier like every other Blast Radius row.
data_source: /Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db and ~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db, table `access` (service, client, client_type, auth_value, auth_reason, last_modified), opened read-only and joined by bundle id to the installed AI-app census
honest_limit: Verified on this machine that BOTH TCC databases refuse to open without Full Disk Access ('authorization denied'), so without FDA every column is NULL and the attempt is a counted scan_access denial — never a zero and never an empty list rendered as 'no grants'. TCC records the grant, not its use: Vole can say an app MAY read the screen and never that it did. SIP-protected system services and per-invocation 'allow once' decisions do not appear in this table.
competitive_note: EDR vendors read TCC through a kernel or Endpoint Security entitlement, and the market file's own do-not-build list rules an ES sensor out for Vole; this gets the same table from a plain read-only SQLite open under the Full Disk Access grant Vole already requests and already accounts for.
gap_area: The non-developer AI surface: browser extensions with declared reach, agentic browsers, and OS-level intelligence

name: terms_basis: the contract tier that selects the terms, measured per surface
description: The register cannot be keyed on the auth path alone — a personal OAuth login and a Max subscription and an enterprise seat all look like 'OAuth' to the account-class classifier, yet they sit under three different vendor agreements. This reads the contract-tier fields the agents already write: `~/.claude.json` `oauthAccount.{organizationType,billingType,seatTier,organizationRole,organizationRateLimitTier,hasExtraUsageEnabled}` (verified here: organizationType='claude_max', billingType='stripe_subscription'), the Codex rollout `token_count.rate_limits.plan_type` ('team' in 43 rollouts, 'free' in 4), Grok `paywall_check_result.ctx.subscription_tier` ('GrokPro'), OpenCode `account.json` `accounts[].serviceID` + `credential.type`, and Claude's `bridge-session.ownerOrganizationUuid` (HMAC'd, never stored raw). Adds table `terms_basis(surface_id, vendor, plan_token, plan_source, contract_scope, org_ref, first_seen, last_seen, evidence_ref, source)` with a NULL-only widening upsert, since the tokens-only-grow rule on usage_events cannot carry them. contract_scope is a closed enum {consumer, team, enterprise, unknown} and 'unknown' is a stored value, not a default guess.
desktop_surface: A 'Plan' column on the Shadow AI screen and on each surface card in People view, showing the plan token verbatim beside its source file; clicking it opens the evidence drill-down with the file path and the first/last-seen dates. Surfaces with no plan evidence render an em dash in the column, never 'consumer'.
data_source: ~/.claude.json (oauthAccount.*), ~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl (token_count.rate_limits.plan_type), ~/.grok/logs/unified.jsonl (paywall_check_result.ctx.subscription_tier), ~/.local/share/opencode/account.json (accounts[].serviceID, credential.type), Claude transcript bridge-session lines (ownerOrganizationUuid)
honest_limit: A plan token is what the client last cached, not what billing says today; ~/.claude.json is rewritten on login so a mid-window plan change leaves only the newer value, and the first_seen date is the first time Vole saw it, not the date the plan started. Cursor, Antigravity and Devin write no plan field at all, so their contract_scope stays 'unknown' forever. The token names a tier, not a signed agreement — a negotiated DPA is invisible here.
competitive_note: Anthropic's own Compliance API excludes API-key, Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry and personal accounts, so the vendor console cannot tell an admin which tier a laptop session actually ran under; JetBrains Console excludes BYOK and provider-account agents for the same reason.
v1_ref: Account-class classifier from the auth path
gap_area: AI-vendor processing register: where the data landed, under whose law, and on what default terms

name: Grant and override ledger: which file granted this authority, and what weakens the guardrails
description: One posture_grants table answering both halves of 'who gave the agent this authority'. First, resolve each autonomy interval against the settings precedence chain, highest first - /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json (absent here), ~/.claude/settings.json (skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt=true here, a host-level do-not-even-ask flag), ~/.claude/settings.local.json, the repo's own .claude/settings.local.json, ~/.claude.json projects[cwd].allowedTools - and store the winner as granted_by with a path_class of managed / user / project / repo_controlled / unknown. Second, the same pass normalises every cross-agent switch that weakens a guardrail, quoting the literal value: Claude Desktop preferences.bypassPermissionsOptInByAccount and bypassPermissionsGateByAccount (both true for account 909a1169-... here) plus coworkScheduledTasksEnabled, ccdScheduledTasksEnabled and remoteToolsDeviceName; ~/.codex/config.toml [projects."<redacted-local-path>"].trust_level = "trusted" (the entire home directory); ~/.grok/config.toml [ui].yolo and permission_mode; Claude remoteControlAtStartup and enableAllProjectMcpServers. Two rules: grant_repo_controlled (critical - the file that granted the authority lives inside the repository the agent is working on, the CVE-2026-21852 project-file shape) and credential_in_agent_config, storing file, key name and shape class only - verified live, ~/.codex/config.toml [shell_environment_policy.set] carries a literal ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN value and ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4141.
desktop_surface: Supply Chain > Grants: a 'where the autonomy came from' table (one row per grant source with its class, the keys it sets, how many sessions it covered, red flag on repo-controlled sources) above an Overrides table grouped by agent, each row printing the literal key = value, the file it came from and a scope column (global / per-project / per-account), with home-directory and wildcard scopes flagged amber.
data_source: /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json; ~/.claude/settings.json (verified: permissions.allow 9 entries, skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt=true, remoteControlAtStartup=false, effortLevel xhigh); ~/.claude/settings.local.json; <repo>/.claude/settings.local.json; ~/.claude.json projects[*].allowedTools; ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json preferences.*; ~/.codex/config.toml [projects.*].trust_level and [shell_environment_policy.set]; ~/.grok/config.toml [ui].
honest_limit: The CLI invocation appears in no log, so a session launched with --dangerously-skip-permissions and one switched with /permissions at the first turn are indistinguishable; when no settings file explains the observed posture, granted_by is 'unknown' and the panel says so rather than guessing a flag. These are snapshots of now and must never be stamped onto historical rows (backup replay is the only route to earlier states); settings files are mutable with no history, so a grant edited between polls is unrecoverable and the table records only what Vole observed and when. Values are stored as sha256 plus a class, never verbatim, the exception being switch names with their boolean literals; the Desktop account UUID is an opaque id and nothing is read from the adjacent oauthAccount block. Whether an override is a violation is policy input - there is no numeric posture score.
competitive_note: v1 mentions skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt and checks managed-settings presence and hash, but never resolves which layer actually won for a given session, and does not normalise Claude Desktop's per-account bypass opt-in, Codex home-directory trust_level or Grok yolo/permission_mode into one cross-agent table. Nx s1ngularity (2025-08-26) weaponised exactly these switches across three agents at once, and Lakera (2026-04-27) found 33 live credentials in .claude/settings.local.json files shipped on npm. Snyk Agent Scan and Invariant inventory these files without resolving precedence; Zenity reads hooks and OTel but not the chain.
v1_ref: Permission allowlist and managed-settings posture; Workspace trust and repo-controlled permission exposure
field_verified: Every override verified verbatim. `~/.claude/settings.json`: `"skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt": true`, `"effortLevel": "xhigh"`, `"remoteControlAtStartup": false`, permissions.allow with 9 entries. Claude Desktop `preferences`: `"bypassPermissionsOptInByAccount": {"909a1169-d7f6-4e37-9a6b-576514ef1ef9": true}`, `"bypassPermissionsGateByAccount": {"909a1169-...": true}`, `"coworkScheduledTasksEnabled": true`, `"ccdScheduledTasksEnabled": true`, `"remoteToolsDeviceName": "shivas-macbook-pro-local"` (17 preference keys total; `enableAllProjectMcpServers` is NOT among them). `~/.codex/config.toml`: `[projects."<redacted-local-path>"] trust_level = "trusted"` and `[shell_environment_policy.set] ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN = "litellm-899D6018-..."`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL = "http://localhost:4141"`. `~/.grok/config.toml`: `[ui] yolo = false`, `permission_mode = "auto"`. TWO SOURCES DO NOT EXIST: `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json` (`No such file or directory`), and `defaults read com.anthropic.claudecode` -> `Domain does not exist`. AND THE PRECEDENCE CHAIN'S PROJECT LAYER IS EMPTY: 21 of 23 projects carry an `allowedTools` KEY but `[(p,v['allowedTools']) for p,v in projects.items() if v.get('allowedTools')]` returns `[]` — every one is `[]`.
constraint: Principle 1 and C5, at the design level. With the managed layer absent and every project allowedTools empty, 'which layer won' is predicted from two files — that is Vole guessing the agent's resolution order, which is precisely inventing a number. Reconciliation, and it inverts the feature: the observed mode is already recorded per turn. Across ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl, `permissionMode` on `user` lines counts auto 754, bypassPermissions 626, default 47, plan 5, plus 86 `type='permission-mode'` bypassPermissions and 13 auto entries — 1,384 raw `bypassPermissions` occurrences. Read the observed mode first, then attribute it to a layer, and stamp granted_by='unknown' when no file explains it. Also: C6 (posture_grants needs a source column), and grant_repo_controlled needs `git ls-files` inside a user repo — the same subprocess consent class as codesign, opt-in and slow.

name: detection_epochs: rules have a birthday, and an empty history has to say which kind of empty it is
description: A retro-hunt applies today's knowledge to yesterday's evidence, which makes "no incidents before March" ambiguous between nothing happened and nothing was looking. Adds `detection_epochs(rule, content_rev, evaluated_from, evaluated_to, first_run_at)`, written by the same insert-gated detection pass that already keeps scan cursors, and extended backwards only as far as a hunt or pack-bump re-scan genuinely scanned. Backdated incidents keep the constraint intact — `anomaly_key = rule:indicator_id:evidence_row_identity`, never now() — while `window_start` carries when it happened and `detected_at` when it was found, plus a basis string ("found by hunt run 41 on 7 Sep; rule shipped 2 Sep; evaluated back to 15 Aug"). Every read model that would render an empty rule history renders "not evaluated before <evaluated_from>" instead of a zero.
desktop_surface: A left-hand cutoff marker on every rule's history sparkline, and a line in the incident detail sheet separating occurred-at from evaluated-at so a months-old incident that surfaced today cannot be misread as a months-old alert nobody acted on. Feeds the same two dates into the evidence bundle.
data_source: detect pass scan cursors; content_packs registry and content_rev on incidents; hunt_runs; anomalies.window_start / detected_at
honest_limit: An epoch proves a rule ran over an interval, not that the evidence the rule needed existed in it — it must be read beside answerable_from, and the two will legitimately disagree when a rule was evaluated over a window whose sources were already pruned. It also cannot speak for rules that were never shipped at all.
competitive_note: An auditability point no vendor in the matrix makes: SIEM and EDR retro-hunts return hits without stating the detection's own effective date, so a quiet quarter reads as a clean quarter. This is the same class of claim as EU AI Act Art. 12 logging evidence (market.md L160) and is what makes a backdated incident defensible rather than alarming.
gap_area: Indicator retro-hunt: 'an advisory just named X — were we exposed, when, and what happened next'

name: Workspace-trust transitions and untrusted-execution rule
description: Snapshot ~/.claude.json projects[<cwd>].{hasTrustDialogAccepted, allowedTools, mcpServers, enabledMcpjsonServers, hasClaudeMdExternalIncludesApproved, hasClaudeMdExternalIncludesWarningShown} into workspace_trust each poll - 23 projects here, 14 with hasTrustDialogAccepted=false - alongside Codex [projects.*].trust_level and OpenCode session.directory, and own the transitions the static override ledger cannot see. Three rules: untrusted_workspace_execution (tool calls executed in a cwd whose trust flag is false), fresh_clone_then_trusted (a trust flag flipping true within N seconds of the first session in a directory whose .git birthtime is the same day - the Keyv worm and Claude Code project-file RCE shape) and external_includes_approved (hasClaudeMdExternalIncludesApproved flipping true, the exact moment repo-controlled instructions are allowed into the context).
desktop_surface: Supply Chain > Workspaces: a table of directory class, trust state, MCP servers enabled from repo config and tool calls executed, with a timeline strip of trust flips per workspace; a flip inside the fresh-clone window renders as a critical incident card quoting both poll timestamps.
data_source: ~/.claude.json projects[*].{hasTrustDialogAccepted, allowedTools, mcpServers, enabledMcpjsonServers, hasClaudeMdExternalIncludesApproved, hasClaudeMdExternalIncludesWarningShown}; .git/ birthtime of the cwd; ~/.codex/config.toml [projects.*].trust_level; ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db project.worktree and session.directory.
honest_limit: ~/.claude.json is a single mutable JSON file with no change history, so Vole can only report 'this key differed between poll N and poll N+1' and cannot attribute the change to a session or a person unless a tool call in the same interval named the file; a flip and flip-back inside one poll interval is invisible. Directory paths are stored as a salted hash plus a coarse class (home / repo / tmp / node_modules), so the panel names the class, not the path. Only Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode expose a trust concept at all - every other collected tool's column is NULL. localSettingsSeenGitTracked is null everywhere despite the file being git-tracked in three repos here, so the repo-controlled edge is driven by `git ls-files`, and the flag is quoted as 'tool reports null'.
competitive_note: v1 reads the same flags but as a static snapshot with home_directory_trusted / repo_controlled_permissions / all_project_mcp_auto_enabled; the transition rules - trust flipping on a same-day clone, external includes being approved mid-stream, calls executing under trust=false - are what the Keyv worm and CVE-2026-21852 actually look like. No competitor reads hasTrustDialogAccepted: vendor telemetry does not emit it and the SASE and proxy vendors (Netskope, Zscaler, Cato) never see the file.
v1_ref: Workspace trust and repo-controlled permission exposure
field_verified: Verified, and one inherited claim is now wrong. `~/.claude.json` has 23 projects; `Counter(hasTrustDialogAccepted)` = `{False: 14, True: 9}` — exactly as claimed. Key frequency across projects: hasTrustDialogAccepted 23, allowedTools 21, enabledMcpjsonServers 21, hasClaudeMdExternalIncludesApproved 21, hasClaudeMdExternalIncludesWarningShown 21, mcpServers 16. `hasClaudeMdExternalIncludesApproved` is false on all 21, so external_includes_approved has no positive example and can only ever fire on a future flip. THE INHERITED CLAIM IS FALSE: the write-up repeats v1's 'localSettingsSeenGitTracked is null everywhere' — it appears on exactly one project, `<redacted-local-path>`, with the value `True`. Codex side verified: `[projects."<redacted-local-path>"] trust_level = "trusted"` plus two more trusted paths. Fresh-clone detection is feasible: `stat -f "%SB" .git` -> `Aug 29 18:57:08 2026` (birthtime available, reachable as fs.statSync().birthtime).
constraint: C3 is the unresolved one. anomaly_key must be deterministic and must never include now(), but a trust flag that goes true -> false -> true produces an identical (project, key, old, new) tuple twice, and INSERT OR IGNORE (db.ts:137) silently swallows the second — the flip-back-and-flip-again case, which is the interesting one, disappears. Reconciliation: key on (project, key, old, new, transition_ordinal) where the ordinal comes from a monotone counter in the snapshot table, not from the clock. The path-hashing proposal conflicts with C7 and with usage_events.project the same way it does in the blanket-approval entry: cwds are already stored in cleartext, so hash them here and the panel cannot join to the sessions that ran under the flag — store the path, mask on export.

name: Policy screen: effective rule thresholds with provenance, read-only by design
description: Render ~/.vole/policy.json and the built-in defaults side by side: for each rule show window, group key, gates, fire and critical thresholds, and where the effective value came from — module default, policy.json global, or a scoped override — plus the sanctioned-agent, sanctioned-model and MCP-server allowlists that the Agents and Posture screens compare against. The app stays a read-only consumer: it explains, diffs and copies a proposed JSON patch and offers Reveal in Finder rather than writing the file behind the operator's back. A drift row appears when the file's hash changed since the last collector pass, and the effective figures come from the anomalies.tuning column, which records what was actually in force at fire time.
desktop_surface: A Policy screen listing rules with their effective values and a provenance chip per value; an Allowlists section for agents, models and MCP servers; a diff view when the file differs from defaults; Copy patch and Reveal in Finder actions.
data_source: ~/.vole/policy.json (the Tier-1 RuleConfig); detect module constants burn-rate.ts:4-7, loop.ts:4-8, error-storm.ts:4-6, rate-limit.ts:4-5, context-pressure.ts:5-7; the anomalies.tuning column.
honest_limit: The screen reflects the policy file this machine reads — under MDM the authoritative copy is a managed preference and a local edit may be overwritten silently, which the screen must label 'managed by your administrator'. It shows configured thresholds, not enforcement: nothing here prevents an agent from doing anything.
competitive_note: v1 defines the RuleConfig contract and the tuning column but gives the desktop app no surface to read them, so the effective threshold is visible only inside an incident detail string. Platform leads asked specifically for policy-drift checks over managed-settings.json, requirements.toml and Gemini system settings because the vendors themselves say those files are bypassable; rendering the effective value with its provenance is the check no vendor console offers.
v1_ref: RuleConfig contract, effective threshold in every incident, conformance tests
field_verified: The five constant blocks exist at exactly the cited lines: burn-rate.ts:4/6/7 (WINDOW_MS, MIN_TOKENS_IN_WINDOW = 20_000, SPIKE_MULTIPLE = 3), loop.ts:4/5/6/8, error-storm.ts:4/5/6, rate-limit.ts:4/5, context-pressure.ts:5/6/7. But there is NO RuleConfig plumbing -- collect.ts calls `detectBySource(all, { live: rateLimits }, Date.now())` with no config argument, and the rules read module constants directly. And the key claim is false today: anomalies HAS NO `tuning` COLUMN (pragma table_info(anomalies) returns 19 columns: id, anomaly_key, rule, severity, tool, session_id, model, window_start, window_end, title, detail, observed, baseline, threshold, confidence, source, detected_at, user, machine). tuning is proposed by roadmap-v1 L24, not shipped. ~/.vole/policy.json does not exist.
constraint: C11: adding `tuning TEXT` is a legal add-nullable-column migration, but migrate() must learn it and DB.swift assumes newest columns are present. C12: a whole screen with a provenance chip per value is written twice. C14: policy.json is another runtime read to declare.

name: MCP server-instruction rug-pull detector
description: Claude Code persists the full text every MCP server injects into the system prompt: attachment entries of type mcp_instructions_delta carry addedNames[] and addedBlocks[] - 665 occurrences across 622 transcripts here, containing the complete context7 and github instruction blocks verbatim. A posture_injected_text table stores (source, mcp_identity, server_name, block_sha256, block_len, first_seen, last_seen, session_count) - hash and length only, never the text - and mcp_instructions_changed fires when a stable mcp_identity emits a new block_sha256, quoting both hashes, both lengths, both dates and the intervening agent version. Keying on mcp_identity rather than the display name is what makes this a rug-pull detector rather than an inventory: in the MCPoison shape the approved name survives and the endpoint plus its steering text do not.
desktop_surface: Supply Chain > MCP row expands to an 'injected instructions' sub-row: current hash, length in characters, the sessions it was injected into, and a change-history strip; a changed hash renders as a critical incident card carrying both hashes, both lengths and the two dates.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl entries where type='attachment' and attachment.type='mcp_instructions_delta' (fields addedNames, addedBlocks, removedNames), joined to posture_mcp_servers.mcp_identity by server name within the same session's client config.
honest_limit: This is server INSTRUCTIONS, not per-tool descriptions: the poisoned-description variant of the attack (a single tool's description carrying hidden directives) is not in this field, Claude Code does not persist per-tool schemas, and Codex thread_dynamic_tools remains the only place that variant is visible. A first observation cannot be judged good or bad - the rule fires only on change, so a server that was already poisoned at first sight is invisible. Coverage is Claude Code only; Codex, OpenCode, Grok, Cursor, Devin and Antigravity emit no equivalent record and the table says so per tool.
competitive_note: v1's two entries contradict each other: the injection-scan entry states flatly that 'Claude Code does not persist MCP tool descriptions locally' while the census entry counts the same mcp_instructions_delta rows - the instruction blocks are on disk in 665 places and give exact hash-based rug-pull detection, only per-tool descriptions are genuinely absent, and neither entry keys the hash on the endpoint identity. Invariant Labs' 2025-04-01 tool-poisoning writeup names changed descriptions as the core attack and ATLAS CS0053 (postmark-mcp) is a version swap between sessions; no local-first tool detects either.
v1_ref: Offline injection-indicator scans: MCP tool descriptions and ingress content; System-prompt and injected-context census
field_verified: Verified, count corrected. Parsing all 634 transcripts, `attachment.type='mcp_instructions_delta'` = 467 (not 665), and the shape is exactly as described: `{"type":"mcp_instructions_delta","addedNames":["context7","github"],"addedBlocks":["## context7\nUse this server to fetch current documentation...","## github\nThe GitHub MCP Server provides tools..."]}` — the complete instruction text both servers inject, verbatim, on disk. The shortfall is explained and matters: `~/.claude/.last-cleanup` reads `2026-09-07T05:13:50.752Z`, so Claude Code prunes its own transcripts and the corpus shrinks over time.
constraint: C7 (the DB holds no content) — addedBlocks is multi-kilobyte model-steering text; hash and length only, as the feature states. C3 (deterministic anomaly_key, never now()) is satisfied by keying on (mcp_identity, old_sha, new_sha), and that composite also survives INSERT OR IGNORE correctly because a genuine second change carries a different pair. C6: posture_injected_text needs the source column. Hard dependency on F2: the whole claim to being a rug-pull detector rather than an inventory rests on mcp_identity existing, so these two ship together or neither works.

name: processing_terms pack with an as-of-the-evidence lookup, not an as-of-today one
description: A vendor-signed content pack (existing content_packs trust classes, preflight and checksum path unchanged) whose entries carry legal entity, processing region(s), trains-on-input default, retention default, sub-processor status, the plan condition that changes them, a citation URL and an `asserted_as_of` date — plus, critically, `in_force_from`/`in_force_to`, so the resolver `termsAsOf(recipient_id, plan_token, evidence_ts)` returns the terms that were published when the bytes moved, not the terms published today. This is the correction of a live bug: `pricing.json` already carries `effective_from` and `pricing.ts` never reads it, so Vole's one existing dated-fact table silently applies today's figure to last month's row. Adds table `processing_terms`, view `v_processing_register` (one row per recipient × contract_scope × surface with evidence count and first/last seen), and rule `terms_unknown_at_time_of_processing` when the oldest in-force entry post-dates the evidence — an explicit unknown, never the nearest entry.
desktop_surface: A 'Processing Register' section under Privacy Center: one row per recipient with entity, region, training default, retention, each cell footnoted 'vendor's published default, in force <from>–<to>, cited <url>'. Rows whose terms were asserted after the evidence date render the terms cells greyed with a 'terms at the time unknown' chip that cannot be dismissed.
data_source: ~/.vole/packs/processing_terms.<version>.json (vendor-signed, offline checksum), joined to dlp_egress rows and terms_basis; citations are URLs recorded in the pack, never fetched
honest_limit: Every field is a dated assertion with a citation, not a measurement — Vole cannot verify what a vendor does with received bytes, and a vendor that quietly changes a default between pack releases leaves a window Vole will describe with the older entry until the bump lands. The pack is only as complete as its authors; an absent recipient must resolve to unknown and must never inherit a sibling's jurisdiction. Free-tier and preview models (`opencode/deepseek-v4-flash-free`, `openrouter/stealth/ox-alpha` here) frequently have no published terms at all.
competitive_note: No vendor in the 62-row matrix ships a terms register at all: Purview's coding-agent coverage is a domain wildcard list of browser sites, and the SASE vendors classify a destination host inline without attaching an entity, a jurisdiction or a training default to it.
gap_area: AI-vendor processing register: where the data landed, under whose law, and on what default terms

name: Instruction-file hidden-Unicode scan and include graph
description: Track every instruction file an agent may load - repo-root CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md, .cursorrules, .cursor/rules/**, GEMINI.md, copilot-instructions.md, plus the installed plugins' own AGENTS.md - with sha256, byte length and mtime, and run one codepoint-class scan over each: zero-width (U+200B-U+200F), bidi overrides (U+202A-U+202E, U+2066-U+2069), Unicode Tags (U+E0000-U+E007F), soft hyphen (U+00AD) and BOM-in-body. Findings store (file, class, codepoint, count, line_no) and never the surrounding text. A second pass over the same read extracts `@path` includes and joins ~/.claude.json projects[].hasClaudeMdExternalIncludesApproved, so an instruction file pulling text from outside the repo becomes a visible edge rather than a footnote. Verified here: CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md pairs in three repos under ~/Developer plus the plugin cache's own AGENTS.md, and 143 nested_memory attachments proving subdirectory files were actually read - zero hidden-codepoint hits, the honest clean baseline.
desktop_surface: Supply Chain > Instructions: a table of files with size, last-changed, an include-count column and a hidden-codepoint column reading em-dash when clean; a hit opens a detail card naming the codepoint, its count and the line number, with 'text not stored' printed underneath; include edges render as a small graph beside the table.
data_source: CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md / .cursorrules / .cursor/rules/** / GEMINI.md / copilot-instructions.md under project cwds already seen in transcripts; ~/.claude/plugins/**/AGENTS.md; ~/.claude.json projects[].hasClaudeMdExternalIncludesApproved and hasClaudeMdExternalIncludesWarningShown; attachment.type='nested_memory' (143 here).
honest_limit: Zero-width and bidi codepoints have legitimate uses (RTL text, emoji ZWJ sequences), so a hit is a flag for human review at warn severity and never a verdict. Vole scans only files under project cwds it has already seen in transcripts - an instruction file in a repo nobody has opened with an agent is never scanned, and the coverage line states how many projects were in scope. Presence on disk is never claimed as 'loaded': only nested_memory attachments prove a subdirectory file was actually read, and the root file is shown as present-on-disk.
competitive_note: v1 tracks sha256 and mtime and fires instruction_file_changed, but has no hidden-Unicode detection at all - which is the entire mechanism of the Rules File Backdoor (Pillar, 2025-03-18) and of the Keyv worm's zero-width payloads in .cursorrules and CLAUDE.md (2026-08-04) - and treats includes as prose rather than as edges. Pillar sells a rules-file scanner but is not an endpoint monitor and keeps no per-session load evidence.
v1_ref: Instruction-file inventory, drift and load evidence
field_verified: Clean baseline confirmed by running the scan. Ten instruction files exist under ~/Developer, ~/Desktop and ~/.claude/plugins — CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md pairs in LaunchSafe/platform, LaunchSafe/launchsafe and LaunchSafe/.platform-e2e plus the plugin tree's own AGENTS.md; a regex pass for U+200B-200F, U+202A-202E, U+2066-2069, the U+E0000-E007F Tag block and U+00AD returned `total hit files 0`. No .cursorrules and no GEMINI.md exist anywhere on this machine. `nested_memory` = 28 attachments (not 143), and the shape carries a field the write-up misses: `{"type":"nested_memory","path":"<redacted-local-path>","content":{"type":"Project","content":"@AGENTS.md\n","contentDiffersFromDisk":false},"displayPath":"platform/CLAUDE.md"}` — the vendor itself reports whether the loaded text matched disk, and the `@AGENTS.md` include syntax is present in the very first sample.
constraint: C7 — this reads file CONTENT, which the constraint permits precisely because 'DLP scanning happens on the raw line in the collector'; storing (file, class, codepoint, count, line_no) and never the surrounding text stays inside it. C6: the findings table needs the source column. The unnamed operational constraint is cadence: the collect loop runs every 5 seconds (collect.ts:29-75) and re-reads everything, so a full-content Unicode scan of every instruction file in every known project on that cycle is an energy bug on a laptop — reuse the (path, size, mtime) cache pattern from the binary ledger and rescan only on change.

name: declared_dpa_scope_mismatch: the agreement you rely on does not cover the account that ran
description: The register must accept an admin override for a negotiated DPA, and the override is where a compliance tool most easily starts lying. This adds `terms_overrides` under the admin-authored trust class (never vendor-signed, never silently merged into pack rows) with a required `covers` predicate naming the vendor, the contract_scope and, where the vendor exposes one, the org identifier. The rule `declared_dpa_scope_mismatch` fires when evidence exists under a scope the override does not cover — here, an override asserting an Anthropic enterprise ZDR agreement against 14,547 Claude Code rows whose measured `contract_scope` is consumer (`organizationType='claude_max'`, `billingType='stripe_subscription'`), or a Codex override against the 4 rollouts whose `plan_type` is 'free'. Provenance is asymmetric by design: an admin override wins on the terms fields (only the admin has read the contract) and always loses on the plan fields (those are measured), and the incident prints both figures side by side.
desktop_surface: A red 'outside your DPA' banner on the Processing Register row, with the declared scope and the measured scope printed as two adjacent figures and a link to the sessions that fall outside; the override itself renders with an 'admin-authored by <principal> on <date>' byline everywhere it appears.
data_source: ~/.vole/policy/terms_overrides.json (admin-authored, preflight-validated) joined to terms_basis (~/.claude.json oauthAccount.organizationType, Codex rate_limits.plan_type, Grok subscription_tier)
honest_limit: Vole cannot read the contract; it compares an admin's declaration against the plan tokens the clients cached, and both can be stale. A DPA may legitimately cover a tier whose local token Vole cannot distinguish (two enterprise workspaces under one entity look identical on disk), so the rule must be suppressible per override with the suppression counted, not hidden. It proves a scope gap, never that a transfer was unlawful.
competitive_note: Every vendor in the matrix sells the DPA as a procurement artifact; none reconciles it against the account class actually observed on the endpoint, which is precisely the 67%-of-AI-access-on-corporate-devices-uses-non-corporate-accounts gap the DBIR figure names.
gap_area: AI-vendor processing register: where the data landed, under whose law, and on what default terms

name: Plugin declared-capability tier from the marketplace catalog
description: The same `~/.claude/plugins/plugin-catalog-cache.json` lists, per plugin, `components:{commands, agents, skills, hooks, mcpServers, lspServers}` — the vendor's own declaration of what the extension is allowed to do. Derive a capability tier per enabled plugin: declaring hooks, mcpServers or lspServers means the plugin executes code or opens a transport and is high tier; skills and commands only is low tier. Store it beside `unique_installs` and `marketplace_sha` so a plugin that gains a hook in a later catalog refresh shows as a tier change against a recorded sha rather than as a silent upgrade.
desktop_surface: Supply Chain → Plugins shows a capability tier badge per installed plugin with the declared component counts, the catalog sha and fetchedAt it came from, and a diff marker when the tier changed since the last recorded sha.
data_source: ~/.claude/plugins/plugin-catalog-cache.json plugins[].components.{commands,agents,skills,hooks,mcpServers,lspServers}, plugins[].unique_installs, catalog.marketplace_sha, fetchedAt (all verified present).
honest_limit: This is a declaration in a cached vendor catalog, not an observation of behaviour — a plugin that declares no hooks may still ship code that runs via a skill, and a plugin declaring hooks may never fire one. Marketplace plugins only: locally installed and inline plugins have no catalog entry and must render as 'not in catalog' rather than as low tier. Tier changes are only detectable from the shas Vole has actually recorded, so the first observation has no baseline to diff against.
competitive_note: No security vendor in the 62-row matrix tiers coding-agent plugins by whether they declare hook, MCP or LSP execution, and v1's hook inventory reads settings files and hooks.json but never the marketplace catalog that says what a plugin is entitled to do before it is invoked.
v1_ref: Hook inventory and execution ledger
field_verified: Verified in full, and the file carries more than the feature claims. All 290 catalog plugins have `components` with the six named keys; counting plugins with a non-empty list: **skills 235, mcpServers 124, hooks 57, commands 51, agents 32, lspServers 14** — so the high-tier population (hooks ∪ mcpServers ∪ lspServers) is large and the tier actually discriminates. `unique_installs` present on 288 of 290; `catalog.marketplace_sha '0620a687ddd518871772eefd78573baff2dcb8cb'` and `fetchedAt '2026-08-29T07:17:37.379Z'` ✓. Additional provenance the entry does not mention and should: each plugin carries `sha`, `source_sha`, `version`, `last_updated`, and `marketplace_entry.source: {source: 'git-subdir', url: 'https://github.com/…', path, ref: 'v1.5.5', sha: '30287f5e…'}` — a git URL, tag and commit sha per plugin, which is a supply-chain bill of materials, not just a tier. Caveat: `installed_plugins.json` lists one plugin (`ponytail@ponytail`) with no catalog entry, so every INSTALLED plugin here renders 'not in catalog'.
constraint: Constraint 7 (the DB holds no content — only counts, ids, names, paths, hashes): component counts, tier, sha and install counts are all metadata, so this stores cleanly; do not store `marketplace_entry.description`, which is prose. Constraint 6 (new tables carry a source column with the live/seed partition and purge). Principle 2/3: a declaration is not an observation, and the entry says so — 'a plugin that declares no hooks may still ship code that runs via a skill' is the right disclaimer and must survive into the UI, not just the roadmap.

name: residency_evidence with a ranked chain, and an inference_geo that is honestly empty
description: Where the processing happened gets four ranks and never a flag emoji below the top two: `vendor_stated` from Claude's own `usage.inference_geo` field, `route_declared` from a Bedrock cross-region inference-profile prefix on the model id (`us.`/`eu.`/`apac.`/`us-gov.`) or a Vertex/Foundry region in the settings env snapshot, `pack_default` from processing_terms, and `unknown`. The honest headline is that `inference_geo` is present on 40,088 assistant lines here and says `"not_available"` on 34,871 of them and `""` on 5,087 — so the field that would settle the question is, on this account, empty. Adds column `residency_rank` and `residency_value` on the egress rows plus view `v_residency_coverage` printing the share of classified egress with a rank above `pack_default`.
desktop_surface: A 'Region' column on the Processing Register and Leak Ledger whose cell always shows the rank badge beside the value; `pack_default` renders in italic with the pack date, `unknown` renders an em dash. A coverage strip at the top of the register prints 'region evidenced above pack default on N of M rows'.
data_source: Claude transcripts: assistant line usage.inference_geo (verified present, values not_available/empty); usage_events.model prefix; ~/.claude/settings.json and settings.local.json env snapshot (AWS_REGION, CLOUD_ML_REGION); processing_terms pack region field
honest_limit: On this machine every inference_geo value is `not_available`, so the top rank is currently unreachable for Claude — the feature must ship being visibly empty rather than falling back to a guess. Zero Bedrock rows exist here, so the geo-prefix parser is untested against real traffic and degrades to NULL. A pack default names where a vendor says it processes by default, which a routing decision inside the vendor can override without telling the client.
competitive_note: Cursor's enterprise OTel export ships per-event tokens and cents with no residency field; Anthropic's Analytics API is daily and excludes Bedrock/Vertex entirely, which is exactly the path where residency is decided.
gap_area: AI-vendor processing register: where the data landed, under whose law, and on what default terms

name: Plugin and marketplace provenance with cross-agent blast radius
description: One walk of the installed plugin trees plus the marketplace registries answers both where a plugin came from and how far a single approval reaches. posture_marketplaces(source, name, source_type, source_url, pinned_revision, install_location, last_updated) is filled from ~/.claude/plugins/known_marketplaces.json, plugin-catalog-cache.json, ~/.claude/settings.json extraKnownMarketplaces, ~/.codex/config.toml [marketplaces.*] and ~/.grok/config.toml [[marketplace.sources]]; posture_plugin_targets(plugin_id, marketplace_url, git_sha, target_agent, manifest_file, component_kind) is filled from the manifests each installed tree ships. Verified live: Codex declares three marketplaces, two with source_type='local' under user-writable paths (<redacted-local-path> and <redacted-local-path>) and claude-plugins-official pinned at last_revision 10dee3b3...; Grok points at github.com/xai-org/plugin-marketplace.git; and the single third-party Claude plugin (ponytail@ponytail v4.9.0, github.com/dietrichgebert/ponytail.git, gitCommitSha 2ed6c52c...) ships hooks/claude-codex-hooks.json, hooks/copilot-hooks.json, hooks/qoder-hooks.json, gemini-extension.json, opencode.json, plugin.yaml, a pi-extension/, its own ponytail-mcp/ server, skills/, commands/ and scripts/ - one approval declaring reach into five agents. Rules: marketplace_revision_changed, marketplace_source_user_writable and plugin_multi_agent_reach.
desktop_surface: Supply Chain > Plugins: a card per plugin listing target agents as icon chips and declared component kinds (hooks / MCP / skills / commands / scripts) with a 'reach: 5 agents' figure, above a Marketplaces table of source-type icon, URL or path, pinned revision short-sha, last-updated date and a warning chip on user-writable local sources; clicking an agent chip filters the Hooks and MCP tabs to that plugin's entries, and revision changes appear in the History timeline.
data_source: ~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json (installPath, version, installedAt, gitCommitSha), known_marketplaces.json (source.url, installLocation, lastUpdated), plugin-catalog-cache.json; the installed tree's hooks/*.json, *-extension.json, opencode.json, plugin.json, plugin.yaml, ponytail-mcp/; ~/.claude/settings.json extraKnownMarketplaces; ~/.codex/config.toml [marketplaces.*] and [plugins.*]; ~/.grok/config.toml [[marketplace.sources]].
honest_limit: Reach is what the package DECLARES, not what a given agent loaded - a copilot-hooks.json in the tree proves intent to target Copilot, never that Copilot read it - and Vole cannot see plugins installed into agents it has no collector for. Vole never fetches: a pinned revision is compared against the already-cloned tree with a read-only `git rev-parse HEAD` in installLocation, so when that tree is absent drift is 'not evaluable', never 'clean'.
