The same table reports the internal contradiction already present here — mcpDisabled:false carrying mcpReason:'admin_disabled' — as control_state_inconsistent rather than picking a winner. profileArn also names the paying AWS account and region, so a Bedrock-routed Kiro seat stops being console-invisible spend of unknown ownership.
desktop_surface: Posture gains an 'Admin says / device did' pair per control, each with the resolved_at that makes staleness visible; Reconciliation gains the hashed tenant reference as a join key into whichever AWS account actually pays for these tokens.
data_source: ~/.kiro/logs/<stamp>/kiro.log lines [GovernanceService] Resolved, [KiroAgent] Resolved capabilities, agent_controller.triggered; ~/.kiro/sessions/<hash>/sess_<uuid>/session.json (autopilot, agentMode, _meta.kiro.policyPreset)
honest_limit: This is the vendor's client-side resolution of policy, not the console's current state: it is only as fresh as the last launch, so a device that has not launched since a policy change shows a stale value and must display resolved_at next to it. It proves what the client received, never what the admin intended. The account id is stored hashed; region and service stay in clear because they are not personal data.
competitive_note: JetBrains Console reports adoption and credits, not enforcement; every vendor console shows the setting an admin chose, and none compares it against what a device then did. This is the only signal that says a control did not take, and it needs no console credential at all.
gap_area: Editor-embedded agent task stores (Cline, Roo/Kilo, Kiro, Zed, JetBrains) across every VS Code fork root

name: Measured collection posture: the vendor turned uploads on remotely, and here are the receipts
description: Grok CLI writes the one thing every other posture feature can only assert: a per-session precedence chain for its own data collection. `trace.upload.decision` carries `{trace_upload, trace_upload_source, telemetry_mode, telemetry_source, in_requirement_pin, in_env_trace_upload, in_env_telemetry_enabled, in_cfg_telemetry_trace_upload, in_cfg_features_telemetry, in_remote_trace_upload_enabled, has_remote_settings, uploads_enabled, upload_reason}` — on this machine 209 decisions with `trace_upload_source:"remote"` and every local input NULL, i.e. the vendor's server enabled trace upload and no local setting contested it. Beside it, 274 `repo_state.upload.enqueued` lines record `{turn_number, size_bytes, gcs_path, blobs}` and `repo_state.upload.start` records `{repo_path, phase}` — measured receipts that whole-repository tarballs left for a Google Cloud Storage object path. Adds `collection_posture_decisions` and `vendor_upload_receipts` tables and rules `upload_posture_set_remotely` (local config had no say) and `repo_body_uploaded` (bytes, repo, object path, turn).
desktop_surface: An 'Uploads' band on the Posture screen listing, per agent, who decided the collection setting (local / env / remote / unset) with the field names as evidence; a drill-down table of upload receipts with repo path, phase, byte count and destination object path, summed per repo on the Blast Radius screen.
data_source: ~/.grok/logs/unified.jsonl msg='trace.upload.decision' ctx.* and msg='repo_state.upload.{start,enqueued}' ctx.{repo_path,phase,turn_number,size_bytes,gcs_path,blobs}
honest_limit: Only Grok CLI logs this; for every other agent the collection posture stays a config reading, and the absence of receipts is not evidence that nothing was uploaded. The gcs_path is an object key inside the vendor's bucket, not a bucket name, region or account — Vole cannot say which cloud region or legal entity holds it. size_bytes is what the client enqueued, not what the server acknowledged.
competitive_note: Market research found no vendor that reads Grok CLI, OpenCode, Devin or Antigravity at runtime — only Snyk scans their configs — so these receipts are currently read by nobody, including xAI's own customers.
v1_ref: Native-telemetry and prompt-logging posture per agent
gap_area: AI-vendor processing register: where the data landed, under whose law, and on what default terms

name: Plugin install-vs-use reconciliation (ghost and orphan plugins)
description: Three registries disagree on this machine and the gap is the finding. ~/.claude.json pluginUsage records the vendor's own counters for seven entries - ponytail@ponytail usageCount 3455 / lastUsedNumStartups 79, ponytail@inline 2434, caveman@inline 2406, caveman@caveman 1296, anthropic-skills@inline 2, rust-analyzer-lsp@claude-plugins-official 0, 1.0.0@inline 0 - while installed_plugins.json lists only ponytail@ponytail, ~/.claude/settings.json enabledPlugins enables only ponytail@ponytail, and ~/.claude.json enabledPlugins is null. A reconciliation view joins the three Claude registries plus ~/.codex/config.toml [plugins."name@marketplace"].enabled (15 entries) and emits plugin_used_not_installed (ran, but no install record - the install record was deleted or the plugin loaded from elsewhere) and plugin_installed_not_enabled, each quoting the vendor's own usageCount and lastUsedAt.
desktop_surface: Supply Chain > Plugins gains a Reconciliation section: three columns (enabled / installed / used) with mismatched rows highlighted and the vendor's own usageCount, lastUsedAt and lastUsedNumStartups printed beside each row.
data_source: ~/.claude.json pluginUsage{usageCount, lastUsedAt, lastUsedNumStartups} and enabledPlugins (null here); ~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json; ~/.claude/settings.json enabledPlugins and extraKnownMarketplaces; ~/.codex/config.toml [plugins.*].enabled.
honest_limit: lastUsedAt is a single epoch and the registry keeps no history, so 'used 1296 times' is a lifetime total with one timestamp that can never be split across a date range or attributed to a session. A plugin uninstalled cleanly legitimately leaves a usage record behind, and the four '@inline' entries here are a marketplace-naming artefact rather than a ghost install - so used_not_installed is a question at info severity, never a violation. Codex records enabled/disabled but no usage counter, so its used column is NULL, and Grok exposes neither.
competitive_note: v1 records attributionPlugin per response but never reconciles the vendor's own three registries against each other. Fleet/osquery advertises inventory of MCP servers, AI coding assistants and SKILL files with undocumented depth; nothing in the 62-row matrix surfaces install-registry inconsistency, because it is only visible in the vendor's own local state file, which no proxy or gateway ever reads.
v1_ref: Plugin, skill and marketplace supply-chain inventory
field_verified: All three registries verified to disagree exactly as described. `~/.claude.json` pluginUsage: ponytail@ponytail `{usageCount: 3467, lastUsedAt: 1788799340328, lastUsedNumStartups: 79}` (write-up said 3455 — it is a live counter and has grown, which corroborates rather than contradicts), ponytail@inline 2434, caveman@inline 2406, caveman@caveman 1296, anthropic-skills@inline 2, rust-analyzer-lsp@claude-plugins-official 0, 1.0.0@inline 0. `~/.claude.json` enabledPlugins is `None`. `~/.claude/settings.json` enabledPlugins = `{"ponytail@ponytail": true}` — one entry. `installed_plugins.json` lists ponytail@ponytail only. Codex `[plugins.*].enabled` = 15 entries, no usage counter anywhere in its config. One internal inconsistency worth a column: rust-analyzer-lsp has usageCount 0 but a populated lastUsedAt and lastUsedNumStartups 22.
constraint: Principle 1 — 'used 1,296 times' is a lifetime counter with a single epoch, so it can never be placed in a date range or attributed to a session, and any attempt to show it inside the app's range selector would be inventing a time distribution. Reconciliation: render it outside the range control as an explicitly lifetime figure with its one timestamp, the way the vendor stores it. C6: if this becomes a stored table it needs the source column; better, keep it a view over the registries so there is nothing to purge.

name: Comparability gate: not_comparable is the verdict the third verdict was hiding
description: An indicator can fail to match because it was never here, or because this store cannot express it — and calling the second case "not seen" is the lie this feature refuses. Adds `indicator_matchers(kind, ledger, column, normaliser_id, norm_rev, strength)`: package joins the execution ledger and the resolved lockfile with semver-range semantics; mcp_endpoint joins on the endpoint identity key the registration sweep already uses, never on server name; host normalises to a registrable domain at the same normalisation revision the egress ledger recorded; command_hash is comparable only when the pack's `pattern_id`/`pack_version` equals the store's pattern-pack version. Every hit records `match_strength ∈ identity | shape | prefix`, and any indicator whose construction this store cannot reproduce returns `not_comparable` with the reason ("pattern pack v3 required, store holds v2") instead of a clean negative.
desktop_surface: A fourth counter on the hunt result and a per-indicator reason chip; clicking a not_comparable row shows exactly what would make it answerable (bump the pattern pack, re-scan N retained files, cost in bytes) and offers the bounded re-scan.
data_source: existing round-2 ledgers (package execution, MCP registration by endpoint identity, ai_extensions, context_edges/egress, tool_calls command skeletons with pattern_id + pack_version, secret_sightings); indicator pack files under the signed content-pack path
honest_limit: A shape match over a command skeleton can collide — two different commands can share a skeleton — so shape-strength hits are evidence to read, not proof, and are never promoted to identity. Fixing a not_comparable command_hash requires re-hashing retained evidence under the pack's pattern version, which the retention window and byte budget may not cover.
competitive_note: Every content-storing vendor (Cyberhaven, Nightfall, Harmonic, MintMCP) can grep raw text and will always return seen/not-seen, because they kept the content; Vole keeps hashes, so it must earn the negative. No competitor in the 62-vendor matrix publishes a not-comparable state — the honest cost of not storing prompts, turned into a visible field.
gap_area: Indicator retro-hunt: 'an advisory just named X — were we exposed, when, and what happened next'

name: Pre-Vole residue hunt: the filesystem remembers days the store never saw
description: The store starts on install day; the machine does not, and the s1ngularity-class questions are always about weeks before anybody deployed a monitor. At hunt time only, under a declared byte budget and the existing exclusion-at-open() path, the hunt reads dated residue: `~/.npm/_logs/*-debug-0.log` (bounded by logs-max, 10 here, 14 files present), pnpm's `node_modules/.modules.yaml` and npm's `node_modules/.package-lock.json` under the declared work_roots for exact resolved versions, Homebrew `/opt/homebrew/Cellar/*/*/INSTALL_RECEIPT.json` (`time`, `source.versions`) and `Caskroom/<cask>/<version>/`, and `~/.vscode/extensions/extensions.json` plus `.obsolete`. Adds `residue_hits(indicator_id, artifact_path, recorded_ts, ts_basis, still_present, hunt_run)` as its own evidence class ranked strictly below a ledger hit, and it is the only thing that can move an indicator out of the unanswerable bucket for the pre-install period.
desktop_surface: A separate "before Vole" section under the hunt result, visually demoted, each row labelled with whose clock the date came from (install receipt time, log filename, lockfile mtime) and whether the artifact is still on disk.
data_source: ~/.npm/_logs; node_modules/.modules.yaml and node_modules/.package-lock.json under work_roots; /opt/homebrew/Cellar/*/*/INSTALL_RECEIPT.json; /opt/homebrew/Caskroom/<cask>/<version>/; ~/.vscode/extensions/extensions.json and .obsolete
honest_limit: Residue proves presence, not execution: a lockfile entry proves resolution, an install receipt proves an install, neither proves the postinstall ran or the agent used it. Dates come from the artifact's own recorded time — Vole did not observe them — and a deleted node_modules or a pruned log leaves nothing at all, so absence here is worth less than absence in a ledger.
competitive_note: Fleet/osquery inventories the present state with no history, and every SaaS competitor's timeline starts at deployment day; reading the package manager's own dated receipts is the only way to answer an advisory that predates the pilot — precisely the Nx s1ngularity and Keyv-worm question shape (market-extracts incidents 2025-08-26, 2026-08-04).
gap_area: Indicator retro-hunt: 'an advisory just named X — were we exposed, when, and what happened next'

name: Posture screen with three-state controls and an evidence coverage ratio
description: One card per host control - permission/approval mode per agent, sandbox policy, MCP servers registered, hooks installed, instruction-file drift, binary signing, agent version against the advisory floor, marketplace pinning, vendor upload posture - each rendered as pass / fail / unknown, where unknown is a first-class state that names why (file unreadable, tool not installed, no run recorded). The header shows a coverage ratio, 'evidence for 11 of 17 controls', because a screen of green ticks over missing evidence is the exact failure mode EU AI Act audits and SOC 2 CC7.1 punish. Every card reads the posture_snapshots rows the other features write, keyed by fields the collectors already see: Codex turn_context.approval_policy and sandbox_policy.type, Claude permission-mode entries, ~/.grok/config.toml [ui].yolo and permission_mode, Devin configOptions[mode].
desktop_surface: Posture: control cards grouped by Autonomy / Supply chain / Configuration, each showing state, the evidence path, the last-checked timestamp and a drill-down listing the sessions or files that produced the verdict; a coverage bar in each section header, and an export that carries the unknown count into the evidence pack.
data_source: posture_snapshots and the per-feature tables (posture_binaries, posture_mcp_servers, posture_grants, workspace_trust, posture_hook_runs, posture_marketplaces); Codex rollout turn_context.{approval_policy, sandbox_policy.type, permission_profile}; Claude permission-mode entries and settings layers; ~/.grok/config.toml; Devin meta.info.configOptions[mode].
honest_limit: Absence of evidence is never compliance: a control with no artifact stays unknown and must never count toward the pass ratio, and the ratio itself is the headline rather than a score. Config files record intent, not enforcement - Google states its own Gemini system settings are 'not a foolproof security boundary' - so a 'sandbox on' card proves the setting, not the containment. Every card's query must be written twice (queries.ts and the DB.swift port) or the app cannot render it, which is most of the effort here.
competitive_note: v1 defines the storage and the diff CLI but no screen and no coverage semantics, so nothing stops a partially-collected fleet rendering as all-green. Snyk's agent-scan reads the same config surface for free but keeps no history and has no console; Cyberhaven and CrowdStrike infer posture from a kernel-level sensor and report confidence, not evidence paths. A three-state, evidence-linked posture card with an explicit unknown count is the audit artifact neither shape produces.
v1_ref: Posture snapshots, vole posture CLI and vole_posture MCP tool
field_verified: Every named input verified except one taken from the code map rather than the machine. Codex rollouts (66 files): `"approval_policy":"never"` x21 and `"on-request"` x5; `"sandbox_policy":{"type":"danger-full-access"` x8, `"read-only"` x9, `"workspace-write"` x2 — plus a developer message spelling it out in prose: `sandbox_mode is danger-full-access: No filesystem sandboxing - all commands are permitted. Network access is enabled. Approval policy is currently never.` Claude permission modes are richer than the write-up assumes: `permissionMode` on user lines counts auto 754, bypassPermissions 626, default 47, plan 5, and there are 86 `type='permission-mode'` bypassPermissions entries plus 13 auto. `~/.grok/config.toml` `[ui] yolo = false`, `permission_mode = "auto"`. Devin configOptions[mode] I did not open a .db to confirm — I am citing the code map ("[id=mode] ('bypass'/'accept-edits')") rather than the machine; 54 acp-messages .db files do exist.
constraint: C13 is the whole cost and the write-up half-admits it: DB.swift is 274 lines porting five queries, DashboardView is 709 lines with four sidebar sections (Dashboard, Incidents, Breakdown, Settings). This feature adds a fifth section plus one card per control, each with a drill-down, each query written twice or the app cannot render it. C4 also bites subtly: pass/fail/unknown must NOT be stored in or named after `confidence`, which is exactly two values by policy — it needs its own control_state column, or a reader will eventually run MIN(confidence) across it the way queries.ts:80 already does and produce nonsense. C5: an unknown control must never count toward the pass ratio.

name: Two trust classes: vendor-signed content vs admin-authored policy, and the customer trust anchor
description: The six content artefacts do not share a trust model and pretending they do is the round-2 brief's mistake: Vole can sign dlp_detectors, command_patterns, advisory_floor, semconv and pricing, but it can never sign the customer's own sanctioned-surface allowlist or rule thresholds, because the customer holds no Vole key. `content_packs.trust` splits kinds into `vendor_signed` and `admin_authored`; admin content is trusted by provenance instead — a root-owned file under the packs directory, or the managed-preference domain `/Library/Managed Preferences/com.launchsafe.vole.plist` (the app's real bundle id, apps/mac/Info.plist:8) — and `signed_by` records exactly which of `vole_builtin | anchor:<fp> | managed_pref | root_file_unsigned | user_file` applied. An enterprise that wants its own allowlist signed installs an Ed25519 public key as `ContentTrustAnchor` in that managed profile; matching packs then verify against it and record `anchor:<fp>`. The UI must never render a checkmark or the word "signed" over `root_file_unsigned` or `user_file`.
desktop_surface: The Content table's signer column prints the literal trust string, never an icon; the Policy screen shows each effective threshold and allowlist entry with its trust class beside the provenance it already renders; an admin_authored pack on an unmanaged machine reads "authored on this machine".
data_source: /Library/Managed Preferences/com.launchsafe.vole.plist (absent here — that directory holds only a per-user subdir, so this machine is unmanaged); file ownership and mode of /Library/Application Support/Vole/packs/*.json via fs.statSync; ~/.vole/policy/*.json for the user-authored case.
honest_limit: Provenance-based trust is exactly as strong as the filesystem: where the developer is a local admin, a root-owned pack proves nothing about who wrote it, and Vole labels it root_file_unsigned rather than implying otherwise. Vole also cannot distinguish a managed preference written by MDM from one written by a local root shell, and says so.
competitive_note: Cursor's enterprise control for personal-account login is MDM-only Allowed Team IDs (cursor.com/docs/enterprise/privacy-and-data-governance) — the precedent that a customer's own allowlist arrives by managed preference, not vendor signature. No vendor in the matrix distinguishes vendor-supplied detection content from customer-supplied policy in its audit trail.
gap_area: Detection-content lifecycle: how packs, CVE floors and allowlists reach the fleet offline, age, and re-score history

name: content_stale, per kind, with a rule key that ages in steps instead of firing daily
description: `content_stale` fires when a pack's `built_at` exceeds its per-kind floor — default 90 days, but advisory_floor defaults to 30 because an old CVE table means "unknown", not "clean", and semconv is info-only because a stale one is cosmetic. Thresholds resolve through the same policy provenance chain the Policy screen already renders with its effective values. The key is `content_stale:<kind>:<version>:<floor(age_days/30)>`: deterministic and free of `now()`, satisfying the constraint that detect.test.ts:120 pins, so the incident escalates in 30-day steps rather than duplicating every poll or freezing at its first severity under `INSERT OR IGNORE`. Severity caps at warn and the title says the content is old, never that the person did anything.
desktop_surface: A content-age chip beside the menu bar's six honest states and on the coverage strip — grey when current, amber when stale — reading "content 118d old" rather than a red dot; the Policy screen lists each per-kind floor with its provenance next to the thresholds it already shows.
data_source: content_packs.built_at compared against poll time; per-kind floors from the policy precedence chain.
honest_limit: Staleness is measured against the pack's own declared build date, which the pack author controls; with no network Vole cannot know whether a newer pack exists, only how old the one it holds is. An admin on a quarterly MDM cadence will see this fire forever — that is the accurate report, not a bug, and the copy says so.
competitive_note: EDR vendors surface "sensor out of date" as fleet health backed by their own update channel; Vole's version has to state the inverse plainly — it reports age and can never close the gap. Anthropic's own warning that transcript formats change between versions (market.md L168) makes content age a real detection-coverage claim, not decoration.
gap_area: Detection-content lifecycle: how packs, CVE floors and allowlists reach the fleet offline, age, and re-score history

name: vole packs --preflight: score a candidate pack against this machine's evidence before the fleet gets it
description: `vole packs` prints kind, version, built_at, age, ring, trust, load_state and which entries came from the builtin floor rather than the pack — the support call answered in one line, and the only way a helpdesk can tell a rejected signature from an old pack. `--preflight <file>` goes further: it verifies the candidate's signature, then dry-runs it over the evidence this machine still holds (dlp_scan_state's surviving raw_refs for detector packs, the tool_calls ledger for command-pattern packs, usage_events windows for rule thresholds) and prints findings-added, findings-removed and per-entry hit counts, writing nothing to the store and opening every third-party file read-only. That is the honest way to learn a detector will flood before it reaches 3,000 laptops: run it on the canary ring first, where the evidence is real.
desktop_surface: None by design — an admin CLI, not a user surface. The Settings → Content table's empty state names the command so an admin arriving from the GUI finds it.
data_source: The candidate pack path given on the command line; read-only queries over dlp_scan_state, secret_sightings, tool_calls, anomalies and usage_events in ~/.vole/vole.db.
honest_limit: Preflight measures one laptop's evidence, which is not the fleet's — a detector clean on the canary can still flood elsewhere, and the output labels the sample size it actually saw. It also cannot estimate a true-positive rate, only how many rows would match.
competitive_note: No vendor in the 62-vendor matrix offers a customer-side dry run of a detection-content update: content ships and the false positives arrive with it, which is part of why Harmonic argues blocking is futile and tuning is the real work. A local preflight is only possible because Vole keeps the evidence on the endpoint.
gap_area: Detection-content lifecycle: how packs, CVE floors and allowlists reach the fleet offline, age, and re-score history

name: Approved-baseline snapshot and one-key drift diff
description: Posture is only actionable against a baseline. Add `vole posture baseline` and a Settings button that writes the current posture_snapshots rows — MCP identities, hook command hashes, plugin ids with git shas, marketplace revisions, instruction-file hashes, binary CDHashes, policy-layer hashes — into a human-readable ~/.vole/baseline.json with a capture timestamp and the tool versions in force. Every later poll diffs against it, and the Supply Chain screen shows one 'N changes since baseline' figure expanding to per-item before/after. An admin-owned /Library/Application Support/Vole/baseline.json takes precedence, following the pricing.json override pattern already in the codebase.
desktop_surface: Supply Chain screen header: 'Baseline captured <date> · N changes since', a drift list showing item kind, identity, old hash, new hash and change time, and a 'Set baseline' action whose confirm dialog lists exactly what will be captured and which file is in force.
data_source: posture_snapshots rows keyed on (kind, identity, sha256); ~/.vole/baseline.json; optional admin-owned /Library/Application Support/Vole/baseline.json.
honest_limit: A baseline captured after a compromise blesses the compromise: the UI states the capture date prominently and never calls a matching state 'secure'. A user-writable baseline in ~/.vole proves nothing against the seat owner — only the admin-owned copy is meaningful for enforcement — and items that did not exist at capture time show as 'new since baseline', which is not the same as 'changed'.
competitive_note: v1 gives `vole posture diff --since=7d`, a rolling time-window diff; an explicit approved baseline is the artefact auditors and SOC 2 CC6 reviewers actually ask for, and v1 has no desktop surface for it. Every drift-detection vendor in the matrix (Zenity, Cyberhaven, CrowdStrike) keeps its baseline server-side where the employee cannot inspect it.
v1_ref: Posture snapshots, vole posture CLI and vole_posture MCP tool
field_verified: `posture_snapshots` does not exist; `~/.vole/baseline.json` does not exist. The claimed precedent is half true. The user-level override pattern IS real: paths.ts:21 `pricingOverride: () => process.env.VOLE_PRICING ?? join(home(), '.vole', 'pricing.json')`, merged at pricing.ts:45-52 (`models: { ...BUILTIN.models, ...(o.models ?? {}) }`) inside a try/catch that falls back to BUILTIN. But there is NO admin-directory precedent whatsoever: `/Library/Application Support/Vole` does not exist on this machine, and `grep -rn 'Library/Application Support' packages/core/src apps/mac/Sources` returns exactly one hit — devin.ts:12, a comment about Devin's own path.
constraint: Constraint 8 ('Vole writes only under ~/.vole') — reading an admin-owned /Library file is fine, but the feature should state plainly that Vole never writes there; that file arrives via installer or MDM, not via the app. Constraint 14 is the real one: the SEA collector must do 'no runtime file reads except pricing override and sources', an explicitly enumerated exception list. Adding baseline.json widens that list, which is precisely the quiet widening constraint 14 exists to prevent — amend it in writing to name baseline.json rather than letting the read slip in.

name: Deny-by-default export field registry with a NULL-omitting encoder
description: The 'never a prompt leaves' claim must be structural, not a review habit. Add packages/core/src/export/fields.ts: a frozen table of {column, wire_name, transform} entries (project -> repo_slug|hmac, raw_ref -> dropped, session_id -> passthrough, user/machine -> hmac_or_cleartext per policy identity.mode) and build every payload — OTLP attributes, Splunk HEC event object, Elastic doc, syslog SD-PARAMs — by iterating that table, never from an object literal or a SELECT * spread. The same encoder omits a key entirely when the value is NULL (never 0, never ""), because queries.ts already shows SUM(cost_usd) silently dropping unpriced rows, and it ships sibling counters vole.calls.unpriced / activity_only / model_unknown plus vole.confidence on every metric point and span so a dashboard cannot chart a partial total as a whole one. A post-serialisation guard scans the produced bytes for gen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages, gen_ai.system_instructions, prompt, content, arguments and stdout and throws before any socket write; pnpm verify --content runs that guard over a sample of every sink's real output plus a round-trip row with every nullable column NULL. Putting identity.mode here rather than at the sync writer means the local DB always holds resolved values so the app keeps working, and the transform happens once, in one place, on the way out.
desktop_surface: Settings → Export gains two panels rendered from fields.ts at runtime: 'Fields that leave' (column, wire name, transform, example value) with a second list of columns that are structurally unable to leave, and an 'Absence' strip showing, for the last 24 h of exported rows, the count and share that carried no tokens, no cost and no model — the same three numbers the reference Grafana panel shows. The Privacy Center screen renders the same manifest.
data_source: packages/core/src/schema.ts column list; packages/core/src/db.ts ORIGIN spread; packages/core/src/pricing.ts computeCost returning null; packages/core/src/queries.ts TOKEN_FILTER and SUM(cost_usd); ~/.vole/policy.json identity.mode; the constraint 'the database holds no content' from code-map-extracts.
honest_limit: The registry proves nothing about fields Vole never collected — a reviewer still has to read the collectors to see that tool_use.input was never parsed into memory. HMAC at export is pseudonymisation, not anonymisation, and is meaningless unless the path and hostname transforms run with it: project embeds <redacted-local-path> and machine here is 'Marys-MacBook-Pro.local', a first name. Omission is only half the NULL fix: a downstream sum() still shows a smaller number rather than 'unknown', and Vole can ship the counters and reference dashboards but cannot stop a customer writing a panel that ignores them. A free-text column can also carry content indirectly — anomalies.detail is a rendered English sentence today and must be transformed into parameters or dropped.
competitive_note: Every AI-security vendor in the matrix inspects content (Cyberhaven, Nightfall, Harmonic, Zenity), Cowork's own OTel ships full prompts by default and Gemini CLI's logPrompts defaults true; Cursor labels its exported cost 'best-effort'. A machine-checkable allowlist plus first-class absence counters is the only form in which Vole's differentiator survives a security questionnaire and a FinOps review at the same time.
v1_ref: Redaction manifest and verify --content (prove the DB and exports hold no content)
field_verified: Every input verified present, the output verified absent. schema.ts lists the 25 usage_events columns; db.ts:87 INSERT_EVENT spreads `{...r, ...ORIGIN}`; pricing.ts computeCost returns null for unknown ids; queries.ts:23 `const TOKEN_FILTER = "confidence != 'activity_only'"` and queries.ts:56 `SUM(cost_usd) AS cost` with no unpriced counter beside it — the exact silent-partial the feature names. anomalies.detail is `detail TEXT NOT NULL` (schema.ts:53) and holds rendered English (live row: "Burned 36,751 tokens in 10 min…"). Absent: `grep -rn 'policy.json|export.key|export_state|outbox' packages/core/src apps/mac/Sources` returns nothing, `ls ~/.vole/` is vole.db + wal + shm only, and there is no packages/core/src/export/ directory. The honest_limit's own example checks out verbatim: hostname is `Marys-MacBook-Pro.local`.
constraint: Constraint 7 ('the database holds no content') is what this enforces, not what it strains — good. The real strain is constraint 14 (SEA): the collector must stay zero-runtime-dependency with no runtime file reads except the pricing override and the sources, so fields.ts must be a frozen module inlined by esbuild, and ~/.vole/policy.json must be added to that carve-out explicitly (SECURITY.md says Vole writes only under ~/.vole, so reading a policy file there is consistent). Second: `pnpm verify --content` cannot live in cli/verify.ts as written — it is a 539-line top-level-await script with no argv parsing and is explicitly not importable (code map §7).

name: case_key: the case identity beneath the time bucket
description: Every rule builds anomaly_key ending in the UTC bucket epoch (burn-rate.ts:54, loop.ts:50, error-storm.ts:32, context-pressure.ts:53, rate-limit.ts:24), so the 'stable key' triage assumes is not stable across recurrences: the same runaway loop next window is a different row. Add a nullable case_key column on anomalies plus idx_an_case, emitted by each rule as the identical tuple minus the bucket (rule + source + subject dims, never now(), never a session for burn_rate which groups tool+model). Backfill is exact rather than guessed: on this store the trailing numeric segment equals window_start for 250 of 250 live rows, so rtrim(anomaly_key,'0123456789') recovers the case for every row already written. Dispositions attach to case_key while findings stay one row per window, so a rotated-then-reappearing secret reopens the same case instead of forking it, and the queue's unit of work becomes 49 cases instead of 250 rows.
desktop_surface: Incidents becomes case-first: one row per case carrying 'seen N times, first window / last window', disclosure-triangle expanding to the individual findings with their own figures. The case id is the vole:// deep-link target and the anchor the sidebar open-count counts.
data_source: ~/.vole/vole.db anomalies.anomaly_key and anomalies.window_start (verified 250/250 tail == window_start); key construction in packages/core/src/detect/*.ts
honest_limit: burn_rate_spike's subject is tool+model only, so its case can never be attributed to a session - the session_id on the row is evs[0].session_id (burn-rate.ts:58), the first event in the window, not the case's owner. A pack bump that changes a rule's dimensions produces a new case_key; the old case is retired with the pack version, never silently merged into the new one.
competitive_note: Anthropic states outright that 'anomaly detection, baselining, correlation across sessions, and alerting are the responsibility of your SIEM' (code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage), so no agent vendor ships case identity at all; Sentinel and Splunk ES dedupe by rule+entity but only over what you exported, and Cursor's OTel export has no backfill and no per-session tool attribution, so a SIEM cannot rebuild the case from it either.
v1_ref: Finding lifecycle and acknowledgement

name: Triage queue: the incidents screen the app has never had
description: Today the incident feed (DashboardView.swift:415-525) groups by Calendar.current.startOfDay and prints rule/tool/confidence/detail with no state, no figures and no order but time, over getAnomalies which does not even SELECT observed/baseline/threshold (queries.ts:230). Replace it with a worked queue backed by a new v_triage read model (case_key, rule, worst severity, recurrence count, first/last window, state, state age, principal, the ledger row the case points at) written twice, in queries.ts and DB.swift, per the read-model parity rule. The list is case-first, sorted severity then recurrence then age, with observed/baseline/threshold rendered inline; j/k moves, a/f/x/m disposes, Return opens the ledger row the case points at (tool_calls, secret_sightings, anomaly_context), Escape returns. The sidebar and menu-bar security count switch from findings to open cases, which on this machine is 49 rather than 250.
desktop_surface: New Incidents screen replacing the feed: a left rail of open counts by rule and by disposition, a group-by control (rule | case | principal), a persistent filter bar, a header line reading 'N open / M labelled / K unlabelled', and one-key jump into the evidence viewer.
data_source: anomalies.observed/baseline/threshold/severity/rule/detected_at (schema.ts:42-64) plus finding_actions.state; renders through queries.ts and the DB.swift port
honest_limit: Grouping by principal is a workload view only - counts and ages, never a rate per unit of activity and never a ranking - and it sits behind the same gate and access log as the People view, because 'no productivity axis' has to survive the screen that most tempts you to build one. An empty queue because nobody labelled anything looks identical to an empty queue because nothing fired, which is why the header always carries the unlabelled count rather than a green tick.
competitive_note: None of the 27 agent-covering security vendors in the matrix ships a local queue - all are in-path with a cloud console - and the two OSS comparables on the endpoint, ccusage and agent-audit, have no incidents at all, so 'the analyst's morning list runs on the laptop with no rows leaving it' is unoccupied ground.
gap_area: Incident triage: the analyst's daily loop and detection-quality accounting

name: Timed mute: mandatory expiry, hidden-count and renewal accounting
description: A mute is a finding_actions row with state='muted' and a NON-NULL expires_at; the writer rejects a mute without one, so a mute can never become permanent silence by omission. Detection is untouched - rules still fire and rows still land in anomalies under INSERT OR IGNORE - so the mute only hides the case from the queue and from the notification freshness gate (collect.ts:16,72; Store.swift:151-153), which means the hidden set is fully recoverable. On expiry a sweep flips the case back to open and the queue shows a 'while this was muted' batch with the exact count and window, computed as COUNT(*) FROM anomalies WHERE case_key=? AND detected_at BETWEEN mute_ts AND expires_at. A third consecutive renewal of the same scope emits a suppression_renewed info incident keyed suppression_renewed:<scope_hash>:<renewal_n> - a counter, not a clock, so it fires once per renewal and never absorbs now().
desktop_surface: A mute control in the case row with a required duration picker and a live countdown chip; an Expiring Mutes list in the Policy screen showing scope, expiry, renewals so far and hidden-count to date; the expiry batch appears at the top of the queue as its own group.
data_source: finding_actions.expires_at; anomalies.detected_at and case_key; the notification gate in cli/collect.ts and Store.swift
honest_limit: The hidden count is exact for a mute because the rows were still written, but it is a LOWER BOUND whenever the central suppression register turned the same detector off in the same window - nothing was evaluated then, so both counts must be shown side by side with the register's figure winning. A mute also cannot hide what a stopped collector never saw, so the view joins evidence_gaps and prints unmonitored hours beside the count.
competitive_note: Zscaler and Netskope suppressions are policy-level and open-ended, and v1's own scoped-suppression entry required an expires field but counted nothing and tracked no renewals; the renewal counter is the mechanism behind Harmonic's 'blocking is futile, coach not block' argument applied to the alert itself.
v1_ref: Scoped suppressions stored as auditable info incidents
gap_area: Incident triage: the analyst's daily loop and detection-quality accounting

name: Triage writes take the collector path: the ~/.vole/inbox spool
description: DB.swift opens READONLY and only falls back to READWRITE for WAL edge cases (DB.swift:129-133), and the standing constraint is that it stays a read-only consumer - so triage writes cannot originate in the app process without creating the second writer the store has no busy_timeout for (db.ts:60). Instead the app and the CLIs append one JSON object per line to ~/.vole/inbox/actions.jsonl with O_APPEND and a single write syscall, and an eighth collector reads it using the same byte-offset cursor in collector_state that claude-code.ts:111 already maintains, inserting finding_actions inside the existing single-writer transaction and calling commit() only after the insert succeeds. Every line carries a client-generated action_id that is UNIQUE in finding_actions, so a crash mid-pass replays to a no-op and the whole path is idempotent by exactly the contract usage rows already obey. The same spool carries queue_opened records written when the triage screen comes to the foreground, which is the only way MTTA ever gets an honest denominator.
desktop_surface: Invisible by design, surfaced twice: a pending badge on any action the collector has not yet ingested, and a line in the Privacy Center path receipts naming ~/.vole/inbox/actions.jsonl as a file Vole writes rather than reads.
data_source: new ~/.vole/inbox/actions.jsonl; collector_state byte-offset cursor (schema.ts); paths.ts home() resolution with VOLE_HOME_OVERRIDE honoured
honest_limit: An action taken while the collector is stopped is durable but invisible until the next pass, so the UI shows it from an in-memory echo and the database never learns a fabricated timestamp; two clocks are stored (ts from the app, ingested_at from the collector) and a clock_suspect line is ingested in arrival order, never reordered. Anyone with write access to the home directory can forge a line, so the spool proves an action was requested on this machine, not who requested it.
competitive_note: CrowdStrike, SentinelOne and Jamf all solve this with a privileged Endpoint Security sysext writer, which the research explicitly rules out as unnecessary for file reading and a multi-month Apple process; Santa's four-part layout (app, launchd collector, sync, CLI) is the shape this preserves, and it keeps the single-writer invariant that makes 'no ES entitlement' credible.
gap_area: Incident triage: the analyst's daily loop and detection-quality accounting

name: export_seq change cursor and replay that cannot rewind the live tail
description: Every forwarder needs a resumable cursor, and roadmap-v1's export_state(sink, last_rowid, last_sent_at) is broken by Vole's own upsert: db.ts rewrites an existing row in place when excluded.total_tokens is strictly greater without changing usage_events.id, so a rowid high-water mark never re-sends the corrected row — measured here, 410 of 987 Claude message.id values in one transcript appear 2-3 times, the first copy a streaming placeholder with output_tokens 0, so a rowid-cursor SIEM would keep the zeros forever. Add export_seq INTEGER to usage_events and anomalies, filled from a vole_seq counter in a new export_meta table and bumped inside the same transaction on insert AND on upgrade (the existing ON CONFLICT SET list gains export_seq), with CREATE INDEX idx_ue_export_seq; the cursor becomes WHERE export_seq > ? ORDER BY export_seq, and consumers are told to upsert on document id because the same event_key legitimately arrives twice. On the same column, `vole export --replay --from --to --sink=<name> [--dry-run]` re-reads history through the same encoder and the same outbox but records progress in a separate export_state row (sink:replay), so a backfill can never move the live high-water mark backwards and drop the tail; --dry-run writes payloads to a directory, which is also how the payload inspector and the volume forecast get their bytes.
desktop_surface: Settings → Export: a per-sink row showing last_seq / max_seq and an 'N events behind' number, with a red badge when the gap stops shrinking for two poll intervals; plus a Replay panel with a date-range picker, a dry-run toggle and a cancellable progress row showing rows and bytes sent.
data_source: packages/core/src/db.ts INSERT_EVENT upsert (ON CONFLICT ... WHERE excluded.total_tokens > usage_events.total_tokens); packages/core/src/schema.ts usage_events/anomalies; ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl streaming duplicates of message.id; queries.ts rangeStart.
honest_limit: Only rows whose total_tokens grow are re-emitted. The SET list never touches model, project, git_branch or confidence, so a row corrected downward, or one that merely gains a model value, is invisible to the cursor until that WHERE/SET is widened explicitly. Rows written before the column exists get NULL export_seq and need one ordered backfill UPDATE, which re-sends the whole history to a sink once. Replay reaches only as far back as Vole's own store — rows pruned by retention are gone, and pre-install history is bounded by what the agent still keeps on disk — so a replay window can be silently shorter than the range requested; and on sinks with no server-side dedupe (Splunk HEC, Datadog, syslog) replay creates duplicates by design, which the UI must state before starting.
competitive_note: Cursor's OTel export documents that it has no backfill at all and Copilot's audit stream keeps a 48-hour REST window; Claude Code Analytics is daily with an hour of lag. A correct resumable cursor over a complete local history — replayable after a mapping fix — is a capability the vendor exporters structurally cannot offer.
v1_ref: SIEM forwarder (Splunk HEC / Elastic bulk / Datadog Logs)
field_verified: Premise verified line by line. db.ts:87-101: `ON CONFLICT(event_key) DO UPDATE SET input_tokens=…, total_tokens=…, cost_usd=…, is_error=…, stop_reason=…, tools=…, context_window=…, ts=excluded.ts WHERE excluded.total_tokens > usage_events.total_tokens` — rewrites in place, `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` untouched, so a rowid high-water mark provably never re-sends. The streaming duplicates are real: in one transcript 2,144 unique message.ids across 3,436 assistant lines, 1,070 of them appearing more than once (the feature's '410 of 987' is the same phenomenon in a different file). roadmap-v1.json tier6 feature 9 says verbatim 'export_state(sink, last_rowid, last_sent_at) high-water mark advanced only after 2xx' — the broken design it corrects. No export_seq, no export_meta, no index exists.
constraint: Constraint 2 head-on, and the feature is the required reconciliation rather than a violation: adding export_seq to the ON CONFLICT SET list IS the 'explicit widening' the constraint demands. Two conflicts it under-states. Constraint 11: node:sqlite named binding is strict — export_seq must be added to the INSERT column list, the @params object, the UsageEvent type, schema.ts and migrate() together, or an extra/undefined key throws and aborts the entire batch. Constraint 12: migrate() is add-nullable-column only via PRAGMA probing, so the one-time ordered backfill UPDATE is unavoidable and re-sends all 29.5K rows to a sink once — which on Splunk/Datadog/syslog (no server-side dedupe, per feature 8) means a guaranteed duplicate storm on first upgrade. Say so in the UI before the first drain, not in the docs.

name: control_intents ledger: notification actions that record a request, gated on an exact PID mapping
description: Store.swift:151-176 builds a plain UNMutableNotificationContent with no categoryIdentifier, so an incident notification is informational only. Register a UNNotificationCategory per rule in VoleApp.init with actions Pause session, Quarantine repo, Snooze 1h, Open evidence; pressing one writes a single row to a new control_intents table (intent, target session_id, pid, actor, requested_at, expires_at, state, source) whose state machine is requested -> enforced -> expired_unenforced -> stale_not_sent, and the UI renders that state rather than implying the action happened. Because DB.swift opens SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY (DB.swift:129) and must stay a read-only consumer, and openDb (db.ts:54-64) is a process singleton that mkdirs, execs SCHEMA and migrate and sets no busy_timeout against the collector's 5s writer, the app writes intents to a separate ~/.vole/intents.db (or an append-only JSONL outbox) that the collector folds into vole.db on its next pass through insertEvents' single write path. Pause/Stop renders live only where ~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json supplies an exact pid->sessionId->cwd mapping (verified present here: pid 55648 -> 8d91fabd, cwd <redacted-local-path>, procStart 'Mon Sep 7 05:03:45 2026') and the PID's procStart still matches at press time; everywhere else the button is disabled with the reason on its face.
desktop_surface: Notification Center action buttons per rule; an Actions strip on the incident drill-down; a menu-bar 'action pending' state opening a Requests list showing each intent's state, actor and expiry; disabled Pause/Stop buttons carry their reason inline ('no exact PID mapping for Codex'), and a Requests row that expired shows 'requested, never enforced'.
data_source: apps/mac/Sources/Vole/Store.swift:151-176 and VoleApp.init (UNUserNotificationCenter categories); ~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json {pid,sessionId,cwd,startedAt,procStart,version,entrypoint,kind}; ps lstart for liveness; new control_intents table written through a store the collector owns, never through DB.swift
honest_limit: Vole is out of the request path, so an intent is honoured only where a consumer exists: today that is Claude Code alone (an exact-PID signal, or the hook once it exists). Codex, OpenCode, Grok, Cursor, Devin and Antigravity have no consumer at all, so their rows expire unenforced and the UI must never render that as a completed action. Even the exact mapping is one poll stale: re-verify pid and procStart at press time and record stale_not_sent when it no longer matches. The session file also carries messagingSocketPath (/tmp/cc-socks/<pid>.sock) and peerFeatures ['notify_idle','reply_across_default_dirs','artifact_yield'], an undocumented protocol pinned to CLI version 2.1.263 here, deliberately not used. A second write path is new surface area the read-only DB.swift rule was designed to avoid.
competitive_note: Harmonic, Prompt Security and the SASE vendors (Zscaler, Netskope, Palo Alto, Cato) block inline because they sit in the path, and market.md's own handicap list concedes buyers on Harmonic's 'phase two' will want that. CrowdStrike Falcon Guardian and SentinelOne/Prompt already own the endpoint kill switch with a kernel view Vole does not have; a second, inferred one loses the comparison. Request-and-record with a visible enforcement state is also what CSA's Agentjacking mitigations and the OWASP Agent Control Standard ask for — inspectable and traceable.
v1_ref: Pause / resume / stop a session with confirm-to-act notifications
field_verified: All three named artifacts exist, with two corrections. (a) Store.swift:155-163 is exactly as described — `let content = UNMutableNotificationContent(); content.title = "Vole · \(incident.severity.uppercased())"; content.body = incident.title; content.sound = .default` then `UNNotificationRequest(identifier: "vole-incident-\(incident.id)", content: content, trigger: nil)` — no categoryIdentifier, so informational only. The seam it needs already exists: VoleApp.swift:10 `@NSApplicationDelegateAdaptor(AppDelegate.self)`, AppDelegate at VoleApp.swift:82, and VoleApp.init:33 already calls `requestAuthorization(options: [.alert, .sound])`. (b) ~/.claude/sessions/55648.json verbatim: {"pid":55648,"sessionId":"8d91fabd-b000-440c-bc87-9719dcb5eda1","cwd":"<redacted-local-path>","startedAt":1788757425696,"procStart":"Mon Sep  7 05:03:45 2026","version":"2.1.263","messagingSocketPath":"/tmp/cc-socks/55648.sock","peerFeatures":["notify_idle","reply_across_default_dirs","artifact_yield"]} — mapping confirmed, three live PIDs (22530, 23889, 55648) each with a matching file and socket. CORRECTION 1: procStart is UTC-rendered, `ps lstart` is local — `ps -o lstart= -p 55648` returns "Sun Sep  6 22:03:45 2026" while the file says "Mon Sep  7 05:03:45 2026" (7h = PDT). A literal string compare NEVER matches; the check must be `TZ=UTC ps -o lstart= -p <pid>`, which I ran and which returns "Mon Sep  7 05:03:45 2026" exactly. Ship that as the comparison or the entire gate silently fails closed. CORRECTION 2: the feature's premise that DB.swift is hard read-only is overstated — DB.swift:130-136 tries `sqlite3_open_v2(path, &h, SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY, nil)` and on failure falls back to `SQLITE_OPEN_READWRITE` with a ponytail comment ('WAL databases sometimes refuse a pure READONLY connection'). Read-only is policy (constraint 13), not a lock — which makes the separate-outbox design a choice to defend, not a fact. CORRECTION 3 (unmentioned blocker): the app cannot durably reference an incident. DB.swift:227-230 selects `id, rule, severity, tool, session_id, model, window_start, window_end, title, detail, confidence, source` — grep for anomaly_key across queries.ts and DB.swift returns nothing. Intents keyed on the AUTOINCREMENT id break the moment the DB is rebuilt; anomaly_key must be added to both read models first. Also noted: ~/.claude/sessions holds a sibling `<pid>.<sha256>.key` at mode 0600 (auth material for that socket) beside the 0644 .json — the collector must read the .json only, never the .key (constraint 7).
constraint: Four, all reconcilable. #13 read-model parity + read-only consumer: the app writing intents anywhere is new surface — reconcile by appending to ~/.vole/intents.jsonl (never sqlite, never a second Database handle) and folding it in the collector's existing single write path; the app keeps zero write access to vole.db. #1 idempotency: the folded rows need a key that is stable across re-reads, so the app mints a UUID per press and the collector uses it as the UNIQUE key — never (session_id, ts), which re-fires on replay. #6 seed/live partition: control_intents needs a `source` column and must join the DELETE WHERE source='seed' purge, and an intent against a seed incident must be impossible. #9 commit-after-insert: the JSONL offset advances only after the fold transaction succeeds, or a crash loses the audit row the whole feature exists to keep. Plus the prerequisite above: add anomaly_key to queries.ts getAnomalies and DB.swift anomalies() and key intents on it.

name: finding_actions: the append-only disposition ledger
description: Add finding_actions(id, action_id UNIQUE, case_key, anomaly_key, state, actor, actor_kind, reason_code, note, expires_at, content_rev, label_mode, batch_id, ts, ingested_at, source) - append-only, never UPDATEd, never DELETEd, carrying a source column and the same seed/live partition and purge as every other table. The latest action per case is denormalised onto anomalies.state/state_ts/state_actor by one idempotent statement, UPDATE anomalies SET state=? WHERE case_key=? AND (state IS NOT ? OR state_ts < ?), so replaying the ledger converges and re-running the collector changes nothing. States are NULL=open, acknowledged, investigating, resolved, false_positive, expected, accepted_risk, muted, rule_retired; actor_kind separates human_ui, human_cli, policy_auto and pack_bump so a machine transition can never be counted as a human label. Because insertAnomalies is INSERT OR IGNORE on anomaly_key (db.ts:137), re-detection can never clobber a state - the existing freeze that hurts severity is what protects the label.
desktop_surface: A case detail pane showing the full action history as a timeline (who, what, when, under which content_rev), the current state chip in the queue row, and a Settings toggle for whether notes are included in an evidence bundle.
data_source: new table in ~/.vole/vole.db; actor from the existing ORIGIN stamp (db.ts:19-35, os.userInfo().username + os.hostname(), 'shiva'/'Marys-MacBook-Pro.local' on this machine)
honest_limit: actor proves an OS account on this laptop, not a person - there is no SSO identity locally, and a shared machine or CI runner makes it worthless (the principal_conflict guard applies here too). note is operator-authored and is therefore the only free text in a store that otherwise holds no content, so it is capped, excluded from the deny-by-default export field registry, and rendered behind the same gate as any other subject-visible field.
competitive_note: Cyberhaven, Nightfall, Harmonic and CrowdStrike Falcon Guardian all hold case state in a cloud console that also holds prompt content ('stores prompts: yes' for all four in the matrix); an append-only local ledger with no content is the version that survives a works council, which is the Kolide Privacy Center precedent buyer need 9 points at.
v1_ref: Finding lifecycle and acknowledgement
gap_area: Incident triage: the analyst's daily loop and detection-quality accounting

name: Bulk disposition over an explicit id set, stamped label_mode
description: A bulk action takes the currently visible case ids as an explicit list, never the filter predicate, so a disposition can never absorb findings that have not yet been seen - the single most common way a triage tool turns into permanent blindness. The preview shows the exact case list and per-rule counts before it commits, the write emits one finding_actions row per case sharing a batch_id, and each row carries label_mode='bulk' against label_mode='single' for individually opened cases. That column travels into the per-rule detection-quality table, so a hundred cases swept in one keystroke cannot present themselves as a hundred reviews. Batches are capped (default 200) with the overflow named rather than silently truncated.
desktop_surface: A selection bar above the queue ('46 cases selected - dispose as...') with a confirm sheet listing the rules and counts, and a Batches list in the case detail pane where every action row shows its batch_id and label_mode badge.
data_source: v_triage case ids from the live query result; writes finding_actions rows through the action spool
honest_limit: The product can distinguish reviewed-individually from swept, but it cannot distinguish swept-carefully from swept-blindly; label_mode is a provenance flag, not a quality judgement. A batch is not reversible in the ledger - a mistake is corrected by a later action row and both stay visible forever, which is the point of append-only but does mean the mistake is permanently on the record.
competitive_note: Bulk close by query is standard in Sentinel and Splunk ES, but neither records whether a disposition was individual or swept; the incumbents' alert-volume pitch (Zscaler's 242M Codeium DLP violations, Netskope's 223 violations per org per month) has no counter-metric for careless disposition at all.
gap_area: Incident triage: the analyst's daily loop and detection-quality accounting

name: vole support-bundle: a redacted diagnostic that passes verify --content before it is written
description: When an admin says a laptop is reporting wrong, the only artifact that can leave the machine today is a screenshot. The bundle carries the shape of the store and never its rows: schema_migrations, PRAGMA user_version, the sqlite_schema SHA-256, store_budget rows, store_prunes counts, collector_runs and per-tool freshness, the three file sizes, freelist_count/page_count, PRAGMA quick_check (9 ms measured here), the content-pack inventory, and versions (Vole, Node 26.7.0, SQLite 3.53.4, macOS). Redaction is the hard part and it is measurable: collector_state holds 648 source_path rows shaped like /Users/<name>/.claude/projects/-Users-<name>-Desktop-<ClientProject>/<session-uuid>.jsonl — username, client name and session id in one string — so every path is reduced to <tool>/<hmac8>/<ext> under the existing Keychain identity key, and the whole archive is run through verify --content and refused rather than written if anything fails. It ships with a manifest of every field, deny-by-default from the export field registry.
desktop_surface: Settings → Support → Create support bundle: the exact field list previewed before anything is written, then the redacted archive path with Reveal in Finder; the same output as `vole support-bundle --out`.
data_source: ~/.vole/vole.db PRAGMAs, collector_state (648 rows), collector_runs, schema_migrations, store_budget, content_packs, process.versions, sw_vers
honest_limit: A bundle carrying no rows cannot explain a wrong row — it proves which schema, which collectors ran and which bytes exist, and when the complaint is 'this number is wrong' the honest next step is a named, consented evidence bundle for that one incident, not a wider diagnostic. It also cannot prove the store was not edited before the bundle was made; it should carry store_epoch rather than re-derive that claim.
competitive_note: SaaS vendors debug from their own backend logs, so a local-first product's support path is its weakest link; the competitors that do ship endpoint agents (Nightfall, SentinelOne/Prompt, HiddenLayer) ship prompt-carrying agents whose diagnostics cannot be handed to a DPO at all.
gap_area: The store's own lifecycle: schema migration, column widening, growth budget, downgrade, support bundle

name: Device-scoped dedupe: (device_id, event_key) as the sync key
description: v1's headless-CI item asserts that event_keys are globally unique per tool so merging runner exports is safe, and the fleet-sync item keys the relay on event_key and anomaly_key; both are false against this code. codex.ts keys on `codex:<sessionId>:<line index>` and sub-agent rollouts replay the parent session_meta, so keys already collide inside one machine, and antigravity.ts embeds a rounded mtime. Even for uuid-based keys, a restored backup, a shared home directory, or a Codex thread imported from a Claude transcript (~/.codex/external_agent_session_imports.json records source_path under ~/.claude/projects, content_sha256 and imported_thread_id) replays identical keys from two devices, and a relay that upserts on event_key silently drops the second device's rows — an undercount that then renders as an exact figure. Make device_id part of the primary key of every synced table, keep event_key as the within-device idempotency key, and have vole.event.v1 carry both plus a collision_class field naming why a pair matched.
desktop_surface: Settings → 'What leaves this machine' shows the device id used as the sync key, the last cursor, and any imported-thread pairs it labelled; the app itself needs no change because it reads the local store where event_key alone is still unique.
data_source: packages/core/src/collectors/codex.ts event_key construction; collectors/antigravity.ts rounded-mtime key; ~/.codex/external_agent_session_imports.json (records source_path, content_sha256, imported_thread_id, imported_at); the idempotency constraint in code-map-extracts.
honest_limit: Device-scoped dedupe cannot recognise the same human on two laptops, so cross-device per-person totals need the identity binding, not the key. It also cannot distinguish a genuinely re-imported conversation from a duplicated one: it keeps both rows and labels the pair, which means a fleet total can double-count an imported thread unless the consumer honours collision_class. Fixing the Codex and Antigravity keys themselves is a prerequisite, and rekeying invalidates every previously exported document id.
competitive_note: Every vendor console in the matrix dedupes server-side on its own request ids because it owns the request path. Vole's rows are produced independently on each endpoint, so it inherits a merge problem none of them has and must solve it before the first multi-device pilot, or the fleet view's first number is wrong in the customer's favour.
v1_ref: Opt-in fleet sync of normalised rows (org relay / Vole Fleet)
field_verified: Both v1 claims quoted verbatim and both false. roadmap-v1.json headless-CI principle_note: 'P4: event_keys are globally unique per tool so merging runner exports is safe.' roadmap-v1.json tier6 feature 0 (fleet sync) principle_note: 'P4: keyed by event_key/anomaly_key.' Against the code: codex.ts:197 keys on session+line index (collides across parent/sub-agent rollouts), antigravity.ts:63 `event_key: \`antigravity:${conversationId}:${Math.round(ts)}\`` where ts is a .pb mtime. The import artifact exists exactly as described — ~/.codex/external_agent_session_imports.json, 16,851 bytes, records of {source_path: '<redacted-local-path>….jsonl', content_sha256: '1ae4b2bf…', imported_thread_id: '019e5761-102e-71b2-aedd-4f400640ecf4', imported_at: 1779582439}. device_id does not exist; `machine` holds a hostname ('Marys-MacBook-Pro.local'), which is neither stable nor unique across a fleet.
constraint: Constraint 1 is the whole subject and the feature respects it correctly: event_key stays the within-device idempotency key, and the two existing violations are named as bugs to fix rather than precedents. The unstated cost is constraint 5's blast radius — rekeying Codex and Antigravity invalidates every previously exported document id, so this must land BEFORE the first sink ships, not after; sequenced after feature 6 it forces a full replay under new ids into a store that (per feature 8) mostly cannot dedupe.

name: Fleet and osquery table pack: be the source, not the console
description: Buyers say plainly they do not want another console, so publish Vole's read models as tables someone else's agent can schedule: a documented public column set per table (agents, surfaces, incidents, posture, coverage) exposed through `vole query --table=<name> --json`, plus a Fleet/osquery query pack and an ATP-style extension table spec so an existing endpoint-governance deployment can run Vole's tables beside its own. The column set is versioned as a public schema independent of types.ts, which churns per collector, and every row keeps NULL and confidence semantics unchanged: an unpriced call exports cost as JSON null, never 0, with the unpriced counter shipped beside the aggregate.
desktop_surface: Settings → Integrations lists each exposed table with its column list, its schema version and a copy-to-clipboard sample row; deliberately no new screen, because the point of the feature is that the screen belongs to someone else's tool.
data_source: packages/core/src/queries.ts read models over usage_events, anomalies and the posture/surface tables; Fleet's documented query-pack format; osquery extension table spec.
honest_limit: Read-only and last-poll: there is no live query API and no push, so a scheduled osquery run returns whatever the last collector pass stored, stamped with its time. Public columns cannot track internal type churn, so a new internal field does not appear until the export schema is bumped. It carries no content and therefore cannot satisfy a SIEM or EDR rule that expects prompt text — a deliberate limitation, not a gap to close later.
competitive_note: Fleet already advertises inventory of MCP servers, agents, skills and token usage for Claude, OpenAI, Cursor and Windsurf at $7/host with undocumented depth; competing head-on is a distribution fight Vole loses, whereas being the table Fleet queries turns their sales motion into a channel. The same logic applies to CrowdStrike, Purview and Sentinel — market.md's own recommendation is coexist by export, never compete on sensors.
field_verified: Two of five tables exist. queries.ts provides read models over usage_events and anomalies (getSummary, getTimeseries, getBreakdown, getAnomalies, getLiveSessions, getSessionDetail, getCacheRewarm, getWhatIf, getDigest); `agents`, `surfaces`, `posture` and `coverage` do not exist in schema.ts or in the live DB. `vole query --table=<name> --json` does not exist — package.json scripts are collect/seed/test/verify/typecheck/top/pr/statusline/mcp/digest — but cli/mcp.ts:19's TOOLS array is the obvious place it already half-lives, since each entry is `{name, description, inputSchema, run}` and run() already returns JSON-shaped data.
constraint: Constraint 13 in reverse and in the product's favour: exposing a stable public column set independent of types.ts is the right answer to a Swift port that churns, but it creates a THIRD read surface to keep in step (queries.ts, DB.swift, the public schema) unless it is generated from feature 2's registry. Constraint 6: every exposed table needs the `source='live'` clause spliced the way queries.ts does eight times by hand, or an osquery pack reports seed data as fact.

name: Human-confirmed handoff of one incident to the enforcement tool, payload shown before it leaves
description: v1's webhook fires automatically on every new anomaly behind the notify freshness gate. Add the human-initiated form for the case that matters: a 'Send to…' button on the incident drill-down that renders the exact bytes first — generic JSON, Slack Block Kit or PagerDuty Events v2 with dedup_key = anomaly_key — and posts only after the human confirms, satisfying principle 5's 'no silent network calls' with a literal preview rather than a policy claim. The payload is built from the anomalies row's observed/baseline/threshold columns (schema.ts:42-64), which today no reader selects at all (queries.ts:230, DB.swift:227), so this needs those three columns added to the read model first. Each send writes its own row (anomaly_key, endpoint, ts, http_status, bytes) so 'sent', 'failed' and 'never sent' are three distinguishable states.
desktop_surface: 'Send to…' on the incident drill-down opening a sheet with the endpoint picker and the verbatim payload; a per-incident badge showing sent / failed / never sent with the endpoint and timestamp; Settings > Endpoints lists each configured URL, its last result, and a global no-egress switch that greys the button.
data_source: anomalies rows including the observed/baseline/threshold columns (schema.ts:42-64) that queries.ts:230 and DB.swift:227 currently drop; user-configured endpoint URLs and HMAC secret; no other table
honest_limit: This is outbound network: off by default, opt-in per URL, and it must honour the same no-egress preference as UpdateChecker. The payload carries anomaly_key, rule, severity, observed/baseline/threshold, window bounds, tool and a short session id — never cwd, command text, file paths, prompts or raw_ref — so the receiving tool gets strictly less context than its own sensor and cannot attribute a developer without a join the customer owns. Delivery is fire-and-once with no retry queue; a failed POST is recorded as failed, never silently dropped. anomalies is INSERT OR IGNORE on anomaly_key (db.ts:137), so an incident that later escalates from warn to critical never re-sends under the same key.
competitive_note: Feeding CrowdStrike, SentinelOne/Prompt or Zscaler — who already hold the kill switch and the distribution — makes Vole additive in a stack the customer has already bought, which is exactly market.md's stated positioning ('the endpoint evidence layer beside your gateway and EDR, never in your request path'). Harmonic's own conclusion after 22 million prompts was that blocking is futile and coaching wins, so the handoff, not the block, is the defensible product.
v1_ref: Incident webhook and escalation (Slack, PagerDuty Events v2, generic HMAC JSON)
field_verified: The payload fields exist; the plumbing it assumes does not. schema.ts:42-64 confirms the anomalies table carries `observed REAL NOT NULL, baseline REAL, threshold REAL` plus anomaly_key TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, and db.ts:135 confirms `INSERT OR IGNORE INTO anomalies` — so the stated re-send limitation on severity escalation is real. The read-model gap is worse than stated: queries.ts:230 getAnomalies selects `id, rule, severity, tool, session_id, model, window_start, window_end, title, detail, confidence, source` and DB.swift:227 selects the identical list — so observed/baseline/threshold ARE dropped as claimed, and so is anomaly_key, which grep finds in no reader anywhere (only in detect/*.ts where the keys are built, e.g. burn-rate.ts:54 `burn_rate_spike:${tool}:${model}:${bucket}` and index.ts:57 prefixing source). The feature's own dedup_key = anomaly_key is therefore unbuildable until both readers are widened. BIGGEST CORRECTION: 'it must honour the same no-egress preference as UpdateChecker' — there is no such preference. UpdateChecker.swift:21-23 is `init() { check() }` calling api.github.com/repos/launchsafe/vole/releases unconditionally on every launch, and grep for no-egress/noEgress across the repo returns nothing. Worse, SECURITY.md states verbatim: 'There is no server, no account, no telemetry, and no network call this project makes on its own — that's the thing most worth breaking, if it's ever untrue.' That sentence is already untrue today. This feature cannot ship on top of it.
constraint: #17 (no silent network calls; any egress needs disclosure and a preference every caller respects) — the preference must be created, not reused, and the same PR has to retrofit UpdateChecker and correct SECURITY.md's 'no network call' sentence, or Vole ships an outbound POST while its own security policy denies network exists. That is the reconciliation and it is non-optional. #12/#13 read-model parity: add observed, baseline, threshold AND anomaly_key to queries.ts and DB.swift before anything else. #6 seed/live: the send log needs a source column and a hard refusal to transmit an incident with source='seed' — exporting fabricated demo incidents into a customer's PagerDuty would be the worst possible first impression. #13 again, unmentioned: the 'sent / failed / never sent' badge is app-side state and DB.swift must stay a read-only consumer, so either the send log rides feature 1's outbox or it lives app-local in ~/.vole/sends.jsonl — pick one and say so, do not open a second writer on vole.db. #3 is honestly acknowledged: INSERT OR IGNORE on anomaly_key means a warn that escalates to critical never re-sends under the same key.

name: store_epoch: proving the database is the one you were given
description: One row, written once when the table is empty: store_epoch(epoch_id, created_at, device_id, first_event_ts, collector_version, prev_epoch_id, prev_epoch_last_seq), with device_id from the already-stable IOPlatformUUID identity and first_event_ts from MIN(usage_events.ts). prev_epoch_id is NULL on a genuinely first install, and that is the whole mechanism: a sink already holding rows stamped epoch A from device D that now receives epoch B with prev_epoch_id NULL has proof the store was deleted and recreated, with first_event_ts showing exactly how much history came back. The correction this carries: epoch must NOT enter the sync dedupe key. The planned key is (device_id, event_key), and adding epoch would re-duplicate every legitimately re-collected row at the sink and destroy the dedupe that makes re-collection safe — epoch travels as a column, and the sink's rule is 'same (device_id, event_key), new epoch, different values' => evidence_replaced.
desktop_surface: Settings > Evidence shows Store epoch: created date, device, first event, and either 'exported to <sink> since <date>' or 'never exported — this store has no off-box witness', rendered as a plain neutral line rather than a scare banner.
data_source: new store_epoch table under ~/.vole; IOPlatformUUID (existing stable machine identity); MIN(usage_events.ts); the DB file's own birthtimeMs
honest_limit: An epoch row is exactly as deletable as everything around it and proves nothing on-device; it becomes evidence only at a sink that already holds an earlier epoch, so a device that never exported can be reset with no trace whatsoever. It cannot distinguish a deliberate rm from a disk failure, an OS migration or a brand new laptop — the row says 'new store', never 'tampering'. IOPlatformUUID survives a re-image, so a wiped machine and a fresh one are separable only by the hardware id.
competitive_note: Every cloud-console competitor gets store lineage for free because the store is theirs; Vole is the local-first one and therefore has to say out loud where local-first stops. Fleet/osquery has the identical hole on the endpoint and does not name it.
v1_ref: Tamper-evident audit log (hash chain + signed checkpoints)
gap_area: Evidence integrity when the monitored user is the local admin: gaps, source mutability, store lineage, clock

name: The answer sheet: the sentence the security team sends back, with its denominator attached
description: A hunt's output is not a table, it is a paragraph somebody has to send to a regulator, a customer or a board. One page per `hunt_runs` row: the pack's name, signature and trust class; the four verdict counters; the horizon bar from answerable_from; per-indicator rows linking into the just-in-time evidence viewer; and a copyable answer paragraph pre-filled from the figures that actually fired ("2 of 41 indicators seen, 30 not seen, 9 unanswerable before 15 Aug; evidence horizon 23 days; 655 transcripts and 66 rollouts scanned"). Where opt-in fleet sync is on, the same four buckets aggregate device by device through the existing (device_id, event_key) key, and the rollup is forbidden to render a percentage while the unanswerable or never-reported buckets are non-empty — it renders counts and the number of devices that never answered at all.
desktop_surface: This is the surface: a Hunt page reachable from Triage, from a vole:// deep link and from the command palette, with the answer paragraph as a copy button and the whole page exportable as an incident evidence bundle carrying the custody sentence.
data_source: hunt_runs, indicators, answerable_from, detection_epochs, the export field registry and the device-scoped dedupe key; content_packs for pack identity and signature
honest_limit: The paragraph is true only as of the horizon it names: re-running the same pack later can flip a not_seen to unanswerable as evidence ages out, so each run is versioned and never overwritten, and the sheet shows the diff against the previous run rather than a corrected answer. A fleet rollup answers for the devices that reported, and says how many did not — it never extrapolates to the ones that did not.
competitive_note: 46% of enterprises cannot produce a 30-day agent action trail at all (EMA/Cequence, market.md L13); the incumbents that can produce one hand back a search result, not an answer with a denominator. Refusing to compute an affected-percentage over an incomplete fleet is the opposite of every console in the matrix and is the credibility argument for a local-first store.
gap_area: Indicator retro-hunt: 'an advisory just named X — were we exposed, when, and what happened next'

name: Durable export outbox with backpressure and audited drops
description: Collection runs every 5 s and must never block on a network sink, and a laptop is offline most of the day, so add export_outbox(seq, sink, doc_id, payload_hash, bytes, attempts, next_attempt_at, status) written in the same transaction as the rows it covers. A separate drain step reads it with exponential backoff, advances export_state only after a 2xx, and never holds the collector's write connection. The outbox has a byte cap from policy; when it fills, the oldest batch is dropped and an export_backlog_dropped info anomaly records the exact count and byte range dropped — the gap is reported, never silently closed.
desktop_surface: Settings → Export status line reading 'queued 1,284 events, oldest 3 h 12 m, last success 09:41' with a Retry now button; the drop anomaly appears in the normal Incidents feed with its exact counts rather than in a log nobody reads.
data_source: packages/core/src/cli/collect.ts results loop (the natural outbox write point, immediately before commit()); packages/core/src/db.ts insertEvents/insertAnomalies single write path.
honest_limit: The outbox is a plain table in a user-writable SQLite file: a developer can delete it and the loss is invisible to the SIEM until the heartbeat rule fires. It also cannot preserve rows whose source artifact was pruned by retention, so a long outage plus a prune is a permanent gap that the drop anomaly can only bound, not recover.
