CollectorResult.commit() must still run only after insertEvents succeeds, so the outbox write joins that transaction rather than replacing it.
competitive_note: Gateway and proxy vendors buffer server-side by construction because they own the request path. An endpoint tool that is honest about queue depth and about exactly which bytes it dropped is closer to Fleet/osquery's operational posture than to a DLP agent's, and it is the difference between a SIEM engineer trusting the source and treating it as best-effort.
field_verified: Write seam confirmed, outbox absent. cli/collect.ts drives `collectAll → insertEvents → r.commit?.()` and types.ts:105-109 documents commit-after-insert; db.ts:113-127 is the single transactioned write path (`db.transaction((rows)=>{…stmt.run({...r, ...ORIGIN})…})`). No export_outbox table, no ~/.vole/outbox directory (ls ~/.vole shows only vole.db/-wal/-shm). Note roadmap-v1 is not silent on the concept: tier6 feature 6 already mentions 'the last payload from a sync_log table and ~/.vole/outbox/', so novelty:'new' overstates — this specifies what v1 gestures at.
constraint: Two the description misses. Constraint 6: 'New tables must carry a source column and the same partition/purge' — without it, `pnpm seed`'s 30 days of synthetic rows queue up and ship to a customer's SIEM, and `purgeSeed` leaves the outbox rows behind. Constraint 3: the drop notice is an anomalies row, and anomaly_key must be deterministic and must never include now() (enforced by detect.test.ts:120) — key it on the dropped seq range (`export_backlog_dropped:<sink>:<first_seq>-<last_seq>`), never on drop time, or every restart mints a new incident. Constraint 9 is respected as written: the outbox write joins the insertEvents transaction rather than replacing it.

name: Evidence bundle export with a pre-export field preview and re-identification scan
description: One command (Cmd-E) from any incident, session, person or finding writes a .zip containing exactly the row(s), the anomaly's observed/baseline/threshold and effective rule config, the usage_events rows inside the window, the collector run record and tool versions, PRAGMA user_version, the pricing table version and a manifest.json naming every column included and every transform applied. Before writing, a sheet renders the payload field by field so nothing leaves the machine unseen, and a re-identification scanner runs over every string field looking for the local OS username, the short hostname, the directory-service RealName (dscl . -read /Users/$USER RealName), the local part of oauthAccount.emailAddress and any /Users/<name>/ prefix, emitting a reid_risk finding naming the column and the hit count. On this machine it fires immediately: 26,977 of 28,948 project values begin <redacted-local-path>, machine is Marys-MacBook-Pro.local, raw_ref embeds -Users-shiva, and anomalies.detail is free text carrying session ids and paths. In managed mode the send is refused unless the redaction manifest declares a transform for the offending column, and the same scanner runs on every other outbound payload — SIEM batch, sync outbox, DSAR bundle.
desktop_surface: Cmd-E anywhere plus a context-menu item on incident, session and finding rows; a preview sheet with a per-column table, pass/fail and sample hit counts, finishing on Copy path / Reveal in Finder; a blocking sheet listing the offending columns when hits are unresolved; Privacy Center → 'Export safety' shows the same table standing, one row per column.
data_source: anomalies (all 18 columns), usage_events window rows, collector_state/sources, packages/core/src/sync/manifest.ts column allowlist, PRAGMA user_version, pricing.json version; os.userInfo().username, os.hostname(), dscl RealName, ~/.claude.json oauthAccount.emailAddress; target columns usage_events.project/.raw_ref/.machine/.git_branch, anomalies.detail, collector_state.path.
honest_limit: It is evidence about rows in one SQLite file at export time, not a tamper-proof chain — until the hash chain and signed checkpoints land, integrity rests on the file's own checksum. The re-identification check is lexical only: it cannot catch identity carried by a rare repository name, a team's branch-naming convention it was not told about, or a project path under a shared root, so it reduces accidental leakage and is not an anonymity proof and must not render a green tick implying one. The bundle deliberately contains no prompt, command or file content, which some incident responders will want and cannot have.
competitive_note: v1's pack is a range-scoped compliance zip with no per-incident keystroke, no pre-send preview and no scanner proving that its manifest's 'home prefix and git_branch stripped' promise actually happened. 46% of enterprises cannot produce a 30-day agent audit trail (EMA/Cequence 2026-09-01) and GitHub's audit log excludes local prompts entirely; nothing comparable to the reid scan exists in the matrix, because vendors that inspect content have no reason to check whether their own export re-identifies.
v1_ref: Compliance evidence pack export
field_verified: I reproduced every re-identification hit. os.userInfo().username -> 'shiva' and os.hostname() -> 'Marys-MacBook-Pro.local', both stored on EVERY row (`select distinct user, machine from usage_events` returns exactly that one pair). `dscl . -read /Users/$USER RealName` -> 'RealName: Shiva Nagendra Babu Kore'. oauthAccount.emailAddress local part is present in ~/.claude.json. 27,661 of 29,632 project values begin <redacted-local-path>; raw_ref embeds the Claude slug '-Users-shiva-Developer-...'; anomalies.detail is free text carrying session ids verbatim ('... Session 019e5765.'). TWO corrections: anomalies has NINETEEN columns, not 18 (`pragma table_info(anomalies)` -> 19 rows), and `pragma user_version` -> 0 with no user_version scheme anywhere (code map: 'no version stamp exists'), so citing it as a schema stamp is meaningless today. sync/manifest.ts and a findings table do not exist.
constraint: C11 (schema evolution is add-nullable-column only; no version stamp exists and DB.swift assumes newest columns are present) -- either the bundle drops the PRAGMA user_version claim or this feature owns introducing the scheme for both readers. C7 respected: the bundle deliberately carries no prompt, command or file content. C12 for the preview sheet.

name: Accessibility pass and an exact-numbers toggle
description: A grep across apps/mac finds zero accessibility modifiers and two keyboardShortcut calls. Three concrete gaps: severity and confidence are conveyed by colour plus a glyph set VoiceOver never names (Pal.severity, ConfidenceBadge in MenuPanel.swift:33); every headline figure passes through Fmt.compact so '1.2M' has no exact value anywhere in the UI; and the Sparkline and the Swift Charts timeline expose no audio-graph descriptor. Add accessibilityLabel/value to every status glyph and chip, an accessibilityValue carrying the exact integer beside each compacted figure (also shown on hover), an accessibilityChartDescriptor for the timeline, Dynamic Type support in the Card and MenuRow layouts, an Increase Contrast check on the seven brand series colours, and a Settings toggle that turns compaction off globally.
desktop_surface: Everywhere: menu-bar label, MenuPanel hero and tool bars, KPI tiles, incident and breakdown rows, the timeline; plus a 'Show exact numbers' switch in Settings.
data_source: Theme.swift Fmt.compact/money/pct and Pal.severity/severityIcon; MenuPanel.swift ConfidenceBadge and Sparkline; DashboardView.swift TimelineChart.
honest_limit: An audio-graph descriptor works per series, so the stacked seven-agent timeline gets one descriptor for the total plus per-agent series and will read poorly at 30-day ranges; Dynamic Type at the largest sizes forces the 324pt menu-bar panel to scroll rather than reflow. None of this makes the product conformant — it removes the three defects an evaluator finds first and gives a VPAT something true to say.
competitive_note: No competitor markets accessibility, but a VPAT is a line item in the enterprise procurement questionnaire beside SOC 2 and the DPA; a monitoring tool the monitored employee cannot read is also an awkward answer to a works council asking about transparency and proportionality.
field_verified: Premise verified exactly: `grep -rc accessibility apps/mac/Sources/Vole/*.swift` returns 0 for all eight files, and keyboardShortcut appears exactly twice. Pal.severity (Theme.swift:59-65) and Pal.severityIcon (:68-74) convey status by colour plus an unnamed glyph. Fmt.compact (:89-96) returns '1.2M' with no exact value retained anywhere in the UI. Sparkline (MenuPanel.swift:113-129) is bare RoundedRectangles with no descriptor. The panel width limit is real: VoleApp.swift:65 `.frame(width: 324)`. One correction: ConfidenceBadge (MenuPanel.swift:34-44) renders `Text(Labels.confidence(c))` — actual words, 'exact' or 'no tokens' — so it is already readable; the unlabelled-glyph problem is severity, not confidence.
constraint: None — and the exact-numbers toggle is a quiet principle-1 repair the feature under-sells. Every headline figure in the product passes through Fmt.compact, which ROUNDS ('1.2M'), so today the exact integer is unreachable anywhere in the UI. A product whose first principle is 'never invent a number' currently shows only rounded ones. Frame the toggle as principle 1 reaching the interface, not as an accessibility nicety.

name: Structured incident detail: template key plus parameters
description: anomalies.detail is NOT NULL free text today and it is the column most likely to leave the machine: rows here read 'Burned 36,751 tokens in 10 min (3,675/min) across 2 calls — 3.0x this model's typical 12,149-token window. Session 019e5765.' A forwarder or evidence pack either ships the session id and paths embedded in prose or regex-scrubs free text, and both are bad. Add detail_key plus a detail_params JSON object, render the sentence in util/format.ts and in DB.swift, and let the exporter drop or hash individual parameters per the field registry while the app still shows the full sentence locally. Purely additive: keep detail as the rendered fallback for rows that already exist, since the upsert cannot backfill them.
desktop_surface: No visible change on the Incidents feed — the same sentence, rendered client-side from the key and params — while the Privacy Center's export preview gains a per-incident-type list of which parameters are dropped or hashed on the way out.
data_source: anomalies.detail (NOT NULL free text in schema.ts); the five detect rules that compose it; packages/core/src/util/format.ts; apps/mac/Sources/Vole/DB.swift anomalies().
honest_limit: It only fixes prose written from now on: existing rows keep their rendered string and can only be regex-scrubbed or excluded from export, and the tokens-only-grow upsert gives no path to rewrite them. Localisation is not the goal and the renderer is not a translation layer; the parameter split exists so the exporter has something structured to redact. Two renderers (TypeScript and Swift) must be kept in step or the app and the CLI print different sentences from the same row.
competitive_note: Not in roadmap-v1, whose SIEM forwarder ships anomalies rows as-is. It is the prerequisite that makes the OTLP, HEC, syslog and evidence-bundle exports manifest-bounded rather than best-effort, which is the difference between a DPO signing off on export and blocking it outright.
field_verified: Verified verbatim, character for character. schema.ts:53 `detail TEXT NOT NULL`, and the live store's first burn_rate_spike row reads: "Burned 36,751 tokens in 10 min (3,675/min) across 2 calls — 3.0x this model's typical 12,149-token window. Session 019e5765." — the exact sentence the description quotes, session id embedded in prose. MIS-SOURCED, though: the sentence is not rendered in util/format.ts, which contains only compact/usd/mmss/ago. It is composed inside each rule — burn-rate.ts:63-66 builds it with template literals over fmt() and shortId(). So the change lands in the five detect files plus a new renderer, not in format.ts.
constraint: Constraint 3 makes the backfill genuinely impossible, and the description is right to concede it: anomalies are INSERT OR IGNORE (db.ts:130) with no upsert path, so existing rows keep their prose forever and can only be excluded or regex-scrubbed on the way out. Constraint 12: detail_key/detail_params are add-nullable-columns, which migrate() supports. Constraint 13 is the ongoing tax — two renderers in TypeScript and Swift that must print the same sentence from the same row, which is precisely what feature 23's parity check would catch.

name: Command palette, section shortcuts and a persistent filter bar
description: Twelve screens with drill-downs need navigation that is not a mouse; the app today has exactly two keyboardShortcut calls, both in MenuPanel. Add Cmd-1..9 for sections, Cmd-K for a palette over sessions, people, agents, repos, rules and incident ids, Cmd-F for a per-section filter bar (person, agent, repo, severity, time range) whose state persists per section as removable chips, and J/K plus Space/Escape for row traversal and expansion. All of it searches only indexed identifier columns — session_id, user, machine, project, tool, rule, anomaly id — because there is no content in the database to search.
desktop_surface: A palette sheet over the window; a filter bar under the toolbar in every list section showing active filters as removable chips; keyboard traversal in Incidents, Breakdown, People and every ledger table.
data_source: Existing indexed columns in usage_events and anomalies; the vole.section AppStorage key already shared between MenuPanel and DashboardView.
honest_limit: The palette searches ids, names and paths and never content, so a query like 'find the session that leaked the AWS key' resolves only through a finding's fingerprint, not through text. Filter state is per-machine UserDefaults, so it is not part of any evidence trail, and a filter over a column that is NULL on historical rows (user, machine) silently excludes them unless the bar shows an 'unknown origin' chip.
competitive_note: The competing consoles are all web apps where keyboard navigation and search come from the browser; a desktop app with twelve sections and no palette is slower than the console it replaces, which is the first thing a security analyst notices in a bake-off.
field_verified: Premise exact: `grep -rn keyboardShortcut apps/mac/Sources` returns precisely two hits, MenuPanel.swift:235 and :238, both in the footer. The shared `vole.section` AppStorage is real (MenuPanel.swift:139, DashboardView.swift:242). FACTUAL ERROR in the justification: the feature says it 'searches only indexed identifier columns — session_id, user, machine, project, tool, rule, anomaly id'. The live index list is `sqlite_autoindex_usage_events_1` (event_key), `idx_ue_ts`, `idx_ue_tool_ts`, `idx_ue_session`, `idx_ue_source_ts`, `sqlite_autoindex_anomalies_1` (anomaly_key), `idx_an_detected`, `idx_an_source`. So `user`, `machine`, `project` and `rule` are NOT indexed — a palette scan over project paths is a full scan of 29.6K rows.
constraint: No constraint break. Unnamed hard dependency: every filter here binds TEXT, which DB.swift:141 cannot do, so this cannot ship before feature 1's Bind enum. Constraint 13 applies to any new query. The 'no content to search' framing is correct and worth keeping — it is a feature, not an apology.

name: Label carry-over across a pack bump, and the re-review queue
description: Every finding_actions row records the content_rev in force when the human labelled it. When a pack bump re-scores a case, the human state is kept verbatim - a machine transition never overwrites a human label, which is what actor_kind exists to prove - and the case gains a recheck_reason only when the re-score crossed a boundary that would plausibly have changed the verdict: severity changed class, observed moved to the other side of threshold, or the rule's dimensions changed and so minted a new case_key. Those and only those appear in a filtered re-review view rendering the old figures beside the new with both content_revs named. A rule the pack retires moves its open cases to state='rule_retired' stamped with the retiring pack version rather than deleting them, so an auditor can still see what fired, under which rule text, and why it stopped mattering.
desktop_surface: A 'Re-review (7)' filter chip in the Incidents queue, and in each affected case a before/after figures block showing observed, baseline, threshold and severity under each content_rev with the label the human gave and the date they gave it.
data_source: finding_actions.content_rev; anomalies.observed/baseline/threshold/severity/content_rev; the content_packs registry
honest_limit: Re-scoring can only run over evidence still retained, so a case whose evidence aged out gets recheck_unavailable and keeps its old label with the gap named on the row - the product cannot tell whether the human would have labelled it differently, only that the figures moved and it could not re-check. A retired rule's cases keep a state that no longer has a live definition behind it, so the rule text has to be preserved in the pack registry or the label becomes uninterpretable.
competitive_note: Snyk agent-scan and Pillar both ship versioned rule content but neither preserves human dispositions across a version change, and detection-as-code repos (Sigma, the SPL and EQL packs) version the rule while the triage history stays on the consumer's side and quietly desynchronises - keeping both in one local store is only possible because Vole owns the detector and the queue at once.
v1_ref: content_rev on incidents: re-score without duplicating, retire without lying
gap_area: Incident triage: the analyst's daily loop and detection-quality accounting

name: Incidents as OTLP logs carrying the figures that fired
description: The anomalies table already stores observed, baseline, threshold, detected_at and anomaly_key, and no reader selects them — queries.ts getAnomalies projects id/rule/severity/tool/session/model/window/title/detail/confidence/source and DB.swift:223 the same — so a forwarder built on the existing IncidentRow would ship incidents stripped of their evidence and break principle 3 across the wire. The exporter reads anomalies directly and emits one OTLP LogRecord per row with event.name='vole.incident', body omitted, attributes vole.rule, vole.observed/baseline/threshold, vole.window_start/end, vole.confidence and vole.anomaly_key, severity mapped info/warn/critical to SeverityNumber 9/13/17, and trace_id set to the offending session's derived trace so the alert links to the spans. Splunk, Elastic and Datadog receive the same object with _id = anomaly_key.
desktop_surface: The Incidents feed gains the three figures inline (observed vs baseline vs threshold) — exactly the values the SIEM receives — plus a 'copy as SIEM event' action, so the analyst and the alert cannot disagree about what fired.
data_source: packages/core/src/schema.ts anomalies.{observed,baseline,threshold,anomaly_key,detected_at}; packages/core/src/detect/*.ts thresholds; packages/core/src/queries.ts getAnomalies and apps/mac/Sources/Vole/DB.swift anomalies().
honest_limit: INSERT OR IGNORE on anomaly_key freezes the first verdict, so an incident that later worsens is never re-emitted and the SIEM keeps the lower severity; this export is only correct once anomalies move to an explicit upsert-on-greater-observed with a re-notify path, and anomaly_key must stay deterministic and free of now() while that changes. anomalies.detail is a rendered English sentence and is dropped rather than exported until it is split into a template key and parameters, so the SIEM sees figures without the prose.
competitive_note: Anthropic states explicitly that anomaly detection, baselining, correlation and alerting are the SIEM's responsibility and ships none of it; shipping an explainable alert that carries its own baseline and threshold is exactly the layer the vendor says is missing, and no console in the matrix emits a rule verdict with its evidence attached.
v1_ref: OTLP export: sessions as traces, rows as metrics, incidents as logs
field_verified: Confirmed exactly. schema.ts:56-58 declares observed/baseline/threshold, schema.ts:42 anomaly_key, schema.ts:59 detected_at. queries.ts:230 selects `id, rule, severity, tool, session_id, model, window_start, window_end, title, detail, confidence, source` — none of the three figures — and DB.swift:227 selects the identical eleven, so a forwarder built on IncidentRow would ship evidence-free alerts. The values are in the store: a live burn_rate_spike row reads observed=36751.0, baseline=12149.0, threshold=36447.0, severity='warn'; a sibling reads 144948.0/12149.0/36447.0 at 'critical'. db.ts:130 is `INSERT OR IGNORE INTO anomalies`, so the first verdict is frozen — confirmed.
constraint: Constraint 3, and the feature names it correctly but then prices it as S. Moving anomalies to upsert-on-greater-observed requires an explicit ON CONFLICT clause, a re-notify path, and a key that stays deterministic and now()-free (detect.test.ts:120 guards this) — that is not a small change, and without it the SIEM keeps the lower severity forever while the app shows the same stale verdict. Dropping `detail` also makes this dependent on feature 22, or the SIEM gets figures with no sentence.

name: vole:// deep links and addressable notifications
description: Register a vole:// URL scheme in apps/mac/Info.plist, which today declares no CFBundleURLTypes at all, so a filter state, an incident or a session becomes addressable: opening a link raises the window, sets the section, applies the filter and selects the row. Notifications then open the exact drill-down instead of the Incidents list, and an investigator can paste a link into the incident channel for a colleague on the same machine or fleet.
desktop_surface: Deep links from UNNotification actions, from Copy-link actions on incident, session and finding rows, and from the CLI (`vole open <anomaly_key>`); an unresolvable link opens a clear 'this incident is not in your local database' state naming the key it looked for.
data_source: apps/mac/Info.plist (no CFBundleURLTypes today); anomalies.anomaly_key as the stable cross-machine identifier; usage_events.session_id; the vole.section AppStorage key.
honest_limit: Row ids are per-store autoincrements, so a link must key on anomaly_key or session_id and even then is only meaningful on a machine whose database holds that row — on any other Mac it must say so rather than showing an empty screen. A URL scheme is claimable by any app the user installs later, so a link is a convenience, never an authentication or an authorisation boundary.
competitive_note: Web consoles get addressability for free, and pasting a link into the incident channel is the one workflow security teams actually use; a desktop app that cannot be linked to loses it entirely, and v1 never mentions the URL scheme even where its webhook and notification features assume a click-through.
field_verified: Confirmed by reading the whole file: apps/mac/Info.plist is 22 lines and contains CFBundleName, CFBundleDisplayName, CFBundleIdentifier (`com.launchsafe.vole`), CFBundleExecutable, CFBundleIconFile, CFBundlePackageType, CFBundleShortVersionString, CFBundleVersion, LSMinimumSystemVersion, NSPrincipalClass, NSHighResolutionCapable, LSUIElement, NSHumanReadableCopyright — and NO CFBundleURLTypes key. The key identifier claim checks out: `anomaly_key` is UNIQUE (sqlite_autoindex_anomalies_1) so it is stable and portable, while `anomalies.id` is INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT (schema.ts:43) and therefore per-store, exactly as the honest_limit says.
constraint: No egress, so principle 7 and constraint 17 are untouched — but the feature misses the direction that matters. A registered URL scheme is this app's FIRST externally-triggerable input: any web page the user visits can navigate to `vole://...` and drive the app. The reconciliation must be written into the spec — the handler is navigation-only (set section, apply filter, select row), never an action, never a write, never a file read, and never a path it will open. The feature notes the scheme can be hijacked BY another app; it should also note the app is now reachable FROM anywhere.

name: The custody sentence: what an evidence bundle is allowed to claim
description: One derived read model, v_custody(window_start, window_end), joining the outputs of the five mechanisms above to a bundle's own window: run-covered milliseconds over window milliseconds, gap count and total gap minutes, gaps-with-activity, sources whose prefix digest broke, clock_suspect row count, whether a checkpoint covering the window was acknowledged by a sink and when, and orphan sessions overlapping. Every export, evidence bundle, DSAR answer and control-framework mapping renders it as one sentence carrying the actual figures. A bundle whose window contains a gap-with-activity, a rewritten source or an unacknowledged checkpoint is stamped partial custody — never suppressed, never silently downgraded, and there is no override switch, which is the entire point of the feature.
desktop_surface: A persistent Evidence Integrity header on the Privacy Center and on every export and bundle preview: 'Monitored 96.2% of 2026-08-08 to 2026-09-07. 3 unmonitored intervals (61 min total, 1 with agent activity). 1 source rewritten. Clock stable. Checkpoint 4471 acknowledged by splunk-prod 2026-09-06 22:14 UTC.' Bundle cards carry the partial custody stamp inline.
data_source: v_evidence_gaps; collector_state integrity columns; store_epoch; usage_events.clock_suspect; export_checkpoints; orphan_sessions
honest_limit: The sentence describes Vole's own observation, not the truth: a fully covered period can still be one in which the subject worked on another machine, in a browser, or under an account Vole never sees. It is a coverage statement, not an innocence statement, and the screen must say that in those words. All of it is computed from the same store it describes, so on a store with no off-box witness the custody sentence is self-reported and worth what the subject's honesty is worth — which is why the never-exported case must print 'no external witness' instead of a percentage.
competitive_note: The market finding that nobody is out-of-path, exact and prompt-free at once cuts both ways: being out-of-path is exactly why Vole owes the buyer its own coverage number. No row in the 62-vendor matrix states retention or coverage — CrowdStrike's is literally 'retention not stated' — so publishing a measured custody line is a claim no competitor currently makes.
v1_ref: Compliance evidence pack export
gap_area: Evidence integrity when the monitored user is the local admin: gaps, source mutability, store lineage, clock

name: OTLP wire contract: pinned semconv snapshot and deterministic ids
description: Two contracts the OTLP exporter needs before anyone can trust it. First, pin the conventions: vendor packages/core/src/export/semconv/genai-<version>.json — the attribute registry extracted from a named upstream commit — emit its schema_url on every OTLP resource, and add a test asserting that every attribute name the serializer can produce exists in the snapshot with the same type; `vole export --semconv=<version>` selects among vendored snapshots and can dual-emit old and new names during a migration window. Second, make ids a pure function of the row, because re-sends are guaranteed (the upsert re-emits corrected rows and replay exists) and a random id forks a new trace on every retry: trace_id = HMAC-SHA256(install_key, 'trace|' + session_id)[0:16] and span_id = HMAC(install_key, 'span|' + event_key)[0:8] using node:crypto and a per-install key generated once into ~/.vole/export.key (0600), so ids are stable across restarts and unlinkable across companies, with the matching W3C traceparent written onto the Splunk/Elastic document so it joins to the OTLP trace with no lookup table. The semconv version in force is recorded in export_meta so an exported batch is self-describing.
desktop_surface: Settings → Export gains a 'Semantic conventions' row (pinned version, upstream commit, snapshot date, dual-emit toggle showing the exact extra attribute names it would add) and a copyable traceparent for the most recent event, so an analyst can paste it into their trace UI and confirm the join.
data_source: vendored OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic-conventions registry (market.md §6: still Development, no tagged release); packages/core/src/export/fields.ts; usage_events.event_key and session_id; node:crypto; ~/.vole/export.key.
honest_limit: Pinning does not make the attributes stable upstream — a customer's collector processor may already expect a newer spelling and Vole cannot know which — and attributes with no semconv home (cost, confidence, the cache-write 5m/1h split, subagent roll-up) live under a vole.* prefix and are non-portable by definition. The install key is a file the seat owner can read and change; rotating it renames every future trace and orphans history in the SIEM. The ids are Vole's own: they join Vole's rows to each other, never to Anthropic's or OpenAI's internal traces.
competitive_note: Cursor and Claude Code both ship OTel without naming the semconv revision they target, so a dashboard built on either can break silently under an upstream rename; a published, pinned snapshot with a conformance test is a procurement answer neither gives. Anthropic's own guidance is that correlation across sessions is the SIEM's responsibility — supplying stable trace ids is precisely the work being handed off.
v1_ref: OTLP export: sessions as traces, rows as metrics, incidents as logs
field_verified: Local inputs confirmed: usage_events.event_key and session_id exist (schema.ts:8,11), node:crypto is a builtin, and the re-send pressure it guards against is real — the db.ts upsert rewrites rows in place, so retries with random ids would fork a trace on every corrected row. No semconv snapshot is vendored and no ~/.vole/export.key exists (ls ~/.vole: vole.db, -wal, -shm only). The upstream instability claim comes from market.md §6 and is the one part I could not check on-machine (no network); it is an external citation, correctly labelled as such in data_source.
constraint: Constraint 14, sharply, and the feature does not see it: the SEA collector must be CJS-bundleable with 'no runtime file reads except pricing override and sources'. `vole export --semconv=<version>` selecting among vendored snapshots at runtime is exactly that forbidden read. Reconciliation: inline every snapshot at build time the way esbuild already freezes data/pricing.json, and make the flag a selector over inlined objects. ~/.vole/export.key needs the same explicit carve-out that the pricing override has, and being 0600 in the seat owner's home it is disclosure, not protection — which the honest_limit already says.

name: gen_ai.provider.name normalisation with an explicit unknown bucket
description: Semconv wants a provider from a closed enum (anthropic, openai, aws.bedrock, gcp.vertex_ai, azure.ai.inference, x_ai) while Vole stores raw model ids of at least five shapes: claude-opus-4-5, anthropic/claude-* (OpenCode composite), gpt-5.5, grok-composer-2.5-fast, and — seen in a real Codex rollout on this machine — claude-opus-4.6 served through litellm behind a GitHub Copilot exception. Add a provider_map table loaded the way pricing.ts loads rates (id prefix or exact match to an enum value, with an org override file) that emits gen_ai.provider.name, gen_ai.request.model and a separate vole.model_id_raw, and resolves to the literal string 'unknown' — never a guess — when no rule matches, counted by the vole.calls.model_unknown series. contextWindow's existing provider-prefix strip is reused so the same id parses identically everywhere.
desktop_surface: The Breakdown pane gains a provider column above the model rows, with an 'unknown provider' row that is clickable through to the raw model ids behind it, so the gap is a thing you can open rather than a rounding error.
data_source: usage_events.model; packages/core/src/pricing.ts rateFor/contextWindow prefix handling; ~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl turn_context.payload.model_provider and task_complete text showing a litellm-routed claude id.
honest_limit: The provider is the one declared locally, not the one that served the request: a gateway or an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL override can route an anthropic-shaped id to anything and the transcript records no evidence of the hop. 46 of 83 Codex rows here carry no model at all because mid-thread switches land in thread_settings_applied, which the collector ignores, so provider is NULL for those rather than defaulted. The org override file makes the mapping a policy artefact that must be versioned with the export.
competitive_note: Vendor consoles are single-provider by construction — Cursor sees Cursor, Copilot sees Copilot, Claude Code Analytics excludes Bedrock and Vertex entirely. A normalised provider dimension spanning Claude, Codex, OpenCode, Grok, Cursor, Devin and Antigravity in one series is the whole point of an endpoint collector, and the honest 'unknown' bucket is what stops it becoming a fiction.
v1_ref: Provider, service-tier and gateway attribution columns
field_verified: Mostly confirmed, one field mis-sourced, one shape missing. Codex model ids on this machine: gpt-6-astra (28), gpt-5.5 (22), gpt-5.6-sol (15), gpt-5.6-terra (6) and — not in the feature's list — `openrouter/stealth/ox-alpha` (6), a sixth shape that is itself a routing tell. 'claude-opus-4.6' appears 300 times inside codex rollouts and the string 'litellm' is present, so the cross-served-id case is real. 46 of 83 stored codex rows have model NULL — exactly as claimed. MIS-SOURCED: model_provider is on session_meta.payload, NOT turn_context.payload — verified by dumping the line that contains it: type=session_meta, payload keys ['id','timestamp','cwd','originator','cli_version','source','thread_source','model_provider','base_instructions','dynamic_tools'], value 'openai' in 67 files and 'claude-code-router' in 1. That one 'claude-code-router' value is a shadow-routing signal worth more than the enum mapping.
constraint: Constraint 14: the org override file is a runtime file read, permitted only because pricing.ts already has that carve-out — so the loader must mirror pricing.ts:55 exactly (load once at import, merge over the inlined default) rather than inventing a second config mechanism. Constraint 18 adjacent: pricing already warns that cost definitions must not mix silently; a provider column that is 'declared locally, not who served it' has the same hazard and must never be used to attribute spend to a vendor.

name: Span model: real execute_tool durations, honestly zero-length chat spans
description: Roadmap-v1 says Claude spans have no duration and should be demoted to span events; that is right for the model call and wrong for tool calls. Verified on this machine: an assistant line's timestamp plus the matching user line's tool_result timestamp (joined on content[].tool_use.id and confirmed by sourceToolAssistantUUID) gives true intervals — 127 ms for a Read, 1178 ms for a Bash — and system/subtype=turn_duration carries a real durationMs (621321 ms observed) as does stop_hook_summary.hookInfos[].durationMs. So emit execute_tool spans with genuine start and end for Claude Code, invoke_agent spans for turns that have a turn_duration line, and the chat span as an explicitly zero-length span carrying vole.duration_source='absent' — never a synthesised width. OpenCode (message.data.time.created/time.completed) and Grok (inference_done.ctx.model_elapsed_ms, ttft_ms) carry real model-call durations and get true chat spans.
desktop_surface: Incidents and session detail gain a 'timing' column reading exact / tool-only / none per tool, matching the vole.duration_source badge carried in the exported trace, so what the app shows and what the trace UI shows cannot diverge.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl assistant timestamp + message.content[].tool_use.id, user tool_result.tool_use_id + timestamp, system/turn_duration.durationMs, stop_hook_summary.hookInfos[].durationMs; opencode.db message.data.time.completed; ~/.grok/logs/unified.jsonl inference_done.ctx.model_elapsed_ms.
honest_limit: turn_duration is rare — 10 of 591 transcripts here have one — so most invoke_agent spans stay zero-length too. Tool durations are wall-clock between two transcript writes, so they include the agent's own serialisation and any human approval wait; they are a transcript gap, not the tool's execution time, and must be labelled duration_kind rather than 'latency'. A zero-length span still renders as '0 ms' in Tempo or Jaeger and no attribute prevents a human misreading it, so the docs must say so plainly.
competitive_note: Cursor's OTel export ships no traces and no per-session tool attribution at all; Datadog LLM Observability and Langfuse only see what a vendor SDK chose to send. Real tool-call spans reconstructed from files already on disk, for agents that never emitted a span, are unique to the transcript-parsing approach.
v1_ref: OTLP export: sessions as traces, rows as metrics, incidents as logs
field_verified: The best-evidenced feature in the shard; I reconstructed it directly. Joining assistant `message.content[].tool_use.id` to the matching user `tool_result.tool_use_id` by timestamp over one transcript yielded 1,945 real intervals — ('Bash',2508), ('Bash',1603), ('Read',19), ('Bash',32), ('Bash',47), ('Edit',1029) ms — and sourceToolAssistantUUID is present in the same file. turn_duration is real and rare: `{'type':'system','subtype':'turn_duration','durationMs':621321,'messageCount':228,…}`, found in 10 files (of 633 transcripts here, not 591). stop_hook_summary carries `hookInfos: [{'command':…,'durationMs':69}]`. OpenCode: `select data from message` → assistant row `{'created':1780757623926,'completed':1780757625798}`. Grok unified.jsonl: "model_elapsed_ms":5115 / 36833 / 24025 and "ttft_ms":2355 / 1223.
constraint: Not an export mapping — a collector change, which the effort should reflect. Code map §3.1 records that claude-code.ts ignores `user` lines ENTIRELY, so the tool_result side of every join is unparsed today; and there is no table to hold a duration (tool_calls does not exist), so this cannot land as an exporter-only feature. Constraint 7 applies to the parse: tool_result payloads carry stdout/stderr/newString, which must never leave the collector loop — only the two timestamps and the tool name may be kept. duration_kind is the right label; 'latency' would be inventing a meaning the number does not have.

name: Sink capability matrix and truthful delivery semantics
description: Roadmap-v1 claims 'idempotent re-sends via event_key document ids' for Splunk HEC, Elastic bulk and Datadog Logs alike — only Elastic supports that. Encode the truth as a per-sink descriptor in packages/core/src/export/sinks/*.ts: Elastic _bulk with {"index":{"_id": event_key}} is exactly-once by id; OTLP with deterministic span ids is deduped only if the backend dedupes at all; Splunk HEC has no server-side dedupe (the best available is an indexed vole_event_key field plus HEC indexer acknowledgement, which is a delivery guarantee, not a duplication one); Datadog Logs and syslog have neither. Each descriptor declares dedupe, max_batch_bytes, retry_on and ack_mode, and both the UI and the docs print that sink's real guarantee instead of a blanket claim.
desktop_surface: Settings → Export sink cards each show a one-line guarantee next to the endpoint — 'exactly-once by _id' or 'at-least-once, duplicates possible' — taken from the descriptor and not editable by the user.
data_source: packages/core/src/export/sinks/* descriptors; usage_events.event_key and anomalies.anomaly_key as document ids; sink vendor documentation cited in the descriptor.
honest_limit: Even on Elastic the guarantee is only as good as the id, and Codex's event_key is `codex:<session>:<line index>` which collides across parent and sub-agent rollout files, so Codex rows can overwrite each other in the index until that key is fixed. Nothing in this descriptor makes a customer's own downstream ingest pipeline idempotent, and a sink's documented behaviour can change under a version upgrade Vole cannot see.
competitive_note: Nightfall's and MintMCP's export pages name sinks without stating delivery semantics, and Cursor's OTel docs say nothing about duplication. It is the first question a SIEM engineer asks of a new log source, and answering it in the product rather than in a support thread is cheap credibility.
v1_ref: SIEM forwarder (Splunk HEC / Elastic bulk / Datadog Logs)
field_verified: The false claim it corrects is verbatim in roadmap-v1.json tier6 feature 9: 'Ship usage_events, anomalies and findings rows … in batches with _id = event_key' applied uniformly to 'Splunk HEC / Elastic bulk / Datadog Logs'. The Codex key caveat is confirmed at codex.ts:197 `event_key: \`codex:${sessionId ?? filePath}:${index}\`` with sessionId rebound from every session_meta line (codex.ts:107), so parent and sub-agent rollouts that replay the parent meta collide on line index. No packages/core/src/export/sinks/ exists.
constraint: None. It is a descriptor object plus a non-editable UI string, and stating a weaker guarantee is principle 1 applied to delivery semantics rather than to numbers. The only note: the descriptor's own truthfulness decays silently when a sink changes behaviour under a version upgrade, which the honest_limit already concedes — pin the doc-read date the way feature 24 does for vendor coverage.

name: Heartbeat export and the log-source-stopped dead-man's switch
description: The first thing an attacker or an annoyed developer does is stop the collector, and a SIEM only notices if the source was emitting a heartbeat. Every drain writes one vole.heartbeat record per host carrying up=1, collector version, poll interval, per-tool last-seen timestamps and rows-since-last-beat, keyed idempotently on (machine, interval bucket); the matching dead-man's-switch detection ships in the Sigma pack, alerting when no heartbeat arrives from an enrolled host for two intervals. The local counterpart writes a collector_runs row per pass so the same freshness answer exists offline with no sink configured.
desktop_surface: Settings → Export shows the last heartbeat time and the per-tool freshness table it contained; the existing StaleBanner reads from the same source so the app and the SIEM never disagree about whether collection is running.
data_source: collector_state.last_scanned_at; packages/core/src/cli/collect.ts per-pass results (filesScanned, notes); package version; the collector_runs table from v1's self-health item.
honest_limit: collector_state is written only by the Claude Code collector — every row on this machine is claude_code — so per-tool freshness is genuinely unknown for the other six until the heartbeat is written from the results loop; until then those cells must read 'no run record', never zero. Backlog depth exists only for Claude Code because the other six re-read their sources in full each pass. And a host that was never enrolled cannot be missed: this detects silenced hosts, not unmanaged ones.
competitive_note: Endpoint DLP and EDR vendors get liveness from their cloud console by construction, which is one of their strongest arguments against a local-first tool. A local-first product has to ship the dead-man's switch explicitly and let the customer's own SIEM own the alert, or it concedes the tamper-detection argument to CrowdStrike without a fight.
v1_ref: Collector self-health: collector_runs, vole doctor, coverage matrix, freshness attestation
field_verified: The gap is exactly as stated and worse than it sounds. `select tool,count(*) from collector_state group by tool` returns a single row: ('claude_code', 633). claude-code.ts:111 `for (const [p, off, mtime] of pending) setState(db, p, 'claude_code', off, mtime)` is the only setState call in any collector. DB.swift:244 reads `SELECT MAX(last_scanned_at) FROM collector_state` for the whole app's liveness, under a comment claiming the collector 'stamps every source it touches, every pass' — which is false. collector_runs does not exist. So per-tool freshness is genuinely unknown for six of seven tools today.
constraint: Constraint 9: the heartbeat must be written from cli/collect.ts's results loop AFTER insertEvents succeeds, not before, or a failed pass advertises itself as healthy. Constraint 1: the idempotency key '(machine, interval bucket)' is well formed — it contains no now() — but the interval bucket must use util.ts bucketOf's UTC epoch-anchored integer math (constraint 19) or heartbeats from two machines land in different buckets for the same minute.

name: Incident evidence bundle with byte-offset provenance and the figures that fired
description: `vole evidence <incident_id>` writes one JSON and one markdown file holding the anomaly row including observed, baseline and threshold — columns that exist in schema.ts but that no reader selects today (queries.ts getAnomalies and DB.swift:223 both project title/detail/confidence only), which breaks principle 3 in the one place it matters most — plus the autonomy_interval and its granted_by, every tool_call in the window with its authority state and path classes, the bounding human-origin entries, and for each fact a raw_ref of <transcript path>#<byte offset> so an auditor can re-read the original line. Rows are hash-chained with prev_hash so a later edit to the store is detectable, and the bundle records the agent version, the rule thresholds in force and the mapping version. It requires the Claude collector to persist into usage_events.raw_ref the byte offset it already computes for its incremental reader.
desktop_surface: An 'Export evidence' button on the incident detail that writes the bundle and reveals it in Finder, with the three figures (observed vs baseline vs threshold) shown inline and a preview of the hash chain in the detail pane, so the reviewer sees exactly what would leave before anything leaves.
data_source: anomalies.{observed,baseline,threshold,anomaly_key,detected_at}; tool_calls; autonomy_intervals; posture_grants; usage_events.raw_ref (needs the Claude collector to write the offset it already tracks in collector_state.last_offset).
honest_limit: Claude Code deletes transcripts after cleanupPeriodDays — unset on this machine, so the tool default applies — and a byte offset is re-readable only inside that horizon; the bundle records the horizon and marks each raw_ref verifiable or expired at export time. The hash chain proves the store was not edited afterwards, not that the source log was authentic: a forged transcript would be faithfully cited, and a chain in a developer-writable SQLite with a developer-readable key is not tamper-evident against the seat owner. Nothing in the bundle carries prompt text, tool arguments or file contents — classes, hashes, counts and pointers only.
competitive_note: v1 has both a secrets incident-response bundle and a Tier 7 tamper-evident audit log, but neither closes the observed/baseline/threshold gap that already exists in the schema and neither carries a re-readable pointer into the source artifact. Market research lists a reconstructable 30-day agent action trail as a top CISO need with most enterprises unable to produce one; the byte-offset pointer is what makes Vole's version checkable rather than merely believable.
v1_ref: Compliance evidence pack export
field_verified: The gap is real and the offset claim is FALSE. Verified present: schema.ts:56-58 `observed REAL NOT NULL, baseline REAL, threshold REAL`, and neither reader selects them — queries.ts:230 projects `id, rule, severity, tool, session_id, model, window_start, window_end, title, detail, confidence, source` and DB.swift:227 the identical eleven columns. Live rows carry the figures: observed=36751.0, baseline=12149.0, threshold=36447.0. Verified FALSE: 'the byte offset it already computes'. util/jsonl.ts readNewLines returns `{lines, newOffset, mtimeMs}` where newOffset is the END of the whole consumed chunk, and claude-code.ts:178 writes `raw_ref: filePath` — a bare path, confirmed in the DB: '<redacted-local-path>….jsonl' with no fragment. No per-line offset is computed anywhere. Codex, by contrast, already writes `raw_ref: ${filePath}#${index}` (codex.ts:220) — a LINE index, not bytes. cleanupPeriodDays is indeed unset (absent from ~/.claude/settings.json and ~/.claude.json). tool_calls, autonomy_intervals and posture_grants do not exist.
constraint: Constraint 2, and it is fatal if unaddressed: the upsert SET list does not include `raw_ref`, and Claude Code coalesces 2-3 transcript copies of the same message.id (measured: 1,070 of 2,144 unique ids duplicated in one 10,139-line transcript). So a row upgraded from the streaming placeholder keeps the FIRST copy's pointer — the auditor is sent to the output_tokens:0 placeholder line, not the final one. Reconciliation: add raw_ref to the SET list in the same widening that feature 6 needs for export_seq, or stamp the offset only on the final copy. Second, smaller: jsonl.ts `.split('\n').filter(l => l.length > 0)` drops blank lines, so a running Buffer.byteLength sum desynchronises on any blank line — the offset must be accumulated before the filter. Third: the two collectors would disagree about what follows '#', so the shape must declare the unit (bytes vs line index).

name: Source-prefix integrity: a chained digest beside every byte offset
description: readNewLines already holds exactly the bytes it consumed, so chain a digest over them instead of throwing them away: prefix_sha256 = sha256(prev_digest || newly_consumed_bytes), cost O(new bytes) and never a re-read. Add prefix_sha256, head_sha256 (first 4 KiB, the O(1) per-poll probe), inode and birthtime_ms to collector_state, all of which fs.statSync already returns and Vole discards. Each poll compares four things: size < last_offset means truncation (today util/jsonl.ts silently restarts at 0 and forgets it happened), ino or birthtime changed means the file was replaced rather than appended, head_sha256 changed means the prefix was rewritten in place, and mtime moving backwards while ctime is recent means a backdated mtime — utimes cannot move ctime backwards without root. Any hit fires source_rewritten carrying the path, the offset, the first 8 hex of the digest before and after, and how many rows Vole already ingested from that file; `vole verify --integrity` recomputes the full chain by re-reading, opt-in and never in the 5-second loop.
desktop_surface: Each source row in the Coverage strip gets a shield state (verified / rewritten / no offset). A source_rewritten incident card shows path, offset, digest before and after, and the ingested row count now in question. Settings > Evidence shows 'last full integrity verify: <date>' with a Run now button.
data_source: collector_state {source_path, last_offset, last_mtime} (641 rows here); fs.statSync {ino, dev, birthtimeMs, ctimeMs, nlink} already returned by util/jsonl.ts's statSync call; the consumed byte range readNewLines already holds in memory
honest_limit: Only incrementally-read files have offsets, and today that is claude_code alone — all 641 collector_state rows. Codex, Grok, OpenCode, Cursor and Devin re-read in full every poll, so there is no prefix to chain until they get offsets. SQLite sources rewrite themselves legitimately (OpenCode's 507 MB store VACUUMs), so hash page count and schema version there and never call a change tampering. A rewrite performed while Vole is stopped, then re-appended past the old offset with a matching head, is undetectable. The digest lives in the same writable DB as everything else.
competitive_note: Every in-path competitor (Nightfall, Harmonic, Cyberhaven) sidesteps this by reading the request rather than the log — but all three store prompt content to do it. Nobody who reads agent logs out-of-path publishes an integrity check on the log they read, which is the claim that makes byte-offset provenance mean anything.
gap_area: Evidence integrity when the monitored user is the local admin: gaps, source mutability, store lineage, clock

name: Per-rule detection quality with a labelled-fraction floor
description: Add v_rule_quality: per rule and per content_rev, findings, cases, labelled cases split by state (false_positive, expected, accepted_risk, resolved), unlabelled cases, and the label_mode split between individually opened and bulk-swept. The precision ratio is printed only when labelled cases clear a floor (default 20 cases and 20% of the rule's cases); below it the cell renders an em dash and the literal denominator, '9 of 21 cases labelled'. No label is ever inferred: not from the human-interrupt ledger, not from a session ending, not from time-to-close - the interrupt ledger exists and is deliberately not joined here, because 'a human hit Escape' is evidence about the agent, not about the detector. The same table is what vole assess and the digest print, so the buyer sees the honest version and the demo cannot show a fabricated one.
desktop_surface: A Detection Quality table in the Policy screen, one row per rule with fired / cases / labelled / false-positive / unlabelled / precision-or-em-dash, and the same table appended to the weekly digest markdown.
data_source: finding_actions.state and label_mode joined to anomalies.rule/case_key/content_rev in ~/.vole/vole.db
honest_limit: Precision is knowable only over labelled cases and labellers choose the interesting ones, so the figure is biased upward or downward in a direction the product cannot measure - the view says so in the column header rather than in a footnote. Recall is never shown at all, because Vole cannot count the findings it failed to produce. On this store 0 of 49 cases carry a label, so every rule renders an em dash on day one, which is the correct output and not a defect to be engineered away.
competitive_note: No vendor in the matrix publishes per-rule precision; volume is the marketing number instead (Zscaler's 242M Codeium DLP violations, Netskope's 223 monthly violations per org), which makes 'here is how often our own rules were wrong, with the unlabelled count beside it' a claim only an open-source local product can afford to make.
v1_ref: Rule dry-run and weekly tuning facts
gap_area: Incident triage: the analyst's daily loop and detection-quality accounting

name: Noise budget per host per week, and the rules that blew it
description: Add v_noise_budget grouping anomalies by (machine, rule, ISO week) on detected_at, against a budget shipped as a content pack (~/.vole/policy/noise.json, admin-overridable in managed mode) giving findings-per-host-per-week per rule and overall. A noise_budget_exceeded info incident fires with anomaly_key noise_budget:<machine_hash>:<rule>:<iso_week> - anchored on the week, so it fires once per rule per week and cannot re-fire on every five-second poll - and the meta-rule is excluded from its own count. To make the count mean 'alerts that reached a human', stamp a discovery column at insert ('backfill' when window_end predates the previous pass's last_scanned_at, else 'live') and count only live discoveries. The grounding is this laptop: five rules produced 250 findings across 106 days, with 29 in a single day and 20-29 on every active day; at round two's ~40 rules the same laptop is a several-hundred-per-week queue before any fleet exists.
desktop_surface: A budget strip at the top of the Incidents queue ('this week: 61 of 40 budgeted - burn_rate_spike 38, loop_suspected 14') with the offending rules linking into Detection Quality, and the same figures in the digest.
data_source: anomalies.detected_at, machine, rule in ~/.vole/vole.db (250 live rows, 174 sharing one backfill detected_at); new ~/.vole/policy/noise.json
honest_limit: The budget counts findings written, so a week when the collector was down looks quiet - the view joins evidence_gaps and prints the unmonitored hours beside the count rather than letting silence read as calm. Muted cases still count toward the budget because the rows were written, but a detector switched off centrally contributes nothing at all, so that week's figure is a lower bound and is labelled as one.
competitive_note: Alert volume is a selling point for the incumbents and a cost for the buyer - Netskope's 223 violations per org per month and Zscaler's 242M events are quoted as evidence of coverage; treating volume as a budget with a named owning rule inverts that, and no coding-agent vendor does it because none of them detects locally in the first place.
gap_area: Incident triage: the analyst's daily loop and detection-quality accounting

name: MTTA and MTTR from Vole's own clocks, with unattended as a first-class state
description: Compute MTTA as the median of (first finding_actions.ts minus anomalies.detected_at) per rule over cases that actually have an action, and MTTR as the same against the first terminal-state action - both only from timestamps Vole itself wrote, never from a vendor clock and never from window_end. Beside every median sits the complementary count of cases with no action at all, split by whether a queue_opened record (from the action spool) ever landed during the case's open life: a case nobody could have triaged because the app was never opened is reported as unattended, and a case left alone while the queue was demonstrably open is unactioned. That split is the only defensible answer to 'nobody triaged this is indistinguishable from nobody opened the app' - it makes the distinction observable instead of assumed. Medians over fewer than n cases print the count instead of a number.
desktop_surface: A response panel in Detection Quality showing MTTA/MTTR per rule with the unattended and unactioned counts as their own columns, plus a queue-header line naming the last time the triage screen was opened.
data_source: anomalies.detected_at joined to finding_actions.ts; queue_opened rows from ~/.vole/inbox/actions.jsonl
honest_limit: detected_at is Vole's discovery time, not the event time - 174 of the 250 live rows here share a single detected_at because they were all found in the first pass - so discovery='backfill' rows are excluded from MTTA entirely rather than handed a plausible-looking number. queue_opened proves a window was foregrounded, not that a human read it, and the unattended split needs the spool, so on a build without it every unlabelled case reports as unknown rather than as slow.
competitive_note: EMA/Cequence found 46% of enterprises cannot produce a 30-day agent action trail, so response-time evidence is downstream of a trail nobody has; SIEM MTTR dashboards compute from ticketing systems Vole has no access to, which is precisely why the figure here is scoped to the actions Vole wrote and refuses to estimate the rest.
gap_area: Incident triage: the analyst's daily loop and detection-quality accounting

name: Versioned export shapes for the secret and tool-call ledgers
description: One versioned row shape per new ledger, both bound by the field registry. vole.secret_sighting.v1 is {fingerprint, key_epoch, detector_id, pack_version, class, provider_key, host, transport, direction, normalisation, tool, session_id, agent_id, path_hmac, dir_prefix, first_seen, last_seen, occurrences, reached_model, status, user, machine} — no value, no path, and deliberately no byte offset, because an offset is a pointer into a plaintext file still sitting on the endpoint and shipping it hands the SIEM a map to the secret. The tool-call shape ships pattern_id, pack_version, category, name, server, outcome, status_source, duration_ms, duration_kind, agent_id and hashes — never the skeleton, never a command, never args content — over both `vole export --table=tool_calls` NDJSON and a new session-scoped vole_tool_calls MCP tool. As OTLP log records both carry gen_ai.provider.name and never gen_ai.input.messages. Scoping is part of the feature, not a footnote: cli/mcp.ts today lets any agent that can spawn the server enumerate every session on the machine, and a tool ledger makes that materially more sensitive, so vole_tool_calls is session-scoped at the tool boundary before it ships.
desktop_surface: Settings → Export 'What leaves this machine' gains both column sets with a sample record for each; the Behaviour panel shows the tool_calls manifest inline and the Privacy Center renders the same list, so the field list a reviewer reads is the one the serializer uses.
data_source: secret_sightings and dlp_egress tables; tool_calls and agent_edges tables; packages/core/src/cli/mcp.ts TOOLS array; packages/core/src/export/fields.ts.
honest_limit: path_hmac means the receiving SIEM cannot name the file — an admin who needs the path must re-identify on the endpoint, which is intentional and documented rather than worked around. Correlating sightings across machines requires a shared org key, which changes the threat model and is a separate opt-in from the local key epoch. Skeletons stay local by policy, so a SIEM consumer sees a pattern id and must resolve it against the published pack, which is why pack_version travels on every row. And a ledger row proves a call was recorded, not that it executed: outcome is NULL wherever status_source is 'none'.
competitive_note: v1 scopes the forwarder to usage_events and anomalies 'until secret_findings lands' and never defines the findings shape. Cursor's OTel export ships no prompts but also no per-session tool attribution; Copilot's EMU session streaming carries bodies up to 1 MB; Speakeasy and MintMCP gateways forward tool args and results. A findings shape that is useful in a SIEM while being provably value-free is the wedge for 'coexist with your gateway and EDR, export to both' — and market.md flags IETF draft-klrc-aiagent-auth-03 as the audit shape to align these rows with.
v1_ref: SIEM forwarder (Splunk HEC / Elastic bulk / Datadog Logs)
field_verified: FALSE for the tables, TRUE for the scoping fix. Neither `secret_sightings`, `dlp_egress`, `tool_calls` nor `agent_edges` exists — sqlite_master returns three tables and schema.ts declares three. The MCP half is real and independently checkable: cli/mcp.ts:19 declares `const TOOLS: {name; description; inputSchema; run}[]` with vole_summary, vole_live_sessions, vole_session, vole_incidents, vole_breakdown, vole_whatif, vole_digest — none of them takes a scope, all call queries.ts with includeSeed=false and no session restriction, and serverInfo is pinned `version: '0.1.0'` (mcp.ts:94) against package version 0.1.4. So 'any agent that can spawn the server can enumerate every session on the machine' is confirmed.
constraint: Constraint 6 is the one it misses: 'New tables must carry a source column and the same partition/purge' — a secret-sighting or tool-call row from `pnpm seed` must never reach a SIEM, and neither declared shape carries `source`. Add it to both wire shapes or make the exporter filter `source='live'` the way every production query already splices `AND source='live'`. Otherwise no conflict: refusing to ship offsets and skeletons is constraint 7 applied outward.

name: Asset labels in the export field registry: tier travels, names are opt-in, basis never
description: Asset fields enter the deny-by-default export field registry explicitly and split three ways, because a crown-jewel list is itself intelligence: asset_tier and asset_match (the chain link) are exportable by default so a SIEM can prioritise; asset_id and owner are opt-in per sink; basis and the register's raw match strings (declared hosts, DSNs, path globs, salted literals) are never exportable at any setting, enforced by an encoder test that fails if they appear in a serialized payload. Over OTLP they ride as attributes on the existing incident log record under vendor-namespaced keys (vole.asset.tier, vole.asset.match) because the pinned gen_ai.* semconv snapshot has no asset concept and inventing one there would break the parity check.
desktop_surface: The Privacy Center export-payload inspector shows every asset field with its three-state marker (always / opt-in / never), and the field dictionary explains in one line why basis cannot leave the device.
data_source: the export field registry and NULL-omitting encoder; anomalies.asset_tier / asset_id; assets.basis and assets.match_norm as the denied fields.
honest_limit: Tier alone still leaks structure: a SIEM that sees 'tier 1' on 14 incidents learns the org has tier-1 assets and roughly how many. The honest answer is the sink capability matrix showing what each destination receives, not a claim of zero disclosure.
competitive_note: Copilot's EMU audit streaming can carry 1MB bodies and Cowork's OTel includes full prompts by default; a deny-by-default asset split that a buyer can read in the shipped encoder is the opposite posture and is verifiable rather than promised.
gap_area: The company's own asset and data-class register (what 'sensitive' and 'customer data' mean here)

name: Vendor-join key ledger (event_links) for pivoting into vendor records
description: A SIEM's value comes from joining Vole rows to the vendor's own records, which needs the ids the vendors themselves use — all present on disk and all discarded today. Beyond v1's three correlation columns, add an `event_links(event_key, kind, value)` table for the many-valued ids: Claude message.content[].tool_use.id (toolu_…) and the bridge-session ownerAccountUuid/ownerOrganizationUuid, and Codex token_usage_record.payload.{response_id, turn_id, root_turn_id, thread_id} plus the line ordinal. These export as vole.vendor.request_id, vole.vendor.response_id, gen_ai.tool.call.id and gen_ai.conversation.id, so an analyst can pivot from a Vole incident to an Anthropic Compliance API row or an OpenAI response record.
desktop_surface: Session detail gains a copyable 'join keys' block per call (request id, response id, tool call ids, thread id); the Incidents feed exposes the same block for the session that fired.
data_source: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl requestId/uuid/parentUuid/promptId and content[].tool_use.id, type:'bridge-session' owner uuids; ~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl token_usage_record.payload.{response_id, turn_id, root_turn_id, thread_id} and the top-level ordinal.
honest_limit: requestId appears only on assistant lines that reached the API, so cached, aborted and local-only turns have none, and promptId lives on user lines, so linking it to an assistant row needs a persisted uuid chain that incremental offset reads can lose. response_id exists only in Codex's newer token_usage_record type, so older rollouts cannot be joined at all. The org uuid is Anthropic's tenant id, not the customer's IdP identity, and the whole ledger is useless for any vendor whose console the customer cannot query.
competitive_note: Claude's Compliance API excludes API-key, Bedrock/Vertex and personal accounts and Cursor's admin API is Enterprise-only; supplying the join key from the endpoint is what lets a customer stitch the partial vendor view onto complete local evidence.
v1_ref: Correlation ids: request_id, turn_id, entry_uuid columns
field_verified: Codex confirmed exactly: `token_usage_record` lines carry payload keys {thread_id, turn_id, session_id, root_turn_id, response_id, usage, turn_token_usage, thread_token_usage} — 39 lines, response_id on all 39. BUT those 39 lines live in only 4 of 66 rollout files, so 94% of this machine's Codex sessions have no response_id at all — the honest_limit's 'older rollouts cannot be joined' is confirmed and is more severe than the wording suggests. Claude-side ids (requestId, uuid, parentUuid, promptId, content[].tool_use.id) are catalogued in the code map's field inventory as parsed-but-discarded, and claude-code.ts:93 confirms only assistant lines are examined. SECOND BLOCKER, shared with feature 1: Claude is the only incremental collector and all 632 collector_state rows already point past every existing byte, so historical requestIds are unreachable — event_links is forward-only unless a rescan path exists that does not disturb those offsets.
constraint: C7 is the sharp one: content[].tool_use.id sits in the same object as tool_use.input, which the code map names as 'the DLP surface'. The entry must state that it stores the id and never the input — a reader will assume otherwise. C1/C5: event_key stability is fine since event_links is keyed on an existing event_key. Also shard-misfiled: this is tagged telemetry_export, not identity_attribution, though it is what makes feature 16 useful.

name: Clock sanity from boot-anchored uptime, with a clock_suspect tag that reorders nothing
description: Record both wall_ms and boot_epoch_s = floor(Date.now()/1000) - os.uptime() on every collector_runs row; verified on this machine that pair equals sysctl kern.boottime to the second (1788227235), so it needs no subprocess, no network and works inside the SEA. Within one boot the derived boot epoch is constant, so a wall-clock change moves it: boot_epoch shifting while uptime keeps increasing gives the exact shift in seconds, and wall_ms going backwards between consecutive runs is a rollback. Rows ingested in a run whose boot_epoch differs from the previous run get clock_suspect=1 on usage_events, written by an explicit UPDATE keyed on the run because the tokens-only-grow upsert will never rewrite that column. Rule clock_shifted reports the measured shift and nothing else — all bucketing stays UTC-epoch integer math, and not one ts is reordered, re-bucketed or corrected.
desktop_surface: A clock chip on the Coverage strip; affected timeline buckets and incident cards carry a small clock marker reading the measured shift, e.g. 'wall clock moved -3h 12m at 2026-08-14 09:41 UTC; 42 rows in that window tagged'. The tag rides along into exports and evidence bundles.
data_source: node:os uptime() and Date.now() at each collector pass, written to collector_runs; new nullable usage_events.clock_suspect column
honest_limit: A reboot resets uptime, so a clock change made while the machine was powered off is invisible — only the post-boot NTP correction shows, and it is indistinguishable from a legitimate first sync on a machine that was off for a week. Shifts smaller than the poll interval are lost. It proves no intent: DST, VM suspend/resume and a long sleep all move the pair. And every agent timestamp is the agent's clock, not Vole's, so a shifted clock taints the sources too — the tag says 'affected window', never 'wrong number'.
competitive_note: v1's licence entry proposes MAX(usage_events.ts) < expires_at to 'defeat clock rollback without NTP', which only defends the licence against forward fraud and says nothing about the evidence. Boot-anchored uptime is the offline local substitute for the NTP-signed timestamps every SIEM ingestion path assumes it is getting.
v1_ref: Collector self-health: collector_runs, vole doctor, coverage matrix, freshness attestation
gap_area: Evidence integrity when the monitored user is the local admin: gaps, source mutability, store lineage, clock

name: Two clocks on every row and measured observation lag per tool
description: Vole reads files the agent wrote after the fact, so its true detection latency is flush time plus poll interval, and its rows already mix two clocks — the agent's own timestamp from the transcript and the moment Vole read it — which today collapse into one ts column and, worse, into Date.now() when the source timestamp is missing (claude-code.ts and codex.ts both fall back). Stamp observed_at at insert in db.ts and export both vole.event_time and vole.collected_at with vole.time_source reading 'source' or 'collector', so a row whose timestamp was invented is labelled rather than trusted; roll observed_at - ts into a source_lag view exposing p50/p95 per tool, which will differ by an order of magnitude between Claude Code (incremental byte-offset reads, seconds) and Antigravity or Devin (session-level artifacts, potentially hours). When a sink returns an HTTP Date header, record the signed difference against local time as vole.clock_offset_ms on subsequent batches — measured, never assumed, and NULL when no sink has replied.
desktop_surface: Settings → Sources gains a lag column per tool (p50 / p95 over the range) with a plain-language line, 'incidents for this tool are detected on average N seconds after the call'; Settings → Export shows 'clock offset vs <sink>: +1.4 s (measured 09:41)' or an em dash when no sink has replied; session detail marks calls whose timestamp came from the collector, and the incident detail footer stamps 'as of last poll hh:mm:ss'.
data_source: usage_events.ts; packages/core/src/collectors/claude-code.ts and codex.ts Date.now() fallbacks; a new observed_at column stamped in packages/core/src/db.ts; collector_state.last_scanned_at; the HTTP Date response header from a configured sink.
honest_limit: For the six collectors that re-read their whole source each pass, observed_at is the poll that noticed the row, so the measured lag is an upper bound that folds Vole's own interval together with the agent's flush delay and cannot separate them. Rows imported during a machine's first scan have a meaningless lag and are excluded by a first-scan flag rather than folded in. The clock offset is against one sink's clock, not UTC — a skewed sink makes Vole look skewed — and there is deliberately no NTP call because that would be undisclosed egress. Rows written before observed_at exists cannot say which clock produced their ts, so time_source is NULL for history rather than backfilled with a guess.
competitive_note: Every inline vendor (Prompt/SentinelOne, Harmonic, Nightfall, Zscaler, Netskope, Lakera) leads with real-time blocking, a comparison Vole cannot win by assertion; Copilot's metrics lag about two days and Claude Code Analytics is daily with an hour of lag. Publishing the measured number turns the weakness into the credibility asset the rest of the honesty positioning trades on, and it is the concrete input to the monitor-first, coach-not-block rollout buyers say they want.
field_verified: Fallbacks confirmed verbatim. codex.ts:124 `const ts = entry.timestamp ? Date.parse(entry.timestamp) : Date.now();` — an invented timestamp indistinguishable from a real one once stored; claude-code.ts has the same shape. schema.ts has `ts INTEGER NOT NULL` and no observed_at. collector_state.last_scanned_at exists but is written by one collector (633 rows, all claude_code), so a per-tool lag view can only be computed for Claude Code today; for the other six, observed_at would be the first poll that noticed the row, which is exactly the upper bound the honest_limit describes.
constraint: Constraint 2, unstated and consequential: observed_at is stamped at insert and the upsert SET list does not include it, so an upgraded row keeps its FIRST observation time. For Claude Code's placeholder-then-real pattern that is arguably the right semantics ('when Vole first saw this call'), but it must be documented, and vole.time_source will describe the first insert's clock, not the surviving row's. Constraint 11 for the new column (INSERT list + @params + type + schema + migrate together). Constraint 17 is respected and well handled: reading an HTTP Date header off a request the user already authorised is not new egress, and refusing NTP is the correct call.

name: Witness-orphan sessions: the ones that left no row at all
description: Left-anti-join every session id seen by a survivor artifact against both the transcripts on disk and usage_events.session_id, writing three distinct outcomes into orphan_sessions: pruned (no transcript, last witness older than .last-cleanup and outside the retention period — the tool's own housekeeping, not a finding), deleted (no transcript, but the witness timestamp is newer than the last cleanup or inside the retention window), and never_ingested (no transcript and no usage_events row, so Vole never saw it and no raw_ref can ever point at it). On this machine that is 1 of 13 Claude history session ids with no transcript, and 0 of 55 Codex index ids missing. This is not the v1 entry: v1's retention-loss disclosure and verify's 'report pruned sources' both start from a stored row whose raw_ref path is now gone (563 distinct Claude paths here, 0 missing, exactly matching the 563 files that contain assistant lines), so a session deleted before Vole's first poll of that file leaves no row, no raw_ref, and is invisible to that check — and neither one separates a policy prune from a hand deletion.
desktop_surface: A Sessions gap list under Coverage: id, which witness saw it, its timestamp, a classification chip (pruned / deleted / never ingested), and the project. The People view's attribution-coverage figure gains '+N sessions witnessed but not ingested' so the denominator stops flattering itself.
data_source: ~/.claude/history.jsonl {sessionId, timestamp, project}; ~/.claude.json projects[].{lastSessionId, lastStartTime, lastCost}; ~/.claude/file-history/<sessionId>/ (32 dirs); ~/.codex/session_index.jsonl (55 ids); ~/.codex/logs_2.sqlite logs.thread_id (13 distinct); ~/.codex/.codex-global-state.json {thread-workspace-root-hints, projectless-thread-ids}; ~/.claude/.last-cleanup (2026-09-07T05:13:50.752Z here); cleanupPeriodDays (unset here)
honest_limit: The witnesses are ordinary user-writable files in the same home — deleting the transcript and the history.jsonl line together leaves nothing, and ~/.claude.json keeps only the last session per project, so a deleted middle session is unwitnessed. never_ingested recovers not one token: it establishes that a session existed and roughly when, and every token, model and cost column stays NULL. pruned is a classification from a date comparison, not a statement about intent. Each tool can change its own housekeeping layout at any release, so every witness carries its own present/absent state rather than being assumed.
competitive_note: The vendor-native path (Anthropic Compliance and Analytics APIs) keeps a server-side record and does not need this — but it excludes API-key auth, Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry, personal accounts, Cursor and Codex, which is precisely the population Vole exists to cover. For those sessions there is no server-side copy and the local witnesses are the only ones that exist.
v1_ref: History horizon and retention-loss disclosure
gap_area: Evidence integrity when the monitored user is the local admin: gaps, source mutability, store lineage, clock

name: evidence_gaps: unmonitored intervals proved by the agents' own clocks
description: Derive gaps, never assert them: sort collector_runs by started_at within one store epoch and treat any interval longer than 3x the effective poll interval as a candidate. Then count activity timestamps that fall inside the interval from witnesses that need no Vole run at all — usage_events.ts ingested later, ~/.claude/history.jsonl timestamps (18 lines here), ~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json startedAt, ~/.codex/session_index.jsonl updated_at (55 ids), ~/.codex/logs_2.sqlite logs.ts (3,965 rows spanning 1788757180-1788758921, written independently of the rollouts), and collector_state.last_mtime (641 rows).
